additional_notes: Used to ask how to say a word or phrase in Portuguese (or another language). Often followed by the word/phrase you want translated or explained. Can be used in questions directed at someone (Como se diz 'apple' em português?) or rhetorically (Não sei como se diz...).
target_language_example: Como se diz 'library' em português?
native_language_example: How do you say 'library' in Portuguese?

meaning: as if
additional_notes: Used to compare something to a hypothetical, imagined, or unreal situation. It often introduces a clause with the imperfect subjunctive: como se fosse, como se tivesse, como se quisesse. In negative expressions like não é como se..., it means 'it’s not like...'.
target_language_example: Ela me olhou como se me conhecesse.
native_language_example: She looked at me as if she knew me.

meaning: 'roommate' or 'flatmate' (person you share a room or apartment with).
additional_notes: Used in Brazil and Portugal to refer to someone you share living space with. 'Quarto' literally means 'room' so this is a compositional phrase. You can also say 'colega de quarto' or simply 'roommate' (loanword) in casual speech. Gender-neutral; sometimes 'companheira de quarto' or 'companheiro de quarto' reflects the person's gender, but 'companheiro de quarto' is commonly understood for any gender in neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Meu companheiro de quarto voltou tarde ontem.
native_language_example: My roommate came back late yesterday.

meaning: to make up for lost time; to recover time that was wasted or lost.
additional_notes: Used when someone wants or needs to recover time lost (e.g., by working faster, staying longer, or speeding up tasks). Often appears as 'compensar o tempo perdido' (make up for lost time). Can be followed by a gerund or an explanation of how the time will be made up.
target_language_example: Vou compensar o tempo perdido trabalhando neste fim de semana.
native_language_example: I'll make up for lost time by working this weekend.

meaning: to buy this (one).
additional_notes: Literally 'to buy this'. Used before a noun (or implied noun) to say you will purchase a specific item near the speaker or that has been mentioned. Word order: comprar + demonstrative (este). In questions the subject/auxiliary can change (Vai comprar este carro? = Are you going to buy this car?).
target_language_example: Ela vai comprar este livro hoje.
native_language_example: She is going to buy this book today.

meaning: bought a
additional_notes: "compraram" is the simple past of comprar and is used with eles/elas/vocês: "they bought" or "you all bought." "um" is usually the masculine singular indefinite article ("a/an") before a masculine noun, but it can also mean "one" depending on context. With a feminine noun, use "uma" instead.
target_language_example: Eles compraram um presente para mim.
native_language_example: They bought a present for me.

meaning: shopping with (someone) / purchases with (something)
additional_notes: Used to indicate who you're shopping with or what payment/method accompanies a purchase. Often appears in phrases like 'compras com amigos' (shopping with friends) or 'compras com cartão' (purchases with a card). Verb: 'fazer compras com...' or noun phrase: 'as compras com...'. Word order and prepositions matter: 'compras com' is followed by the person, method, or thing accompanying the shopping.
target_language_example: Vou fazer as compras com meu irmão amanhã.
native_language_example: I'm going shopping with my brother tomorrow.

meaning: 'shopping' or 'to do shopping at (a place)'.
additional_notes: Used with a place to say you go shopping at that location. 'Fazer compras no/na/num/no(s)' is the common structure: fazer compras no shopping, no supermercado, no mercado, na loja, etc. 'No' = 'em + o' (masculine singular). Use 'na' for feminine (na loja), 'nos'/'nas' for plural.
target_language_example: Ela foi fazer compras no supermercado.
native_language_example: She went shopping at the supermarket.

meaning: 'I bought this/that' (past tense with a nearby or specific item)
additional_notes: Comprei = first-person past of comprar (to buy). Esse points to a specific item, often near the listener or previously mentioned; in English it can be translated as 'this' or 'that' depending on context. Word order may vary (Eu comprei esse... / Comprei esse...). When referring to people as source (bought from), use 'do'/'da' (ex.: 'comprei esse carro do Tom' = I bought this/that car from Tom).
target_language_example: Comprei esse presente para você ontem.
native_language_example: I bought this/that gift for you yesterday.

meaning: I bought this / I purchased this.
additional_notes: Used to say that the speaker purchased a specific item. 'Comprei' is the first-person singular past (pretérito perfeito) of 'comprar'. 'Este' (this) agrees in gender/number with the noun it refers to (este/esta/estes/estas). In spoken Portuguese you can also include the subject pronoun 'eu' (Eu comprei este...) but it's optional unless you want emphasis.
target_language_example: Comprei este casaco na semana passada.
native_language_example: I bought this coat last week.

meaning: I bought a pair (of ...).
additional_notes: Used to say you purchased two matching items that form a pair (gloves, shoes, socks, scissors, etc.). Usually followed by 'de' + item (comprei um par de luvas). In Portuguese 'par' implies two items; some nouns (like 'tesouras') are plural even when used with 'um par de'.
target_language_example: Comprei um par de meias novas.
native_language_example: I bought a pair of new socks.

meaning: bought some / did you buy any (feminine or unspecified item)
additional_notes: Comprou is the past (pretérito perfeito) of comprar (to buy). 'Alguma' is a feminine indefinite pronoun/adjective meaning 'some' or 'any' and agrees with a feminine noun that may be omitted. Together, 'comprou alguma?' is a short question meaning 'Did (you/he/she) buy any (feminine item)?' Context and subject can be added: 'Você comprou alguma coisa?' (Did you buy anything?) or 'Ela comprou alguma roupa?' (Did she buy any clothes?). For masculine nouns use 'algum' instead.
target_language_example: Você comprou alguma coisa para o jantar?
native_language_example: Did you buy anything for dinner?

meaning: 'did you buy this' (part of the question 'Where did you buy this?')
additional_notes: Used when asking where someone bought a specific item the speaker can see or has been mentioned. 'Comprou' is the past (pretérito perfeito) of 'comprar' (to buy). 'Essa' is a demonstrative meaning 'this/that' (feminine), matching a feminine noun like 'camisa' or 'agenda'. For masculine nouns use 'esse' (e.g., 'comprou esse livro?').
target_language_example: Onde você comprou essa bolsa?
native_language_example: Where did you buy this bag?

meaning: 'bought these' (past tense) — used to ask or say where/why/when someone bought specific items.
additional_notes: Comprou is the third-person singular past (pretérito perfeito) of comprar (to buy). 'Esses' is a demonstrative meaning 'these' (masculine plural) or 'those' near the listener. Together they appear in questions like 'Onde comprou esses ...?' or 'Quando você comprou esses ...?'. In spoken Brazilian Portuguese, subject pronouns (você/ele/ela) are often omitted: 'Onde comprou esses óculos?' = 'Where did you/he/she buy these glasses?'. Use 'essas' for feminine plural nouns (essas bolsas).
target_language_example: Onde você comprou esses sapatos?
native_language_example: Where did you buy these shoes?

meaning: do you/one agree that...; (he/she/they) agree(s) that...
additional_notes: Used to ask or state agreement about a clause introduced by 'que' (that). In questions with 'você' or omitted subject it becomes 'Concorda que...?' meaning 'Do you agree that...?'. With a named subject use third person: 'Ele concorda que...'. Common in both formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Você concorda que devemos mudar o plano?
native_language_example: Do you agree that we should change the plan?

meaning: agreed with
additional_notes: Past tense (they) of 'concordar com' — to agree with or approve of someone or something. Use 'concordar com' when expressing agreement with an idea, proposal, decision, or person. For other subjects/tenses change the verb (e.g., 'concordo com' = I agree with; 'concordaram com' = they agreed with).
target_language_example: Eles concordaram com a nova regra.
native_language_example: They agreed with the new rule.

meaning: confessed the / admitted the
additional_notes: Past tense of confess (confessar). Used with a direct object introduced by the definite article or possessive (o, a, seu, sua). Means to admit having done something or to reveal feelings (e.g., confessar um crime, confessar o amor). Pronunciation tip: stress on second syllable: con-FES-sou.
target_language_example: Ele confessou o crime ontem à noite.
native_language_example: He confessed the crime last night.

meaning: Do you know my... / (He/She) knows my... (depending on context and subject).
additional_notes: Conjugation depends on subject: 'Você conhece meu...' or 'Conhece meu...' (informal question). 'Conhece' is the 3rd-person singular or polite 2nd-person form of 'conhecer' (to know/meet). 'Meu' is the masculine singular possessive 'my' and will change to 'minha/meus/minhas' to match gender/number (e.g., 'minha filha', 'meus filhos'). Common in introductions or when asking if someone knows a family member.
target_language_example: Você conhece meu irmão mais velho?
native_language_example: Do you know my older brother?

meaning: we know the
additional_notes: A first-person-plural (nós) form of conhecer + definite article 'o' before a masculine noun. Most commonly translates as 'we know the...' (familiarity) but can mean 'we met the...' in past contexts when referring to having met someone before. Use 'conhecemos a' for feminine nouns. Word order: verb + article + name/ noun (e.g., conhecemos o Tom = we know Tom / we all know Tom).
target_language_example: Nós conhecemos o vizinho novo.
native_language_example: We know the new neighbor.

meaning: to meet you / to get to know you
additional_notes: Used when meeting someone for the first time or expressing pleasure at getting to know them. In Brazilian Portuguese, word order more commonly is 'conhecer você' or 'conhecer você' in informal speech, but more natural written forms often use 'conhecê-lo/conhecê-la' (formal) or 'conhecer você' in casual contexts. Can be used after adjectives like 'foi incrível' or 'foi um privilégio' to say 'it was great to meet you.'
target_language_example: Foi um prazer conhecer você ontem.
native_language_example: It was a pleasure to meet you yesterday.

meaning: "I met your..." or "I got to know your..." — first-person singular, simple past (pretérito perfeito) of conhecer + the possessive seu/sua (your/his/her depending on context).
additional_notes: Conheci is the 1st person singular past of conhecer (to meet, to get to know). 'Seu' (or sua) is a possessive meaning 'your' in many varieties of Portuguese but can also mean 'his' or 'her' depending on context, so the owner may be ambiguous without clarification. In Brazil, 'seu/sua' is commonly used for 'your' (both formal and informal contexts); 'teu/tua' is a less common informal alternative in some regions. The phrase is compositional: conhecer + possessor; it must be followed by the thing possessed (e.g., amigo, irmão, pai). Word order: verb + possessor + noun (e.g., 'conheci seu amigo').
target_language_example: Eu conheci seu amigo ontem.
native_language_example: I met your friend yesterday.

meaning: 'I met your' or 'I got to know your' (past tense + possessive).
additional_notes: Literal combination of the verb conhecer in the past tense (conheci = I met/knew) + the possessive pronoun sua (your, hers). By itself it's incomplete — usually followed by a noun (e.g., conheci sua irmã = I met your sister) or a clause. Context determines whether 'conheci' means 'met' (first encounter) or 'came to know/learned about'. Formality: neutral; 'sua' can be ambiguous (your, his, her, its, their depending on context and formality).
target_language_example: Ontem conheci sua amiga no restaurante.
native_language_example: Yesterday I met your friend at the restaurant.

meaning: 'I know this' (feminine singular object).
additional_notes: Used to say you are familiar with a person, place, song, etc. 'Conheço' = I know (to be acquainted with or recognize). 'Esta' is the feminine singular demonstrative (this). Use 'este' for masculine nouns (ex.: conheço este lugar). For negative: 'Não conheço esta...' or 'Não conheço este...'. 'Já conheço esta...' can mean 'I already know this.'
target_language_example: Conheço esta cidade muito bem.
native_language_example: I know this city very well.

meaning: I don't know anyone / I don't meet anyone.
additional_notes: Used to say you do not know any people in a place or situation. Often appears with a negation (não) before 'conheço' or omitted in casual speech ('Não conheço ninguém'). 'Conhecer' means 'to know' (people, places, be familiar with). In Portuguese the negative word 'ninguém' (nobody) pairs with verbs without doubling the negative (use 'não' + verb + 'ninguém').
target_language_example: Eu não conheço ninguém no trabalho ainda.
native_language_example: I don't know anyone at work yet.

meaning: 'managed to open' or 'was able to open'.
additional_notes: Past tense of conseguir + infinitive. Used to say someone succeeded or failed at doing something (conseguiu abrir = succeeded in opening; não conseguiu abrir = failed to open). Often implies effort or difficulty. Can refer to physical opening (box, door) or metaphorical openings (breach, opportunity).
target_language_example: Ela conseguiu abrir a janela sozinha.
native_language_example: She managed to open the window by herself.

meaning: 'managed to get' or 'obtained' (past, informal neutral), followed by a masculine noun/pronoun (e.g., o trabalho, o empréstimo).
additional_notes: Conseguiu is the past (pretérito perfeito) of conseguir (to get/achieve/manage to). When followed by o, it combines with a masculine noun: conseguiu o trabalho = got the job. Can also appear with other articles/pronouns (conseguiu a, conseguiu os). Use to ask or say whether someone obtained something or succeeded in doing something.
target_language_example: Ele conseguiu o visto para viajar.
native_language_example: He got the visa to travel.

meaning: managed to solve / was able to solve
additional_notes: Past (preterite/imperfect) form indicating that someone succeeded in solving something. 'Conseguiu' comes from 'conseguir' (to manage/to succeed) + infinitive verb (resolver). Commonly used to say someone succeeded in doing an action. Can be used in questions, statements, and with a named subject (e.g., Tom conseguiu resolver).
target_language_example: Ela conseguiu resolver o exercício antes da aula.
native_language_example: She managed to solve the exercise before class.

meaning: considers (someone) a / considers oneself a
additional_notes: Form of the verb considerar + indefinite article 'um'. Can be used with third person (ele/ela considera um...) to say someone regards another as something, or with reflexive 'se considera um...' to say someone considers themselves (e.g., 'se considera um cidadão'). Followed by a noun or adjective. Verb changes with subject (considero, considera, consideram).
target_language_example: Ela se considera um artista talentoso.
native_language_example: She considers herself a talented artist.

meaning: 'I consider (someone) a' / 'I regard (someone) as a'.
additional_notes: Used to state an opinion or judgment about a person (or about oneself with reflexive 'me considero um'). Often followed by a noun or noun phrase (e.g., amigo, cientista, idiota). With a direct object pronoun (o/a) it becomes 'Eu o considero um...' — 'I consider him a...'.
target_language_example: Eu me considero um aprendiz dedicado.
native_language_example: I consider myself a dedicated learner.

meaning: I can’t talk to / I can’t speak with (someone or something).
additional_notes: Consigo falar com is the negative form of 'conseguir falar com' (to be able to talk to). In these examples 'não consigo falar com' means the speaker is unable to talk to a person or is unable to speak (e.g., physically unable to use their mouth). Use with a person (com + name/pronoun) or with body parts/objects when describing inability to speak. Conjugation changes by subject (ex.: 'não consigo' = I can't, 'não consegue' = he/she/you formal can't, 'não conseguimos' = we can't).
target_language_example: Não consigo falar com o médico agora.
native_language_example: I can't talk to the doctor right now.

meaning: '(I) can't (do it) anymore' / 'I can't take it anymore'.
additional_notes: Used with first-person singular (eu) + não consigo mais to express inability or that one has reached a limit (emotionally, physically, or mentally). Often followed by an infinitive or direct object: não consigo mais + [infinitive] (confiar, segurar) or + isso. Informal/neutral spoken phrase common in frustration or exhaustion.
target_language_example: Eu não consigo mais aguentar essa situação.
native_language_example: I can't take this situation anymore.

meaning: 'I can't stop (doing)'.
additional_notes: Used to say you are unable to stop an action or thought. Literally built from 'conseguir' (to be able to) in the first person singular present ('consigo') + 'parar de' (to stop doing). Often followed by a verb in the gerund (pensar → pensar / thinking) or by the verb itself (parar de chorar). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Não consigo parar de sorrir quando penso em você.
native_language_example: I can't stop smiling when I think about you.

meaning: bank account.
additional_notes: Used to refer to an account at a bank where money is deposited, withdrawn, transferred, or where authorizations are given. Common verbs: abrir (open), fechar (close), mandar/enviar (send money to), acessar (access). In Portuguese the adjective bancária follows conta.
target_language_example: Preciso abrir uma conta bancária para receber meu salário.
native_language_example: I need to open a bank account to receive my salary.

meaning: 'countdown' (the act of counting backward toward zero, often before an event starts).
additional_notes: Used to announce or describe a countdown before something begins (e.g., launch, start of an activity, New Year's). Common in spoken and written Portuguese; can appear with or without an article. Often preceded by verbs like começar, iniciar, fazer.
target_language_example: Vamos começar a contagem regressiva!
native_language_example: Let's start the countdown!

meaning: 'provided that' / 'as long as' (introduces a condition)
additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition that must be met. Can often be swapped with 'desde que' or 'desde que' in many contexts. Usually followed by the subjunctive when referring to hypothetical/non-real conditions (e.g. 'contanto que não haja...'), but indicative is possible when the condition is presented as factual. Common in formal and informal speech.
target_language_example: Você pode sair, contanto que volte antes das dez.
native_language_example: You can go out, provided that you return before ten.

meaning: 'to count up to' (to count numbers up to a given number); also used in commands like 'I'll count to (three)' to give someone time to do something.
additional_notes: Literally 'count until'. Common in two uses: 1) describing the ability to count to a certain number (Meu filho sabe contar até cem = my child can count to one hundred), and 2) as a short command/threat to give someone a brief countdown (Vou contar até três — do it before I finish). Often followed by a number (três, cem, etc.).
target_language_example: Vou contar até cinco e você precisa estar pronto.
native_language_example: I'll count to five and you need to be ready.

meaning: to tell everything from (the) — used to say you'll tell the whole story starting at a point (e.g., the beginning).
additional_notes: Commonly completed with words like 'o começo', 'o princípio' or 'o início' (all meaning 'the beginning'). Appears in polite/formal requests with verbs like 'deixa', 'deixem', 'permita', 'permita-me' meaning 'let me' or 'allow me'. Use to introduce a full account or story.
target_language_example: Deixa-me contar tudo desde o início para que não haja mal-entendidos.
native_language_example: Let me tell everything from the beginning so there are no misunderstandings.

meaning: eye contact
additional_notes: Refers to looking directly into another person's eyes. Used for social cues (attention, confidence, honesty). Can be used literally (meeting someone's gaze) or as advice (maintain/avoid eye contact). Common collocations: manter contato visual, fazer contato visual, evitar contato visual, perder/recuperar contato visual.
target_language_example: Quando falar, mantenha contato visual por não mais que cinco segundos.
native_language_example: When speaking, keep eye contact for no more than five seconds.

meaning: 'keeps (on) me' — indicates someone keeps doing something to/with me (continues to [verb] me).
additional_notes: Often appears with a verb after (e.g., continua me pedindo = keeps asking me). 'Continua' is the 3rd-person singular of 'continuar'. Word order in Portuguese often places the object pronoun after the verb in spoken Brazilian Portuguese ('continua me'), though written European Portuguese may more commonly use enclitic or mesoclitic forms (e.g., 'continua-me' or 'continua a pedir‑me'). Use to describe repeated or ongoing actions directed at the speaker.
target_language_example: Ele continua me ligando todas as noites.
native_language_example: He keeps calling me every night.

meaning: fairy tale; a magical or fantastical story, usually for children.
additional_notes: Used to refer to traditional stories with magic, kings/queens, creatures, and moral lessons. Can also be used figuratively in Portuguese to describe something unrealistically perfect (e.g., 'vida de conto de fadas' = 'fairy-tale life').
target_language_example: Ela leu um conto de fadas para as crianças antes de dormir.
native_language_example: She read a fairy tale to the children before bed.

meaning: 'told what' or 'told (someone) what...'.
additional_notes: Combination of the verb contar (to tell) in past tense (contou) plus o que ('what' / 'that which'). Used to report that someone told you details or explained what happened. Often followed by a clause explaining the content (e.g., contou o que estava acontecendo / contou o que viu).
target_language_example: Ela contou o que realmente aconteceu na festa.
native_language_example: She told (me) what really happened at the party.

meaning: 'told (you) where' or 'told where' (past tense of 'contar' + question/relative word 'onde')
additional_notes: Used to ask or say that someone told someone else the location of something or where an event/person/place is. 'Contou' is the third-person singular past (pretérito perfeito) of 'contar' (to tell). 'Onde' means 'where'. Word order can vary (e.g., 'Quem te contou onde eu moro?' or 'Quem te contou onde moro?').
target_language_example: Ela me contou onde está o endereço.
native_language_example: She told me where the address is.

meaning: told (me/you/others) yesterday; 'contou' = (he/she/you formal) told, 'ontem' = yesterday.
additional_notes: This is the past tense (pretérito perfeito) of 'contar' (to tell, to count) plus 'ontem' (yesterday). Commonly used to report information or stories someone told you the day before. Context/subject is often explicit (ele me contou = he told me) or implied. 'Conte' (imperative) appears in examples asking someone to tell again; 'contou' is the simple past, used for completed actions. Informal pronouns and contractions (pro = para o) appear in spoken Brazilian Portuguese.
target_language_example: Ela me contou ontem sobre o novo emprego.
native_language_example: She told me yesterday about the new job.

meaning: against the current / against the flow; figuratively: going against the norm or majority.
additional_notes: Used literally for moving opposite to a water current (or flow) and figuratively to describe doing something contrary to popular opinion, trends, or obstacles. Common in phrases about difficulty or resistance (e.g., nadar contra a corrente = to swim against the current).
target_language_example: Ela decidiu seguir sua carreira contra a corrente da família.
native_language_example: She decided to follow her career against her family's expectations.

meaning: remote control (device used to operate electronics from a distance).
additional_notes: Commonly refers to a TV remote but can mean any handheld device that controls electronics remotely. In Portuguese, the adjective follows the noun (controle + remoto). Used in everyday situations (asking where it is, saying who has it, or referring to the era of remote controls).
target_language_example: Cadê o controle remoto da TV?
native_language_example: Where is the TV remote?

meaning: idle talk; nonsense; small talk with no substance.
additional_notes: Used to dismiss something as meaningless, insincere, or unimportant. Can refer to pointless chatter, excuses, or attempts to deceive. Tone is often annoyed or skeptical. Equivalent to 'cut the small talk' or 'don't give me that'.
target_language_example: Chega de conversa fiada — vamos ao que interessa.
native_language_example: Enough with the small talk — let's get to what matters.

meaning: 'very' + 'conversation' — used to modify a noun (conversa) meaning a very (something) conversation, e.g. very interesting, very heated, very offensive conversation.
additional_notes: Portuguese word order places the adverb 'muito' after the noun to modify an adjective that describes the conversation (often collapsed in examples: 'conversa muito interessante' = 'a very interesting conversation'). It can also appear with an adjective after it ('conversa muito acalorada'). On its own 'conversa muito' is incomplete — you normally need an adjective after 'muito' (or context that supplies it). 'Conversa' = conversation; 'muito' = very/very much.
target_language_example: Tivemos uma conversa muito honesta ontem à noite.
native_language_example: We had a very honest conversation last night.

meaning: 'talking in' or 'talking at/inside (a specific place)'.
additional_notes: Present participle 'conversando' (talking) + preposition 'na' (a + a = in the/at the, feminine). Used to say people are speaking inside or in a particular room or location. Change 'na' to 'no' (masculine), 'na(s)/no(s)' for plural, or drop/replace preposition depending on context.
target_language_example: Eles estão conversando na varanda.
native_language_example: They are talking on/in the porch.

meaning: to talk more; to have a longer or further conversation
additional_notes: Used to express a desire or need to continue or increase conversation. Common in personal and informal contexts (friends, family, partners). Can be followed by about what (conversar mais sobre isso) or used alone. Polite/requesting tone when used with precisamos/queria/esperava.
target_language_example: Podemos conversar mais sobre seus planos amanhã?
native_language_example: Can we talk more about your plans tomorrow?

meaning: converted to (a religion or belief).
additional_notes: Used to say someone changed their religion or faith. Often appears with reflexive pronoun se (converteu-se ao / se converteu ao) but can be written as converteu ao in past narratives. The preposition ao = a + o = 'to the' and is followed by the name of the religion (ao catolicismo, ao Islã, ao islamismo).
target_language_example: Ela se converteu ao budismo no ano passado.
native_language_example: She converted to Buddhism last year.

meaning: pink (color; literally "color of rose").
additional_notes: Used as an adjective (often hyphenated) to describe anything pink. Can refer to shades of pink; agrees in gender/number with the noun (e.g., vestido cor-de-rosa, sapatos cor-de-rosa). Common and neutral, not slang.
target_language_example: Ela comprou uma camisa cor-de-rosa ontem.
native_language_example: She bought a pink shirt yesterday.

meaning: pink (color).
additional_notes: Used to describe the color pink. Literally 'color of rose' — common in everyday speech to describe objects, clothing, or tones. Can also appear in expressions (e.g., ver a vida cor de rosa = to see life through rose-colored glasses).
target_language_example: Ela comprou um vestido cor de rosa.
native_language_example: She bought a pink dress.

meaning: 'broken heart' — emotionally hurt after love or loss.
additional_notes: Used to describe emotional pain from romantic breakup, unrequited love, or deep sadness. Common in literal and figurative contexts (songs, stories). Often preceded by 'estar/de' (estar de coração partido = to have a broken heart).
target_language_example: Depois do término, ela ficou de coração partido por semanas.
native_language_example: After the breakup, she had a broken heart for weeks.

meaning: 'her body' (refers to the physical body of a female person).
additional_notes: A possessive phrase: corpo = 'body', dela = 'of hers'/'her'. Commonly used in neutral contexts (anatomy, health) and in news/crime contexts (found a body, injured body). Context determines whether it refers to a living person's body (e.g., 'her body hurt') or to a deceased person's body (e.g., 'found her body'). Pronunciation note: 'dela' contracts in speech but is written as two words.
target_language_example: A polícia encontrou o corpo dela perto do rio.
native_language_example: The police found her body near the river.

meaning: runs every (feminine plural time period) — e.g. 'runs every morning'.
additional_notes: The phrase combines the verb 'correr' (to run) in the 3rd person singular 'corre' with 'todas as' ('all the' / 'every' for feminine plural nouns). Use 'todas as manhãs' = 'every morning', 'todas as noites' = 'every night'. For masculine plural nouns use 'todos os' (e.g. 'corre todos os dias' = 'runs every day').
target_language_example: Ela corre todas as tardes no parque.
native_language_example: She runs every afternoon in the park.

meaning: to chase (literal); to pursue or work hard to achieve something (figurative).
additional_notes: Used both literally (someone or something chasing another) and figuratively to mean actively pursuing a goal, opportunity, or trying hard to get something (e.g., a job, a client, success). Often appears as "correr atrás de [algo/alguém]". Tone can be neutral or informal depending on context; common in advice or everyday speech (e.g., "Você precisa correr atrás").
target_language_example: Só que correr atrás dá muito trabalho.
native_language_example: But pursuing it requires a lot of work.

meaning: 'take the risk' or 'run (something)' depending on context; often used in the phrase 'correr o risco' = 'to take the risk'.
additional_notes: Alone 'correr' means 'to run'. When followed by 'o risco' it forms the idiom 'correr o risco' = 'to take/run the risk'. In other sentences above (e.g. 'correr o mais rápido que podia') 'correr o' is simply part of 'correr o mais...' meaning 'to run as...'. So check the words that follow: if it's 'risco' it's the risk idiom; if it's 'mais rápido' it's the physical action 'to run'.
target_language_example: Não vou correr o risco de perder o emprego.
native_language_example: I won't take the risk of losing my job.

meaning: 'ran' + part of the comparative phrase 'as ... as possible' (ran as ... as he/she could).
additional_notes: correu is the past (pretérito perfeito) of correr (to run). In these examples, correu o appears as part of the fixed comparative structure 'correu o mais rápido que (pôde/podia)' = 'ran as fast as (she/he) could.' You will often see either pôde (simple past, more common in European Portuguese) or podia (imperfect, common in spoken/colloquial contexts) after 'que'.
target_language_example: Ele correu o mais rápido que pôde para apanhar o autocarro.
native_language_example: He ran as fast as he could to catch the bus.

meaning: I ran as fast as (possible / I could).
additional_notes: Common way to say you ran at your maximum speed. Often followed by possível, que eu podia/pude, or para + infinitive (to catch someone). Use corri (past of correr, eu) for 'I ran'; replace with correu, corremos, etc., for other persons. You can shorten to 'corri o mais rápido que pude' or 'corri o mais rápido possível'.
target_language_example: Eu corri o mais rápido que pude para alcançar o ônibus.
native_language_example: I ran as fast as I could to catch the bus.

meaning: lawn mower
additional_notes: Refers to a machine used to cut grass in yards or gardens. Can be gas-powered (a gasolina) or electric. Used in everyday contexts when talking about yard work or borrowing equipment.
target_language_example: Preciso comprar um cortador de grama novo para o quintal.
native_language_example: I need to buy a new lawn mower for the yard.

meaning: usually does / tends to do
additional_notes: Combines the verb 'costumar' (to usually do/tend to) in the present with an infinitive ('fazer' = to do). Used to talk about habitual actions or routines. For questions, it asks whether someone usually does something. In Portuguese, you can replace 'fazer' with any other infinitive (ex.: 'costuma comer', 'costuma viajar').
target_language_example: Você costuma fazer exercícios de manhã?
native_language_example: Do you usually exercise in the morning?

meaning: 'to cook so/that well' — used to say someone cooks to a high degree (with 'tão' = so/that).
additional_notes: This phrase pairs the verb cozinhar (to cook) with the adverb tão (so/that) plus an adjective (e.g., bem = well). Common in questions and statements about how or where someone learned to cook so well. The full structure in examples: 'cozinhar tão bem' = 'to cook so well'. You can replace cozinhar with other verbs (e.g., 'falar tão bem').
target_language_example: Como ela aprendeu a cozinhar tão bem?
native_language_example: How did she learn to cook so well?

meaning: to believe that / to think that
additional_notes: Used to express belief or conviction about a statement or situation. Often followed by a clause introduced by 'que' (that). Can be used in both literal and figurative senses (e.g., being led to believe). Formality: neutral; common in writing and speech.
target_language_example: Temos motivos para crer que ambos estão perto.
native_language_example: We have reason to believe that both are nearby.

meaning: 'raised in' (referring to the place or environment where someone grew up).
additional_notes: Used with a place or environment to say where someone was brought up. Often appears with a form of the verb 'ser' (fui criado, foi criado, foi criada). Can refer to a physical location (cidade) or a type of upbringing/family (um lar católico). Gender/number of 'criado' changes with the subject (criada for feminine, criados/criadas for plural). Common in both formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Apesar de ter nascido em Osaca, fui criado em Tóquio.
native_language_example: Although I was born in Osaka, I was raised in Tokyo.

meaning: 'created/raised by' or 'made by' (passive voice: someone/something was created or raised by...).
additional_notes: Used in passive constructions. Can mean 'created by' (made by, often for things or beings: Tudo foi criado por Deus = Everything was created by God) or 'raised by'/'brought up by' (for people or animals: Você foi criado por lobos? = Were you raised by wolves?). Context determines whether it refers to creation (manufacture, divine creation) or upbringing.
target_language_example: Esse quadro foi criado por um artista famoso.
native_language_example: This painting was created by a famous artist.

meaning: when I/you/he/she was a child; 'as a child'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce memories or habitual actions from childhood. Common variants: 'quando criança' (shorter) or 'quando era criança' (fuller). Often followed by the imperfect tense to describe repeated or ongoing past actions (costumava, ia, ficava, sabia). Can be used with other subjects: 'quando eu era criança', 'quando ela era criança'.
target_language_example: Quando eu era criança, eu costumava brincar na rua até anoitecer.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I used to play in the street until it got dark.

meaning: 'crime against' (used to indicate an offense directed at someone or something)
additional_notes: Used before a noun or pronoun to specify the victim or target of a crime (e.g., crime contra a pessoa — crime against a person). Common in legal contexts and formal writing. In everyday speech, speakers might simply say 'crime' plus the victim (um crime contra mim) or use other constructions.
target_language_example: Eles investigam um crime contra o patrimônio público.
native_language_example: They are investigating a crime against public property.

meaning: crime against humanity; an offense that attacks civilians on a large scale (e.g., slavery, genocide, torture).
additional_notes: Used for very serious international crimes that target civilians or groups. Often used in legal, historical, and moral contexts. Plural: crimes contra a humanidade. Pronunciation tip: 'crime' like English 'kreem', 'contra' = against, 'humanidade' = humanity.
target_language_example: A escravidão é um crime contra a humanidade.
native_language_example: Slavery is a crime against humanity.

meaning: to take care of
additional_notes: Used with a person or thing that receives care. Often followed by a pronoun or noun (e.g. cuidar de mim, cuidar das plantas). Can mean self-care when reflexive (cuidar de si mesmo). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ela precisa cuidar de suas plantas enquanto viaja.
native_language_example: She needs to take care of her plants while she travels.

meaning: 'costs the' (used to say how much something costs, often followed by a noun or measurement)
additional_notes: Common construction with the verb custar (to cost). 'Custa o preço de...' = 'costs the price of.../costs as much as...'. Also used in questions: 'Quanto custa o...?' = 'How much does the ... cost?'. The article (o/a) agrees with the noun that follows (o preço, o quilo, o seguro).
target_language_example: Essa viagem custa o dobro do que eu esperava.
native_language_example: That trip costs twice as much as I expected.

meaning: how much does a/an ... cost?
additional_notes: Used to ask the price of a single item or one unit (a/an). 'Quanto custa' = 'How much does it cost?'; adding 'um' specifies 'a' or 'one' (masculine). For feminine nouns use 'uma' (e.g., 'Quanto custa uma passagem?'). You can add quantity and measure after: 'um quilo de', 'um saco de', etc.
target_language_example: Quanto custa um livro na livraria?
native_language_example: How much does a book cost at the bookstore?

meaning: cost of living (the amount of money needed to cover basic expenses like housing, food, transportation, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to talk about how expensive it is to live in a place or for a household. Commonly appears with verbs like aumentar (to rise), diminuir (to fall), comparar (to compare) and expressions such as 'alto custo de vida' (high cost of living) or 'baixo custo de vida' (low cost of living).
target_language_example: O custo de vida nesta cidade é muito alto.
native_language_example: The cost of living in this city is very high.

meaning: 'cost (me/you/etc.) a' — used to say something required a large amount (often followed by a noun like 'fortuna' or a time period).
additional_notes: Literally 'it/this/that cost a...'. Commonly followed by nouns such as 'fortuna' (a fortune), 'semana' (a week), etc. When used with an indirect object pronoun (me/te/lhe) it indicates who paid the cost: 'isso me custou uma semana' = 'that cost me a week.' Useful to express monetary cost or non-monetary cost (time, effort).
target_language_example: Esse projeto me custou uma noite inteira.
native_language_example: That project cost me an entire night.

meaning: 'between us' or 'just between us' — used to introduce a confidential, frank, or off-the-record remark.
additional_notes: Common colloquial phrase to signal that what follows is meant to be kept private, candid, or slightly taboo. Often used before a blunt opinion, gossip, or a candid admission. Tone can be playful, conspiratorial, or critical depending on context.
target_language_example: Cá entre nós, eu não gostei daquele filme.
native_language_example: Just between us, I didn't like that movie.

meaning: camera (for taking photos); photographic camera.
additional_notes: Refers to a device used to take photographs. Common in everyday speech; can be shortened to just 'câmera' in context. 'Fotográfica' specifies it's for photography (not, for example, a video camera). Plural: 'câmeras fotográficas'.
target_language_example: Ela comprou uma câmera fotográfica nova para a viagem.
native_language_example: She bought a new camera for the trip.

meaning: 'a camera in/on/at the' (camera + preposition + definite article contraction).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a combination: câmera (camera) + no (contraction of em + o = 'in/on/at the' or 'on the/at the' depending on context). Use 'no' before masculine singular nouns (o). Context determines English preposition: 'in the', 'on the', 'at the', or 'on (website)' (e.g., 'no eBay' = 'on eBay').
target_language_example: Achei uma câmera no armário.
native_language_example: I found a camera in the closet.

meaning: lung cancer.
additional_notes: A medical term referring to malignant tumors in the lungs. Used the same way as in English: to say someone has, died of, or that something causes lung cancer. 'Câncer' is spelled with an accent on the first a. In Portuguese word order: câncer (disease) + de (of) + pulmão (lung).
target_language_example: Meu avô foi diagnosticado com câncer de pulmão.
native_language_example: My grandfather was diagnosed with lung cancer.

meaning: 'the sky was' (simple past description of the sky's condition).
additional_notes: Used to describe the weather or appearance of the sky in the past (imperfect/past continuous sense). 'Céu' = sky; 'estava' is the imperfect past of 'estar' (to be) for he/she/it or general statements. Commonly followed by adjectives (azul, nublado, escuro, etc.).
target_language_example: Ontem à tarde o céu estava limpo e ensolarado.
native_language_example: Yesterday afternoon the sky was clear and sunny.

meaning: 'the sky is' (used to describe the sky's current appearance or weather-related color/condition).
additional_notes: Combines céu (sky) + está (third-person singular of estar). Use to state how the sky looks right now (color, cloudiness, darkness, etc.). Estar indicates a temporary/state condition. Often followed by colors or descriptions: azul (blue), negro (black/dark), vermelho (red), nublado (cloudy).
target_language_example: O céu está nublado hoje; devemos levar um guarda-chuva.
native_language_example: The sky is cloudy today; we should take an umbrella.

meaning: the sky became / the sky got (followed by a description).
additional_notes: A common sequence: 'o céu ficou + adjective/phrase' to describe a change in the sky's appearance (e.g., nublado, escuro, vermelho). Use to report a sudden or gradual change. Literal parts: 'céu' = sky, 'ficou' = became/got (past of ficar).
target_language_example: De repente, o céu ficou muito escuro.
native_language_example: Suddenly, the sky became very dark.

meaning: vicious circle; a self-perpetuating negative cycle
additional_notes: Used to describe a situation where one problem causes another, which in turn makes the first problem worse, creating a repeating negative loop. Common in everyday and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Se não pagar as dívidas, os juros aumentam e cria um círculo vicioso.
native_language_example: If you don't pay the debts, the interest increases and it creates a vicious circle.

meaning: of the morning; used in the phrase 'café-da-manhã' = breakfast.
additional_notes: da manhã literally means 'of the morning' and is used after words (most commonly 'café') to form expressions referring to morning activities or items. In Brazilian Portuguese, 'café-da-manhã' (or 'café da manhã' with spaces) is the standard word for 'breakfast'. The hyphenated form appears in some fixed expressions but spacing is also common.
target_language_example: Eu faço caminhada depois do café-da-manhã.
native_language_example: I go for a walk after breakfast.

meaning: an insult meaning 'son(s) of a b****' or 'b*****' (used to call someone very offensive names).
additional_notes: Highly vulgar. Often appears as part of the compound expression 'filho(s)-da-puta' (singular filho-da-puta) meaning 'son of a bitch' or 'bastard'. Used to express anger or contempt; avoid in polite conversation. Can be pluralized (filhos-da-puta) and combined with articles/pronouns (vocês são um bando de filhos-da-puta).
target_language_example: Ele é um filho-da-puta — não quero falar com ele.
native_language_example: He's a son of a bitch — I don't want to talk to him.

meaning: from head to toe; completely, all over.
additional_notes: Used to describe something applying to the entire body or something total/complete (e.g., covered, dressed, soaked). Literal phrase: 'from the head to the feet.' Common in everyday speech and neutral register.
target_language_example: Ela estava molhada da cabeça aos pés após a caminhada.
native_language_example: She was wet from head to toe after the walk.

meaning: of the force / by force (depending on context)
additional_notes: Literal composition: 'da' = 'of the' (de + a) and 'força' = 'force' or 'strength'. Can indicate possession ('of the force'), source ('from the force'), or means ('by force' / 'through force') depending on the sentence. Context decides whether it refers to a physical force, a military force, or the abstract idea of using force.
target_language_example: Recuperaram a cidade da força invasora.
native_language_example: They recaptured the city from the invading force.

meaning: of the sentence / of the phrase.
additional_notes: A possessive + noun phrase: 'da' = contraction of 'de' + 'a' (of the). Used to indicate something belonging to or related to a specific sentence or phrase (e.g., meaning, construction, punctuation). 'Frase' can mean 'sentence' or 'phrase' depending on context.
target_language_example: Eu não entendi o sentido da frase.
native_language_example: I didn't understand the meaning of the sentence.

meaning: 'cool' / 'awesome' (slang); or literal 'of the time' depending on context.
additional_notes: Informal, slang use meaning 'cool' or 'awesome' (common in Brazil). But 'da hora' can also appear literally as 'da hora' = 'of the time' (e.g., 'lembrar da hora' = remember the time) or in time expressions ('passou da hora' = it's past the time). Context determines meaning—when exclaimed alone or describing an object ('uma bicicleta da hora'), it's the slang 'cool'.
target_language_example: Que camiseta da hora!
native_language_example: What a cool T‑shirt!

meaning: literally 'of the morning is' — part of a time/description phrase, usually following a noun to indicate something happening/being in the morning (e.g., 'A temperatura da manhã está...').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself but a sequence that appears when describing morning qualities (temperature, calm, rotina, etc.). In Portuguese, time-of-day phrases use "da manhã" (in the morning). "Está" is the present form of "estar" (to be) used for temporary states. Combine with a noun before "da manhã" and an adjective or clause after "está".
target_language_example: A temperatura da manhã está muito agradável hoje.
native_language_example: The morning temperature is very pleasant today.

meaning: overnight; suddenly, from one day to the next.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens very quickly or suddenly (often implausibly). Common in negative sentences to mean 'not overnight' (i.e., it takes time). Equivalent to English 'overnight' or 'from one day to the next.'
target_language_example: O sucesso não veio da noite para o dia; levou anos de trabalho.
native_language_example: Success didn't come overnight; it took years of work.

meaning: from the tap; (coming) out of the faucet
additional_notes: Literal phrase made of 'da' (de + a = from/of the) + 'torneira' (tap/faucet). Used to refer to water or something that comes directly from the household tap (e.g., water, smell, or taste). Can appear in contexts like 'água da torneira' (tap water) or 'cheiro da torneira' (smell from the tap).
target_language_example: Prefiro beber água da torneira depois de filtrá‑la.
native_language_example: I prefer to drink tap water after filtering it.

meaning: of life
additional_notes: Literal meaning is 'of life' and it appears in many expressions (e.g., 'temper o da vida' = 'spice of life'). In questions like 'O que você faz da vida?' or 'O que vocês fazem da vida?' it's informal and asks about someone's job/occupation or what they do with their life (equivalent to 'what do you do for a living?'). Context determines whether it refers broadly to life in general ('part of life', 'rest of life') or to a person's occupation/way of living.
target_language_example: Ela quer saber o que eu faço da vida.
native_language_example: She wants to know what I do for a living.

meaning: 'of the voice' / 'the voice's' — a possessive phrase using the preposition 'de' + definite article 'a' (da = de + a).
additional_notes: Used to indicate possession or relation to 'voz' (voice). 'Da' is the contraction of 'de' + 'a' and agrees with the feminine noun 'voz'. Common in phrases like 'o tom da voz' (the tone of the voice) or 'a amostra da voz' (the sample of the voice). In English you usually translate it as 'of the voice', 'the voice's', or simply 'voice' depending on context.
target_language_example: Gosto do timbre da voz dela.
native_language_example: I like the tone of her voice.

meaning: 'given the' or 'having given the' (past participle phrase using 'dar' = to give).
additional_notes: This is a combination of the past participle 'dado' (given) and the masculine singular definite article 'o' (the). It appears in contexts where something was given (e.g., dado o passo = the step having been taken / given the step) or as part of a passive/perfect construction (ele me deu o livro → ele me deu o livro / eu tinha dado o livro = I had given the book). In many sentences from the examples, 'dado o' is actually just 'dado' + the following noun 'o livro', 'o dinheiro', 'o primeiro passo' etc. Not a fixed idiom — treat it as 'dado' + 'o' + noun.
target_language_example: Eu já tinha dado o presente antes da festa.
native_language_example: I had already given the gift before the party.

meaning: 'bridesmaid' (a woman who helps the bride at a wedding).
additional_notes: Used to refer to one of the bride's attendants in a wedding. Can mean the general role (bridesmaid) or a specific person (the bridesmaid). In some contexts it may refer to the maid of honor if specified, but usually 'madrinha' or 'madrinha de casamento' can be used for a principal sponsor; 'dama de honra' is commonly used for bridesmaids. Plural: 'damas de honra'.
target_language_example: Ela foi dama de honra da melhor amiga.
native_language_example: She was her best friend's bridesmaid.

meaning: 'getting along' or 'doing well (with someone)'.
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the pronominal construction 'se dar bem (com alguém)' meaning to have a good relationship or to get along with someone. Common in conversational Portuguese to ask if people are compatible or interacting well. Tense/number/person changes with 'dar' and the reflexive pronoun (e.g., 'está se dando bem', 'estão se dando bem').
target_language_example: Eles estão se dando bem desde que começaram a trabalhar juntos.
native_language_example: They have been getting along well since they started working together.

meaning: 'giving the' or 'giving (someone) the' / part of continuous verb + definite article construction (gerund + o).
additional_notes: This is the gerund of 'dar' (to give) followed by the masculine singular definite article 'o'. It often appears before a noun (e.g., 'dando o dinheiro' = 'giving the money') or before a superlative/idiomatic phrase (e.g., 'dando o melhor' = 'giving the best / doing one's best'). Context determines the full meaning. The phrase itself is grammatical rather than idiomatic. Watch word order: Portuguese often uses gerund + article + noun; English usually uses 'giving' + noun without an article if indefinite.
target_language_example: Ele está dando o seu melhor no trabalho.
native_language_example: He is giving his best at work.

meaning: 'forget it' / 'to hell with it' — an expression to dismiss something or show you don't care
additional_notes: Informal and rude; used to show annoyance, resignation, or contempt. Can be like 'screw it', 'to hell with it', or 'I don't care' depending on context and tone. Often standalone or followed by the thing/person being dismissed (e.g., 'Dane-se isso' or 'Dane-se, cara'). Avoid in formal situations.
target_language_example: Dane-se, vou fazer do meu jeito.
native_language_example: Screw it, I'm going to do it my way.

meaning: 'from here' or 'out of here' followed by 'and' — used to connect commands or statements that start with 'daqui' (often in imperatives or descriptions).
additional_notes: This construction appears when 'daqui' (meaning 'from here' or 'out of here') is followed by 'e' ('and') to link another clause. Common in commands (Saia daqui, e ... = Get out of here, and ...). In spoken Portuguese the comma may be omitted; intonation or pausing separates the ideas. 'Daqui' can mean 'from here' (location) or 'from now' depending on context, but with imperatives it usually means 'out of here' or 'leave'.
target_language_example: Saia daqui, e não volte mais.
native_language_example: Get out of here, and don't come back.

meaning: in/after (a period of) — used to say when something will happen from now (e.g., 'in two hours').
additional_notes: Common time expression meaning 'from now' + a time interval. Used with days, hours, minutes, years, etc. Can translate to 'in' (British/US English) or 'from now.' Often followed by a number and a time unit (duas semanas, quinze minutos, uma hora).
target_language_example: O filme começa daqui a meia hora.
native_language_example: The movie starts in half an hour.

meaning: in a little while; shortly; soon.
additional_notes: Commonly used to indicate a short, unspecified amount of time from now. Can mean within minutes or a short period later depending on context and speaker. Used for future actions (I'll do it soon), requests (Come back soon), or warnings (you'll regret it soon). Tone can be neutral or informal depending on situation.
target_language_example: Ligo para você daqui a pouco.
native_language_example: I'll call you in a little while.

meaning: to give one's hand; to hold hands (literal) — also used figuratively to mean to help, support, or assist someone
additional_notes: Primary literal meaning is to offer or hold hands with someone (e.g., romantic gesture or to guide someone). Common figurative use: 'dar a mão a alguém' means to help or support a person. Context or added words (e.g., 'dar a mão a alguém', 'dar-lhe a mão') clarify whether it's physical or figurative.
target_language_example: Ela decidiu dar a mão a alguém que precisava de ajuda.
native_language_example: She decided to give a hand to someone who needed help.

meaning: to care (about); to give a damn (about) — commonly used in negative or interrogative contexts to say someone doesn't care.
additional_notes: Informal expression. Frequently appears in negative sentences or questions (e.g., 'não dou a mínima'). Can be followed by 'para' or 'por' + noun/pronoun, or used alone. Avoid in very formal contexts; tone can be blunt or dismissive.
target_language_example: Ele disse que não vai dar a mínima para as críticas.
native_language_example: He said he won't give a damn about the criticism.

meaning: to give someone the floor / to allow someone to speak; to hand over the turn to speak
additional_notes: Used when formally or politely letting someone speak, e.g. in meetings, ceremonies, or speeches. Equivalent to 'give the floor' or 'yield the floor' in English. Can also mean 'to promise' in some contexts when using 'dar a palavra a alguém' as 'give one's word', but the more common use is to grant speaking time.
target_language_example: Vou dar a palavra ao presidente para que ele fale sobre o projeto.
native_language_example: I'll give the floor to the president so he can talk about the project.

meaning: "to teach" (to give a class; to work as a teacher).
additional_notes: Used to say someone teaches a subject or gives classes. Often followed by the subject or the preposition 'de' + subject (dar aula de música) or by a direct object with preposition 'a/para' indicating the students (dar aula para os alunos). Can also appear impersonally: 'gosto de dar aula' = I like teaching. Informal register: neutral, common in spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: Ela vai dar aula de português na escola.
native_language_example: She will teach Portuguese at the school.

meaning: to pay attention to someone or something; to respond (often used in negative: 'not pay attention' = ignore)
additional_notes: Colloquial Brazilian Portuguese expression. Frequently used in the negative form 'não dar bola' to mean ignoring or not caring about someone or something. Positively, 'dar bola' can mean to show interest or give attention. Common in spoken informal contexts.
target_language_example: Ela tentou falar comigo, mas eu não quis dar bola.
native_language_example: She tried to talk to me, but I didn't want to pay attention / I ignored her.

meaning: to send/hand over letters; (idiomatic) to be skillful or to have influence/control in a situation (to call the shots, to have clout).
additional_notes: Literally 'to give letters'. Used both literally (to deliver or send written letters) and idiomatically — common in Brazilian Portuguese to indicate someone who has authority, power, or skill in a situation. More colloquial when idiomatic. Context determines meaning.
target_language_example: Na reunião, quem realmente dava cartas era a diretora; ela sabia como dar cartas e resolver os problemas.
native_language_example: At the meeting, the director was the one who really called the shots; she knew how to call the shots and solve the problems.

meaning: 'to manage' / 'to cope' / 'to handle' (something); also 'to realize' in reflexive use 'dar-se conta'.
additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone can handle a task or situation (dar conta de algo / de alguém). In reflexive form 'dar-se conta' (or 'dar conta' with 'nos'/'se' as in sentence 4) means 'to realize' or 'become aware'. Context determines meaning—followed by 'de' + noun = manage/handle; with 'se/nos' = realize. Often appears in questions (Vai dar conta?) meaning 'Will (you/they) manage?'.
target_language_example: Ele não conseguiu dar conta do trabalho sozinho.
native_language_example: He couldn't handle the work alone.

meaning: 'to work hard' / 'to put in a lot of effort'.
additional_notes: Common informal expression used to say someone is working or studying very hard, or trying very much. Can refer to physical labor or effort in general (e.g., studying, practicing, working). Often used in present tense: 'dar duro' (infinitive) or conjugated: 'dou duro' is not common—more typical: 'ele deu duro', 'vou dar duro', 'tá dando duro'.
target_language_example: Vou dar duro para terminar o projeto a tempo.
native_language_example: I'm going to work hard to finish the project on time.

meaning: to hit on someone; to flirt with someone (often sexually/romantically).
additional_notes: Informal phrasal expression used when one person makes advances toward another — can be playful or unwanted. Common in Brazil and Portugal. Use with care: can imply direct or persistent flirting. Typical structure: dar em cima de + person (dar em cima dela / dele / dele/a).
target_language_example: Ele ficou bêbado e começou a dar em cima de todo mundo na festa.
native_language_example: He got drunk and started hitting on everyone at the party.

meaning: to annoy someone a lot; to get on someone's nerves.
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression used to say that something or someone is irritating, stressful or frustrating. Commonly used in constructions like 'isso/ele/ela me dá nos nervos' (that/they drive me crazy). Replace the indirect object pronoun to indicate who is annoyed (me, te, lhe, nos, vos, lhes). Informal and widely used in spoken Portuguese.
target_language_example: Esse barulho constante me dá nos nervos.
native_language_example: That constant noise gets on my nerves.

meaning: make the
additional_notes: A combination of the verb dar (to give/do) plus the definite article o. Often used idiomatically where English uses verbs like "make" or "place" with a noun: e.g. "dar o primeiro lance" = "make/place the first bid/offer." The exact translation depends on the noun that follows. Contraction with pronouns (dar-lhe o) is possible in full sentences.
target_language_example: Quem vai dar o primeiro lance?
native_language_example: Who will make the first bid?

meaning: to leave, get out, or to break up/ditch someone (colloquial).
additional_notes: Colloquial Brazilian Portuguese. Depending on context, it can mean 'to leave a place' (e.g., 'Let's get out of here') or 'to dump/end a relationship' / 'to ditch someone' (e.g., 'he dumped her'). Often used in informal speech. Not literal (contains 'dar' + 'o fora').
target_language_example: Depois da briga, ela decidiu dar o fora.
native_language_example: After the fight, she decided to leave/ditch him.

meaning: to give mine / to give my (one).
additional_notes: Literal construction: dar (to give) + o meu (my/mine). Used before a noun (dar o meu carro = give my car) or with a pronoun (dar o meu = give mine). Common in everyday speech when offering or handing something (number, phone, name, object). Word order can be shortened (Vou te dar o meu → I'll give you mine / my...).
target_language_example: Vou dar o meu livro a você se quiser.
native_language_example: I'll give you my book if you want.

meaning: to listen to (someone); to pay attention to what someone says.
additional_notes: An idiomatic phrase. Often used with a person as indirect object (dar ouvidos a alguém) or without 'a' in colloquial speech. Can imply giving someone attention, taking their advice, or heeding warnings. Commonly used in negative (não dar ouvidos = not listen) and imperative contexts.
target_language_example: Eu vou dar ouvidos ao conselho dela desta vez.
native_language_example: I'll listen to her advice this time.

meaning: to give to
additional_notes: Used when giving something (a thing, opportunity, chance) to a person. Followed by the recipient introduced by 'a' or a person name. Can also be used with abstract items (a chance, a gift). Not to be confused with 'dar para' meaning 'to be possible' in other contexts (e.g. 'isso não dá para' = 'that won't work').
target_language_example: Vou dar para a Maria um presente amanhã.
native_language_example: I'll give Maria a present tomorrow.

meaning: to give everything; also used idiomatically in 'dar tudo certo' = 'turn out well' or 'be all right'.
additional_notes: Literally means 'to give everything' when used with a direct object (dar tudo a alguém = give someone everything). Separately, the phrase 'dar tudo certo' is a common fixed expression meaning 'it will all work out' or 'everything will be fine.' Context determines meaning.
target_language_example: Se você quiser, eu posso te dar tudo o que tenho.
native_language_example: If you want, I can give you everything I have.

meaning: to find a way / to manage / to fix (informal).
additional_notes: Common informal expression meaning to make something work, to solve a problem, or to arrange something somehow. Can imply improvisation or making adjustments. Often used with de/para/na/etc. depending on context (dar um jeito de + infinitive = find a way to do something; dar um jeito em + noun = fix/put in order).
target_language_example: Vou dar um jeito de consertar isso amanhã.
native_language_example: I'll find a way to fix that tomorrow.

meaning: to give someone a hand; to help someone (informal).
additional_notes: Common informal expression meaning to help or assist with a task. Often used with 'dar uma mão em' + place/task or 'dar uma mão para/para alguém'. Equivalent to English 'give (someone) a hand' or 'lend a hand.'
target_language_example: Você pode me dar uma mão com as malas?
native_language_example: Can you give me a hand with the suitcases?

meaning: to act like; to pretend to be (someone or something); to put on an attitude
additional_notes: Used before a noun or noun phrase to say someone is behaving as if they were that person/role. Often implies imitation, affectation, or pretense — sometimes playful, sometimes critical. Common patterns: 'dar uma de + [profissão/personagem/expressão]' (dar uma de esperto, dar uma de médico). Can be followed by an infinitive clause in informal speech: 'dar uma de sabichão e...'. Tone and meaning depend on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Ele começou a dar uma de entendedor na reunião, mas não sabia do que falava.
native_language_example: He started acting like he was an expert at the meeting, but he didn't know what he was talking about.

meaning: 'to value' or 'to give importance to' (to consider something important or worthwhile).
additional_notes: Used when saying you appreciate, respect, or consider something/someone important. Can be followed by a noun or a clause (dar valor a algo / a alguém; dar valor ao que alguém diz). Close in meaning to 'valorizar'. Not commonly used to mean assigning a price (use 'avaliar' or 'avaliar o valor').
target_language_example: Eu sei dar valor ao tempo que passamos juntos.
native_language_example: I know how to value the time we spend together.

meaning: to go for a walk/ride; to take a turn around (a place); to circle/turn around.
additional_notes: Common, versatile phrasal expression. Context determines exact sense: can mean 'to take a walk' or 'to go for a drive' (dar uma volta), 'to go around something' (dar a volta), or 'to turn something over/around' in a literal sense. Often used with an indefinite article: dar uma volta. Can be used casually for a short outing to relax or check surroundings.
target_language_example: Vamos dar volta no parque?
native_language_example: Shall we go for a walk in the park?

meaning: 'to give birth' (to deliver a baby).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone is giving birth. Often used with a person as subject (e.g., Ela deu à luz) or with alguém as object when speaking about helping (e.g., ajudar a dar à luz). The construction combines the verb dar (to give) with the feminine singular article + noun à luz (to the light); it's idiomatic and not literal.
target_language_example: A irmã vai dar à luz em julho.
native_language_example: The sister is going to give birth in July.

meaning: would give (to)
additional_notes: Conditional form of dar (eu daria = I would give). When followed by a direct object introduced by the preposition a, it means 'would give (something) to (someone)' or 'would grant (someone) [something]'. Often used politely to make requests/offers or to express hypothetical willingness: 'Você me daria a honra...' = 'Would you grant me the honor...'. Word order and presence of the object determine exact translation.
target_language_example: Você me daria a chave se eu precisasse?
native_language_example: Would you give me the key if I needed it?

meaning: old-fashioned; from the old days; classic/old (often with fondness or respect).
additional_notes: Used to describe people, objects, or things that are from an earlier time or have an old-style/retro quality. Can imply nostalgia or admiration (e.g., a classic car, an old recipe, or someone with traditional values). Literally means "of the old ones/old times."
target_language_example: Aquela rádio é das antigas, toca músicas dos anos 70.
native_language_example: That radio is old-fashioned/from the old days; it plays songs from the 1970s.

meaning: literally 'from there the' — often used to introduce a result or consequence ('therefore'/'that's why') or appears in imperatives telling someone to leave a place when followed by verbs/objects ('out of there, ...'). Meaning depends on context and surrounding words.
additional_notes: 'daí' = contraction of 'de' + 'aí' ('from/there' or 'then/so'). The phrase 'daí o' is compositional: 'o' can be the definite article introducing a noun ('Daí o branco' = 'That's why it's white') or part of an imperative construction when combined with verbs and pronouns ('Saia daí o mais rápido possível' = 'Get out of there as quickly as possible'). Pay attention to verb forms and politeness: 'sai'/'saiam'/'saia' etc. Punctuation and stress can affect meaning.
target_language_example: Saia daí o mais rápido possível.
native_language_example: Get out of there as quickly as possible.

meaning: 'of Jesus' / 'about Jesus' depending on context.
additional_notes: The preposition 'de' can mean possession ('of'), origin, description, or topic ('about'). With a proper name like Jesus, 'de Jesus' often appears in surnames (e.g., 'Alexandre de Jesus') meaning 'of Jesus' as part of the family name. In other sentences it can mean 'about Jesus' (talking about him) or indicate something belonging to or related to Jesus (e.g., 'the birth of Jesus'). Context decides the best translation.
target_language_example: Ela escreveu um livro sobre a vida de Jesus.
native_language_example: She wrote a book about the life of Jesus.

meaning: 'of such' / 'of that kind' (used to describe a type or quality previously mentioned)
additional_notes: Used after a noun to indicate 'of such a ...' or 'of that kind'. Often appears in phrases like 'um homem de tal caráter' (a man of such character) or in formal/written contexts. Be careful: capitalized 'Tal' can be a surname—context matters. Not a stand-alone phrase; it modifies a noun.
target_language_example: Ela é uma pessoa de tal honestidade que todos confiam nela.
native_language_example: She is a person of such honesty that everyone trusts her.

meaning: 'in agreement' / 'agree' (expressing agreement with someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to say you agree (fully, partially, or not). Often appears with qualifiers: totalmente de acordo (completely agree), parcialmente de acordo (partially agree), nunca de acordo (never agree). Can function as a short reply (like 'Agreed' or 'Okay'). When followed by 'com' it indicates agreement with a person or idea: 'de acordo com você'.
target_language_example: Estou de acordo com essa proposta.
native_language_example: I agree with that proposal.

meaning: 'according to' / 'in agreement with' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Common phrase used to report sources (according to...), to indicate conformity with something (in accordance with / based on), or agreement. Followed by a noun, source, rule, situation, or a pronoun phrase. Can introduce reported information (De acordo com o jornal...) or indicate behavior that matches something (de acordo com a sua idade).
target_language_example: De acordo com as instruções, desligue o aparelho antes de limpar.
native_language_example: According to the instructions, turn off the device before cleaning.

meaning: 'from now on' or 'from this point forward'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a change that begins at the present moment and continues into the future. Common in both spoken and written Portuguese to set a new rule, habit, or state.
target_language_example: De agora em diante, vou chegar mais cedo ao trabalho.
native_language_example: From now on, I will arrive at work earlier.

meaning: to rent a (something) / to have to rent a (something) (depends on context)
additional_notes: This phrase combines the preposition 'de' with the verb 'alugar' (to rent) and the indefinite article 'um/uma' (a). In many sentences here 'gostaria de alugar um...' means 'I'd like to rent a...'. In others (Eu tive de alugar um, Tom tinha de alugar um) 'ter de' means 'to have to' (past obligation): 'I had to rent a...'. Replace 'um' with 'uma' for feminine nouns (uma casa, uma bicicleta). For a specific item use 'o/a' (o carro).
target_language_example: Gostaria de alugar um apartamento por um mês.
native_language_example: I'd like to rent an apartment for a month.

meaning: made of or containing peanuts; 'peanut' as an ingredient or flavor (of/from peanuts).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to indicate something is made with, filled with, flavored with, or related to peanuts. Common in food contexts (e.g., 'creme de amendoim' — peanut butter). In Portuguese word order, 'de + ingredient' often means 'made of' or 'with'.
target_language_example: Bolo de amendoim está delicioso.
native_language_example: The peanut cake is delicious.

meaning: in advance; beforehand.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is known, done, or expected before a certain time or event. Common in thanks (e.g., 'Obrigado de antemão') and to express prior knowledge or warning.
target_language_example: Obrigado de antemão por responder ao e-mail.
native_language_example: Thanks in advance for replying to the email.

meaning: 'to turn off the' (followed by a feminine noun like 'luz' or 'fogos') — expresses forgetting or remembering to switch something off.
additional_notes: This is the preposition 'de' + infinitive 'apagar' + feminine article 'a' and is used before a feminine noun (e.g., a luz, a fogueira). Common in phrases about forgetting or remembering to switch off lights, fires, appliances, etc. The verb before this phrase is often verbs like esquecer(se) or lembrar(se): 'esquecer de apagar a...' / 'lembrar de apagar a...'.
target_language_example: Não esqueça de apagar a luz quando sair.
native_language_example: Don't forget to turn off the light when you leave.

meaning: of/for learning English; used to talk about the purpose or topic of learning English.
additional_notes: This fragment typically appears after nouns or verbs that require a prepositional phrase indicating purpose, topic, or content (e.g., 'dicas de aprender Inglês' — tips for learning English; 'a necessidade de aprender Inglês' — the need to learn English). 'Inglês' is capitalized in Portuguese. If you want to say 'to learn English' as an infinitive purpose, use 'para aprender Inglês' (more common) or 'a aprender Inglês' in some contexts.
target_language_example: Ela comprou um curso de aprender Inglês online.
native_language_example: She bought a course for learning English online.

meaning: “to learn English in order to get to know / to experience (something or someone).” Expresses purpose: learning the English language so one can meet people, visit places, or learn about cultures.
additional_notes: This phrase combines a purpose marker (para = in order to) with the verb conhecer (to know, to meet, to become acquainted with, to visit/experience). Often used to explain why someone wants to study English (e.g., to meet people, visit countries, or learn about cultures). Note: in Portuguese orthography, 'inglês' is normally lowercase unless at the start of a sentence; however many writers capitalize language names. For more natural alternatives, you can say: "Quero aprender inglês para conhecer outras culturas."
target_language_example: Gostaria de aprender Inglês para conhecer novas culturas; por isso procuro um curso intensivo.
native_language_example: I would like to learn English to get to know new cultures; that's why I'm looking for an intensive course.

meaning: of learning things / to learn things (depends on context)
additional_notes: This is a phrase fragment combining the preposition/deverbal complement 'de' with the verb infinitive 'aprender' and the plural noun 'coisas'. It often appears after verbs, adjectives, or nouns that require 'de' + infinitive (e.g., 'tenho vontade de aprender coisas' — 'I want to learn things') or in lists (e.g., 'gosto de aprender coisas novas'). Alone it is not a complete sentence; context determines exact translation.
target_language_example: Gosto de aprender coisas novas todos os dias.
native_language_example: I like to learn new things every day.

meaning: of fireworks / firework (as in 'fogos de artifício' = fireworks).
additional_notes: Usually appears in the phrase 'fogos de artifício' (fireworks). 'Artifício' by itself can mean 'trick' or 'device', but in this set phrase it specifically refers to pyrotechnic displays. Used in plural: 'fogos de artifício'.
target_language_example: Vamos assistir aos fogos de artifício na praia.
native_language_example: Let's watch the fireworks on the beach.

meaning: 'on good terms' / 'in a good mood' / 'from far away' depending on context
additional_notes: This expression has several uses: 1) 'ficar de bem (com alguém)' = to be on good terms / to reconcile with someone; 2) standalone 'De bem!' is an informal, positive exclamation (like 'All good!' or 'Sounds good!'); 3) in phrases like 'de bem longe' it means 'from (a) long way/afar'; 4) in quantified contexts ('de bem mais') it can mean 'much more' or 'a lot more'. Context decides the exact English equivalent.
target_language_example: Depois da conversa, conseguimos ficar de bem.
native_language_example: After the talk, we managed to be on good terms.

meaning: relaxed / fine / in good faith / of good background (depends on context).
additional_notes: Informal expression with several uses: 1) 'estar de boa' = to be relaxed, fine, or not bothered (e.g., Estou de boa; Não, tô de boa). 2) 'de boa fé' (with fé) = in good faith, honestly/formally used. 3) 'de boa família' / 'de boa aparência' = indicates good family background or good appearance; here 'boa' describes a positive quality. Context determines meaning—most common in speech is the relaxed sense. Often used without the article: 'tô de boa'.
target_language_example: Tô de boa hoje, não quero sair.
native_language_example: I'm relaxed today, I don't want to go out.

meaning: 'willingly', 'of good will', or 'with goodwill' — indicating willingness or a friendly/charitable intent.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone acting willingly, voluntarily, or with kind/positive intentions. Can refer to accepting something gladly (willingly), offering help voluntarily, or a benevolent gesture (goodwill). Context determines whether to translate as 'willingly', 'gladly', 'voluntarily' or 'as a gesture of goodwill.'
target_language_example: Ela ajudou os vizinhos de boa vontade.
native_language_example: She helped the neighbors willingly.

meaning: of (cake) — part of the noun + de + noun structure used to indicate the type, filling or flavor of a cake (e.g., 'bolo de chocolate' = chocolate cake).
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase on its own; it's the internal sequence appearing in constructions like 'bolo de X'. Use with quantities or verbs: 'um pedaço de bolo de X' (a piece of X cake), 'gosta de bolo de X' (likes X cake), 'sirva-se de bolo de X' (help yourself to X cake).
