target_language_example: Eu quero um pedaço de bolo de chocolate.
native_language_example: I want a piece of chocolate cake.

meaning: 'willingly', 'gladly', or 'with pleasure'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone accepts or does something willingly and without reluctance. Common in formal and neutral contexts; conveys readiness or pleasure in doing the action. Often placed after the verb or phrase it modifies (e.g., "aceitou de bom grado").
target_language_example: Aceito de bom grado sua ajuda.
native_language_example: I gladly accept your help.

meaning: 'of/with shit' — vulgar expression used to describe something worthless, dirty, or literally covered in feces
additional_notes: Very vulgar. Can be literal (referring to actual feces) or figurative (insulting an object/person as worthless or disgusting). Common in informal, angry speech. Avoid in polite settings.
target_language_example: Para de usar esse carro de bosta e compra um decente.
native_language_example: Stop using that piece-of-shit car and buy a decent one.

meaning: 'head-first' or 'by heart' / 'from memory' depending on context
additional_notes: This phrase has two common uses: 1) Literally 'head-first' (doing something with the head leading, e.g., saltar de cabeça = dive head-first). 2) Figuratively 'de cabeça' can mean 'by heart' or 'from memory' when referring to knowing or reciting something without notes. Context determines meaning. It also appears in descriptions like 'de cabeça pra cima/para baixo' = 'with the head up/down'.
target_language_example: Ele mergulhou de cabeça no lago.
native_language_example: He dove head-first into the lake.

meaning: upside down; (figuratively) turned upside down / in chaos
additional_notes: Used both literally (an object physically inverted) and figuratively (a situation or life disrupted or in disorder). Common in everyday speech. Can be used with estar/ficar/virar: 'o livro está de cabeça para baixo' (literal) or 'virou minha vida de cabeça para baixo' (figurative).
target_language_example: Depois da mudança, a minha casa ficou de cabeça para baixo.
native_language_example: After the move, my house was upside down.

meaning: completely; from beginning to end; thoroughly.
additional_notes: Used to say someone knows or has done something very thoroughly or entirely. Common with places (knows a city/neighbourhood 'from top to bottom') or tasks (done completely). Informal to neutral register. Literal image is 'from head to tail'.
target_language_example: Ela leu o livro de cabo a rabo.
native_language_example: She read the book from cover to cover.

meaning: of coffee per day; used to say how many cups/glasses of coffee someone drinks each day.
additional_notes: Commonly follows a quantity (e.g., 'três xícaras de café por dia') to express daily consumption. 'Xícaras' (cups) and 'copos' (glasses) are typical containers; 'de' links the container to the content (coffee). Often appears after a range or number.
target_language_example: Eu tomo duas xícaras de café por dia.
native_language_example: I drink two cups of coffee per day.

meaning: of/with hot coffee; (used to describe something that contains or is accompanied by hot coffee).
additional_notes: Commonly follows a noun like 'xícara' (cup) to specify that the coffee is hot. Can appear after quantity words or suggestions (e.g., 'uma xícara de café quente', 'Que tal uma de café quente?'). Literally 'of hot coffee' or 'with hot coffee.'
target_language_example: Eu quero uma xícara de café quente, por favor.
native_language_example: I want a cup of hot coffee, please.

meaning: 'in bed' or 'bed-related' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Used in two main ways: 1) as part of compounds meaning 'bed linen' or 'bedclothes' (roupas de cama = bed sheets/linen) — here it's descriptive/nominal. 2) as an idiom meaning 'confined to bed' or 'in bed because of illness' (estar de cama = to be bedridden/to be in bed). Context tells you which meaning applies. Commonly used with estar/ficar/andar/continuar for the bedridden sense.
target_language_example: Depois da gripe, ela ficou uma semana de cama.
native_language_example: After the flu, she stayed in bed for a week.

meaning: 'suddenly/face-to-face' or an idiomatic marker meaning 'immediately' / 'plainly' depending on context.
additional_notes: Several uses: 1) 'dar de cara com' = to run into, meet unexpectedly (face-to-face). 2) 'de cara' alone can mean 'immediately' or 'right away' (e.g., 'não de cara' = not right away). 3) In informal/emotional contexts it can describe facial expression: 'de cara amarrada' = with a sour/angry face. Also appears in slang insults ('cortar de cara') meaning to dismiss or cut someone off. Common in spoken, informal Portuguese.
target_language_example: Ontem dei de cara com a minha professora no supermercado.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ran into my teacher at the supermarket.

meaning: literally 'of meat for the' — used to say 'meat for the...' (e.g., meat given to or meant for someone/something).
additional_notes: This is a sequence of words, not a fixed idiom. It combines 'de carne' (of meat) with 'para o' (for the + masculine noun). The masculine article 'o' will agree with a masculine noun that follows (e.g., 'o cachorro' — the dog). In many examples the noun appears after 'o' (e.g., 'para o cachorro'). For a feminine noun use 'para a' instead. Context determines translation: it can mean 'give meat to the...' or describe something 'meat for dinner' depending on sentence structure.
target_language_example: Vou comprar um pedaço de carne para o jantar.
native_language_example: I'm going to buy a piece of meat for dinner.

meaning: in a way; in some respects; kind of.
additional_notes: Used to soften or qualify a statement — indicates that what follows is true to some extent or from a certain perspective. Can be placed at the start, middle, or end of a sentence. Similar to English 'in a way', 'to some extent', or 'in a sense.'
target_language_example: De certa forma, aprendi mais com os erros do que com os sucessos.
native_language_example: In a way, I learned more from mistakes than from successes.

meaning: certainly; for sure; without doubt.
additional_notes: Used to express certainty or to emphasize that something is sure. Common in European and Brazilian Portuguese in informal and neutral contexts. Can appear alone as a short response (e.g., “De certo.” = “Certainly/For sure.”) or inside a sentence (e.g., “Isso vai acontecer de certo.” = “That will certainly happen.”).
target_language_example: Ele vai chegar de certo.
native_language_example: He will arrive for sure.

meaning: of/for hats; related to hats (possession or association).
additional_notes: A simple prepositional phrase: 'de' + plural noun 'chapéus' means 'of hats', 'from hats', or 'about hats' depending on context. Commonly shows possession, origin, purpose, or association (e.g., 'loja de chapéus' = 'hat shop', 'uma dúzia de chapéus' = 'a dozen hats'). Word order and surrounding words determine the exact English translation.
target_language_example: Ele trabalha na loja de chapéus da esquina.
native_language_example: He works at the hat shop on the corner.

meaning: of/from Chinese; used to indicate language or origin (e.g. 'Chinese' as in 'language of Chinese').
additional_notes: Commonly appears after nouns to show relationship to China or the Chinese language. In these examples it means 'Chinese' as in 'Chinese language' (e.g., 'a teacher of Chinese' or 'lessons of Chinese'). When referring to the language, Portuguese often uses 'chinês' alone (Falo chinês) or with 'de' after another noun (aulas de chinês, professor de chinês).
target_language_example: Tenho aulas de chinês às terças.
native_language_example: I have Chinese lessons on Tuesdays.

meaning: part of an infinitive construction meaning 'to put' or 'to place' (used after words like 'de' or as part of a verb phrase).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but the root 'colocar' (to put/place) with the particle 'de' and the infinitive form (often written with an accent when followed by a pronoun: colocá‑lo, colocá‑la, colocá‑las). Appears in constructions like 'de colocá-las' (of putting them) or imperative/infinitive with clitic pronouns attached (colocá-lo = to put it). In written Portuguese the accent marks the stressed vowel when a pronoun is attached to the infinitive.
target_language_example: Antes de colocá‑lo no armário, lave bem.
native_language_example: Before putting it in the cabinet, wash it well.

meaning: 'of command' or 'command (as an attributive phrase)'.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to indicate that the noun is related to command, control, or leadership (e.g., sala de comando = command room, posto de comando = command post). Common in military, naval, or control-room contexts. It functions like English 'of command' or simply 'command' as an adjective.
target_language_example: Ele retornou ao seu posto de comando.
native_language_example: He returned to his command post.

meaning: of committing / to commit (used after verbs expressing fear, avoidance, completion, etc.)
additional_notes: This is the preposition 'de' + infinitive 'cometer' (to commit). It appears after verbs or expressions (e.g., medo de, livre de, acabar de) to mean 'to commit' or 'of committing'. Context determines translation: after 'medo de' = 'afraid of committing'; after 'acabar de' = 'have just committed'.
target_language_example: Tenho medo de cometer o mesmo erro de novo.
native_language_example: I'm afraid of committing the same mistake again.

meaning: 'to buy a' (phrase combining a preposition/infinitive + indefinite article)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed expression but a sequence: 'de' often appears after verbs or expressions that require it (e.g., 'gostar de', 'acabar de', 'dar conta de', 'ter condições de') followed by the verb 'comprar' (to buy) and the indefinite article 'um/uma' (a). Literal order in English is 'to buy a'. Choose 'um' for masculine nouns (um carro, um sofá, um cachorro) and 'uma' for feminine nouns.
target_language_example: Ela precisa de comprar um vestido para a festa.
native_language_example: She needs to buy a dress for the party.

meaning: 'of tales' or 'related to (fairy) tales'.
additional_notes: Used to describe something connected to stories or tales (often 'contos de fadas' = 'fairy tales'). Appears after a noun to form phrases like 'coisas de contos de fadas' (things of fairy tales) or to indicate origin/relationship ('criaturas de contos de fadas' = creatures from fairy tales). Not a fixed idiom on its own—usually part of a larger phrase.
target_language_example: Ela contou histórias de contos de fadas para as crianças.
native_language_example: She told fairy-tale stories to the children.

meaning: 'by heart' (from memory); or 'of [a] color' depending on context.
additional_notes: Most commonly used in the phrase 'aprender/decorar de cor' meaning to learn something from memory (learn by heart). Alone, 'de cor' can also be part of a phrase meaning 'of color' when describing origin/appearance (e.g., 'filhos de cor' or 'garoto de cor'), though that latter use can be archaic or carry racial connotations in some contexts. Pay attention to context: in studying/learning contexts it means memorized; in descriptive contexts it relates to color/ethnicity.
target_language_example: Ela sabe o poema de cor.
native_language_example: She knows the poem by heart.

meaning: relating to mail or the postal service (of mail).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to indicate connection with mail/postal items or services. Common in phrases like 'caixas de correio' (mailboxes), 'pilha de correio' (pile of mail), or 'posto de correio' (post office). Not a standalone phrase — usually part of a noun phrase.
target_language_example: Encontrei uma caixa de correio cheia de cartas.
native_language_example: I found a mailbox full of letters.

meaning: 'as usual' or 'customarily' (refers to what normally happens)
additional_notes: Used to compare current behavior or events to what normally happens. Often appears in phrases like 'mais cedo do que de costume' (earlier than usual) or 'do que de costume' (than usual). Can be placed after verbs or time expressions.
target_language_example: Hoje eu acordei mais tarde do que de costume.
native_language_example: Today I woke up later than usual.

meaning: to cook for (someone).
additional_notes: Used to indicate cooking on behalf of or as a favor to someone — the person who benefits is introduced by 'para' (for). Common in sentences like 'cozinhar para a família' (to cook for the family). Verb 'cozinhar' is often conjugated; 'para' stays before the person/recipient.
target_language_example: Eu gosto de cozinhar para meus amigos no fim de semana.
native_language_example: I like to cook for my friends on the weekend.

meaning: of credit; credit (used to describe cards, lines, or accounting).
additional_notes: Commonly appears after a noun to indicate that something is credit-related, e.g. cartão de crédito (credit card), linha de crédito (line of credit). In Portuguese word order many noun + de + qualifier phrases work like English 'of' or the adjective form. Not a standalone phrase — usually part of a compound noun.
target_language_example: Preciso solicitar um cartão de crédito novo.
native_language_example: I need to apply for a new credit card.

meaning: 'during the day' or 'in the daytime'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate something that happens or is true in daylight/ daytime hours (as opposed to 'de noite' = at night). Common in everyday speech: can describe routines (e.g., works during the day), how something appears under daylight (e.g., filmed during the day), or contrast day vs night. Often appears with verbs like dormir, trabalhar, ser, filmar.
target_language_example: Eu estudo de dia e trabalho à noite.
native_language_example: I study during the day and work at night.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase by itself; appears when 'de' (of/from) is followed by a word starting with 'e-' (here, 'e-mail').
additional_notes: This is not a standalone expression. In the examples, 'de' is the preposition used with 'endereço de e-mail' or 'chamado de e-mail'. In Portuguese you can say 'endereço de e-mail' (email address) or 'e-mail' alone. Pay attention to word order: Portuguese uses 'endereço de e-mail' rather than 'e-mail address' (English).
target_language_example: Ela recebeu uma mensagem de e-mail importante.
native_language_example: She received an important email message.

meaning: 'wrong' or 'bad' about (used in phrases like "what's wrong with..." or "there's nothing wrong with...")
additional_notes: Used inside questions or statements to ask or state whether something is wrong or problematic. Common patterns: "O que há de errado em.../O que tem de errado em..." (What's wrong with...?), and "Nada de errado em.../Não há nada de errado em..." (There's nothing wrong with...). Followed by an infinitive verb or noun phrase.
target_language_example: O que há de errado em pedir desculpas?
native_language_example: What's wrong with apologizing?

meaning: to brush (one's) ... (used with a body part or item that follows; here: 'to brush one's teeth').
additional_notes: This construction combines the preposition 'de' (part of the infinitival complement after verbs like 'lembrar-se', 'tratar de', 'gostar de', etc.) + the verb 'escovar' (to brush) + the definite article 'os' used with a masculine plural noun (e.g. 'dentes'). In the examples, the full phrase is 'escovar os dentes' = 'brush the teeth' → idiomatically 'brush one's teeth'. Common verbs that take 'de' before an infinitive include: 'lembrar de', 'tratar de', 'gostar de', 'esquecer de'.
target_language_example: Não se esqueça de escovar os dentes antes de dormir.
native_language_example: Don't forget to brush your teeth before sleeping.

meaning: of the living
additional_notes: This phrase appears as part of the compound noun 'sala de estar' meaning 'living room'. 'de estar' on its own is not a standalone phrase in English but functions as 'for being' or 'for sitting/being' in literal Portuguese — however in fixed expressions like 'sala de estar' it contributes to the meaning 'living' (room). Use it mainly within that set phrase rather than alone.
target_language_example: Quero que Tom limpe a sala de estar.
native_language_example: I want Tom to clean the living room.

meaning: 'of ghosts' or 'about ghosts' (used after verbs or nouns to indicate relation to ghosts)
additional_notes: A prepositional phrase made of 'de' + 'fantasmas' (plural). Can mean 'of ghosts' (possession/existence) or 'about ghosts' (talking/concerning). Common after verbs like 'acreditar em/na existência de' (believe in the existence of) and nouns like 'medo de' (fear of). Use context to choose the best English translation.
target_language_example: Ele falou de fantasmas durante a reunião.
native_language_example: He talked about ghosts during the meeting.

meaning: 'indeed', 'in fact' or 'actually' (used to confirm or emphasize a statement).
additional_notes: Use to confirm or emphasize what was just said, similar to English 'indeed' or 'in fact'. Can appear at the start of a sentence (as a discourse marker) or after a comment to reinforce it. Not to be confused with 'de fato' meaning 'of fact' literally — here it's idiomatic. Formality: neutral — fine in spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: De fato, ele esqueceu o encontro.
native_language_example: In fact, he forgot the meeting.

meaning: of a slot, slotted; used to describe something that has or fits into a slit/slot (literal) — often seen in compound labels like 'chave de fenda' (screwdriver).
additional_notes: Alone, 'de fenda' is not a standalone phrase; it's typically part of a compound noun (e.g., 'chave de fenda' = screwdriver). 'Fenda' means crack, slit, fissure or slot. 'De' shows possession or composition ('of' or 'with'). Use it when talking about objects that involve a slit/slot or a slotted/flat shape.
target_language_example: Preciso comprar uma chave de fenda para apertar os parafusos.
native_language_example: I need to buy a screwdriver to tighten the screws.

meaning: '(type) movies' or 'movies of (a certain genre)'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone likes, dislikes or is afraid of a genre of film. Structure: verb + de + filmes + de + [genre]. In English this is usually rendered as 'movies of/ about' or simply '... movies' (e.g., 'terror movies' = 'filmes de terror'). The first 'de' often follows verbs like gostar de, ter medo de, gostar, gostar de, etc.
target_language_example: Eu não gosto de filmes de comédia.
native_language_example: I don't like comedy movies.

meaning: 'by no means' / 'in no way' / 'not at all'.
additional_notes: Used to strongly negate a statement. It emphasizes impossibility or complete absence. It often appears after 'não' (not) or at sentence start; in English it corresponds to strong negatives like 'by no means' or 'absolutely not.' Formal register.
target_language_example: Isso não é de forma alguma aceitável.
native_language_example: This is by no means acceptable.

meaning: 'for free' or 'free of charge'.
additional_notes: Used to say something is given without payment. Common in spoken and written Portuguese. Can modify nouns or follow demonstratives (e.g., 'Esse aqui é de graça'). Not to be confused with 'com graça' (with grace/humor).
target_language_example: Posso levar? É de graça?
native_language_example: Can I take it? Is it free?

meaning: from now on; from today onward
additional_notes: Used to indicate a new rule, habit, or situation that starts now and continues into the future. Common in both formal and informal contexts; often placed at the beginning of a sentence but can appear elsewhere for emphasis.
target_language_example: De hoje em diante, vou estudar uma hora por dia.
native_language_example: From now on, I will study one hour a day.

meaning: 'of honor' / 'honorary' (used to indicate respect, prestige, or a formal pledge)
additional_notes: Used after a noun to show that something relates to honor, respect, prestige, or an oath. Common contexts: 'código de honra' (honor code), 'palavra de honra' (a solemn promise), 'lugar de honra' (place of honor), 'guarda de honra' (honor guard). Can be literal ('of honor') or translated as 'honorary' or 'honor guard' depending on context.
target_language_example: Ele recebeu um posto de honra na cerimónia.
native_language_example: He received a place of honor at the ceremony.

meaning: 'of age' / 'years old' (used after a number to express someone's age).
additional_notes: Placed after a number (anos) to indicate age: X anos de idade = X years old. Common in both formal and informal contexts; often omitted in casual speech (e.g., Tenho 20 anos). Can also follow other time words (e.g., 'idade' emphasizes the age).
target_language_example: Ela tem vinte e cinco anos de idade.
native_language_example: She is twenty-five years old.

meaning: a phrase used to introduce going to a specific place or destination (literally 'to go to the').
additional_notes: Commonly appears before a noun indicating a place (o/a + place): de ir para o parque, de ir para o exterior, de ir para o ginásio. It often follows verbs or nouns that express intention, decision, desire, or a prior action (e.g., 'decisão de ir para o...', 'antes de ir para o...'). Choose the correct article (o/a/os/as) to match the gender and number of the place word.
target_language_example: Ela falou sobre a ideia de ir para o Brasil no verão.
native_language_example: She talked about the idea of going to Brazil in the summer.

meaning: in a way / in such a manner; often used in expressions like 'de jeito nenhum' (no way) or 'de jeitos' (somehow).
additional_notes: Alone, 'de jeito' is a fragment meaning 'in a manner' or 'in a way' and usually appears in combinations: e.g. 'de jeito nenhum' = 'no way/absolutely not'; 'de algum jeito' = 'somehow'. It is informal-to-neutral and common in spoken Portuguese. Not usually used alone without another word to complete the phrase.
target_language_example: Não consigo resolver isso de jeito nenhum.
native_language_example: I can't solve this no way / I can't solve this at all.

meaning: 'no way' / 'not at all' (strong negative)
additional_notes: A colloquial emphatic negation used to refuse, deny, or reject something strongly. It often appears alone as a short reply ('De jeito nenhum.') or after/within a sentence to stress impossibility or unwillingness. Can be impolite when combined with strong language (e.g., 'porra').
target_language_example: De jeito nenhum vou aceitar essa proposta.
native_language_example: No way am I going to accept that offer.

meaning: 'of reading' / 'reading' (used to describe something related to reading)
additional_notes: Commonly used to form noun phrases that describe rooms, activities, lists, or skills related to reading (e.g., sala de leitura = reading room; lista de leitura = reading list; habilidades de leitura = reading skills). It is compositional and literal: de = of/from, leitura = reading. Use to show a relationship to the act or subject of reading.
target_language_example: Ela passava horas na sala de leitura da biblioteca.
native_language_example: She spent hours in the library's reading room.

meaning: of reading this / to finish reading this (part of a verb phrase meaning 'to finish reading this')
additional_notes: This sequence appears as part of the verb phrase 'terminar de ler este...', meaning 'to finish reading this...'. 'Terminar de + infinitive' is the common structure for 'to finish (doing) something' in Portuguese. 'Este' is a demonstrative meaning 'this' (near the speaker) and agrees in gender with a masculine noun like 'livro' (this book).
target_language_example: Ainda preciso terminar de ler este livro amanhã.
native_language_example: I still need to finish reading this book tomorrow.

meaning: by far the (used to add strong emphasis before a superlative or comparative phrase)
additional_notes: Placed before a superlative or comparative phrase to emphasize that something stands out clearly (equivalent to English 'by far'). Commonly appears as 'de longe o + [superlative/comparative phrase]' — e.g., 'de longe o melhor', 'de longe o mais sábio'. Neutral tone; used in both spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: Ele é de longe o mais sábio dos três.
native_language_example: He is by far the wisest of the three.

meaning: in mourning; wearing/observing mourning after a death.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that a person, group, or place is grieving for someone who died. Can refer to emotional state (they are in mourning) or to wearing black or mourning clothes (vestir roupas de luto). Common in formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Toda a família está de luto pela avó.
native_language_example: The whole family is in mourning for their grandmother.

meaning: 'of monkey' or 'monkey's', used in descriptions or as part of expressions referring to a monkey or calling someone a monkey.
additional_notes: Literally means 'of monkey' or 'monkey's'. In the example sentences it appears in phrases where someone is called a 'macaco' (monkey) or describes being 'in the body of a monkey'. Calling someone 'macaco' can be offensive depending on context (insult or racist). 'De macaco' is compositional — you can usually understand it from the component words. Use carefully in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Ele tem o rosto de macaco na fantasia.
native_language_example: He has a monkey face on the costume.

meaning: an adult; of legal age (18+).
additional_notes: Used to describe a person who is legally an adult. Common in phrases like 'ser de maior' (to be an adult) or 'maior de idade'. Often appears in formal/legal contexts (ID checks, forms) but also in everyday speech. Opposite: 'de menor' (a minor).
target_language_example: Ele já é de maior, pode votar nas eleições.
native_language_example: He is already an adult; he can vote in the elections.

meaning: ‘more people like’ — used to say that more people with the same qualities/behavior are needed.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in phrases like 'Precisamos de mais pessoas como você' (We need more people like you). Followed by a pronoun or name (você, ele, o Tom). Used to praise someone's qualities and suggest others with those qualities are desirable. Word order can vary: 'Precisamos de mais pessoas como o Tom' or 'Precisamos de mais pessoas como Tom.'
target_language_example: Gostei do trabalho dela — precisávamos de mais pessoas como ela.
native_language_example: I liked her work — we needed more people like her.

meaning: an additional one; one more; a bit more (of something)
additional_notes: Used to request or offer an extra item or a little more of something. Often appears in phrases like 'de mais um pouco' or 'de mais um copo' when specifying the thing. Frequently used with verbs like 'gostar' or 'querer' (e.g., 'Gostaria de mais um?') or with quantities (e.g., 'de mais um pouco de água'). Politeness is achieved by adding 'gostaria de', 'queria', or 'por favor'.
target_language_example: Eu gostaria de mais um pouco de água, por favor.
native_language_example: I would like one more little bit of water, please.

meaning: 'upset', 'angry', or 'in a bad mood' (used with estar: estar de mal).
additional_notes: Commonly used in the expression estar de mal (com alguém) to mean 'to be angry with someone' or 'to be in a bad mood'. Literal components: 'de' (of) + 'mal' (bad), but the phrase functions idiomatically with the verb estar. Example: Estou de mal com ele = I'm upset/angry with him. Not used alone without a verb in normal speech.
target_language_example: Ela está de mal comigo desde ontem.
native_language_example: She has been upset with me since yesterday.

meaning: not at all / by no means
additional_notes: Used to strongly deny or reject something. Functions like English 'not at all' or 'absolutely not'. Often appears alone as an exclamation or after 'não' (e.g., 'Não, de maneira alguma.'). Formal but common in spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: De maneira alguma vou concordar com isso.
native_language_example: I will not agree with that under any circumstances.

meaning: 'of memory' / 'related to memory' (used to talk about memory or memory problems)
additional_notes: Used after nouns to indicate something concerning memory (e.g. 'problemas de memória' = memory problems). Also appears in fixed expressions like 'perda de memória' (memory loss). Not used to mean 'by heart' — that phrase is 'de cor' or 'de memória' can sometimes mean 'from memory' (i.e. recalling without notes) depending on context; here examples show the clinical/possessive sense.
target_language_example: Ela tem dificuldade de memória desde o acidente.
native_language_example: She has memory difficulties since the accident.

meaning: 'fake' or 'not real' (used to describe something that is pretend or imitation).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say that the thing is fake, pretend, or for show (e.g., 'um anel de mentira' = a fake ring). Can also describe playful/pretend situations (e.g., 'briga de mentira' = mock fight). Tone is neutral; context determines if it's criticism (fake) or playful (pretend).
target_language_example: Ela comprou uma bolsa de mentira para usar no desfile.
native_language_example: She bought a fake bag to wear in the parade.

meaning: called a liar / of (being) a liar
additional_notes: This phrase follows verbs like chamar (to call) or expressions about being labeled. 'Chamar alguém de mentiroso' = 'to call someone a liar.' The preposition 'de' links the verb to the label. It can be used in questions, negatives, and statements. Not idiomatic beyond literal accusation; in sentence 5 it appears in a playful expression ('nariz de mentiroso' = 'liar's nose').
target_language_example: Ela me chamou de mentiroso na frente de todo mundo.
native_language_example: She called me a liar in front of everyone.

meaning: of/shitty; used to describe something as bad, worthless, or contemptible.
additional_notes: Informal and vulgar. Used after a noun to express strong dislike, contempt, or poor quality (literally “of shit”). Can modify people, things, situations, decisions, etc. Avoid in polite/formal contexts; used in casual speech, frustration, or insults.
target_language_example: Ele trabalha numa empresa de merda.
native_language_example: He works at a shitty company.

meaning: not at all; by no means; in no way.
additional_notes: A negative phrase used to strongly deny or reject something. It usually appears after verbs or at the start of an exclamation. Equivalent to English 'not at all' or 'by no means.' Can be replaced by 'de jeito nenhum' or 'de maneira nenhuma' in informal contexts.
target_language_example: Eu não estou de modo algum interessado nesse projeto.
native_language_example: I am not at all interested in that project.

meaning: 1) soaking/in soaking liquid (literal); 2) laid up/recovering and resting because of illness or injury (idiomatic).
additional_notes: Used literally when something is submerged in liquid (e.g., clothes or food). Used idiomatically in Brazilian Portuguese to say someone is staying home and resting because they're sick or injured (similar to 'laid up' or 'on bed rest'). Context and verb tense show which meaning applies. Not informal slang — common everyday phrase.
target_language_example: Ele está de molho por causa de uma torção no pé.
native_language_example: He's laid up/recovering because of a sprained ankle.

meaning: 'holding hands' (literally 'of hands held') — used to say people are physically holding hands or metaphorically closely connected.
additional_notes: Common phrase for two or more people walking or standing while holding hands. Also used figuratively to express close cooperation or a close relationship (e.g., ideas, feelings, or concepts going 'hand in hand'). Appears after verb constructions (estão de mãos dadas, caminhar de mãos dadas, ver alguém de mãos dadas).
target_language_example: Eles caminharam de mãos dadas pela praia.
native_language_example: They walked hand in hand along the beach.

meaning: empty-handed; with nothing (brought or gained).
additional_notes: Used to say someone returns or leaves without anything — no purchase, gift, or success. Common in contexts like shopping, visiting, or trying to obtain something. Often follows verbs like chegar (to arrive), voltar/retornar (to return), sair (to leave).
target_language_example: Não vou voltar de mãos vazias depois dessa viagem.
native_language_example: I won't return empty-handed after this trip.

meaning: you're welcome
additional_notes: Commonly used as a polite response to 'obrigado/obrigada' meaning 'you're welcome'. In other contexts 'de nada' can appear in negative structures to mean 'of nothing' or 'not ... anything' (e.g., 'culpado de nada' = 'guilty of nothing', 'suspeitar de nada' = 'suspect nothing'). Pay attention to context: as a standalone reply it means 'you're welcome'; inside a sentence it expresses absence ('nothing').
target_language_example: — Obrigada pela ajuda. — De nada.
native_language_example: — Thanks for the help. — You're welcome.

meaning: 'to swim in' (part of a verb phrase meaning 'to like to swim in' when combined with gostar de)
additional_notes: This sequence appears when using gostar de + infinitive (gostar de nadar = to like to swim) followed by a definite article + noun (no = em + o = in the [masculine] place). 'No' contracts 'em o' and is used before masculine singular nouns (verão is masculine but typically uses 'no verão' to mean 'in summer'; mar and oceano are masculine so 'no mar', 'no oceano'). The full structure: [subject] gostar de nadar no + [place].
target_language_example: Ela gosta de nadar no lago.
native_language_example: She likes to swim in the lake.

meaning: from birth; congenital (since birth).
additional_notes: Used to say that a trait, condition or characteristic has been present since birth (not acquired later). Common with medical or personal descriptions: e.g., 'cego de nascença' = blind from birth. Usually follows the adjective or noun it modifies (e.g., 'cego de nascença').
target_language_example: Ela é surda de nascença.
native_language_example: She is deaf from birth.

meaning: at night; during the night.
additional_notes: Used to indicate something happens in the nighttime hours. Often interchangeable with "à noite" in many contexts; "de noite" commonly appears in spoken Portuguese and in expressions like "trabalho de noite" (I work nights). When referring to a specific night (e.g., last night), Portuguese often uses "ontem à noite" rather than "ontem de noite", though "ontem de noite" can be heard informally.
target_language_example: Eu costumo ler de noite antes de dormir.
native_language_example: I usually read at night before sleeping.

meaning: again
additional_notes: A very common way to say that something happens one more time. In some contexts it can suggest starting over or doing something from the beginning, but for beginners it is usually best understood as "again."
target_language_example: Vou tentar de novo amanhã.
native_language_example: I'll try again tomorrow.

meaning: watching; keeping an eye on; paying attention to
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is being observed or monitored. Common in phrases like 'estar de olho' (to be keeping an eye on) or 'ficar de olho' (to stay alert/watch out). Can imply cautious attention, suspicion, or interest (e.g., watching a person, an object, or a situation).
target_language_example: Estou de olho naquele pacote na mesa.
native_language_example: I'm keeping an eye on that package on the table.

meaning: 'of gold' or 'made of/containing gold'.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to indicate material (made of gold), possession (gold items), or that something is golden/precious. Can be literal (moedas de ouro = gold coins; cruz de ouro = gold cross) or figurative (selo de ouro could mean a 'gold seal'—a valuable or high-quality mark).
target_language_example: Ela usa um anel de ouro todos os dias.
native_language_example: She wears a gold ring every day.

meaning: 'to pay the' (part of a verb phrase meaning to pay something specific)
additional_notes: This is the preposition 'de' + infinitive 'pagar' + definite article 'a' used before a feminine noun (e.g., 'a conta', 'a casa'). In European Portuguese, 'ter de' or 'ter que' and 'alguém tem de' express obligation ('have to'). 'Esqueci de pagar a...' means 'I forgot to pay the...'. The phrase itself is not idiomatic; it appears as part of larger structures (e.g., 'esqueci de pagar a conta', 'tenho de pagar a casa').
target_language_example: Preciso de pagar a multa amanhã.
native_language_example: I need to pay the fine tomorrow.

meaning: for going for a walk; for strolling; to go out for a walk
additional_notes: Commonly appears after verbs expressing habits, preferences or purposes (e.g., gostar de, ter o costume de). 'Passear' means to walk/stroll or take something/someone out (a dog, a person) for leisure. 'De passear' indicates the activity (to go for a walk) rather than a location. Use with subjects: passear sozinho, passear com alguém, passear com o cachorro.
target_language_example: Ela saiu de casa de passear com o cachorro.
native_language_example: She left the house to go for a walk with the dog.

meaning: of loss / loss of (used to indicate something that is being lost)
additional_notes: Commonly appears after verbs like sofrer (sofrer de perda de ...) or nouns to describe types of loss (perda de memória, perda de cabelo, risco de perda). It links the noun 'perda' (loss) to what is lost. Use 'perda de X' to say 'loss of X.'
target_language_example: Ela sofre de perda de audição desde jovem.
native_language_example: She has been suffering from hearing loss since she was young.

meaning: 'closely' or 'from up close' (near to someone/something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about physical closeness or inspecting something closely. Can be used as an adverbial phrase: olhar de perto = to look closely / ver de perto = to see up close. In commands, it can mean 'come closer' or 'away from' depending on context (e.g., tirar alguém de perto de mim = remove someone away from me).
target_language_example: Quero ver o quadro de perto.
native_language_example: I want to see the painting up close.

meaning: of piano / piano lessons + when (used to say someone took piano lessons at a certain time in the past)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a sequence seen in sentences like "aulas de piano quando..." — literally 'piano lessons when...'. Use to say someone began or took piano lessons at a particular age or period (e.g. 'quando tinha seis anos', 'quando era menino'). Word order: 'aulas de piano quando...' or 'fez aulas de piano quando...'.
target_language_example: Ela fez aulas de piano quando era criança.
native_language_example: She took piano lessons when she was a child.

meaning: to be able to speak / to be able to talk (about having the ability to speak).
additional_notes: Used after verbs or expressions of desire/hopes (e.g., gostar de, a fim de) to express the ability to speak a language or to talk to someone. Literally 'of being able to speak.' Common in phrases like 'gostar de poder falar' (would like to be able to speak) or 'a fim de poder falar' (in order to be able to speak).
target_language_example: Eu gostaria de poder falar espanhol fluentemente.
native_language_example: I would like to be able to speak Spanish fluently.

meaning: 'cutting-edge' or 'high-quality/point' depending on context.
additional_notes: Has two common senses: (1) as part of 'tecnologia de ponta' or 'instrumentos de ponta' meaning 'cutting-edge, state-of-the-art, top-quality'; (2) when describing pens or tips ('ponta fina', 'caneta de ponta'), it relates to the physical tip/point (fine-point). Also appears in fixed expression 'de ponta a ponta' meaning 'from end to end' or 'throughout'. Context determines the right translation.
target_language_example: A empresa investe em tecnologia de ponta.
native_language_example: The company invests in cutting-edge technology.

meaning: upside down; in a state of disorder
additional_notes: Used to say something is physically upside down (turned over) or figuratively in disarray/chaos. Common with objects (mesa, livro) and situations (está tudo de ponta-cabeça). Often appears after estar or verbs of turning (virar).
target_language_example: O carrinho está de ponta-cabeça depois do acidente.
native_language_example: The stroller is upside down after the accident.

meaning: upside down; in disorder or turned over
additional_notes: Used to describe something physically flipped over (e.g., a container, a room) or a situation in disorder/confusion. More commonly written as 'de ponta-cabeça' or 'de cabeça para baixo' in Brazilian Portuguese. Can be used literally (the box is upside down) or figuratively (plans are turned upside down).
target_language_example: Depois do vento, a sala ficou de ponta cabeça.
native_language_example: After the wind, the room was upside down.

meaning: not talkative; speaks little; succinct.
additional_notes: Used to describe a person who speaks rarely or briefly. Often implies someone reserved, concise, or who prefers actions over words. Can describe speech style (economical with words) rather than rudeness. Common in phrases like 'um homem de poucas palavras' (a man of few words).
target_language_example: Ela é de poucas palavras, mas muito confiável.
native_language_example: She is a woman of few words, but very reliable.

meaning: 'preferably' or 'if possible'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a preference or desired option. Can soften requests or suggest the best choice among options. Often placed at the start of a sentence (— de preferência, ...) or before the preferred item.
target_language_example: Traga água, de preferência sem gás.
native_language_example: Bring water, preferably without gas (still water).

meaning: top-quality; first-rate; immediately (in some contexts).
additional_notes: Commonly used to describe something excellent or top-tier (e.g., 'serviço de primeira' = first-rate service; 'madeira de primeira' = top-quality wood). In informal contexts, when used with verbs (e.g., 'não acreditou no Tom de primeira'), it can mean 'right away' or 'at first/initially' (often in negative: 'didn't believe Tom right away'). Context determines whether it refers to quality or immediacy.
target_language_example: O restaurante é de primeira.
native_language_example: The restaurant is first-rate.

meaning: 'on standby' or 'ready/standing by'.
additional_notes: Used to say that people or units should be ready and available to act if needed. Common in military, police, emergency, or work contexts. Can be used with verbs like ficar, estar, colocar (to put someone on standby).
target_language_example: Fiquem de prontidão até novas ordens.
native_language_example: Remain on standby until further orders.

meaning: on purpose; purposely; intentionally.
additional_notes: Used to say that an action was done intentionally (not by accident). Common in spoken and written Portuguese. Can appear alone (e.g., "Foi de propósito") or after the verb/phrase. Synonyms: "intencionalmente", "de maneira intencional".
target_language_example: Ele bateu na porta de propósito para chamar atenção.
native_language_example: He knocked on the door on purpose to get attention.

meaning: related to the lung; pulmonary
additional_notes: Used after a noun to indicate something pertains to the lungs (medical context) or describes a lung-related condition (e.g., 'doença de pulmão' = lung disease). Common in compound phrases: 'câncer de pulmão' (lung cancer), 'problema de pulmão' (lung problem). Formal/neutral register.
target_language_example: O médico diagnosticou câncer de pulmão.
native_language_example: The doctor diagnosed lung cancer.

meaning: standing; upright (physically) or 'planned/ongoing' (when referring to events).
additional_notes: Most commonly used to mean 'standing' (as in people standing up). Can describe posture (estar de pé = to be standing). In some contexts (especially with events or plans) it can mean 'in place', 'set up', or 'still happening' (e.g., 'o almoço está de pé?' = 'is lunch still on?'). Use estar de pé for current states; can appear after nouns (almoço de pé — less common) or after verbs/adjectives.
target_language_example: Fiquem de pé enquanto cantamos o hino.
native_language_example: Stand up while we sing the anthem.

meaning: of good quality; high-quality.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe that something has good quality or is well made. Can describe products, materials, services, or abstract things (e.g., 'tempo de qualidade' = meaningful/good-quality time). Not informal. Common collocation: 'produto de qualidade', 'tempo de qualidade'.
target_language_example: Comprei uma jaqueta de qualidade que vai durar anos.
native_language_example: I bought a high-quality jacket that will last for years.

meaning: 'anyway' / 'in any case' / 'anyhow' — used to return to a point or to show resignation.
additional_notes: Common discourse connector. Use at the start of a sentence to change topic, emphasize that something doesn't change the conclusion, or to downplay importance. Tone can be neutral or dismissive depending on context. Synonyms: 'de qualquer jeito', 'de qualquer modo'.
target_language_example: De qualquer forma, não podemos voltar atrás agora.
native_language_example: Anyway, we can't go back now.

meaning: anyway / in any case / no matter what / carelessly (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used in several senses: (1) 'anyway' or 'in any case' to indicate an action will happen regardless of circumstances (examples 1–3); (2) 'no matter how' or 'by any means' when implying determination (example 2); (3) 'carelessly' or 'sloppily' to describe appearance or manner (example 4). Context and tone determine which meaning applies. Common in spoken Portuguese.
target_language_example: Vou terminar o projeto de qualquer jeito.
native_language_example: I'll finish the project anyway / no matter what.

meaning: 'anyway' / 'in any case' / 'regardless'.
additional_notes: Used to say that something will happen despite circumstances, to change the topic, or to downplay details. Can mean 'anyway', 'in any case', 'regardless', or (less commonly) 'in any way' depending on context. Common in spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: Não importa o que digam — eu vou de qualquer maneira.
native_language_example: It doesn't matter what they say — I'll go anyway.

meaning: anyway; in any case; no matter what.
additional_notes: Used to change the subject, return to a main point, or indicate that something is true regardless of other factors. Can appear at the start of a sentence followed by a comma. Similar to 'de qualquer forma' or 'a qualquer custo' (not exact).
target_language_example: De qualquer modo, vou terminar o trabalho hoje.
native_language_example: Anyway, I'll finish the work today.

meaning: 'of four' / 'four (something)' — indicates quantity or measurement: four of something, four (units), or four‑fold.
additional_notes: Used to indicate number or measure (four months, four siblings, four hours). Also appears in fixed expressions: 'de quatro' can describe position (e.g. 'ficar de quatro' = get on all fours). Context decides whether it means 'of four' (part of a quantity), 'four' as an option ('de quatro ou cinco' = about four or five), or a positional phrase. Not formal or slang—neutral. Translate according to context.
target_language_example: Ela tem dois filhos e está grávida de quatro meses.
native_language_example: She has two children and is four months pregnant.

meaning: 'how' or 'in what way/manner'.
additional_notes: Used to ask about the manner, method, or way something should be done. Interchangeable with 'de que modo' or 'como' in many contexts; slightly more formal than 'como'. Can be followed by verbs or clauses.
target_language_example: De que forma você quer que eu organize os arquivos?
native_language_example: In what way do you want me to organize the files?

meaning: 'how' or 'in what way / manner'.
additional_notes: Used to ask about the manner, method, or way something is done. Often interchangeable with 'como' but slightly more informal and conversational. Common in questions like 'De que jeito devo pedir?' (How should I ask?) or when asking preferences (e.g., how someone wants something prepared).
target_language_example: De que jeito você prefere o café?
native_language_example: How do you prefer your coffee?

meaning: 'how' or 'in what way/manner'.
additional_notes: Used to ask about the manner, method, or way something is done. Can be equivalent to 'como' but slightly more formal or specific. Often appears in questions; can be followed by a verb or subject. Can be answered with a description of steps, reasons, or characteristics.
target_language_example: De que maneira você resolveu o problema?
native_language_example: In what way/how did you solve the problem?

meaning: what (about)? / what (kind of)? — asks about the thing, reason or category being referred to
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask 'about what', 'what for', 'what kind', or 'what are you talking about'. Common in spoken Portuguese. Tone and context determine exact sense: e.g. 'Medo de quê?' = 'Afraid of what?' ; 'Piloto de quê?' = 'What kind of pilot?' or 'pilot of what?'. Often appears after verbs or nouns: 'falando de quê?', 'cheiro de quê?'.
target_language_example: Você está reclamando de quê?
native_language_example: What are you complaining about?

meaning: suddenly
additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens quickly and unexpectedly. Commonly placed at the start, middle (set off by commas), or end of a sentence. Tone can be neutral or dramatic depending on context.
target_language_example: De repente começou a chover forte.
native_language_example: Suddenly it started to rain hard.

meaning: besides; otherwise; as for the rest; moreover (used to add a comment or move on).
additional_notes: Common discourse connector. Used at the start of a sentence or clause to introduce an additional remark, a contrasting point, or to indicate 'apart from that' / 'in any case'. Tone is neutral and suitable for formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: De resto, não tenho mais nada a dizer.
native_language_example: Besides that, I have nothing more to say.

meaning: on wheels; wheeled (made to roll on wheels)
additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something that has wheels or is movable on wheels (e.g., cadeira de rodas = wheelchair, mala de rodas = suitcase with wheels). Common in compound nouns. Not a complete phrase by itself — usually follows the item it describes.
target_language_example: Comprei uma mala de rodas para a viagem.
native_language_example: I bought a suitcase with wheels for the trip.

meaning: used to describe a habit of biting (usually nails): 'to bite' as part of 'o hábito de roer'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the fixed phrase 'o hábito de roer (as unhas)' or 'o mau hábito de roer'. 'Roer' alone means 'to gnaw' or 'to nibble'; when used with 'hábito' or 'costume' it refers to a repetitive habit like nail-biting. Use reflexive 'se livrar do hábito de roer' to say 'get rid of the habit of biting.'
target_language_example: Ele quer parar com o hábito de roer as unhas.
native_language_example: He wants to stop the habit of biting his nails.

meaning: routine; routine/standard (as in usual or regular).
additional_notes: Used to describe something habitual, standard, or part of normal procedure (e.g., a routine check, a routine question, or something done regularly). Can be used as adjective or adverbial phrase: 'exame de rotina' = routine exam, 'falou de rotina' = spoke as usual/standard. Often contrasts with something exceptional ('não será uma visita de rotina' = it won't be a routine visit).
target_language_example: Eles fizeram apenas perguntas de rotina durante a reunião.
native_language_example: They only asked routine questions during the meeting.

meaning: fed up; fed up with something; tired of (something).
additional_notes: Informal idiom used to say you're annoyed, frustrated or tired of a situation or person. Common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese. Often appears with 'estar/estou' (to be) + 'de saco cheio de' + noun/verb. Stronger than 'cansado' (tired) — expresses irritation or exasperation.
target_language_example: Estou de saco cheio de esperar sempre o mesmo atraso.
native_language_example: I'm fed up with always waiting for the same delay.

meaning: relating to salary / of salary.
additional_notes: Used after a noun or phrase to indicate that something concerns or belongs to salary (e.g., 'termos de salário' = 'terms regarding salary'). Common in phrases like 'aumento de salário' (salary raise) or 'adiantamento de salário' (salary advance). It is compositional and literal: 'de' = of/about, 'salário' = salary.
target_language_example: O contrato inclui cláusulas de salário e benefícios.
native_language_example: The contract includes clauses about salary and benefits.

meaning: 'on Monday' or 'from Monday' (depends on context); often part of 'de segunda a ...' meaning 'from Monday to ...'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate the day Monday or the start of a range beginning on Monday. In 'de segunda a sábado' it means 'from Monday to Saturday'. In contexts like 'antes de segunda' it means 'before Monday' (i.e., by Monday). Can be followed by other days or by a deadline expression. Not idiomatic/slang.
target_language_example: Preciso terminar o relatório antes de segunda.
native_language_example: I need to finish the report before Monday.

meaning: second-hand; used (not brand new).
additional_notes: Used to describe items (clothes, books, furniture, etc.) that were previously owned. Common in phrases like "loja de segunda mão" (second-hand shop) or "comprar de segunda mão" (to buy used). Neutral register; can sometimes imply lower quality depending on context.
target_language_example: Comprei uma jaqueta de segunda mão e está como nova.
native_language_example: I bought a second-hand jacket and it's like new.

meaning: 'as always' or 'the usual'.
additional_notes: Used to describe something ordinary, habitual or unchanged — e.g., the usual place, the usual things, or the same as always. Common in informal and neutral contexts. Often appears after a noun (a galeria de sempre = the usual gallery) or after pronouns/phrases (o mesmo de sempre = the same as always).
target_language_example: Vou ao café de sempre antes do trabalho.
native_language_example: I go to the usual café before work.

meaning: 'of your/his/her/their room' or 'from your/his/her/their room' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Phrase combines the preposition 'de' + possessive 'seu' + noun 'quarto'. 'Seu' can mean your (formal or familiar), his, her, or their — use context to know the possessor. 'De' often marks possession ('as paredes de seu quarto' = 'the walls of your room') or origin/movement ('saiu de seu quarto' = 'left your room'). Note that in spoken Brazilian Portuguese contractions with definite articles are common (e.g. 'do seu quarto' = 'de o seu quarto'), but 'de seu quarto' is used in more formal/register-neutral contexts or when no article is required. To avoid ambiguity about the possessor, use 'dele' (his), 'dela' (hers) or specify the person: 'o quarto do Tom'.
target_language_example: As paredes de seu quarto estavam cobertas de pôsteres.
native_language_example: The walls of your/his/her/their room were covered with posters.

meaning: more than enough; extra; leftover
additional_notes: Used after a noun to indicate there is an excess or plenty of something (time, space, money, reasons, etc.). Common in everyday speech to say you have plenty or something is abundant. Can be used with quantifiers: 'muito tempo de sobra' = 'lots of spare time'.
target_language_example: Tenho comida de sobra em casa.
native_language_example: I have more than enough food at home.

meaning: from time to time; occasionally; every now and then.
additional_notes: Used to indicate something that happens irregularly but more than rarely. Can be placed after the verb or at the end of the sentence. Synonyms: 'de vez em quando', 'ocasionalmente'. Common in both spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: Eu faço exercício de tempos em tempos.
native_language_example: I exercise from time to time.

meaning: anyway; in any case; regardless
additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement that holds despite previous information or objections. Can appear at the start or end of a sentence. Equivalent to 'de qualquer modo' or 'de qualquer forma'. Common in both spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: De todo modo, vou terminar o trabalho hoje.
native_language_example: Anyway, I'll finish the work today.

meaning: at all
additional_notes: Meaning depends on context. As a negation intensifier (with não, nunca, etc.) it means 'at all' (Não gostei de todo = I didn't like it at all). As an intensifier after adjectives it can mean 'completely' (limpo de todo = completely clean). Used after nouns with definite article it can mean 'of all' or 'of every' (o livro de todo o grupo = the book of the whole group). Pay attention to word order and surrounding words to determine the exact sense.
target_language_example: Eu não entendi de todo o que ele quis dizer.
native_language_example: I didn't understand at all what he meant.

meaning: to have/receive (a) — used before types of drinks, shots, or blows (e.g., have a coffee, take a shot).
additional_notes: Commonly follows 'acabar' (acabar de tomar um = just had one) or appears in questions about willingness/fear (tomar um tiro = to get shot). 'Tomar' here means 'to take' or 'to have' (for drinks/consumption) and also 'to receive' (for blows/shots). The article 'um' agrees with a masculine noun implied or stated (um café, um tiro).
target_language_example: Ela acabou de tomar um suco antes de sair.
native_language_example: She just had a juice before leaving.

meaning: after everything we did / after all we've done
additional_notes: Used to refer back to many actions or efforts made by the speaker and others (we). Often expresses surprise, disappointment, or emphasis (e.g. 'after all we've done, and this happens'). Can appear with or without a following clause or question mark. 'Tudo que' can be replaced by 'tudo o que' in more formal speech.
target_language_example: Depois de tudo que fizemos por você, isso é o mínimo que podia fazer.
native_language_example: After everything we did for you, that's the least you could do.

de um dia para o outro

target_language_multi_word_term: de um dia para o outro
meaning: suddenly; overnight; very quickly (from one day to the next).
additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens rapidly or with little warning — often translated as "overnight" or "from one day to the next." Can describe events, changes in feelings, status, or situations. Neutral register; common in spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: A fama dela cresceu de um dia para o outro.
native_language_example: Her fame grew overnight.

meaning: a little (of), some (amount of)
additional_notes: Used to indicate a small quantity of something. Often appears as part of the phrase 'um pouco de' (a little of). Word order can change (e.g., 'um pouco de vinho' or 'de um pouco' when embedded in a larger phrase). Common with uncountable nouns and abstract needs (attention, money, wine).
target_language_example: Ela pediu de um pouco de pão para a sopa.
native_language_example: She asked for a little bread for the soup.

meaning: once and for all; immediately; all at once (depends on context).
additional_notes: Used to urge someone to do something immediately, to finish something finally, or to do several things at the same time. Tone can be impatient or emphatic: e.g. 'Decidam de uma vez!' = 'Decide already!' or 'Vamos resolver isso de uma vez' = 'Let's settle this once and for all.' Context determines whether it means 'immediately' or 'all at once.'
target_language_example: Decida de uma vez e me diga onde vamos.
native_language_example: Decide already and tell me where we're going.

meaning: once and for all; finally (permanently, decisively).
additional_notes: Used to indicate doing something decisively so it is finished permanently or to urge someone to stop delaying. Common in commands and statements expressing finality or resolution.
target_language_example: Decida-se de uma vez por todas e diga o que quer.
native_language_example: Decide once and for all and say what you want.

meaning: to use protection for the (e.g., body part) — part of the phrase 'deixar de usar proteção para os...' meaning 'to fail/neglect to use protection for the...'.
additional_notes: This fragment appears in negative imperatives and warnings: 'Não deixe(n) de usar proteção para os olhos' = 'Don't fail to use eye protection' / 'Be sure to use eye protection.' 'Deixar de' means 'to stop/neglect/omit'; in negatives with 'não deixar de' it functions as 'make sure to' or 'don't fail to'. The final word(s) indicate the body part (os olhos = the eyes). Useful in safety instructions and polite formal warnings.
target_language_example: Por favor, não deixe de usar proteção para os olhos durante a experiência.
native_language_example: Please don't fail to use eye protection during the experiment.

meaning: of values; relating to values (moral, cultural, or numerical like stock values)
additional_notes: A prepositional phrase: 'de' (of/from) + 'valores' (values). Context determines meaning: moral/cultural values (valores morais) or numeric/financial values (valores de mercado). Often appears in phrases like 'sistema de valores' (value system), 'educação de valores' (values education), or 'valores de mercado' (market values).
target_language_example: A escola trabalha na formação de valores dos alunos.
native_language_example: The school works on forming the students' values.

meaning: really
additional_notes: Used to emphasize sincerity, authenticity, or truth. Can modify nouns (um amigo de verdade = a true/genuine friend), adjectives (um herói de verdade = a real hero), or verbs/clauses (você me ama de verdade = you really love me). Tone can be neutral or emphatic depending on context.
target_language_example: Ela é minha amiga de verdade.
native_language_example: She is my real friend.

meaning: for good
additional_notes: Most commonly used as part of expressions: 'de vez' or 'de vez em quando'. Alone, 'de vez' often implies a permanent or complete change (e.g. 'de vez' = 'for good' / 'completely' or 'once and for all'). In other contexts it can appear in questions or exclamations to emphasize whether something really happened ('Mas de vez?' = 'Really?/Seriously?'). To say 'occasionally' use the full phrase 'de vez em quando'.
target_language_example: Ele parou de fumar de vez.
native_language_example: He quit smoking for good.

meaning: occasionally
additional_notes: Common adverbial phrase used to describe actions that happen infrequently or at irregular intervals. Can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence and is interchangeable with similar expressions like "às vezes" (sometimes), though "de vez em quando" often implies a bit less frequency. No change for gender or number.
target_language_example: De vez em quando eu assisto a filmes antigos.
native_language_example: Occasionally I watch old movies.

meaning: 'about you at' or 'of you in/at' — used to say someone spoke/thought about you in a specific place or event.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a sequence of words: 'de' (about/of) + 'você' (you) + a location/time introduced by 'na' (in the/at the). Common in sentences like 'Falaram bem de você na reunião' = 'They spoke well about you at the meeting.' Word order: verb + de você + na + [place/event].
target_language_example: Falaram bem de você na escola ontem.
native_language_example: They spoke well about you at school yesterday.

meaning: 'yours' (plural) + 'is' — used to say something belongs to 'you' (plural) and state that it is/feels/appears a certain way.
additional_notes: This combines the possessive phrase 'de vocês' (your/yours, plural you) with the verb 'está' (is — third person singular of estar). It's used when talking about one thing that belongs to or is associated with a group of people (you all). In many cases you can separate the parts: 'a resposta de vocês está correta' = 'your answer is correct.' For Brazilian Portuguese, 'de vocês' is common in informal and neutral contexts; in European Portuguese 'de vocês' can sound less common than 'vosso'.
target_language_example: O carro de vocês está na garagem.
native_language_example: Your car is in the garage.

meaning: back
additional_notes: Used to talk about returning to a previous place, state, or owner. Very common in phrases like estar de volta ('to be back'), trazer de volta ('to bring back'), and pegar de volta ('to get/take back').
target_language_example: Quando você estiver de volta, me avisa.
native_language_example: When you're back, let me know.

meaning: 'to vomit' (used in expressions meaning 'to feel like vomiting' or 'makes me want to vomit')
additional_notes: Often appears after verbs or expressions of feeling (e.g., 'estar com vontade de vomitar' = 'to feel like vomiting'; 'dar vontade de vomitar' = 'to make one want to vomit'). Used both for literal nausea and figuratively to express disgust toward people or things. Common in everyday/informal speech.
target_language_example: Só de ver aquele lixo me dá vontade de vomitar.
native_language_example: Just seeing that trash makes me want to vomit.

meaning: 'of/ some water for' or 'water for' — used to indicate that water is intended for someone or some place.
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'de água' (of/about water / some water) with 'para' (for / to). In these examples it marks the thing being brought or given (water) and the recipient (a person or place). Common in spoken Portuguese when asking or telling someone to get/bring water for someone. Word order: object + para + recipient.
target_language_example: Traga uma garrafa de água para mim, por favor.
native_language_example: Bring a bottle of water for me, please.

meaning: a tattletale; someone who informs on others (snitch).
additional_notes: Informal, used to describe a person who tells authority figures or outsiders about others' misdeeds or secrets. Can be negative and insulting. Often used in social, school, or group contexts (e.g., 'don't be a dedo-duro').
target_language_example: Não conte nada a ele — ele é dedo-duro.
native_language_example: Don't tell him anything — he's a tattletale.

meaning: 'I realized' or 'I became aware'.
additional_notes: Literal infinitive is 'dar conta' used reflexively here: 'dar-se conta (de/que)' = to realize, notice, become aware. Commonly appears in past tense 'me dei conta' (I realized) or other persons/tenses: 'ele se deu conta', 'percebi' is a synonym. Often followed by 'de' + noun or 'de que' + clause.
target_language_example: Quando me dei conta, já era tarde demais.
native_language_example: When I realized, it was already too late.

meaning: to leave the door (open/closed); to allow the door to remain in a certain state or position.
additional_notes: Often used with an adjective or past participle (e.g., aberta/fechada). Can indicate intentional or accidental action. Common in requests, statements of habit, and warnings. Can be followed by purpose or beneficiary phrases (e.g., 'pra você').
target_language_example: Ele tem o hábito de deixar a porta aberta.
native_language_example: He has the habit of leaving the door open.

meaning: stop (doing)
additional_notes: Two common uses: 1) 'deixar de' + infinitive = to stop or quit doing something (e.g., deixar de fumar = stop smoking). 2) In negative constructions like 'não pude/deixei de' or 'não pude deixar de' it means 'cannot help (doing)' or 'couldn't help (doing)'. Context determines meaning. Can also appear in phrases like 'deixar de lado' meaning 'set aside'.
target_language_example: Decidi deixar de fumar este ano.
native_language_example: I decided to stop smoking this year.

meaning: to leave (someone) alone; to stop bothering or disturbing someone.
additional_notes: Used when asking or telling someone to stop interrupting, bothering, or disturbing another person. Can be a polite request (Pode me deixar em paz?) or a threat/firm statement (Não vou te deixar em paz). Tone and context determine formality. Literal components: deixar = to leave/let; em paz = in peace.
target_language_example: Pode me deixar em paz, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you leave me alone, please?

meaning: 'to let slip' or 'to let escape' — to accidentally reveal information or to fail to keep/hold onto something (literal or figurative).
additional_notes: Commonly used both figuratively (to unintentionally reveal a secret, spoiler, or information) and literally (to allow something to escape, fall away, or be lost). Context and objects that follow (e.g., 'um segredo', 'uma oportunidade', 'o balão') indicate the sense. Can appear in various tenses and persons: 'deixei escapar', 'deixa escapar', 'deixaram escapar', etc.
target_language_example: Ela foi falar demais e acabou por deixar escapar o segredo.
native_language_example: She talked too much and ended up letting the secret slip.

meaning: to let it go; to drop the subject or stop worrying about something.
additional_notes: Used when you decide not to pursue a topic, argument, problem, or worry anymore. Can be used imperatively or in different tenses: e.g. 'Deixa para lá' (Let it go), 'Deixei para lá' (I let it go). Common in casual speech.
target_language_example: Deixar para lá às vezes é a melhor escolha quando não compensa discutir.
native_language_example: Sometimes letting it go is the best choice when it's not worth arguing.

meaning: to let someone/something pass; to allow through.
additional_notes: Used when permitting movement or entry. Can be literal (letting a person or vehicle go by) or figurative (allowing something to happen). Often appears with an object (deixar + pessoa/coisa + passar) or in requests (Pode me deixar passar?). In negative contexts it means to prevent someone/something from passing (não deixar passar).
target_language_example: Pode me deixar passar, por favor?
native_language_example: Please let me pass, please?

meaning: to leave (someone/something) alone; to let it be; to stop bothering or interfering
additional_notes: Used when telling someone to stop interfering, to leave something as it is, or to stop talking about a topic. Can be used transitively (deixar alguém quieto — leave someone alone) or impersonally (deixa quieto — never mind / forget it). Common in spoken Portuguese.
target_language_example: É melhor deixar quieto — não adianta mexer nisso agora.
native_language_example: It's better to leave it alone — there's no point in fiddling with that now.

meaning: leave her (or it) in/by/at (followed by a noun like 'paz' — 'leave her alone').
additional_notes: Imperative form of 'deixar' + object pronoun 'a' (feminine) + preposition 'em'. Commonly used as 'deixe-a em paz' = 'leave her alone'. The pronoun attaches to the verb with a hyphen in writing. Context and the following noun determine the exact translation of 'em' (e.g. 'em paz' = 'alone/peace', 'em casa' = 'at home').
target_language_example: Deixe-a em casa enquanto eu volto.
native_language_example: Leave her at home while I return.

meaning: let (him/it) (do something)
additional_notes: Imperative plural form of 'deixar' + definite article 'o'. Used to tell a group to allow or permit someone/thing (masculine) to do something, or to tell them to leave him/it alone. Context determines whether it means 'let' (permit) or 'leave'. The subject is 'vocês' or 'eles' (you plural). If referring to a feminine noun use 'deixem a'.
target_language_example: Deixem o João terminar a tarefa.
native_language_example: Let João finish the task.

meaning: 'her ... was' — a combination showing possession (dela = her/hers) followed by the verb 'was' (estava).
additional_notes: Used to describe a state or situation of something that belongs to or is associated with 'her'. 'Dela' follows the noun in Portuguese (A mãe dela = her mother). 'Estava' is the imperfect/past progressive of 'estar' (was/were being). Together they form phrases like 'a vida dela estava...'(her life was...) or 'a casa dela estava...'(her house was...). Not a fixed phrase — it's simply two words often seen together in sentences.
target_language_example: A bolsa dela estava na cadeira.
native_language_example: Her bag was on the chair.

meaning: literally 'his/its/ of him is' + 'is' — used to say where something of his/that belongs to him is, or to describe its state.
additional_notes: Dele is a possessive pronoun meaning 'his'/'of him' (can also mean 'hers' in Brazilian usage when context requires gender-neutral) and is used after the noun (A casa dele = his house). Está is the 3rd-person singular present of estar, used for location, temporary states, conditions, or ongoing situations. Together they appear when describing where or how something belonging to someone is (e.g., location, condition, sale status, health). Word order: noun + dele + está or noun + dele + estar-conjugated in questions (O notebook dele está na mesa?).
target_language_example: O carro dele está na oficina.
native_language_example: His car is in the shop.

meaning: police station; local office of the police.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the building or office where police work, report crimes, file complaints, or handle administrative matters. Commonly used with verbs like ir (to go), estar (to be), entrar (to enter), and pisar (to step/go). In Brazil 'delegacia' alone is often understood as 'police station.'
target_language_example: Tenho de ir à delegacia de polícia para registrar um boletim.
native_language_example: I have to go to the police station to file a report.

meaning: too ... for
additional_notes: Used to say something exceeds someone's ability, capacity, tolerance, or appropriateness. Followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., mim, nós, uma criança) or an infinitive/verb phrase (context can imply 'to do/handle/eat/etc.'). Word order: 'demais para + [pronoun/noun]' or 'é demais para + [infinitive/agent]'. 'Demais' by itself can mean 'too much' or 'very' depending on context.
target_language_example: Este trabalho é demais para mim.
native_language_example: This job is too much for me / too much for me to handle.

meaning: 'democracy is' — a way to start a definition or opinion about democracy.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement, definition, or opinion about democracy. Often followed by a noun phrase (e.g., 'a base'), a clause (e.g., 'o governo do povo...'), or an evaluative comment (e.g., 'o menos ruim'). In Portuguese the article can be omitted ('Democracia é...') or included ('A democracia é...') with no change in basic meaning; including the article is slightly more formal/definite.
target_language_example: A democracia é a melhor forma de governo quando há liberdade e direitos.
native_language_example: Democracy is the best form of government when there is freedom and rights.

meaning: in/within (a time period) or inside (a place); often 'within' when referring to time.
additional_notes: Commonly used to indicate something will happen 'within' a certain time (e.g., dentro de meia hora = within half an hour). It can also mean physically 'inside' when followed by a noun (dentro de casa = inside the house). Context determines translation: with time expressions, translate as 'in/within X'; with locations, 'inside'.
target_language_example: Dentro de duas horas teremos notícias.
native_language_example: Within two hours we'll have news.

meaning: after
additional_notes: Used before a noun or an infinitive verb to say that one thing happens after another. Compare with depois on its own, which often means "afterward" or "later."
target_language_example: Depois de jantar, fomos passear.
native_language_example: After dinner, we went for a walk.

meaning: the day after tomorrow.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the day two days from now. Common in everyday speech and appears in both present and future tense contexts. Literal components: 'depois' = after, 'amanhã' = tomorrow.
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar depois de amanhã às oito.
native_language_example: Let's meet the day after tomorrow at eight.

meaning: 'they gave the' (masculine singular direct object) — past tense of 'dar' (to give) used with a masculine singular noun or pronoun following.
additional_notes: Deram is the third-person plural preterite of dar (they gave). The short phrase 'deram o' appears before a masculine singular noun or an implied masculine object (e.g., 'o número', 'o diagnóstico', 'o melhor', 'o crédito'). Portuguese requires gender and number agreement in objects; if the object is feminine use 'deram a'. Context shows 'they/you (plural formal) gave' or 'people gave'. The subject can be explicit (os médicos) or implied (me deram = they gave me).
target_language_example: Eles me deram o presente ontem.
native_language_example: They gave me the gift yesterday.

meaning: 'bloodshed' — the violent spilling of blood, often used for deaths in fights, wars, or massacres.
additional_notes: Used to refer to violent loss of life or injuries in conflicts. Common in warnings or statements aiming to avoid violence (e.g., 'We want to avoid bloodshed'). Formal or neutral register; not slang. Often appears with verbs like evitar (to avoid), causar (to cause), impedir (to prevent), or falar sobre (to speak about).
target_language_example: Precisamos negociar para evitar derramamento de sangue.
native_language_example: We need to negotiate to avoid bloodshed.

meaning: 'rest in peace' (used when someone has died).
additional_notes: A standard expression used to express sympathy or a wish that the deceased may rest peacefully. Commonly abbreviated in writing as 'RIP' in English; in Portuguese you may also see 'Descanse em paz' (formal) or 'Descansem em paz' (plural). Can be used on tombstones, messages of condolence, or social media tributes.
target_language_example: Que ele possa descansar em paz.
native_language_example: May he rest in peace.

meaning: 'find out that' / 'discover this' (to learn or uncover some information or fact).
additional_notes: Literal components: descobrir = to discover/find out; isso = this/that. Commonly used to say you learned something or instruct someone to find something out. Can refer to discovering a fact, solution, or location. Tense and context change meaning: e.g. 'acabei de descobrir isso' = 'I just found out this (an hour ago)'; imperative 'tem que descobrir isso' = 'you have to find this out'.
target_language_example: Você precisa descobrir isso antes da reunião.
native_language_example: You need to find that out before the meeting.

meaning: 'apology to' or 'to apologize to (someone)'.
additional_notes: Used when addressing the person you are apologizing to. Common forms: 'pedir desculpa a [alguém]' or shortened 'peço desculpa a [alguém]'.
