In Brazil you may also hear 'desculpe' or 'peço desculpas' (plural) without 'a' followed by the person: 'Desculpe, João.' Formality: neutral — suitable in both polite and casual contexts. If you want to apologize for something, add 'por [motivo]': 'Desculpa a você por isso.'
target_language_example: Quero pedir desculpa a você pelo erro.
native_language_example: I want to apologize to you for the mistake.

meaning: 'sorry for the' or 'excuse the' (used to apologize for something specific).
additional_notes: Common opening for brief apologies. Followed by a noun or noun phrase (e.g., 'atraso' = delay, 'incômodo' = inconvenience, 'mau humor' = bad mood). Polite and can be used in formal and informal contexts. To apologize for an action you did, you can also say 'desculpe pelo(a) ...' (contraction of 'por + o/a') or 'desculpe' alone.
target_language_example: Desculpe o barulho, vou terminar logo.
native_language_example: Sorry for the noise, I'll finish soon.

meaning: since then; from that time onward.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a point in the past mentioned or implied earlier. Often appears at the start or end of a sentence. Can introduce ongoing actions or states that started at that past time and continue or have relevance now.
target_language_example: Eles se conheceram em 2010 e, desde então, viajam juntos todo ano.
native_language_example: They met in 2010 and, since then, they travel together every year.

meaning: since last year / since the year (followed by specification).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the starting point in time from a specific year (often 'desde o ano passado' = 'since last year'). Commonly followed by 'passado' (past) or a specific year: 'desde o ano passado', 'desde o ano de 2020'. Can appear at the beginning of a sentence ('Desde o ano passado...') or inside it. Expresses continuity from that time until now.
target_language_example: Desde o ano passado estou estudando mais inglês.
native_language_example: Since last year I've been studying more English.

meaning: "since when" (asks how long something has been true) or
additional_notes: Used to ask about the start time or duration of a situation. Often appears in questions expressing surprise, disbelief, or curiosity. Can introduce a literal time frame (Desde quando eu parei...) or a rhetorical challenge (Desde quando você se importa?). In informal contexts it can be stronger, even confrontational.
target_language_example: Desde quando você fala francês?
native_language_example: Since when do you speak French?

meaning: since
additional_notes: Primary uses: (1) time — 'since' / 'ever since' to indicate when something started (e.g. Desde que eu comecei... = Since I started...); (2) conditional/temporal with subjunctive in some contexts meaning 'as long as' or 'provided that' (e.g. desde que você esteja disposto = as long as you are willing). Context and verb mood determine meaning. Common in both spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: Desde que a aula terminou, ele não parou de estudar.
native_language_example: Since class ended, he hasn't stopped studying.

meaning: cartoon; animated (film/show).
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to an animated short, film, or TV show aimed at children (or in cartoon style). Can be used as a noun (um desenho animado = a cartoon) or attributively (uma personagem de desenho animado = a cartoon character).
target_language_example: Depois do almoço, as crianças assistiram a um desenho animado.
native_language_example: After lunch, the children watched a cartoon.

meaning: hung up on me / (someone) cut me off abruptly (often on the phone).
additional_notes: Informal, typically used when someone ends a phone call rudely by hanging up or abruptly breaking off contact. Literally 'hung up on my (face)', used in Brazil. Often expresses annoyance or offense. Can be adapted with different pronouns (desligou no meu / desligou na minha cara).
target_language_example: Ela desligou na minha quando eu perguntei pelo chefe.
native_language_example: She hung up on me when I asked for the boss.

meaning: 'to say goodbye to' or 'to bid farewell to' (someone).
additional_notes: Used when taking leave of a person. Do not confuse with despedir (without de) which often means 'to fire' (dismiss someone from a job). With de + person it means to say goodbye to that person. Common constructions: despedir de alguém (often reflexive: despedir-se de alguém) or despedir alguém de um emprego (to fire someone).
target_language_example: Vou despedir de todos antes de partir.
native_language_example: I will say goodbye to everyone before leaving.

meaning: 'destiny is' or 'the destiny/fate is (somewhere or in someone's hands)'.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone's destiny or fate depends on or is controlled by someone/something. Commonly appears in phrases like 'meu destino está em tuas/vossas/suas mãos' — 'my destiny is in your hands.' Remember to match possessive and preposition (em + suas = nas when plural feminine).
target_language_example: O meu destino está nas suas mãos agora.
native_language_example: My destiny is in your hands now.

meaning: 'I hate the' or 'I hate' (followed by a masculine singular noun or a verb phrase when using 'o' as a clitic pronoun).
additional_notes: Detesto is the first-person singular present of detestar (to hate). When followed by the masculine singular article 'o' it usually introduces a specific masculine noun (Detesto o inverno = I hate the winter). If you want to hate a feminine noun use 'detesto a' (detesto a chuva). For general dislikes you can also say 'detesto' + infinitive (Detesto esperar = I hate waiting). Tone is strong—use carefully in polite contexts.
target_language_example: Detesto o trânsito da cidade.
native_language_example: I hate the city traffic.

meaning: behind (something) / at the back of (feminine plural noun).
additional_notes: Used to indicate physical location behind something or a figurative idea of what lies behind (e.g., meaning, motive). 'Por detrás de' is the base phrase; 'das' is the contraction of 'de' + 'as' (feminine plural). Use 'do'/'dos' for masculine, 'da'/'das' depending on the gender and number of the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Há algo por detrás das portas fechadas.
native_language_example: There is something behind the closed doors.

meaning: 'realized' or 'became aware that'.
additional_notes: Literal verb phrase from 'dar conta' used in the past: 'se deu conta de que' = 'he/she realized that'. Used to say someone suddenly noticed or understood something. Common with reflexive pronoun 'se' (se deu conta). Can be followed by a clause introduced by 'que' or by 'de' + noun/infinitive (e.g., 'se deu conta do erro', 'se deu conta de ter errado').
target_language_example: Ela se deu conta de que tinha perdido o ônibus.
native_language_example: She realized that she had missed the bus.

meaning: 'gave this' or 'gave that' (past-tense of 'dar' + demonstrative)
additional_notes: Combines the past-tense verb deu (he/she/you formal gave) with the demonstrative esse (this/that). Used to ask or say who gave something or to state that someone gave a specific item. Context and intonation determine whether esse refers to something near the listener (that) or previously mentioned. In questions, subject can be omitted or expressed (Quem deu esse...? / Quem lhe deu esse...?).
target_language_example: Quem te deu esse presente?
native_language_example: Who gave you this gift?

meaning: Greek god (a god from ancient Greek mythology).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a god from Greek mythology (e.g., Zeus, Athena, Apollo). Can be used literally (mythology) or figuratively/ironically to describe someone acting grand or majestic. Gendered: 'deus grego' (masculine); the feminine form is 'deusa grega'.
target_language_example: Ele se comporta como um deus grego no palco.
native_language_example: He behaves like a Greek god on stage.

meaning: 'must/should speak' or 'ought to speak' (expresses obligation or advice about speaking)
additional_notes: Combination of the modal verb dever (must/should/ought to) + the infinitive falar (to speak). Depending on context and intonation, it can express obligation (must), strong advice (should/ought to), or prohibition when negated (não deve falar = should not/must not speak). The subject may be implied (ele/ela/você/deve falar) or explicit (você deve falar).
target_language_example: Você deve falar com a professora sobre o problema.
native_language_example: You should speak to the teacher about the problem.

meaning: 'should/ought to take' or 'must take' (expresses obligation, advice, or necessity) depending on context.
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb dever (must/should) in the 3rd person singular with the infinitive tomar (to take; to have—for drinks; to take a shower—depending on context). Use to give advice, recommendations, or obligations: e.g. tomar banho (take a shower), tomar cuidado (be careful/take care), tomar líquido (drink fluids), tomar como exemplo (take as an example). Tone ranges from soft advice (should) to stronger obligation (must) depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Você deve tomar remédio quando estiver doente.
native_language_example: You should take medicine when you are sick.

meaning: 'homework' (school assignments to be done at home).
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to schoolwork given by teachers. Can be singular 'dever de casa' or plural 'deveres de casa' (or simply 'deveres' / 'lição' in some regions). Often used with possessive: 'meu dever de casa', 'seu dever de casa'.
target_language_example: Preciso fazer meu dever de casa antes de jantar.
native_language_example: I need to do my homework before dinner.

meaning: should tell / should tell (someone) / ought to tell
additional_notes: Combines the conditional/modal verb deveria (from dever = should/ought to) with the verb contar (to tell). Used to express that someone thinks it would be appropriate or advisable to tell someone something. Often followed by a direct object (what to tell) and/or a prepositional phrase with the person (a/para/ao/à + person). Formality: neutral; common in speech and writing.
target_language_example: Eu deveria contar a verdade para ela.
native_language_example: I should tell her the truth.

meaning: 'should rest a' (start of a suggestion that someone should rest for a certain time or take a short rest)
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself — it's the beginning of a sentence like 'deveria descansar um pouco' (should rest a little) or 'deveria descansar um dia' (should rest a day). 'Deveria' is the conditional of 'dever' (should/ought to), used to give advice or say what would be advisable. Use with a time/duration or 'pouco'/'pouco mais' to complete the idea.
target_language_example: Você deveria descansar um pouco antes de voltar ao trabalho.
native_language_example: You should rest a little before going back to work.

meaning: 'should wash' or 'ought to wash' (a suggestion or mild obligation to wash something)
additional_notes: Deveria is the conditional of dever (to must/should) and is used to give advice, suggestions, or indicate what is expected. Put the thing to be washed after the verb (e.g., lavar as frutas). You can add polite emphasis by using 'você deveria' (you should) or switch to 'deves'/'deverias' in other dialects/levels of formality.
target_language_example: Você deveria lavar as mãos antes de comer.
native_language_example: You should wash your hands before eating.

meaning: because of; due to.
additional_notes: Used to give a reason or cause. Followed by a noun, pronoun, or phrase (often artigo + noun). Can appear at sentence start or mid-sentence. Formal register; common in writing and speech. If followed by a verb, use 'por causa de' or a subordinate clause (e.g., 'porque').
target_language_example: O voo foi cancelado devido ao mau tempo.
native_language_example: The flight was cancelled due to bad weather.

meaning: 'what should I do with' (used to ask what to do with someone/something).
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask for instructions about handling, using, disposing of, or dealing with an object, person, money, etc. Often appears as 'o que devo fazer com...' or 'o que eu devo fazer com...'. Can be followed by a pronoun, noun, or noun phrase.
target_language_example: O que devo fazer com essas roupas velhas?
native_language_example: What should I do with these old clothes?

meaning: I owe (my) — used to say you owe something (often credit) to someone.
additional_notes: Common structure: devo + (possessive) + [thing] + a + [person]. Here 'devo meu sucesso a...' means 'I owe my success to...'. 'Devo' comes from the verb dever (to owe, to have to). The possessive (meu/minha/meus) agrees with the noun (sucesso). Use 'a' or 'ao/à' (a + o/a) before the person: 'a meu amigo', 'à minha amiga', 'aos meus amigos'.
target_language_example: Devo meu novo emprego à minha família.
native_language_example: I owe my new job to my family.

meaning: 'I owe you one' — a way to thank someone and say you'll return a favor.
additional_notes: Informal expression used to show gratitude and promise to repay help or a favor in the future. Often said to friends or acquaintances; can be abbreviated as 'te devo uma' (I owe you one to you) or 'devo uma' in context. Tone is casual and friendly.
target_language_example: Valeu pela ajuda com a mudança — te devo uma!
native_language_example: Thanks for helping with the move — I owe you one!

meaning: daily life; day-to-day routine.
additional_notes: Used to talk about everyday activities, routines, or what happens regularly. Can describe someone's usual life (o meu dia a dia), gradual change (cresce dia a dia = grows day by day), or the everyday experience of a role (no dia a dia).
target_language_example: O barulho do trânsito faz parte do meu dia a dia.
native_language_example: Traffic noise is part of my daily life.

meaning: a school/class day; a day when classes are held (e.g., first day of class, last day of class).
additional_notes: Used to talk about specific days in an academic context (first day of class, last day of class, a regular teaching day). Commonly appears with adjectives or ordinal words: primeiro dia de aula (first day of class), último dia de aula (last day of class).
target_language_example: Amanhã é o primeiro dia de aula do semestre.
native_language_example: Tomorrow is the first day of classes of the semester.

meaning: one of these days; sometime soon (in the near future or an unspecified upcoming day).
additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified day in the near future. Can be casual; context determines urgency/seriousness (e.g., a friendly visit or a joking threat). Often appears at the start of a sentence (Um dia desses...) or after the verb (veio me ver um dia desses).
target_language_example: Vamos almoçar um dia desses.
native_language_example: Let's have lunch one of these days.

meaning: day and night; all the time, continuously
additional_notes: Used to say something happens continuously or both during the day and at night (i.e., around the clock). Can be literal (referring to day and night) or idiomatic (meaning constantly, nonstop). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ele estudou dia e noite para o exame.
native_language_example: He studied day and night for the exam.

meaning: a long (tiring or drawn-out) day.
additional_notes: Used to describe a day that felt long because of fatigue, many tasks, stress, or length. Often implies tiredness or that the day was difficult. Can be used in casual conversation; word order is normal adjective after noun in Portuguese.
target_language_example: Depois de tanto trabalho, hoje foi um dia longo.
native_language_example: After so much work, today was a long day.

meaning: an emphatic/informal way to say 'what on earth/what the hell are you (doing/saying)?' (expresses surprise, anger or disbelief).
additional_notes: Placed after or before a question word (Que/O que/Sobre que) to add strong emotion. Informal and mildly vulgar — avoid in polite situations. Can translate as 'what the hell' or 'what on earth' depending on tone. Word order in examples: 'Que diabos você está fazendo?' or 'O que diabos você está fazendo?'.
target_language_example: Que diabos você está pensando em fazer?
native_language_example: What the hell are you thinking of doing?

meaning: 'in front of', 'facing', or 'before' (used both physically and figuratively).
additional_notes: Used for physical position (in front of/facing something) and for situations or contexts (faced with / in the presence of / before a problem). Commonly followed by a noun. Equivalent to 'in front of', 'facing', or 'in the face of' depending on context.
target_language_example: Ele ficou diante de mim sem saber o que dizer.
native_language_example: He stood in front of me not knowing what to say.

meaning: the dictionary is (located) / 'the dictionary is ...'.
additional_notes: This is the noun 'dicionário' (dictionary) + the verb 'está' (third-person singular of 'estar') used to state the current location or condition of the dictionary. Use 'está' for temporary states or locations. Common prepositions follow (em, na, sobre, em cima de). For a full sentence, include the location: e.g., 'O dicionário está na mesa.'
target_language_example: O dicionário está dentro da mochila.
native_language_example: The dictionary is inside the backpack.

meaning: 'the dictionary can also (do something)'.
additional_notes: This is a short sequence showing verb ability/possibility: 'dicionário' (dictionary) + 'também' (also) + 'pode' (can). It's followed by an infinitive verb or an object pronoun + infinitive (e.g. 'ajudá-la' = help her). Note pronoun placement: formal written Portuguese often attaches object pronouns to the infinitive (ajudá-la, ajudá-lo), while informal spoken Portuguese may place the pronoun before the verb or use 'te' after the verb ('te ajudar'). Adjust pronouns for gender/number: -la/-las (feminine), -lo/-los (masculine).
target_language_example: Este dicionário também pode corrigir seus erros.
native_language_example: This dictionary can also correct your mistakes.

meaning: different from the (plural/feminine) or different from the (plural/masculine) depending on context; used to compare someone/something with a group.
additional_notes: diferente means 'different'. das is the contraction of de + as (or de + os in masculine contexts becomes 'dos'). In examples here 'diferente das' is used to say someone is different from other people/items (the group that follows is plural). Use 'diferente do' or 'diferente dos' when the following noun is masculine singular or plural respectively. Common structure: 'ser/estar diferente de/da/do/das/dos + noun' — 'diferente de' and 'diferente de + article' are both used; pronunciation and regional preference vary.
target_language_example: Ela é diferente das amigas dela; tem gostos próprios.
native_language_example: She is different from her friends; she has her own tastes.

meaning: difficulty in / difficulty with / trouble (doing something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone finds something hard or has trouble doing or obtaining something. Followed by a verb in the infinitive (dificuldade de respirar, dificuldade de conseguir) or a noun (dificuldade de achar trabalho). Common in everyday and formal speech.
target_language_example: Tenho dificuldade de entender matemática.
native_language_example: I have difficulty understanding math.

meaning: more difficult than (used in comparisons).
additional_notes: Used as part of comparative structures: 'mais difícil do que' = 'more difficult than'. Often appears with 'mais' before the adjective. Can compare tasks, situations, people, etc. Example sentence shows a superlative/comparative idea: 'There is no task more difficult than this.'
target_language_example: Esta prova é mais difícil do que a última.
native_language_example: This exam is more difficult than the last one.

meaning: Tell me how / Tell me (followed by a question word) — used to ask for explanation or instructions.
additional_notes: This sequence appears in questions as a polite prompt: 'Me diga, como...?' = 'Tell me, how...?' 'Me diga' (imperative polite) + a question word (aqui 'como' = how). Common in spoken and written Portuguese to request information, clarification, or instructions. You can replace 'me' with outro pronoun (e.g., 'Diga-me' more formal) and 'como' with other question words (o que, quando, por que).
target_language_example: Me diga, como faço para chegar ao centro?
native_language_example: Tell me, how do I get to the city center?

meaning: 'let it be said' or 'it should be said' — a parenthetical phrase used to add a comment or clarification.
additional_notes: Used to insert a remark, clarification, or aside into a sentence. Often appears at the start of an aside: 'Diga-se que...' (It should be said that...) or 'Diga-se de passagem...' (by the way / it should be mentioned). Formality: neutral to slightly formal. Common in spoken and written Portuguese to emphasize or qualify information.
target_language_example: Diga-se que ele trabalhou muito para conseguir o contrato.
native_language_example: It should be said that he worked hard to get the contract.

meaning: tell him/her/it
additional_notes: Imperative form plural of dizer (vocative or command to multiple people). 'Digam' is the polite/neutral plural command (you all) and 'o' is a direct object pronoun meaning 'him', 'it' (masculine) or a neutral 'it' referring to something mentioned. Context decides whether it refers to a person (tell him) or a thing (say it). In Brazilian Portuguese, 'digam-no' is less common in speech; 'digam o' appears in informal spoken contexts where pronoun appears after a pause. Use with groups (vocês or vocês/eles).
target_language_example: Digam o nome quando chegarem.
native_language_example: Tell him/them the name when you arrive.

meaning: 'let's say' / 'so to speak' / 'you could say that'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a tentative explanation, rephrase, or approximation. Softens a statement or signals the speaker is choosing words carefully — similar to English 'let's say', 'so to speak', or 'you might say'. Common in spoken Portuguese.
target_language_example: Ele é, digamos assim, um pouco teimoso, mas muito competente.
native_language_example: He is, let's say, a bit stubborn but very competent.

meaning: 'money on me' / 'money with me' — money you are carrying right now
additional_notes: Used to say whether you currently have cash (or money) physically with you. Common in everyday situations (shopping, lending, paying). Often follows verbs like ter, não ter, querer; literal meaning is transparent.
target_language_example: Desculpe, não tenho dinheiro comigo, posso pagar com cartão?
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't have any money on me; can I pay with a card?

meaning: 'her money' (money that belongs to her).
additional_notes: A possessive phrase: dinheiro (money) + dela (of her / hers). Used to talk about money belonging to a female person. Context can be neutral (ownership) or negative (e.g., accusing someone of taking or extracting money from her). Dela contracts gender/number to the possessor (dela = of her).
target_language_example: Não toque no dinheiro dela sem pedir.
native_language_example: Don't touch her money without asking.

meaning: 'the right to (do something) to/over me' — used to say someone has (or doesn't have) the right to tell, judge, take, etc., the speaker.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in phrases like 'ter o direito de me dizer', 'ter o direito de me julgar', or negative ('não tem direito de me...') to complain that someone shouldn't have authority or permission regarding the speaker. 'Me' is the object pronoun 'me' (to/over me). Verb after 'direito de' is usually in the infinitive.
target_language_example: Você não tem o direito de me criticar assim.
native_language_example: You don't have the right to criticize me like that.

meaning: human right (a right that belongs to every person).
additional_notes: Used to talk about rights like freedom of speech, education, equality, etc. Often appears in plural as "direitos humanos" (human rights). Can be used in legal, political, and everyday contexts.
target_language_example: Todos têm o direito humano à educação.
native_language_example: Everyone has the human right to education.

meaning: the director/ principal of (feminine noun follows); 'director of' or 'principal of' when referring to a specific institution.
additional_notes: Literal: 'diretor' = director/principal; 'da' = contraction of 'de' + 'a' (of the, feminine). Use before a feminine noun like 'escola' (school) or other feminine institutions. Can refer to film/theater director or the head of an institution depending on context. Word order: 'diretor da escola' = 'the school's principal/director'. Informal/emphatic language in examples (e.g., 'diretor da porra do...') adds strong emotion or insult; avoid in polite speech.
target_language_example: O diretor da escola falou com os pais hoje.
native_language_example: The school's principal spoke with the parents today.

meaning: 'director of' or 'head of' (someone who directs or manages something).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to indicate the person in charge of an organization, place, or production (e.g., film, museum, studio). 'Diretor' is masculine; for a female use 'diretora'. The preposition 'do' = 'de + o' (of the). For feminine nouns use 'da' (de + a) and for plurals 'dos'/'das'. Agreement with the following noun is required (e.g., 'diretor do filme', 'diretor da escola').
target_language_example: Ainda não se sabe quem deverá ser o diretor do filme.
native_language_example: It is not yet known who will be the director of the film.

meaning: driving the (masculine singular vehicle).
additional_notes: Present participle of 'dirigir' (to drive) + definite article 'o' (the). Used to say someone is driving a specific vehicle (carro, ônibus). Word order can vary: you may also see 'está dirigindo o carro' or 'o homem que está dirigindo o ônibus'. The participle is used for continuous actions (equivalent to 'is/was driving').
target_language_example: Ela estava dirigindo o carro quando eu cheguei.
native_language_example: She was driving the car when I arrived.

meaning: hard drive (computer storage device).
additional_notes: Refers to a computer's storage device (internal or external). Can mean traditional HDDs (mechanical) or more generally a drive where data is stored; often used with qualifiers like 'externo' (external) or 'interno' (internal). Common verbs: 'proteger' (protect), 'formatar' (format), 'substituir' (replace), 'remover' (remove).
target_language_example: Eu comprei um disco rígido externo para fazer backup dos meus arquivos.
native_language_example: I bought an external hard drive to back up my files.

meaning: to discuss the / to talk about the (followed by a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Discutir o is the verb discutir ('to discuss') followed by the masculine definite article 'o' before a masculine noun (e.g., 'o assunto', 'o seu trabalho'). Use discutir sobre or discutir + noun without article in some contexts, but 'discutir o' + noun is a very common and neutral way to say 'discuss the [thing]'. The verb can mean 'talk about' or, in other contexts, 'argue' (e.g., 'discutir com alguém' = argue with someone).
target_language_example: Podemos discutir o plano amanhã?
native_language_example: Can we discuss the plan tomorrow?

meaning: said that he was — introduces what someone reported about a man's/state or condition.
additional_notes: Used to report speech (third person) about a male subject's state, feeling, location, or ongoing action. Common in past narrative: 'disse' (said) + 'que' (that) + 'ele estava' (he was). The clause after 'estava' can be an adjective (satisfeito), a participle (atordoado), a location (próximo) or a progressive/reflexive action (se perguntando).
target_language_example: Ela disse que ele estava cansado ontem.
native_language_example: She said that he was tired yesterday.

meaning: 'said that my' — part of a reported-speech phrase introducing what someone said about something belonging to the speaker.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone expression; it's the start of a clause in reported speech. 'Disse' = 'said', 'que' = 'that', 'meu' = 'my' (masculine singular). You will usually see it followed by a noun or clause (e.g., 'disse que meu carro...' or 'disse que meu amigo...'). For feminine nouns use 'minha' instead of 'meu'. Verb tense and subject can change (e.g., 'ela disse que o meu...' or 'ele disse que meu...').
target_language_example: Ela disse que meu carro está no estacionamento.
native_language_example: She said that my car is in the parking lot.

meaning: said that you (plural)
additional_notes: A reporting phrase: 'disse' is past of 'dizer' (to say/tell) and 'vocês' is the plural 'you' (Brazilian Portuguese). Use with a person who reported something about the group: e.g. 'Tom me disse que vocês...' = 'Tom told me that you (all)...'. The subject (he/she/they) is often explicit or understood from context. Can be used with different indirect objects (me, nos) to indicate who received the information.
target_language_example: Ela nos disse que vocês chegarão amanhã.
native_language_example: She told us that you (all) will arrive tomorrow.

meaning: we said that
additional_notes: 'dissemos' is the simple past of 'dizer' for nós ('we'). It introduces reported speech or a statement. The subject pronoun 'nós' is often omitted because 'dissemos' already shows 'we'.
target_language_example: Dissemos que voltaríamos amanhã.
native_language_example: We said that we'd come back tomorrow.

meaning: distance from here; how far (from this place).
additional_notes: Used to ask or state how far something is from the speaker's current location. Common in questions with verbs like ficar, ser, or estar and prepositions até/para/até à. Equivalent to 'how far is... from here' or 'the distance from here to...'.
target_language_example: A que distância daqui fica o centro da cidade?
native_language_example: How far is the city center from here?

meaning: 'How far (do you... / is ...)?' — asks about physical distance or how far away something/someone is or how far someone is going.
additional_notes: Common question pattern for asking distances. Often followed by a verb or location: 'A que distância você mora?' (How far do you live? / How far away do you live?). Can be used for distance to a place or how far someone is traveling or how far something is from the speaker. Formality: neutral; suitable for everyday use. Word order can vary: 'Que distância você mora?' is informal/colloquial but less standard than 'A que distância...'.
target_language_example: A que distância você mora do trabalho?
native_language_example: How far do you live from work?

meaning: "I mean, what..." — a spoken filler followed by a question asking for clarification or specifics.
additional_notes: Used in casual speech to introduce or soften a question, often translating the English filler 'I mean' + 'what...'. Common at the start of a sentence to ask for clarification, explanation, or details about something just mentioned. Tone is conversational; you can drop 'Quero' and just say 'Dizer, o que...'? — no, that would be unnatural. Typical full form is 'Quero dizer, o que...'.
target_language_example: Quero dizer, o que você quis dizer com isso?
native_language_example: I mean, what did you mean by that?

meaning: Used as a discourse marker meaning 'I mean' or 'that is to say' when addressing 'you'.
additional_notes: This combination appears as 'quero dizer, você...' or 'devo dizer, você...' and functions to introduce clarification, emphasis, or an opinion directed at the listener. It's colloquial and common in spoken Portuguese. It doesn't change the literal meaning of 'dizer' (to say) but works as a filler/softener like English 'I mean, you...'. Use it before a statement about the listener.
target_language_example: Quero dizer, você fez um ótimo trabalho hoje.
native_language_example: I mean, you did a great job today.

meaning: to tell (someone) how; to explain how (something is or happened).
additional_notes: Used when asking someone to explain the manner, reason, or process of something. Often appears in questions: 'Pode dizer como é?' (Can you say how it is?) or 'Você pode me dizer como...?' (Can you tell me how...?). 'Dizer' = to tell/say; 'como' = how. The pronoun or object (e.g., 'me', 'isso') often appears between 'dizer' and 'como' or after.
target_language_example: Você pode me dizer como funciona este aplicativo?
native_language_example: Can you tell me how this app works?

meaning: to tell (someone) how to get somewhere / give directions
additional_notes: Used when asking someone to explain the route or directions to a place. Often appears in polite questions with poderia/ você pode/ poderia me dizer. Can be followed by 'a' or 'ao/à' + destination (e.g., ao zoológico, à Embaixada).
target_language_example: Poderia me dizer como chegar ao metrô mais próximo?
native_language_example: Could you tell me how to get to the nearest subway?

meaning: to say more; to add something else (spoken).
additional_notes: Commonly used to indicate adding another remark or to urge someone to stop speaking (negative form). Often appears as 'dizer mais uma coisa' (say one more thing) or 'dizer mais alguma coisa' (say anything else). Used in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Posso dizer mais uma coisa antes de sairmos?
native_language_example: Can I say one more thing before we leave?

meaning: to say/claim that he is a ... (used to introduce an evaluation or judgment about 'he')
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a noun like 'gênio' (genius). Often used in impersonal constructions (pode-se dizer, não é exagero dizer) to soften or emphasize the judgment. Equivalent to 'one can say that he is a ...' or 'it can be said that he is a ...' in English. Use to present an opinion or evaluation about a male person.
target_language_example: Pode-se dizer que ele é um professor dedicado.
native_language_example: One can say that he is a dedicated teacher.

meaning: to say that the (masculine singular) — literal sequence used when reporting speech or clauses that begin with the masculine singular definite article 'o'
additional_notes: Compositional: 'dizer que' = 'to say that'; 'o' = masculine singular definite article 'the'. Appears when the reported clause or noun phrase starts with 'o' (e.g., 'dizer que o livro...'). The article will change to 'a', 'os' or 'as' to match gender/number as needed. Common in reported speech and indirect statements.
target_language_example: Ele vai dizer que o projeto precisa de mais tempo.
native_language_example: He is going to say that the project needs more time.

meaning: 'to say that I will' or 'to tell (someone) that I will...'
additional_notes: Used to introduce an upcoming action the speaker intends to do. Often followed by a verb in the infinitive or a reflexive infinitive (e.g., 'me atrasar', 'te mimar', 'ter'). Common in spoken and written Portuguese to report intentions or inform someone.
target_language_example: Só queria dizer que vou chegar às oito.
native_language_example: I just wanted to say that I will arrive at eight.

meaning: carbon dioxide (CO2).
additional_notes: A common gas produced by respiration, combustion and decay; plants use it for photosynthesis. Used in scientific, environmental and everyday contexts. Pronunciation tip: 'dióxido' stress on 'ó'.
target_language_example: As plantas absorvem dióxido de carbono durante o dia.
native_language_example: Plants absorb carbon dioxide during the day.

meaning: of love / belonging to love
additional_notes: A prepositional phrase: 'do' = contraction of 'de' + 'o' (of the). Used to indicate possession, origin, type, or relationship with 'amor' (love). Appears in contexts like 'poção do amor' (love potion), 'deus do amor' (god of love). Translate depending on context: 'of love', 'love's', or 'the ... of love.'
target_language_example: Ela encontrou a carta do amor que recebeu há anos.
native_language_example: She found the love letter she received years ago.

meaning: inside out; turned inside out; (figuratively) very upset or turned upside down.
additional_notes: Literally means 'from the reverse' and is used for clothing (wearing something inside out) and for turning things so the inside is outside. Figuratively, it can describe a person who is emotionally disturbed/upset or a place turned upside down. Context determines literal vs. figurative meaning.
target_language_example: Ele estava com a camiseta do avesso o dia todo.
native_language_example: He had his T-shirt on inside out all day.

meaning: 'of the grandfather' / 'from the grandfather' (possessive: belonging to or related to the grandfather).
additional_notes: Do = contraction of de + o (of the / from the). Used to show possession or relation (e.g., nome do avô = grandfather's name) or source (present do avô = present from the grandfather). Often appears with a noun that follows (do avô + noun). Informal register: neutral, everyday Portuguese.
target_language_example: Ele achou a foto do avô.
native_language_example: He found his grandfather's photo.

meaning: very (intensifier), extremely; used to insult or emphasize strong feeling (crude/vulgar).
additional_notes: A highly vulgar slang phrase attached to nouns or adjectives to intensify emotion — can be positive (e.g., 'prazer do caralho' = huge pleasure) or negative/insulting (often following insults like 'vadia do caralho'). Strong profanity; avoid in polite situations. Tone is aggressive and coarse.
target_language_example: Isso foi divertido do caralho.
native_language_example: That was fucking/insanely fun.

meaning: of the cellphone / from the cellphone
additional_notes: A contraction of de + o (do) plus celular. Used to indicate possession (the cellphone belonging to someone) or origin/source (a message, call, or recording coming from a cellphone). Context determines whether it's 'of' (possession) or 'from' (origin).
target_language_example: Recebi a foto do celular dela ontem.
native_language_example: I received the photo from her cellphone yesterday.

meaning: of the corridor / in the corridor / at the end of the corridor (depending on context).
additional_notes: A prepositional phrase: 'do' = de + o (of the / from the). Commonly used to indicate location related to a corridor. Phrases in examples use 'no fim do corredor' or 'no final do corredor' meaning 'at the end of the corridor'; 'do corredor' by itself usually links something to the corridor (e.g., 'porta do corredor' = 'corridor door').
target_language_example: A janela do corredor está aberta.
native_language_example: The corridor's window is open. / The window in the corridor is open.

meaning: of the day on which / 'on the day that' (introduces a specific day when something happened).
additional_notes: Used to link an event to a specific day: 'o dia em que...' = 'the day when...'. Often appears as part of the phrase 'do dia em que' after a time expression (manhã/tarde/noite) or possession: e.g. 'na manhã do dia em que...' You can also say simply 'no dia em que...' without 'do' depending on the preceding words.
target_language_example: Lembro-me da tarde do dia em que nos mudamos para cá.
native_language_example: I remember the afternoon of the day on which we moved here.

meaning: of teaching / of education (possessive/genitive phrase).
additional_notes: A contraction of de + o (do) + ensino. Used to show possession or association with 'ensino' (teaching, education). Common in phrases like 'sistema do ensino' (the education system), 'nível do ensino' (level of education), or 'instituições do ensino' (educational institutions). Adjusts to gender/number of the article: de + a = da, de + os = dos, de + as = das.
target_language_example: O nível do ensino melhorou nos últimos anos.
native_language_example: The level of education has improved in recent years.

meaning: from the bottom of my (heart); deeply, sincerely
additional_notes: Used before a body-part word (commonly coração = heart) to emphasize deep or intense feeling. Literal structure: 'do' (of the) + 'fundo' (bottom) + 'do meu' (of my). Common in expressions of love ('do fundo do meu coração' = from the bottom of my heart) but can be used with other emotions (e.g., ódio) for emphasis. Formality: neutral; suitable for heartfelt or emphatic statements.
target_language_example: Eu te agradeço do fundo do meu coração.
native_language_example: I thank you from the bottom of my heart.

meaning: 'of the bad' or 'because of the bad' when part of expressions like 'por causa do mau tempo' meaning 'because of the bad (weather)'
additional_notes: Do mau is the contraction of 'de' + 'o' + adjective 'mau' (bad). It often appears in set phrases such as 'do mau tempo' (bad weather) or 'do mau cheiro' (bad smell). On its own it is not a complete phrase — you usually see it followed by a noun (e.g. 'do mau tempo'). When used with 'por causa' it expresses reason: 'por causa do mau tempo' = 'because of the bad weather'.
target_language_example: Por causa do mau tempo, a viagem foi cancelada.
native_language_example: Because of the bad weather, the trip was canceled.

meaning: in the world
additional_notes: Contraction of de + o. Very often used with superlatives like o melhor, o maior, o mais famoso to mean "in the world". In other contexts, it can mean more literally "of the world."
target_language_example: Ela é a cantora mais famosa do mundo.
native_language_example: She is the most famous singer in the world.

meaning: suddenly; out of nowhere; unexpectedly
additional_notes: Common informal expression used to say something happened without warning or for no apparent reason. Often used in spoken Portuguese: 'ele apareceu do nada' = 'he appeared out of nowhere.' Literally 'from nothing.'
target_language_example: Ela começou a chorar do nada.
native_language_example: She started crying out of nowhere.

meaning: of the name of / the name of (used to refer to someone's or something's name).
additional_notes: Composed of the preposition do (de + o) + nome + de; commonly appears in questions or statements asking/mentioning a person's or thing's name. Often used with lembrar(se) (to remember) or esquecer (to forget). In English it corresponds to 'the name of' or 'of the name of' depending on sentence structure.
target_language_example: Você se lembra do nome de quem fez isso?
native_language_example: Do you remember the name of who made this?

meaning: of the eye; used in expressions meaning 'blind in (one) eye' or 'missing an eye'.
additional_notes: Used after adjectives like 'cego' (blind) to specify which eye is affected: 'cego do olho direito' = blind in the right eye. Literally 'of the eye'. Common in fixed phrase 'cego do olho direito/esquerdo'.
target_language_example: Ele ficou cego do olho esquerdo após o acidente.
native_language_example: He became blind in his left eye after the accident.

meaning: of the sunset / relating to sunset
additional_notes: This phrase appears as part of 'do pôr-do-sol' meaning 'of the sunset' or 'after/before sunset' depending on context. 'Pôr-do-sol' = 'sunset'. Common combinations: 'antes do pôr-do-sol' (before sunset), 'depois do pôr-do-sol' (after sunset), 'ao pôr-do-sol' (at sunset). Use 'do' when indicating 'of' or when combining with prepositions (antes do, depois do).
target_language_example: Vamos caminhar pela praia antes do pôr-do-sol.
native_language_example: Let's walk along the beach before sunset.

meaning: of what
additional_notes: In this use, it introduces an indirect question after a word that takes de, as in ideia do que... = 'idea of what...'. It is essentially de + o que.
target_language_example: Ninguém sabe do que ele está falando.
native_language_example: No one knows what he is talking about.

meaning: 'about/what I am' — used in phrases like 'do que estou falando' (about what I am talking) or 'do que estou dizendo' (about what I am saying).
additional_notes: This is a fragment that combines the preposition 'de' + definite article 'o' (contracted to 'do') + relative pronoun 'que' + present continuous 'estou'. Common in expressions meaning 'about what I am ...' or 'what I am ... about'. You'll usually see it followed by verbs like 'falando' (talking) or 'dizendo' (saying). Use it when referring back to a topic you mentioned. Literal translation to English is possible but word order differs: 'do que estou falando' = 'about what I am talking (about)'.
target_language_example: Não entendes do que estou falando?
native_language_example: Don't you understand what I'm talking about?

meaning: 'what (you/he/she) are/is ... about' — used to ask or refer to what someone is talking about or doing
additional_notes: Commonly appears in questions like "Do que está falando?" meaning "What are you talking about?" 'Do' is a contraction of 'de' + 'o' (or 'de' + 'que' in some contexts) and here introduces 'what' (do que = 'about what' / 'what ... about'). Often used in informal spoken Portuguese; you can also see the full form 'do que você está falando' or 'do que ele/ela está falando'. Word order can change: 'Do que está falando?' = 'What are you talking about?'
target_language_example: Do que está falando? Não entendi.
native_language_example: What are you talking about? I didn't understand.

meaning: 'of what' / 'what (about)' — used to ask for clarification about the object, reason, or topic (informal spoken Portuguese).
additional_notes: Common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese. Often appears after a noun, verb, or clause to ask 'what?' about that thing (e.g., 'Você está com medo do quê?' = 'What are you afraid of?'). Can be used alone as a short question: 'Do quê?' = 'Of what?/What about?'. It contracts 'de' + 'o' + 'quê' in some contexts but here functions as 'de quê' with a preceding word. Tone and word order may be informal.
target_language_example: Ele falou sobre o projeto — do quê exatamente?
native_language_example: He talked about the project — about what exactly?

meaning: of/from the taxi; belonging to or coming from the taxi
additional_notes: This is the contraction of de + o (do) + táxi. Use 'do táxi' to indicate possession ('the driver of the taxi') or origin/motion from something ('got out of the taxi'). Context decides whether it means 'of the taxi' (possession) or 'from the taxi' (movement). For feminine/other articles, forms change (da, dos, das).
target_language_example: Ela pegou a mala do táxi e saiu apressada.
native_language_example: She grabbed the taxi's suitcase and left hurriedly.

meaning: from scratch; starting at nothing.
additional_notes: Used to say something is started again or created without using existing work, materials, or progress. Common with verbs like começar, fazer, refazer. Equivalent to English 'from scratch' or 'from zero.'
target_language_example: Ela construiu o site do zero em duas semanas.
native_language_example: She built the website from scratch in two weeks.

meaning: twice as much (of), double the amount of
additional_notes: Used to compare quantities: 'o dobro de X' = two times X. Can appear with numbers, nouns, or pronouns (e.g., 'o dobro de livros', 'o dobro de dinheiro'). Often followed by 'que' when comparing people or things (e.g., 'o dobro de livros que ele').
target_language_example: Ela tem o dobro de paciência que eu.
native_language_example: She has twice as much patience as I do.

meaning: twice as much as; double (of/from).
additional_notes: Used to compare quantity, price, size, time, etc. Structure: 'X é/está/tem o dobro do/de + [noun or clause]' or 'verbo + o dobro do que + [clause]'. Often followed by 'do que' before a clause (e.g. 'o dobro do que eu como') or 'do' + article + noun (e.g. 'o dobro do preço').
target_language_example: Esta câmera custa o dobro do que eu paguei pela minha.
native_language_example: This camera costs twice as much as what I paid for mine.

meaning: document (that is) for/to (someone) or for translation into (a language).
additional_notes: A combination of 'documento' (document) plus the preposition 'para' (for/to). Depending on context, 'para' can indicate the recipient ('for Tom') or the target language in translation requests ('para o francês' = into French). Word order can vary (e.g., 'traduzir este documento para o francês' or 'para mim este documento').
target_language_example: Enviei o documento para o gerente.
native_language_example: I sent the document to the manager.

meaning: literally 'two brothers'; can be a place name (e.g., town, neighborhood) or refer to two male siblings.
additional_notes: Capitalization matters: 'dois Irmãos' with capitals often appears as a proper noun — the name of towns in Brazil or Portugal (e.g., Dois Irmãos, a municipality). In normal sentences about siblings, you'd write 'dois irmãos' (lowercase). Use context to tell if it's a place or simply 'two brothers'.
target_language_example: Eu nasci em Dois Irmãos, mas tenho dois irmãos de verdade.
native_language_example: I was born in Dois Irmãos, but I actually have two brothers.

meaning: two more years; an additional two years
additional_notes: Used to indicate an extra period of two years added to a previous duration or from now. Context determines whether it modifies a verb (e.g., 'stay for two more years') or a noun phrase (e.g., 'two more years of experience'). Can often appear as 'mais dois anos' in speech; both are understood.
target_language_example: Vou ficar aqui dois anos mais.
native_language_example: I'll stay here for two more years.

meaning: two years older (masculine)
additional_notes: Used to say someone is older by two years. 'Mais velho' agrees in gender with the person described (masculine here). For feminine use 'mais velha'. Common structure: [person] é dois anos mais velho que [other person]. Can be used with names or pronouns. Variations: 'dois anos mais velho do que' (both 'que' and 'do que' are possible).
target_language_example: Meu irmão é dois anos mais velho que eu.
native_language_example: My brother is two years older than me.

meaning: 'you two are' / 'the two of you are' (present tense)
additional_notes: Used when addressing or referring to two people (vocês dois) to ask about their state, action, or relationship. In Portuguese, 'vocês dois' (you two) + verb 'estão' (are). The phrase itself isn't standalone; it appears in contexts like questions: 'Vocês dois estão ...?' Replace 'vocês' with names or 'eles/elas' for third person. Informal to neutral register.
target_language_example: Vocês dois estão prontos para sair?
native_language_example: Are you two ready to leave?

meaning: two or (used as part of 'two or three', 'two or so' -> about a small number/short time).
additional_notes: Usually appears in the pattern 'dois ou três' (two or three) to mean 'about two or three' or 'a couple of (small number/time)'. Used with countable nouns and time expressions (dias, meses, minutos). It's informal-neutral and common in spoken and written Portuguese to indicate approximation.
target_language_example: Vou terminar em dois ou três minutos.
native_language_example: I'll finish in two or three minutes.

meaning: 'two points' — can mean a score difference of two points or a value of two points (e.g., in grading).
additional_notes: Used both for scores (losing/winning by two points) and for point value (an assignment worth two points). Context tells whether it's a margin or a value. Pronunciation: [doysh POHN-toosh].
target_language_example: Perdemos por dois pontos no último minuto.
native_language_example: We lost by two points in the last minute.

meaning: 'two are' or 'both are' (used to say something about two people/things).
additional_notes: Combines the numeral 'dois' (two) with the verb 'são' (3rd person plural of ser = to be). Used to state a fact about two items or people (e.g., identity, origin, quality). In spoken Portuguese you will often see variations: 'os dois são' (the two are), 'vocês dois são' (you two are), or simply 'vocês são' when context makes 'two' clear. For counting or arithmetic, 'dois e dois são quatro' = 'two and two are four.'
target_language_example: Vocês dois são bem-vindos aqui.
native_language_example: You two are welcome here.

meaning: 'the two (of them) are going to' or 'you two are going to' (future with plural subject)
additional_notes: Dois (or vocês dois/ambos) indicates two people; 'vão' is the 3rd-person plural present of 'ir' used to form the near future (going to). Depending on context, it can mean 'the two of them will...' or address 'you two will...'. Often appears as 'vocês dois vão' (you two will) or 'os dois vão' (the two of them will).
target_language_example: Vocês dois vão viajar para Portugal no verão?
native_language_example: Are you two going to travel to Portugal in the summer?

meaning: housewife; a woman who manages the household and may not work outside the home.
additional_notes: Common term referring to a woman whose primary role is running the home (cleaning, cooking, caring for family). Can be neutral, descriptive, or carry stereotypical/negative connotations depending on context (e.g., 'só uma dona de casa' can sound diminishing). Female-specific; the male equivalent is 'dono de casa' or more often 'homem que cuida da casa'.
target_language_example: Minha avó foi dona de casa a vida inteira.
native_language_example: My grandmother was a housewife her whole life.

meaning: 'owner of' (masculine; used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to indicate ownership or proprietorship of something. Portuguese uses gendered articles: dono da = owner of the (feminine) + noun (da = de + a). If the noun is masculine, use dono do. Can refer to businesses, houses, objects, or metaphorical ownership (e.g., 'dono da colmeia' = owner/controller of the hive).
target_language_example: Ele é dono da loja no centro.
native_language_example: He is the owner of the shop downtown.

meaning: headache; pain in the head.
additional_notes: Common, neutral phrase used to describe any headache (mild to severe). Often used with verbs like ter, estar com, acordar com, and with adjectives (leve, forte, terrível). Can be treated as countable in Portuguese (uma dor de cabeça).
target_language_example: Estou com uma dor de cabeça desde esta manhã.
native_language_example: I've had a headache since this morning.

meaning: pain in the (female plural) — used before a body part (e.g., 'dor nas costas' = pain in the back)
additional_notes: This is the feminine plural contraction of 'dor' (pain) + the preposition 'em' + the plural feminine article 'as' (dor nas = dor em + as). It is followed by a plural feminine noun (nas costas, nas pernas). For singular or masculine use you'd say 'dor no' (masc. sing.) or 'dor na' (fem. sing.). Commonly used to describe location of pain.
target_language_example: Tenho dor nas costas desde ontem.
native_language_example: I've had pain in my back since yesterday.

meaning: 'sleeps in/on the' (third-person singular of 'dormir' + definite article or contraction 'no').
additional_notes: Used for third-person singular (ele/ela) or impersonal/imperative forms to say where someone/something sleeps. 'No' is the contraction of the preposition 'em' + definite article 'o' (in the/at the). For feminine nouns use 'na' (dorme na). Can also appear with places like carro (in the car), chão (on the floor), hotel (at the hotel).
target_language_example: Ele dorme no sofá esta tarde.
native_language_example: He sleeps on the sofa this afternoon.

meaning: 'to sleep at' or 'to sleep in/at (a place)'.
additional_notes: A combination of the verb dormir (to sleep) + the preposition na (contraction of em + a = in/at the). Used before a feminine singular noun (e.g., casa) to say you will sleep at/in that place. For other genders/forms use dormir no (masculine) or dormir na/numas depending on article. Common in everyday speech when saying where you will sleep.
target_language_example: Vou dormir na casa da Emma.
native_language_example: I'll sleep at Emma's house.

meaning: to sleep (or not sleep) because of; used to give the reason for sleeping or for not being able to sleep.
additional_notes: Commonly appears as 'dormir por causa de ...' or in negative sentences like 'não consegui/não posso dormir por causa do [ruído/calor]'. Use 'por causa de' + noun or phrase to state the cause. If you want to say 'because' with a verb clause, use 'porque' instead.
target_language_example: Não consigo dormir por causa do barulho da rua.
native_language_example: I can't sleep because of the noise from the street.

target_language_multi_word_term: dormiu o / dormiu o dia todo
meaning: 'slept' (often followed by a time period: e.g. 'slept the whole day')
additional_notes: Common structure: 'dormiu o dia todo' or 'dormiu o dia inteiro' = 'slept all day'. Portuguese often uses the definite article (o/a) with time expressions (o dia, a noite). Use 'dormiu' for he/she/you (formal) past; for questions with você: 'Você dormiu...?' For 'slept enough' use 'dormiu o suficiente?'.
target_language_example: Ela dormiu o dia todo e ainda está cansada.
native_language_example: She slept all day and is still tired.

meaning: 'I give the' (first-person singular of 'dar' + definite article 'o')
additional_notes: Combination of the verb dar (to give) in the present tense (eu dou = I give) followed by the masculine singular definite article 'o'. Used before masculine nouns (e.g., 'dou o recado', 'dou o dinheiro'). In spoken Portuguese you may also hear clitic pronouns or variations (e.g., 'dou-lhe' in more formal/written Portuguese).
target_language_example: Eu dou o presente ao amigo amanhã.
native_language_example: I give the gift to my friend tomorrow.

meaning: gets along with; has a good relationship with
additional_notes: Commonly used in the reflexive form 'se dá bem com' to indicate that someone has a friendly or compatible relationship with another person, group, or animal. Conjugate 'dar' and include reflexive pronouns: eu me dou bem com, tu te dás bem com (Portugal), ele/ela se dá bem com, nós nos damos bem com, vocês se dão bem com. Widely used in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ela se dá bem com todo mundo, menos com a cunhada.
native_language_example: She gets along with everyone, except with her sister-in-law.

meaning: 'give the' (informal spoken imperative/request or simple present: third-person gives the ... / you give the ...).
additional_notes: A combination of the verb dar (to give) in the simple present or imperative and the masculine definite article o. In speech, 'dá o' can be a command/request (Give the ... / Give me the ...) or a statement (he/she gives the ...). Often appears with an object after it (dá o dinheiro, dá o troco). In informal contexts 'me dá' is common for 'give me' (equivalent to 'give me' in English). Word order and pronoun placement: 'me dá o X' = 'give me the X'.
target_language_example: Me dá o passaporte, por favor.
native_language_example: Give me the passport, please.

meaning: 'give some' or 'give any' (polite imperative + feminine object pronoun/quantifier)
additional_notes: Combination of the formal/polite imperative of dar (dê) + the adjective/pronoun alguma. Used to ask someone politely to give or offer some amount/item, often followed by a feminine noun (e.g., 'dê alguma informação', 'dê alguma ajuda'). Can also mean 'give any' in questions or requests ('dê alguma dica?'). Context determines whether it's a request, suggestion or rhetorical. Note: 'dê' is formal/tu-subjunctive or você imperative (use with você). For informal tú/imperative use 'dá alguma'.
target_language_example: Por favor, dê alguma informação sobre o horário.
native_language_example: Please give some information about the schedule.

meaning: Give the (to me / to someone) — imperative form 'give' + masculine singular definite article.
additional_notes: Dê is the formal/imperative/subjunctive form of dar (to give). When followed by o (the), it introduces a masculine singular noun: 'dê o copo' = 'give the glass'. In everyday speech, for requests to another person you might hear 'me dê' ('give me') + noun (e.g. 'me dê o leite'). 'Dê o fora' is an idiomatic expression meaning 'get out' or 'go away' (literally 'give the out'), so word combinations can be idiomatic. Use 'me dê' for 'give me' and change the article to 'a' for feminine nouns (e.g. 'me dê a faca').
target_language_example: Me dê o livro, por favor.
native_language_example: Give me the book, please.

meaning: 'give your' (imperative, polite/formal or neutral request)
additional_notes: Imperative form of dar (dê) + possessive seu (your). Used to ask someone to hand over or provide something that belongs to them (phone, book, consent, etc.). 'Dê' is the formal/you (singular) imperative (also used in neutral polite contexts). If addressing a friend informally, Brazilians often say 'me dá seu...' (present indicative used as an informal imperative) or use 'dá-me o seu...' in European Portuguese. 'Seu' can mean 'your', but be aware it may be ambiguous in Brazilian Portuguese (could refer to 'his/her/your formal'); context usually makes it clear. To specify politeness or number: use 'dê-me' (give me) or 'dê-nos' (give us).
target_language_example: Dê seu número para eu ligar depois.
native_language_example: Give your number so I can call later.

meaning: 'give a little' or 'give a bit' (imperative/request).
additional_notes: Used to ask or tell someone to give a small amount of something (milk, money, etc.). 'Dê' is the formal/third-person singular imperative of 'dar' (you give — pol./fam. depending on context); in casual speech Brazilians often say 'me dá um pouco' (using indicative). Can be followed by 'de' + noun (de leite, de dinheiro) or stand alone when context is clear. Tone can be polite or neutral depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Por favor, dê um pouco de água às plantas enquanto eu viajar.
native_language_example: Please give a little water to the plants while I travel.

meaning: and so on; and the like; etc.
additional_notes: Used to indicate continuation of a list or ongoing actions/things without specifying all items. Equivalent to English "and so on" or "etc." Can stand alone ("E assim por diante.") to mean "and so on" in conversation. Common in both spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: Compramos pão, leite, frutas e assim por diante.
native_language_example: We bought bread, milk, fruit and so on.

meaning: hey
additional_notes: Informal greeting or conversational opener used to check in, get someone's attention, or prompt a response. Tone depends on context: can be friendly ('hey / what's up?'), neutral ('so?'), or expectant ('and then? / what about it?'). Very common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese.
target_language_example: E aí, tudo bem?
native_language_example: Hey, everything ok?

meaning: 'and how' or 'and like' — used to add an explanation, example, or emphasis
additional_notes: Commonly used to introduce an explanation, clarification, example, or to emphasize what was just said. In spoken Portuguese it can be followed by a clause (e como... + clause) or a short phrase/word (e como... + noun/adverb). In informal speech it can also function like English 'and stuff' or 'and so on' when trailing off. Word-for-word translation is 'and' (e) + 'how' (como).
target_language_example: Ele explicou o problema, e como resultado tivemos que mudar o plano.
native_language_example: He explained the problem, and as a result we had to change the plan.

meaning: 'so what?' or 'and then?' depending on context.
additional_notes: Used to challenge or dismiss what was just said (equivalent to 'so what?') or to ask what happened next/what followed (equivalent to 'and then?'). Tone depends on intonation and context: can be confrontational, indifferent, or inquisitive. Common in informal speech.
target_language_example: Ele mentiu para você. — E daí?
native_language_example: He lied to you. — So what?

meaning: a conversational way to say 'so, what...' or 'and then, what...'
additional_notes: Used to prompt for information, a next action, or a consequence. Common in spoken Portuguese to start questions about what happened, what someone will do, or what someone does (for fun). The phrase can appear as 'E então, o que...?' or simply 'E então...?'. Tone is neutral and fits everyday conversation.
target_language_example: E então, o que você vai dizer ao chefe?
native_language_example: So, what are you going to tell the boss?

meaning: 'and Spanish' — used to link Spanish with another language or item.
additional_notes: A conjunction phrase: 'e' means 'and'. Commonly follows a list of languages or nouns. Word order is the same as English: X e espanhol = X and Spanish. Pronunciation: e = /i/ (sounds like English 'ee'). No change for gender or number.
target_language_example: Ela estuda francês e espanhol.
native_language_example: She studies French and Spanish.

meaning: and I like (it/him/her/that).
additional_notes: A simple connector + personal comment: 'e' = 'and', 'eu gosto' = 'I like'. Often follows a statement to express personal approval or enjoyment of something just mentioned. Can refer to a thing (gosto disso), a person (gosto dele/dela) or a general idea; tone can be emphatic or casual depending on context.
target_language_example: Ela me ajuda nos projetos, e eu gosto.
native_language_example: She helps me with the projects, and I like that.

meaning: 'and here we go' / 'and off we go' — used to introduce doing something (often with resignation or inevitability).
additional_notes: Common conversational phrase to signal the start of an action or that something is happening again. Often followed by 'nós' (e lá vamos nós) meaning 'here we go (again)'. Can express excitement, resignation, or inevitability depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: E lá vamos nós outra vez para mais uma reunião longa.
native_language_example: And here we go again for another long meeting.

meaning: and (he/she/it) hurt (himself/herself/it); and injured (someone or a body part).
additional_notes: Commonly follows a verb of motion (caiu, escorregou) to say that someone was hurt as a result. 'Machucar' is a regular verb meaning 'to hurt' or 'to injure'. The subject can be omitted if clear from context; possessive (a perna / sua perna) specifies the injured body part. Use past tense here (simple past/pretérito: machucou).
target_language_example: Ela tropeçou na escada e machucou o braço.
native_language_example: She tripped on the stairs and hurt her arm.

meaning: 'and nine' — the conjunction 'e' (and) followed by the number nine
additional_notes: Used when listing or connecting items where one of them is the number nine. 'e' simply means 'and'. In spoken Portuguese numbers are often connected with 'e' in lists (e.g., 'três e nove' = 'three and nine'). This is literal and compositional.
target_language_example: Comprei uma camiseta, uma calça e nove pares de meias.
native_language_example: I bought a T-shirt, a pair of pants and nine pairs of socks.

meaning: 'and the brother' (used to link a person with their brother)
additional_notes: Commonly used after a name to mention that person's brother (e.g., 'Tom e o irmão dele' = 'Tom and his brother'). In English you might also say 'Tom and his brother' or 'Tom and the brother' depending on context; in Portuguese the possessive can follow ('o irmão dele') or be omitted if context makes it clear. This construction is literal and compositional.
target_language_example: Maria e o irmão dela moram na mesma cidade.
native_language_example: Maria and her brother live in the same city.

meaning: 'and where you' — used to ask or connect to a question about someone's location or where something happened/will happen.
additional_notes: Commonly appears at the start of a question or after another question/statement (the 'e' = 'and' or 'so') to ask about location, origin, or destination. Can be used with different tenses: está/estava (where are/were you), vai achar (where will you find), comprou (where did you buy), quer se encontrar (where do you want to meet). In casual speech 'você' may be replaced by 'tu' in some regions.
target_language_example: E onde você quer se encontrar amanhã?
native_language_example: And where do you want to meet tomorrow?

meaning: 'and why do you' / 'and why are you' — used to ask for a reason about the person addressed
additional_notes: Common conversational phrase that begins a follow-up question. 'E' here functions like 'and' or 'so' to continue or challenge a previous statement. Can be used neutrally to ask for explanation (E por que você está aqui?) or more confrontationally/ironically (E por que você não se manda?). Verb after 'você' can be any conjugated verb. Often pronounced quickly in speech.
target_language_example: E por que você não veio ontem?
native_language_example: And why didn't you come yesterday?

meaning: 'and broke the' (masculine singular object).
additional_notes: This is a short sequence combining the conjunction e (and) + the verb quebrar (to break) in the past tense (quebrou) + the masculine singular definite article o. It appears before a masculine noun (e.g., 'e quebrou o vidro' = 'and broke the glass'). Use o for masculine singular objects; use a for feminine (e.g., 'e quebrou a'). Verb tense is simple past (pretérito perfeito) indicating a completed action.
target_language_example: Ela tropeçou e quebrou o vaso.
native_language_example: She tripped and broke the vase.

meaning: 'and leave' / 'and go out' (imperative, plural or formal plural)
additional_notes: Used to connect an instruction with the command to leave or move out. 'Saiam' is the imperative form of 'sair' for vocês (you plural) or senhoras/senhores in polite plural contexts. Often follows another verb or phrase: 'Larguem as armas e saiam' = 'Drop your weapons and leave.' Tone depends on context—can be urgent, commanding, or simply directional. For one person (informal) use 'e sai' and for formal singular use 'e saia'.
target_language_example: Fechem as portas e saiam do prédio.
native_language_example: Close the doors and leave the building.

meaning: 'and except' or 'and safe' depending on context; most often used in legal/formal phrases meaning 'and except' or 'except for'.
additional_notes: Used as a connector to exclude something from a general statement. Common in formal, legal, or written contexts (similar to 'except' or 'save' in legal English). It can also appear in older or very formal texts meaning 'and, unless' or 'and excepting'. Not commonly used in everyday spoken Brazilian Portuguese; in conversation people more often say 'exceto', 'salvo', or 'a não ser'.
target_language_example: Todos assinaram o documento, e salvo a menção em contrário, a decisão é válida.
native_language_example: Everyone signed the document, and except as otherwise stated, the decision is valid.

meaning: 'and (he/she/they) moved (away or changed residence)'.
additional_notes: This is the conjunction 'e' (and) + the pronominal verb 'mudar‑se' in the simple past (pretérito perfeito): 'se mudou' = 'moved (oneself)', used to say someone changed residence. Subject is implied by context (ele/ela/eles/elas). Common in narratives: 'Fulano trabalhou aqui e se mudou' = 'So‑and‑so worked here and then moved.'
target_language_example: Ela morou na mesma rua por anos e se mudou no mês passado.
native_language_example: She lived on the same street for years and moved last month.

meaning: what if
additional_notes: Often used to introduce a hypothetical possibility, worry, or suggestion: e se...? = 'what if...?' Literally it is 'and if', so in some contexts it can also simply connect clauses with that more literal meaning.
target_language_example: E se chover amanhã?
native_language_example: What if it rains tomorrow?

meaning: and so on; and stuff; etc.
additional_notes: Informal filler phrase used to indicate unspecified similar things, to soften statements, or to trail off. Common in spoken Portuguese. Can be used like 'etc.' or 'and stuff' after listing items or when you don't want to be specific.
target_language_example: Compramos pão, queijo e tal para o café da manhã.
native_language_example: We bought bread, cheese, and stuff for breakfast.

meaning: a strong emphasis meaning 'quite a (something)', 'a real/serious (something)' or 'very impressive'.
additional_notes: Used after a noun or phrase to emphasize size, intensity, importance or impressiveness. Equivalent to 'quite a', 'a real', 'a great' in English. Often follows words like 'explosão', 'feito', 'escolha' to boost impact. Informal to neutral; common in speech and writing.
target_language_example: Foi uma festa e tanto.
native_language_example: It was quite a party.

meaning: and I work / and (I) work
additional_notes: Commonly used after a clause about living or being with someone/place to add that the speaker also works there. The subject pronoun (eu/ele/etc.) is often omitted in Portuguese, so 'e trabalho' means '(and) I work' when the speaker is talking about themselves. Can follow verbs like 'moro' (I live) or 'vivo' (I live).
target_language_example: Moro e trabalho no Brasil.
native_language_example: I live and work in Brazil.

meaning: 'and everything' / 'and all that' (a short, colloquial way to add other related things or emphasize completeness).
additional_notes: Used informally to add unspecified additional items or to emphasize that something includes everything else related. Often appears as 'e tudo o mais', 'e tudo', or in phrases like 'e tudo organizado' to mean 'and everything is organized.' Common in spoken Portuguese.
target_language_example: Ele trouxe os documentos, assinou e tudo.
native_language_example: He brought the documents, signed them, and everything.

meaning: 'and you are' (used to connect a previous statement to something about 'you')
additional_notes: A common connector: 'e' = 'and', followed by the present progressive 'você está' (you are ...). Often introduces an action, state, or contrast about the person 'you'. In spoken Portuguese it can also be used to emphasize or continue a thought ('and you are ...' / 'and you're ...'). The verb that follows determines tense/aspect (e.g. 'e você está indo' = 'and you are leaving'; 'e você está sempre' = 'and you are always').
target_language_example: E você está mentindo para mim?
native_language_example: And you are lying to me?

meaning: 'the e-mail that' or 'the e-mail which' (used to introduce a relative clause about an email).
additional_notes: Combines e-mail (email) with the relative pronoun que. Used to refer to a specific message previously mentioned or known by context. Word order is like English: 'o e-mail que ...' = 'the email that ...'. In spoken Portuguese, e-mail is common; you may also hear 'o email' without the hyphen. The clause after que gives more information (who sent it, when, what happened to it).
target_language_example: Você já respondeu o e-mail que ela te enviou?
native_language_example: Have you already replied to the email that she sent you?

meaning: saving (money) to / saving up for (something).
additional_notes: Used with a verb of purpose (usually 'comprar', 'pagar', etc.) or a noun to indicate saving money with the goal of obtaining something. Common construction: estar + economizando para + infinitive or noun (e.g., 'estou economizando para comprar um carro' or 'estou economizando para um carro'). Can be used in different tenses (economizo, estava economizando, vou economizar).
target_language_example: Estou economizando para viajar no próximo ano.
native_language_example: I'm saving up to travel next year.

meaning: 'education is' — a way to state what education represents or its importance.
additional_notes: Used to introduce an opinion, definition, or general statement about education (e.g., its value, role, or quality). Commonly followed by nouns, adjectives, or phrases like 'a chave para o sucesso', 'fundamental', 'muito importante', or descriptions of benefits. Formal or neutral register.
target_language_example: A educação é a base para uma sociedade justa.
native_language_example: Education is the foundation for a just society.

meaning: side effect; an unintended secondary effect (often negative).
additional_notes: Commonly used in medical contexts for drug side effects, but also used figuratively for any unintended consequence of an action or policy. Plural: efeitos colaterais.
target_language_example: Ele sofreu um efeito colateral inesperado após tomar o medicamento.
native_language_example: He suffered an unexpected side effect after taking the medication.

meaning: 'she still is' or 'she is still'.
additional_notes: Used to say that a female person remains in a certain state, role, age, or quality. 'Ainda' means 'still' (continuation), and 'é' is the present tense of 'ser' (to be). Can be followed by a noun, adjective, or phrase. Context determines nuance (e.g., age, relationship status, reputation).
target_language_example: Ela ainda é estudante, apesar do trabalho.
native_language_example: She is still a student despite the job.

meaning: 'she helps' or 'she is helping'.
additional_notes: Present tense of ajudar (to help) with the subject pronoun ela (she). Used to describe habitual or current acts of assistance. Can be followed by a preposition (em, na, com) plus place or by a direct object (quem/alguma coisa). Common in everyday contexts.
target_language_example: Ela ajuda os vizinhos a carregar as compras.
native_language_example: She helps the neighbors carry the groceries.

meaning: she married / she got married
additional_notes: Used to say that a woman entered marriage. Can appear as 'ela casou' (colloquial) or reflexive 'ela casou-se' (more formal/standard). Often followed by 'com' + person (ela casou com ele) or by circumstances (ex.: 'sem que seus pais soubessem'). In informal speech the reflexive pronoun is often dropped. Can also be used in colloquial exclamations (e.g., 'que ela casou comigo!' meaning 'she actually married me!').
target_language_example: Ela casou-se com um amigo de infância no sábado.
native_language_example: She married a childhood friend on Saturday.

meaning: 'she changed' (past tense of 'mudar' — to change, move, or alter).
additional_notes: Used to say a woman changed something (her mind, clothes, hairstyle, version) or moved residence. Context determines whether it's physical relocation (mudar de cidade), changing an object/state (mudar tudo), changing topic (mudar de assunto) or changing opinion (mudar de ideia). In Portuguese, mudar is intransitive when followed by 'de' + noun (mudar de cidade, mudar de assunto) and transitive when directly followed by an object (mudar a versão).
target_language_example: Depois do desacordo, ela mudou de ideia.
native_language_example: After the disagreement, she changed her mind.

meaning: 'she was not' (past tense of 'to be')
additional_notes: Used to negate a past-state or past-identity of a female subject. 'Ela' = she; 'não' = not; 'era' = imperfect past of 'ser' (was/were). Common for descriptions, identities, or habitual/past characteristics. For simple past completed actions Portuguese often uses 'foi', but 'era' emphasizes ongoing/past state or background.
target_language_example: Ela não era minha professora, era minha vizinha.
