native_language_example: She was not my teacher, she was my neighbor.

meaning: she could / she was able to (past tense, imperfect or conditional depending on context)
additional_notes: Ela podia is the third-person singular of the verb poder in the imperfect (or conditional in some contexts). Use it to talk about ability or possibility in the past (she was able to / could) or to express a tentative/conditional meaning (she could, as in 'she could help us'). Context (tone, other verbs) tells whether it means past habitual/ongoing ability or a conditional possibility.
target_language_example: Ela podia nos ajudar, se tivesse tempo.
native_language_example: She could help us, if she had time.

meaning: part of a sentence meaning 'tell her that I am...' (used when asking someone to inform a female about what you are doing)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom—it's the sequence 'ela' (her) + 'que' (that) + 'estou' (I am). Commonly appears in requests like 'Diga a/para ela que estou...' followed by a verb in the gerund or an activity (me vestindo, ouvindo música, assistindo, comendo). Use 'a ela' or 'para ela' before 'que'.
target_language_example: Diga a ela que estou trabalhando agora.
native_language_example: Tell her that I am working now.

meaning: used to report or tell someone (her) something about you; literally 'to her that you...'.
additional_notes: This sequence appears in reported-speech constructions: 'dizer/ dizer a/ dizer a ela que você...' = 'tell her that you...'. It's formed from the indirect object pronoun 'ela' (her) + conjunction 'que' (that) + subject 'você' (you). Word order can vary: commonly 'dizer a ela que você...' or 'disse a ela que...'. In spoken Portuguese 'pra' or 'para' may replace 'a' (dizer pra ela que...).
target_language_example: Diz a ela que você precisa de ajuda.
native_language_example: Tell her that you need help.

meaning: 'she knows the' or 'she knows it' (depends on what follows).
additional_notes: This is a fragment: 'ela' = she, 'sabe' = knows, 'o' is a masculine singular direct object pronoun or definite article. Most commonly in speech 'o' stands for 'it' (masculine) as a clitic pronoun attached to verbs: ela o sabe → she knows it. In modern spoken Portuguese the pronoun often appears after the verb (ela sabe-o) or more commonly before the verb as 'ela o sabe' (Portugal) or replaced by 'ela sabe' with context (Brazil). If 'o' is an article, it would start a noun (ela sabe o motivo = she knows the reason). Pay attention to gender agreement: 'o' refers to masculine nouns; for feminine use 'a' (ela sabe a / ela a sabe).
target_language_example: Ela sabe o motivo do atraso.
native_language_example: She knows the reason for the delay.

meaning: she sat down near (someone or something).
additional_notes: A simple past action: 'ela se sentou' = 'she sat (herself) down'. 'Perto' means 'near' or 'close to' and is usually followed by a person or place (e.g., 'perto dele' = 'near him'). Commonly used to describe physical proximity. Word order can change (e.g., 'ela sentou-se perto' is more formal).
target_language_example: Ela se sentou perto da janela e começou a ler.
native_language_example: She sat down near the window and began to read.

meaning: she has (in a subordinate clause; used with the subjunctive perfect).
additional_notes: Used in contexts of doubt, possibility, emotion or uncertainty (subjunctive). Commonly appears after verbs/expressions like duvidar que, não acho que, talvez, é possível que. It pairs with a past participle (ex.: tenha feito) to mean 'that she has done' or 'that she did' with an uncertain or hypothetical tone.
target_language_example: Duvido que ela tenha visto o e-mail.
native_language_example: I doubt that she has seen the email.

meaning: she will have
additional_notes: Future tense of ter with ela. It can mean possession or receiving something, and with um bebê/um filho it means she will have a baby. In Portuguese, the pronoun is often omitted, so terá by itself can also mean he/she/you (formal) will have.
target_language_example: Ela terá mais tempo amanhã.
native_language_example: She will have more time tomorrow.

meaning: she had to / she needed to (expresses obligation or necessity in the past)
additional_notes: Common way to express a past obligation or necessity. 'Tinha que' + infinitive = 'had to do something' (imperfect tense). Can imply repeated/ongoing obligation or a specific past necessity depending on context. For a single completed past obligation, Portuguese often uses 'teve que' (preterite).
target_language_example: Ela tinha que estudar todas as noites.
native_language_example: She had to study every night.

meaning: she had to do that / she had to do it
additional_notes: Expresses past obligation or necessity using 'ter que' + infinitive. 'Tinha' is the imperfect of 'ter', implying a past requirement, repeated/ongoing obligation, or a past situation. 'Fazer isso' = 'do that' or 'do it' (refers to a previously mentioned action). Context determines whether translated as 'had to' or 'needed to'.
target_language_example: Ela tinha que fazer isso antes que fosse tarde.
native_language_example: She had to do that before it was too late.

meaning: she takes / she has (used with actions like 'take a bath', 'take care of', or 'borrow').
additional_notes: Toma is the 3rd-person singular present of 'tomar' and combines with nouns or expressions to form common actions: 'toma banho' = takes a bath, 'toma conta' = takes care (of), 'toma emprestado' = borrows. Context and the noun following 'toma' determine the exact English verb. Use 'ela' for 'she'.
target_language_example: Ela toma um copo d'água antes de sair.
native_language_example: She has a glass of water before leaving.

meaning: 'he said that...' followed by a reflexive or subordinate clause starting with 'se' (if/that himself/oneself/etc.)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the sequence of words 'ele disse que se' appears when reporting speech: 'ele disse que' = 'he said that' and 'se' introduces a reflexive pronoun or a subordinate clause (often conditional: 'se' = 'if', or reflexive 'se' = himself/oneself). You will need to look at the words that follow to know the exact sense (e.g., 'ele disse que se lembraria' = 'he said that he would remember' or 'ele disse que se o problema persistir...' = 'he said that if the problem persists...').
target_language_example: Ele disse que se lembraria de ligar amanhã.
native_language_example: He said that he would remember to call tomorrow.

meaning: 'he was lying down' (masculine subject).
additional_notes: Used to describe a male person in a horizontal position (lying), often with a location or body orientation: deitado de costas (lying on his back). 'Estava' is the past imperfect of 'estar' (ongoing or background action). For a female subject use 'ela estava deitada'.
target_language_example: Ele estava deitado no parque olhando para o céu.
native_language_example: He was lying down in the park looking at the sky.

meaning: he is now / where he is now (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literal components: ele (he), está (is), agora (now). Commonly used to ask or state someone's current location or situation. In questions, usually shortened to 'onde ele está agora?' (Where is he now?). Can refer to physical location or current status/state.
target_language_example: Não sei onde ele está agora; vou ligar para descobrir.
native_language_example: I don't know where he is now; I'll call to find out.

meaning: he washes / he is washing (third-person singular of 'lavar').
additional_notes: Simple present (or habitual) form of the verb 'lavar' (to wash). Used for actions like washing clothes, hair, or a car. In Portuguese, context determines tense (present habitual or current action). In sentence 5 ('Ele lava os nomes e aí coloca o dele.') the verb is used figuratively: 'lavar os nomes' suggests manipulating or erasing names (idiomatic) rather than literal washing.
target_language_example: Ele lava a louça depois do jantar.
native_language_example: He washes the dishes after dinner.

meaning: 'he passed (in/on)' — used to say someone passed an exam/test or was accepted (into something).
additional_notes: Used before an exam/test or selection (exame, teste, concurso, vestibular). 'Passar em' = to pass (succeed in) or to get into. Common in statements and questions. Conjugation changes with subject (eu passei, ela passou, eles passaram). With articles it becomes 'passou no' (masculine singular) or 'na'/'no' depending on the noun: 'passou no exame', 'passou na prova'.
target_language_example: Ele passou no vestibular e vai estudar medicina.
native_language_example: He passed the college entrance exam and will study medicine.

meaning: 'he could do that' or 'he would be able to do that' (polite/conditional)
additional_notes: Contains the pronoun 'ele' (he) + conditional/polite verb form 'poderia' (could/would be able to) + 'fazer isso' (do that). Used to talk about someone's ability or possibility in a hypothetical or polite context. Can refer to past or present hypothetical situations depending on context. To make it a question, intonation or punctuation is added (e.g., 'ele poderia fazer isso?').
target_language_example: Eu acho que ele poderia fazer isso se tivesse mais tempo.
native_language_example: I think he could do that if he had more time.

meaning: he solved/fixed the (problem/issue).
additional_notes: Common phrase meaning someone took care of or solved something. 'Resolveu' is past of 'resolver' (to resolve/solve). The noun that follows (e.g., 'problema') completes the phrase. Can imply doing it quickly or by oneself depending on adverbs in the sentence (facilmente, por conta própria, rapidinho).
target_language_example: Ele resolveu o problema sozinho.
native_language_example: He solved the problem by himself.

meaning: he might be a
additional_notes: Used in subordinate clauses expressing belief, doubt or possibility about a man's identity or role. 'Seja' is the present subjunctive of 'ser' and is used after verbs/expressions like acreditar, crer, talvez, or in impersonal constructions (acredita-se). The English equivalent depends on context: often 'he might be' / 'he may be' (possibility) or 'that he is' after verbs of belief. The article following 'um' can change (um/uma/o/o) per noun gender/definiteness.
target_language_example: Talvez ele seja um bom médico.
native_language_example: Maybe he is a good doctor.

meaning: 'he was wearing' or 'he used to wear' (past imperfect of 'usar')
additional_notes: Ele usava is the third-person singular imperfect form of usar. In most contexts it describes what someone was wearing at the time (he was wearing) or a habitual/action in the past (he used to wear). Context (like surrounding verbs or time expressions) tells whether it's continuous/past action or habitual. Usar can mean 'to wear' (clothes, glasses) or 'to use' depending on context.
target_language_example: Ele usava um casaco vermelho naquela noite.
native_language_example: He was wearing a red coat that night.

meaning: 'he used' or 'he made use of'.
additional_notes: Simple past (pretérito perfeito) of 'usar' for 'ele' (he). Can mean physically using an object (use a bike, dictionary), using something as a tool or shield, or using a tone/strategy (make use of). Context determines literal vs. figurative use. Common in everyday speech and writing.
target_language_example: Ele usou meu computador por uma hora.
native_language_example: He used my computer for one hour.

meaning: he (is) the last one (female) / he's the worst (colloquial, ironic)
additional_notes: Literal meaning: 'he is the last (one)'. In Portuguese, última is feminine; this phrase can sound ungrammatical if referring to a male person unless used ironically, jokingly, or to refer to something feminine associated with him (e.g., 'a última' = 'the final move/word/turn'). Informally, it can be used jokingly/ironically to say someone is hopeless, the worst, or the ultimate (in a negative sense). Context matters—without more context, prefer the literal reading: 'he is the last one.'
target_language_example: Ele é a última a chegar na festa.
native_language_example: He is the last one to arrive at the party.

meaning: African elephant (the species of elephant native to Africa).
additional_notes: Refers specifically to elephants from Africa (two species: savanna/forest). Used in biological, zoo, and travel contexts. Gender/number: elefante africano (m. sing.), elefantes africanos (m. pl.). Can be preceded by articles: o elefante africano = the African elephant.
target_language_example: No safári vimos um elefante africano perto do rio.
native_language_example: On the safari we saw an African elephant near the river.

meaning: elephants are
additional_notes: A simple subject–verb phrase used to state facts or descriptions about elephants. 'Elefantes' is the plural noun 'elephants' and 'são' is the 3rd-person plural present of 'ser' (to be). Use for general truths, descriptions, or classifications (e.g., size, conservation status). For temporary states or locations, use 'estão' (from 'estar') instead.
target_language_example: Os elefantes são muito inteligentes.
native_language_example: Elephants are very intelligent.

meaning: chemical element (basic substance defined by its number of protons)
additional_notes: Used in science contexts to refer to elements on the periodic table (e.g., hidrogênio, oxigênio, ouro). Can be used generally to talk about a single kind of atom or element in chemistry.
target_language_example: O oxigênio é um elemento químico essencial para a respiração.
native_language_example: Oxygen is a chemical element essential for respiration.

meaning: somewhere around here; somewhere nearby.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is in the general area but the exact spot is unknown. Common in spoken Portuguese; often followed by words like 'aqui' or left as a short phrase. Equivalent to 'somewhere around here' or 'somewhere nearby.'
target_language_example: Eu esqueci meus óculos em algum lugar por aqui.
native_language_example: I forgot my glasses somewhere around here.

meaning: in progress; ongoing
additional_notes: Used to say that an action, process, project, or discussion is currently happening or moving forward. Common in formal and informal contexts. Can describe temporary or continuous activities.
target_language_example: Tenho dois projetos em andamento no trabalho.
native_language_example: I have two projects in progress at work.

meaning: down; below; underneath.
additional_notes: Used to indicate position below something or a downward direction. Common in spoken Portuguese; often appears as part of phrases like 'lá em baixo' (down there) or 'cair em baixo' (fall down). Not to be confused with 'embaixo' (one word), which is more common in Brazilian Portuguese for 'underneath' — both are understood.
target_language_example: A chave está em baixo da mesa.
native_language_example: The key is under the table.

meaning: in good hands; being well cared for or looked after.
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone that a person or thing is safe, well taken care of, or under competent care. Common in medical, service, or personal-care contexts. Tone is neutral and idiomatic.
target_language_example: Não se preocupe — ele está em boas mãos com o médico.
native_language_example: Don't worry — he's in good hands with the doctor.

meaning: blank; left blank; (figurative) unnoticed or without impact
additional_notes: Literal use: describes something empty or unfilled (a blank space, form left blank). Figurative use: an event or moment that passed 'em branco' means it had no effect, went unnoticed, or was skipped/forgotten. Common in phrases like 'deixar em branco' (to leave blank) and 'passar em branco' (to go unnoticed).
target_language_example: Deixei a resposta em branco porque não sabia.
native_language_example: I left the answer blank because I didn't know.

meaning: soon
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen in the near future. Can be used for both near-immediate returns (e.g., 'Volto em breve') and events happening soon (e.g., 'vai acontecer em breve'). Polite and neutral — appropriate in formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Volto em breve; espere aqui.
native_language_example: I'll be back soon; wait here.

meaning: at home
additional_notes: Used for being at one's home or place where one lives. After some verbs of movement, English often just says "home" while Portuguese still uses em casa, as in chegar em casa = "arrive home."
target_language_example: Hoje vou ficar em casa.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to stay at home.

meaning: at home all day / the whole day at home.
additional_notes: Used to say someone stayed or will stay at home for the entire day. Commonly appears as 'em casa o dia todo' (with 'todo'). In spoken Portuguese the full phrase 'o dia todo' is typical; variants: 'o dia inteiro' or simply 'o dia'. Can be used with past, present, or future tenses.
target_language_example: Vou ficar em casa o dia todo amanhã.
native_language_example: I'll stay at home all day tomorrow.

meaning: on top
additional_notes: Used for something in a higher position. Often appears as em cima de to mean "on top of" or "above" something: em cima da mesa = "on the table / on top of the table." By itself, it can mean "up there" or "upstairs," depending on context.
target_language_example: O livro está em cima da mesa.
native_language_example: The book is on the table.

meaning: at the last minute; very close to the deadline or start time.
additional_notes: Used to say something is done or notified very late, just before it's needed — often implies little time to prepare. Common in spoken and informal contexts but neutral. Can modify actions like avisar (to notify), chegar (to arrive), aceitar (to accept).
target_language_example: Desculpe por avisar em cima da hora, eu tive um imprevisto.
native_language_example: Sorry for notifying at the last minute, I had an unexpected issue.

meaning: 'on', 'on top of' (physically) or idiomatically 'on/over someone' (to hit on someone / be all over someone); can also mean 'right on', 'close to' (in time or pressure).
additional_notes: Primary meaning is physical placement: 'on top of' (e.g., colocar algo em cima de outra coisa). Informally, with people, pode significar 'dar em cima de alguém' = to hit on someone or 'ficar em cima de alguém' = to pester or closely supervise. Context and verbs around the phrase determine whether it's literal or idiomatic.
target_language_example: Tom tirou o casaco e o colocou em cima de uma cadeira.
native_language_example: Tom took off his coat and put it on top of a chair.

meaning: in common; shared between two or more people or things.
additional_notes: Used to say that people or things share a characteristic, connection, acquaintance, interest, etc. Commonly appears after the thing shared (e.g., 'temos X em comum') or after 'amigo'/'algo'. Works for both concrete and abstract shared items.
target_language_example: Nós temos muitos interesses em comum.
native_language_example: We have many interests in common.

meaning: into account; taken into consideration
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like levar (levar em conta = to take into account) or tendo (tendo em conta = given/considering). It indicates that something is considered when making a judgment or decision. Common in formal and everyday speech.
target_language_example: Leve todos os custos em conta antes de aceitar.
native_language_example: Take all the costs into account before accepting.

meaning: in detail; thoroughly; with many specific details.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is described, explained, or examined carefully and with many specifics. Common with verbs like descrever, explicar, contar, ou falar. Can often be replaced by 'detalhadamente' or 'com detalhes'.
target_language_example: Ele explicou o plano em detalhes para a equipe.
native_language_example: He explained the plan in detail to the team.

meaning: up to date; on time; current.
additional_notes: Used to say something is current, kept updated, or paid/done on time. Context determines nuance: 'pôr algo em dia' = bring something up to date; 'manter em dia' = keep up to date; 'pagar em dia' = pay by the due date. Common in both personal tasks and bills.
target_language_example: Preciso pôr meus documentos em dia antes da viagem.
native_language_example: I need to get my documents up to date before the trip.

meaning: from now on; onward; forward (starting at a point in time or space).
additional_notes: Used after a time or place expression (e.g., daqui em diante, desta noite em diante) to indicate that what follows applies from that point forward. Equivalent to 'from now on' or 'henceforth'. Can attach to directions (forward) but most common in temporal sense.
target_language_example: A partir de amanhã em diante, vou estudar todos os dias.
native_language_example: From tomorrow onward, I will study every day.

meaning: especially; in particular
additional_notes: Used to single out one person, thing or situation from others. Can appear at the start or middle of a sentence. Similar to 'especialmente' but slightly more focused on a specific item or person.
target_language_example: Eu gosto de frutas, em especial de maçãs.
native_language_example: I like fruits, especially apples.

meaning: 'in the act' or 'caught in the act' (caught while committing a crime or wrongdoing).
additional_notes: Used when someone is discovered or arrested while actively committing an offense or immediately after; often appears in legal/police contexts. Common short form: 'pego em flagrante' (caught in the act). Not informal — standard Portuguese.
target_language_example: A polícia prendeu o ladrão em flagrante durante o roubo.
native_language_example: The police arrested the thief in the act during the robbery.

meaning: in front of; facing; opposite (location).
additional_notes: Used to describe physical position: something is located directly before or opposite something else. Often followed by a noun or pronoun (em frente da/do/do(a)/ao when combined with articles). Can mean 'opposite' when referring to faces across a street or space; also appears in more abstract contexts (e.g., 'em frente a um problema' = 'facing a problem').
target_language_example: Existe uma agência de correios em frente a estação.
native_language_example: There is a post office in front of the station.

meaning: in general; generally; usually.
additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about people, things, or situations. Can appear at the start of a sentence (with a comma) or before/after the noun it modifies (e.g., 'os estadunidenses em geral'). Equivalent to 'generally speaking.'
target_language_example: Em geral, as pessoas preferem comida fresca.
native_language_example: In general, people prefer fresh food.

meaning: 'on guard' or 'on the lookout'; being watchful or standing guard.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is being vigilant, keeping watch, or standing guard. Can be used literally (a guard on duty) or figuratively (being alert). Short exclamations like "Em guarda!" are common to warn others to be ready/alert. Context determines whether it's temporary duty or a state of alertness.
target_language_example: Fique em guarda durante a noite.
native_language_example: Stay on guard during the night.

meaning: to insist on going shopping with (someone).
additional_notes: This phrase appears in contexts where someone insists on joining another person for shopping. Literally: em (on/about) + ir (to go) + fazer compras (to do shopping) + com (with). In Portuguese, insistir em + infinitive means 'to insist on (doing something)'. The person you're going with follows 'com' (e.g., a mãe, a mãe dela, sua mãe).
target_language_example: Ele insiste em ir fazer compras com a irmã neste fim de semana.
native_language_example: He insists on going shopping with his sister this weekend.

meaning: at stake; in play; at risk.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is at risk, being decided, or involved in a situation. Common in contexts like life, honor, future, money, or competition. It can also mean 'in play' literally (e.g., a game), but most often translates as 'at stake' or 'on the line.'
target_language_example: Meu emprego está em jogo se eu perder mais prazos.
native_language_example: My job is at stake if I miss more deadlines.

meaning: in less (time/quantity) — used to indicate a smaller amount or shorter time
additional_notes: Usually appears before a period of time or quantity: e.g. 'em menos de uma hora' (in less than an hour) or 'em menos quantidade' (in smaller amount). Commonly paired with 'de' (em menos de...) to mean 'in less than...'. Can also contrast two quantities: 'agora é em menos' (now it's less), though that usage is less common.
target_language_example: Consegui terminar o trabalho em menos de duas horas.
native_language_example: I managed to finish the work in less than two hours.

meaning: 'in (someone's) hands' or 'physically in hand / under someone's control'.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is physically held by someone or under someone's control/possession. Can mean 'in hand' (having something with you) or 'in the hands of' (under someone's responsibility or control). Context determines if it's literal (holding an object) or figurative (power/control). Common in phrases like 'entregar em mãos' (to hand over personally) and 'cair em mãos inimigas' (to fall into enemy hands).
target_language_example: Prefiro receber o documento em mãos.
native_language_example: I prefer to receive the document in person / in my hands.

meaning: in the name of; on behalf of; registered to (ownership).
additional_notes: Used to indicate authority, representation, dedication, or legal registration/ownership. Context determines nuance: 'in the name of' when invoking someone (e.g., religious or formal phrases), 'on behalf of' when acting for someone, or 'registered to' when referring to ownership of documents, accounts, or property.
target_language_example: O contrato está em nome de Maria.
native_language_example: The contract is in Maria's name.

meaning: in order; organized; everything ok.
additional_notes: Used to say something is arranged, correct, working properly, or ready. Can be a short exclamation (Em ordem!) meaning “All set!” or “Okay!” Also used in descriptions: meus documentos estão em ordem = my documents are in order. Context determines whether it means physically organized, correct/legal, or simply fine.
target_language_example: Os arquivos estão em ordem para a apresentação.
native_language_example: The files are in order for the presentation.

meaning: in other words; to rephrase or clarify what was just said.
additional_notes: Used to restate or summarize a previous statement more clearly or simply. Often introduces a simpler explanation, a conclusion, or a paraphrase. Common in both spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: Ele não gosta de responsabilidades. Em outras palavras, não quer trabalhar muito.
native_language_example: He doesn't like responsibilities. In other words, he doesn't want to work hard.

meaning: in other (plural).
additional_notes: Used before plural nouns to mean 'in other [things/places/people]'. Gender and number must match the noun that follows (e.g. 'em outros planetas' for masculine plural, 'em outras cidades' for feminine plural). Common in questions and statements about existence or location.
target_language_example: Há restaurantes em outros bairros da cidade?
native_language_example: Are there restaurants in other neighborhoods of the city?

meaning: 'partly' or 'in part'.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is true to some degree but not completely. Common in both spoken and written Portuguese. Often followed by a clause or noun (e.g., em parte verdade, em parte minha culpa).
target_language_example: Eu concordo com você em parte, mas ainda tenho dúvidas.
native_language_example: I agree with you in part, but I still have doubts.

meaning: 'in person' — physically present; personally.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone is physically present or will do something themselves rather than remotely or through a representative. Can emphasize direct, personal involvement (e.g., 'He came in person' or 'You should speak to her in person'). Also used idiomatically for emphasis: 'Ela é a simpatia em pessoa' meaning 'she is the very picture of friendliness.'
target_language_example: Vou falar com o gerente em pessoa amanhã.
native_language_example: I'll speak to the manager in person tomorrow.

meaning: in broad daylight; in the middle of the day (often implying something surprising or shocking happened openly).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that an action or event happened openly during daytime, often with a sense of shock, disbelief, or irony. Can be used literally (something happened during the day) or figuratively (doing something openly). Common in news reports and everyday speech.
target_language_example: Assaltaram o carro em plena luz do dia.
native_language_example: They robbed the car in broad daylight.

meaning: exactly at (a time); on the dot.
additional_notes: Used after a time to mean 'precisely' or 'sharp' (e.g., às seis em ponto = at six o'clock sharp). In other contexts 'ponto' can mean 'point' (geometry) — but the phrase 'em ponto' as shown in time examples means punctuality. Common in spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: A reunião começa às três em ponto.
native_language_example: The meeting starts at three o'clock sharp.

meaning: in a few (hours/days/etc.) / within a short time
additional_notes: Usually followed by a time unit (horas, dias, semanas). Means that something will happen or happened after only a small amount of time. Common in phrases like 'em poucas horas' = 'in a few hours' or 'within hours.'
target_language_example: Em poucas horas ela já se recuperou.
native_language_example: She recovered within a few hours.

meaning: 'in a few words' / 'briefly'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a short summary or concise explanation. Equivalent to English 'in short' or 'to put it briefly.' Often placed at the start of a sentence: 'Em poucas palavras, ...'.
target_language_example: Em poucas palavras, o projeto foi um sucesso.
native_language_example: In a few words, the project was a success.

meaning: 'in black' or 'in black (color)'.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that is black or rendered in black (often paired with 'e branco' to mean 'in black and white'). Common when talking about colors of objects, photos, clothing, or how something is displayed/seen.
target_language_example: Você prefere o carro em preto ou em branco?
native_language_example: Do you prefer the car in black or in white?

meaning: 'in the first place' / 'first' / 'firstly' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Used in several ways: 1) To introduce the first point in a list or argument (meaning 'firstly'/'in the first place'). 2) To indicate priority — someone or something comes first (meaning 'in first place' or 'to put oneself first'). 3) In questions or emphasis, it can mean 'to begin with' or 'in the first place'. Context determines the best English translation.
target_language_example: Em primeiro lugar, precisamos conversar sobre o orçamento.
native_language_example: First of all, we need to talk about the budget.

meaning: 'standing' (position: upright on one's feet) or 'still standing' (intact/upright, e.g. neighborhood).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something in an upright/standing position (physical) or metaphorically to mean 'still standing' or 'not destroyed/damaged'. Commonly follows estar, ficar, or ficar + em pé. Can be used for people (está em pé) or places/things (o bairro está em pé).
target_language_example: Ela ficou em pé durante a reunião inteira.
native_language_example: She stood for the whole meeting.

meaning: in how long; within what time (asks about duration or time until something happens).
additional_notes: Used to ask about the amount of time until an event or how long something will take. More common alternatives are 'quanto tempo' (How long?) or 'em quanto tempo' (in how much time). 'Em quanto' by itself is less common and can sound incomplete; native speakers usually say 'em quanto tempo' or 'quanto tempo falta'.
target_language_example: Em quanto tempo você consegue terminar o relatório?
native_language_example: In how long can you finish the report?

em que ano da faculdade de

target_language_multi_word_term: em que ano da faculdade de
meaning: 'what year of (the) ... college/school are (you)?' — asking which year a student is in within a specific faculty/degree program.
additional_notes: Used to ask someone's year/level in a particular university faculty or degree program. Followed by the area of study (e.g., medicina). Can be addressed formally (senhora/ o senhor), informally (tu) or plural (vocês). In English you'd usually say "what year are you in (medical school)?"
target_language_example: Em que ano da faculdade de engenharia você está?
native_language_example: What year are you in engineering school?

meaning: 'about' / 'regarding' / 'with respect to'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic or thing being referred to. Common in formal and informal speech. Often followed by a noun, pronoun, or clause (e.g., em relação a isso / em relação a você / em relação ao projeto). 'Em relação a quê?' = 'Regarding what?'.
target_language_example: Tenho uma pergunta em relação ao prazo do trabalho.
native_language_example: I have a question regarding the project's deadline.

meaning: afterwards; next; immediately after.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that one action happens right after another. Can mean 'next' in a sequence or 'afterwards' in time. Common in spoken and written Portuguese. Often placed after the verb or at the start of a clause: 'Faremos isso em seguida.'
target_language_example: Eu vou almoçar e em seguida volto ao trabalho.
native_language_example: I'll have lunch and then (right) after I'll return to work.

meaning: 'in second' or 'in second place' (position or ranking).
additional_notes: Used to indicate someone or something is in the second position (e.g., in a race, competition, ranking). Also appears in lists as 'em segundo lugar' meaning 'secondly' or 'in second place/point'. Commonly followed by 'lugar' when emphasizing ranking but 'em segundo' alone is acceptable in context.
target_language_example: Ela terminou em segundo na corrida.
native_language_example: She finished in second in the race.

meaning: 'in time' / 'on time' / 'in time to (do something)' (depends on context)
additional_notes: Can mean 'in time' (soon enough) when followed by an infinitive or context (e.g., em tempo de mudar = in time to change). It also appears inside larger phrases like 'em tempo integral' meaning 'full-time', and 'de tempo em tempo' meaning 'from time to time'. Context determines translation: check surrounding words (e.g., 'em tempo integral' = full-time; 'em tempo de guerra' = in wartime; 'ainda está em tempo' = there's still time / it's not too late).
target_language_example: Ainda estamos em tempo de consertar o erro.
native_language_example: We're still in time to fix the mistake.

meaning: anyway; in any case; regardless
additional_notes: Used to change topic, return to a main point, or indicate that what follows holds despite previous information. Common in spoken and written Portuguese; placed at the start or middle of a sentence. Equivalent to 'anyway' or 'in any case' in English.
target_language_example: Em todo caso, vou ajudar você com o projeto.
native_language_example: Anyway, I'll help you with the project.

meaning: instead of
additional_notes: Used to indicate substitution or preference: one thing replaces another. Can introduce an alternative action, choice, or preference. Often followed by a noun, pronoun, or verb phrase (infinitive).
target_language_example: Eu vou caminhar em vez de pegar o ônibus.
native_language_example: I'll walk instead of taking the bus.

meaning: because of; in view of; considering
additional_notes: Used to give a reason or to indicate that something is considered in light of a situation or fact. Formal or neutral register; common in written and spoken Portuguese. Often followed by a noun phrase (em vista de dificuldades, em vista de novas informações). Preposition 'de' may contract with articles (em vista do, em vista da, em vista dos, em vista das).
target_language_example: Em vista de as chuvas terem aumentado, o evento foi adiado.
native_language_example: Because of the rains having increased, the event was postponed.

meaning: 'around' or 'around (something/someone)'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or position surrounding something (orbiting, circling, wrapped around, standing/sitting around). Often appears with de/da/do/da mim (em volta de mim) or followed directly by the object (em volta da fogueira). Can mean 'look around' (olhar em volta).
target_language_example: Eles se sentaram em volta da mesa.
native_language_example: They sat around the table.

meaning: around
additional_notes: Used to indicate location 'around' (physically surrounding) or an approximate amount/time ('about', 'around'). With physical location it can be interchangeable with 'ao redor de' or 'em torno de'. For quantities or time it means 'approximately' (e.g., em volta de 10 pessoas = about 10 people). Context determines whether it indicates place or approximation.
target_language_example: Havia pessoas em volta de mim o tempo todo.
native_language_example: There were people around me the whole time.

meaning: aloud; out loud (spoken so others can hear).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is spoken audibly, not silently or in your head. Common with verbs like ler (to read), falar (to speak), repetir (to repeat). Can be used literally (reading aloud) or figuratively (thinking something 'out loud').
target_language_example: Leia o parágrafo em voz alta para a turma.
native_language_example: Read the paragraph aloud for the class.

meaning: in vain; without success or result.
additional_notes: Used to say that an action or effort produced no useful result. Common after verbs like 'esperar', 'tentar', or 'ser' (e.g., 'foi em vão'). Can be placed after the verb or at the end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Procurei o documento por horas, mas foi em vão.
native_language_example: I looked for the document for hours, but it was in vain.

meaning: in/at chess; used to say someone has skill or experience in the game of chess.
additional_notes: Commonly used after verbs like ser, estar, ter, ser bom/melhor/ruim to indicate ability, experience, or involvement with chess. 'Em' + activity is a common Portuguese pattern (e.g., 'em música', 'em esporte'). Use 'bom em xadrez' = 'good at chess'.
target_language_example: Ela é excelente em xadrez.
native_language_example: She is excellent at chess.

meaning: under; beneath; below (indicating position under something).
additional_notes: Used to describe physical location directly beneath or underneath an object. Commonly interchangeable with 'debaixo de' in everyday speech, though some sources treat 'embaixo de' as slightly more colloquial. Followed by a noun or pronoun: embaixo de + object. Can also be used figuratively (e.g., embaixo de pressão = under pressure).
target_language_example: O gato está embaixo de a mesa.
native_language_example: The cat is under the table.

meaning: although / even though (introduces a contrast or concession).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that contrasts with or limits the main clause. In Portuguese the conjunction is usually 'embora' followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., 'embora esteja'), but in casual texts you may also see 'embora o' when referring back to a masculine noun or pronoun (e.g., 'embora o rei não o soubesse' — 'although the king did not know it'). 'Embora' can be followed by a full clause or by 'que' + clause ('embora que'), though 'embora' alone is most common. Formal writing favors the subjunctive after 'embora'.
target_language_example: Embora o tempo esteja incerto, iremos à praia amanhã.
native_language_example: Although the weather is uncertain, we'll go to the beach tomorrow.

meaning: 'lend me the...' (informal request asking someone to lend you a specific item)
additional_notes: Common, colloquial way to ask someone to lend you a particular thing. Often used with me (me empresta o...) or você/tu forms (Você me empresta o seu...). In spoken Brazilian Portuguese, people may drop articles or use possessives: 'Me empresta o telefone?' or 'Me empresta seu celular?'. Use a polite tone or add 'por favor' for more politeness.
target_language_example: Me empresta o casaco, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you lend me the coat, please?

meaning: to lend (someone) the ...; used when asking someone to lend a specific item.
additional_notes: Common phrase in requests: 'Pode/Poderia me emprestar o ...?' = 'Can/Could you lend me the ...?' 'Me' indicates the borrower (to me). Replace the noun after 'o' (or 'a', 'os', 'as') to match the gender/number of the item: 'emprestar a carteira', 'emprestar os livros'. Formality: 'Poderia' is more polite than 'Pode'.
target_language_example: Pode me emprestar o celular por algumas horas?
native_language_example: Can you lend me the cellphone for a few hours?

meaning: 'lend me a' or 'to lend (someone) a'.
additional_notes: Used when asking someone to lend you a single item (or speaking about lending one). 'Emprestar' = to lend/borrow depending on perspective: 'emprestar (algo) a (alguém)'. Portuguese often includes the indefinite article (um/uma) before the object. For asking politely, use 'Pode/Pode me emprestar...' or 'Você pode me emprestar...'. When offering to lend, subject and object switch: 'Vou te emprestar...' = I'll lend you...
target_language_example: Você pode me emprestar um lápis?
native_language_example: Can you lend me a pencil?

meaning: to annoy, bother, or pester someone (colloquial).
additional_notes: Informal/slang expression. Literally 'to fill the bag' but means to bother or bother someone repeatedly. Used to tell someone to stop pestering or to complain that someone is being annoying. Common in Brazil; avoid in formal situations.
target_language_example: Pare de encher o saco, eu preciso trabalhar.
native_language_example: Stop annoying me, I need to work.

meaning: finds the
additional_notes: Depends on context and verb form. 'Encontra' is the third-person singular (or polite you) present of 'encontrar' meaning 'to find' or 'to meet'. With a definite article or object after it (here 'o' = 'the' + masculine noun), it usually means 'finds the ...' (e.g. 'encontra o carro' = 'finds the car'). In some contexts (especially asking someone to meet or pick someone up), 'encontrar alguém' can mean 'meet someone' or 'pick someone up' (e.g. 'Alguém me encontra o Ashitaka?' can mean 'Can someone meet/pick up Ashitaka for me?'). Word order and pronouns can change meaning: 'me encontra' = 'finds me' or 'meets/picks me up'.
target_language_example: Você me encontra o passaporte na mochila?
native_language_example: Can you find the passport for me in the backpack?

meaning: 'found dead' (used to report that someone was discovered dead)
additional_notes: Passive construction: 'encontrado' is the past participle of 'encontrar' and agrees with the subject (often omitted in these examples). Common in news reports or factual statements. Use to state that a person or animal was discovered dead at a location; you can add a location after 'encontrado morto' (e.g., 'encontrado morto em casa').
target_language_example: O cão foi encontrado morto no quintal.
native_language_example: The dog was found dead in the yard.

meaning: we found / we met (at/in) — 'encontramos' = we found/met; 'no' = in the/at the (masculine singular).
additional_notes: Used with a location following 'no' (short for 'em + o'). 'Encontramos' can mean either 'we found (someone/something)' or 'we met' depending on context and object pronouns. With reflexive pronoun 'nos' (Nós nos encontramos) it means 'we met (each other)'. Word order of object pronouns may change meaning: 'Nós a encontramos no parque' = We found her at the park. 'Nós nos encontramos no aeroporto' = We met (each other) at the airport.
target_language_example: Nós encontramos no museu às dez horas.
native_language_example: We met/found each other at the museum at ten o'clock.

meaning: 'meet me at' (imperative/request form: ask someone to meet you somewhere).
additional_notes: Used to tell or ask someone to meet you at a specific place. Often appears as 'Me encontre no/na + place' (no = masculine or contraction of 'em + o'; na = em + a). Can be informal or neutral depending on tone. You can also use 'Encontre-me no/na...' (more formal) or 'Vamos nos encontrar no/na...' for 'let's meet at'.
target_language_example: Me encontre no café às 15h.
native_language_example: Meet me at the café at 3 PM.

meaning: I met with her / I ran into her.
additional_notes: Used to say you met or ran into a female person. Can mean a planned meeting (met with her) or an accidental encounter (ran into her) depending on context. In European Portuguese, reflexive word order can vary: 'Eu me encontrei com ela' or 'Me encontrei com ela' are both heard in speech; in Brazilian Portuguese it's more common to say 'Me encontrei com ela' or 'Eu me encontrei com ela', but many speakers prefer 'Eu encontrei ela' or 'Eu a encontrei' (less reflexive).
target_language_example: Ontem me encontrei com ela no café e conversamos por uma hora.
native_language_example: Yesterday I met her at the café and we talked for an hour.

meaning: met with (someone).
additional_notes: Used to say you met or arranged to meet someone. Commonly appears with a person introduced by o/a (the) plus their name or relation (o Tom, a minha amiga). In informal spoken Portuguese the pronoun can be clitic (me encontrei) or separate (eu me encontrei). Also appears as 'me encontrei com' or 'encontrei-me com' (less common).
target_language_example: Me encontrei com o Pedro no café ontem.
native_language_example: I met with Pedro at the café yesterday.

meaning: I found (it) in/on (a place).
additional_notes: ‘Encontrei’ is the first-person past of 'encontrar' (to find). 'Na' is the contraction of 'em' + 'a' (= in/on the, feminine). Together they indicate that the speaker found something at or inside a feminine noun location (na rua, na gaveta). Word order can vary (e.g., 'Encontrei na gaveta uma carta' or 'Eu encontrei na rua'). If the place is masculine use 'no' (em + o).
target_language_example: Encontrei na mesa o meu caderno.
native_language_example: I found my notebook on the table.

meaning: found what (he/she/you) was looking for.
additional_notes: This is part of the full phrase 'encontrou o que estava procurando' (found what [someone] was looking for). 'Encontrou' is the past (pretérito perfeito) of 'encontrar' (to find). 'O que estava' begins a relative clause meaning 'what was' — usually followed by 'procurando' (looking for) or another verb. Use with different subjects: 'eu encontrei...', 'você encontrou...', 'ele/ela encontrou...'. In questions, intonation or question word order marks it as a question (e.g., 'Você encontrou o que estava procurando?').
target_language_example: Você encontrou o que estava procurando?
native_language_example: Did you find what you were looking for?

meaning: atomic energy; energy released from atoms (nuclear energy).
additional_notes: Refers to energy produced by nuclear reactions (fission or fusion). Used in formal and neutral contexts when discussing power generation, scientific topics, history, or peaceful vs. military applications. Pronunciation tip: 'atômica' stresses the first syllable (Á-to-mi-ca).
target_language_example: O país investiu em energia atômica para gerar eletricidade.
native_language_example: The country invested in atomic energy to generate electricity.

meaning: electricity; electrical power.
additional_notes: Refers to the energy supplied to homes, devices, and appliances. Commonly used when talking about power outages (ficar sem energia), electric consumption (consumo de energia), and electricity bills (conta de energia elétrica). Can be shortened in speech to just "energia".
target_language_example: Ficamos sem energia elétrica durante a tempestade.
native_language_example: We were without electricity during the storm.

meaning: nuclear energy; energy produced from nuclear reactions (e.g., power plants).
additional_notes: Used to talk about electricity or power generated by nuclear fission/fusion and related issues (safety, policy, era). Formal term; common in news and discussions about energy and environment.
target_language_example: O país investiu em energia nuclear para reduzir as emissões de carbono.
native_language_example: The country invested in nuclear energy to reduce carbon emissions.

meaning: 'meanwhile' or 'in the meantime'.
additional_notes: Used to link two actions or situations happening at the same time or to contrast what is happening elsewhere while something else takes place. Common at the start of a sentence or clause. Can also be written as 'enquanto' + comma when context implies 'isso'.
target_language_example: Ele preparava o jantar. Enquanto isso, eu terminei o relatório.
native_language_example: He was making dinner. Meanwhile, I finished the report.

meaning: primary and lower-secondary education (elementary school and middle school).
additional_notes: Refers to the stage of basic schooling in Brazil covering early grades through early adolescence (roughly ages 6–14). Used like 'in/at primary school' or 'since primary school'. Can be preceded by prepositions (no/desde/do) and used to indicate when something happened or where someone studied.
target_language_example: Eu e Tom somos amigos desde o ensino fundamental.
native_language_example: Tom and I have been friends since primary school.

meaning: high school (secondary education).
additional_notes: Refers to the stage of education between basic/elementary schooling and higher education. Used to talk about attending, studying, or activities during high school. In some countries it can cover grades roughly equivalent to 9–12.
target_language_example: Ela fez intercâmbio no ensino médio.
native_language_example: She did an exchange program in high school.

meaning: 'taught the' (masculine singular direct object) — used when saying someone taught someone/something (the) [male person/masculine noun] to do something or taught (the) [masculine noun].
additional_notes: Ensinou is the past (pretérito perfeito) of ensinar (to teach). The o is the masculine singular direct object pronoun or the definite article used before a masculine noun. In examples like "ensinou o filho" the o is the article before the masculine noun (o filho = the son). In sentences like "ensinou o alfabeto" it's the article before a masculine noun (o alfabeto). To say "taught him" you would use "lhe ensinou" or "ensinou-lhe" in more formal Portuguese; "ensinou o" is not used to mean 'taught him' when standing alone. Typical structure: [Subject] ensinou o [person/thing] a/como/verbo (taught the [person/thing] to [verb]).
target_language_example: Ela ensinou o aluno a escrever corretamente.
native_language_example: She taught the student to write correctly.

meaning: 'to understand it' or 'to understand the' (depending on context) — literally 'to understand + definite article/neutral object'.
additional_notes: Entender = to understand. When followed by o (the masculine singular definite article) it can mean 'understand the [something]' or stand in for a neutral/referential 'it' (e.g., entender o porquê = 'understand the reason/why'). Commonly used with nouns (entender o significado) or fixed nouns like 'o porquê' (the reason). Word order and context determine the exact translation.
target_language_example: Não consigo entender o motivo dessa mudança.
native_language_example: I can't understand the reason for this change.

meaning: 'I understood that' or 'I got that'.
additional_notes: Used to say you understood something just mentioned or explained. Often appears in questions to check comprehension (Entendi isso direito? = Did I understand that correctly?). 'Entendi' is past tense (I understood); can also be used more generally as 'I get it' in conversational contexts.
target_language_example: Entendi isso, posso seguir em frente?
native_language_example: I understood that, can I go ahead?

meaning: 'I don't understand anything' or 'I don't understand (at all)'.
additional_notes: Informal negative phrase. Combines the verb entender (to understand) with nada (nothing). Often used alone ('Não entendo nada.') or followed by a topic introduced with de/da/do/que. Tone can be blunt or frustrated; adding 'não' at start is required in Portuguese for the negation. A more neutral form is 'não entendo' or 'não entendo nada sobre...'.
target_language_example: Não entendo nada de programação.
native_language_example: I don't understand anything about programming.

meaning: to enter (into)
additional_notes: A versatile phrasal verb meaning physically go into a place (entrar em minha casa), to enter or be accepted into an institution (entrar em Harvard), or to enter into an agreement/negotiation (entrar em acordo). Use with a noun following 'em' (em + place/thing). In English you may translate it as 'enter', 'get into', or 'reach/come to' depending on context.
target_language_example: Ela quer entrar em contacto com o professor.
native_language_example: She wants to get in touch with the professor.

meaning: to panic; to start panicking.
additional_notes: Used to say someone begins to feel panic or lose calm. Common with verbs like começar (to begin), tentar (to try), or as an instruction (Tente não entrar em pânico). Can refer to an individual or a group (os bois entrar em pânico — the cattle panic).
target_language_example: Tente não entrar em pânico durante o exame.
native_language_example: Try not to panic during the exam.

meaning: among these; between these (things/people).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a subset within a group previously mentioned or shown. Matches gender/number of the noun it refers to: 'entre esses' (masculine plural), 'entre essas' (feminine plural). Can be followed by a noun or a clause (e.g., 'entre esses filmes', 'entre esses, o melhor é...').
target_language_example: Entre esses livros, este é o mais interessante.
native_language_example: Among these books, this one is the most interesting.

meaning: 'between me' or 'between me and (someone)'.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is private or concerns only the speaker (and another person). Commonly followed by a person (entre mim e você/ela/ele) or used alone to emphasize confidentiality. In Portuguese, native speakers often prefer 'entre mim e você' although prescriptive grammar sometimes recommends 'entre mim e você' over 'entre eu e você' — note: when the pronoun is the subject of a verb, use 'eu' (e.g. 'eu e você').
target_language_example: Isso fica entre mim e você.
native_language_example: This stays between me and you.

meaning: 'delivery to' or 'hand over to' (indicates the recipient or destination of a delivery/handing over).
additional_notes: Used to show who will receive something or where something should be delivered. Common with packages, documents, or when instructing someone to give an item to a person/department. Often followed by a person, department, or address (entrega para João / entrega para recepção). Can also appear in instructions/forms (endereço de entrega para...).
target_language_example: Coloque a encomenda na porta e escreva: entrega para a Sra. Silva.
native_language_example: Put the package at the door and write: delivery to Mrs. Silva.

meaning: 'so what do you' — used to ask what someone will do, means, or wants next
additional_notes: Commonly starts questions. 'Então' here functions like 'so' or 'then' to prompt a reaction, decision, or clarification. Followed by verbs like 'fará' (will do), 'quer' (wants), or 'quer dizer' (mean). Can be used in hypothetical questions (e.g., 'Se... então o que você faria?'). Neutral register.
target_language_example: Então o que você faria se encontrasse uma carteira na rua?
native_language_example: So what would you do if you found a wallet on the street?

meaning: ashamed/embarrassed of/about (something or doing something).
additional_notes: Used with 'de' + verb infinitive or noun/pronoun. Expresses feeling of shame or embarrassment about an action, situation, or trait. Adjective agrees in gender/number with the subject (envergonhado/envergonhada/envergonhados/envergonhadas). Commonly followed by 'de' + infinitive (de + verb) or 'de' + noun/pronoun.
target_language_example: Você deveria estar envergonhado de seu comportamento.
native_language_example: You should be ashamed of your behavior.

meaning: 'Common Era' (the calendar era equivalent to AD)
additional_notes: Used in dates to mean the same as Anno Domini (AD) but secular; often abbreviated 'EC' in Portuguese (though 'd.C.' for 'depois de Cristo' is more common). Placed after the year: e.g. '2024 era Comum' or abbreviated '2024 EC' or more commonly '2024 d.C.' In formal writing, 'era comum' may appear in lowercase.
target_language_example: O ano 2024 era Comum corresponde a 2024 d.C.
native_language_example: The year 2024 Common Era corresponds to 2024 AD.

meaning: 'was the last person that' / 'was the last person I would expect to...'
additional_notes: Used to express surprise or unexpectedness about someone appearing or being involved. Often followed by a verb in the imperfect or preterite (e.g., 'eu esperava encontrar', 'eu esperava conhecer') and implies that the speaker did not expect that person. Can be used with different subjects (ele/ela/tu).
target_language_example: Ele era a última pessoa que eu imaginava ver naquela festa.
native_language_example: He was the last person I expected to see at that party.

meaning: 'when I was a boy' or 'when (I) was young (male)'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to actions or habits in the speaker's childhood. 'Era' is the imperfect past of 'ser' (to be). 'Garoto' means boy; change to 'era criança' (child) or 'era menina' (when I was a girl) as needed. Commonly followed by verbs in the imperfect (e.g., 'cantava', 'ia') or simple past references.
target_language_example: Brincava no parque quase todos os dias quando era garoto.
native_language_example: I played in the park almost every day when I was a boy.

meaning: 'it was time to' or 'about time to' (expresses that something should have been done already or that the moment to do it has arrived).
additional_notes: Used to say that the appropriate moment for an action has arrived or was overdue. Commonly followed by an infinitive (era hora de sair) or a subordinate clause introduced by que (era hora de você chegar). Can express relief or mild reproach: 'It was about time!'
target_language_example: Era hora de terminar o trabalho.
native_language_example: It was time to finish the work.

meaning: 'once upon a time' — standard phrase used to start fairy tales or stories about the past.
additional_notes: Used to open traditional stories or to introduce a fictional or distant past. It is a fixed formula and not used for literal historical narration in neutral contexts. Equivalent to English storytelling phrase 'once upon a time.'
target_language_example: Era uma vez um pequeno vilarejo onde todos se ajudavam.
native_language_example: Once upon a time there was a small village where everyone helped each other.

meaning: wrong with (something/someone).
additional_notes: Use after expressions like 'há' or 'algo' or in constructions like 'o que havia de errado com...' to say that something is malfunctioning, incorrect, or problematic. Common patterns: 'não há nada de errado com a X' (there's nothing wrong with X), 'algo de errado com a X?' (is there something wrong with X?), 'o que havia de errado com a X' (what was wrong with X). 'Com a' changes to 'com o' or 'com' depending on the gender/number of the noun (e.g. 'errado com o carro', 'errado com as portas').
target_language_example: Tem algo de errado com a geladeira?
native_language_example: Is there something wrong with the refrigerator?

meaning: wrong with (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to say that there is a problem or something isn't right with a person, object, or situation. Followed by the noun (o/a + noun) or a pronoun (ele/ela). In questions and statements you can also see variations like "há algo errado com..." or "o que está errado com..."
target_language_example: Há algo errado com o meu computador.
native_language_example: There is something wrong with my computer.

meaning: 'wrong about' (to be incorrect in one's opinion or belief about someone/something).
additional_notes: Used after a subject to say they had an incorrect opinion or belief regarding a person, thing, or situation. Common structure: [estar/ficar/estar + errado] + sobre + [object]. Can be used in past (estava errado), present (está errado) or with verbs like achar (to think) + errado sobre. Not idiomatic/slang.
target_language_example: Eu estava errado sobre o filme — gostei muito.
native_language_example: I was wrong about the movie — I liked it a lot.

meaning: 'to err is human' — people make mistakes; it's natural to make errors.
additional_notes: A common proverb used to acknowledge that everyone makes mistakes. Often followed by 'perdoar é divino' ('to forgive is divine') when talking about forgiving others. Used in everyday speech and writing; can be said to excuse or explain an error.
target_language_example: Errar é humano; vamos consertar e seguir em frente.
native_language_example: To err is human; let's fix it and move on.

meaning: 'error in' or 'mistake in/on (the)'.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to point out a mistake or an error that occurs within or on something. 'Erro' = error/mistake; 'na' is the contraction of 'em' + 'a' meaning 'in the' or 'on the' (feminine noun). Change 'na' to 'no' for masculine nouns (erro no). Often followed by a noun: erro na escolha, erro na sentença, erro na tela.
target_language_example: Há um erro na gramática desta frase.
native_language_example: There is an error in the grammar of this sentence.

meaning: weed; any unwanted wild plant that grows among cultivated plants.
additional_notes: Used for plants considered invasive or unwanted in gardens, farms, or lawns. Can be used literally for plants or figuratively to describe something or someone harmful or troublesome (figurative use is less common). 'Erva' = herb/plant; 'daninha' = harmful (from 'daninho').
target_language_example: Preciso arrancar cada erva daninha do canteiro antes que se espalhem.
native_language_example: I need to pull every weed from the flower bed before they spread.

meaning: I bumped into / I ran into (someone or something).
additional_notes: Esbarrei com is the first-person past (pretérito perfeito) of the verb phrase 'esbarrar com' and is used to say you accidentally hit or bumped into a person or object, or met someone unexpectedly. It can be physical (bumping into someone on the street) or figurative (running into someone you know). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ontem esbarrei com um amigo no mercado.
native_language_example: Yesterday I bumped into a friend at the market.

meaning: I ran into / I bumped into (someone).
additional_notes: Informal way to say you met someone by chance or physically bumped into them. Use with a masculine person or masculine noun (esbarrei com o Tom / esbarrei com o seu pai). The verb is 'esbarrar (com)' — conjugated here in the first person past 'esbarrei'. Often used for casual, unexpected encounters (at a station, supermarket, etc.).
target_language_example: Eu esbarrei com o Tom hoje.
native_language_example: I ran into Tom today.

meaning: 'the schools are' — subject (escolas) + present tense of 'estar' (estão).
additional_notes: Used to describe the current state or condition of multiple schools (e.g., closed, open). 'Escolas' is plural, so use 'estão' (third person plural of estar). For singular use 'a escola está'. Commonly followed by adjectives or phrases indicating status (fechadas hoje, abertas, vazias, etc.).
target_language_example: As escolas estão fechadas por causa da chuva.
native_language_example: The schools are closed because of the rain.

meaning: 'choose the' (imperative: telling someone to pick something).
additional_notes: A command or polite request using the verb escolher (to choose) in the imperative form. It is followed by a masculine singular noun or a clause (e.g., 'escolha o horário' or 'escolha o que for melhor'). For feminine nouns use 'escolha a'. Can also appear as 'escolha o seu/ sua' for 'choose your'.
target_language_example: Escolha o livro que você quer ler.
native_language_example: Choose the book you want to read.

meaning: to hide (something).
additional_notes: Literal verb phrase: esconder + definite article 'o' (the) before a masculine noun or implied masculine object. In examples, 'esconder o' is followed by a noun or context (esconder o rádio / o seu medo / o meu dinheiro). Commonly used with a direct object to say someone hides an object, a feeling, or information. For feminine objects use 'esconder a' (e.g., esconder a chave).
target_language_example: Preciso esconder o documento antes que cheguem.
native_language_example: I need to hide the document before they arrive.

meaning: toothbrush.
additional_notes: Literal, everyday term for the brush used to clean teeth. Can be modified (escova de dentes elétrica = electric toothbrush). Commonly used with verbs like escovar (to brush), comprar (to buy), trocar/substituir (to replace).
target_language_example: Preciso comprar uma escova de dentes nova.
native_language_example: I need to buy a new toothbrush.

meaning: 'brushes the' (used with a plural body part or object, e.g. escova os dentes = brushes the teeth / brushes one's teeth).
additional_notes: escova is the third-person singular present of the verb escovar (to brush). When followed by a plural noun, escova os means 'he/she/it brushes the ...' or 'you (formal) brush the ...' in contexts using você. Commonly used with dentes (teeth) and cabelos (hair). For first/second/third person conjugations change the verb (eu escovo, tu escovas, ele/ela/você escova, nós escovamos, vocês/eles escovam).
target_language_example: Ela escova os cabelos todas as manhãs.
native_language_example: She brushes her hair every morning.

meaning: write the (imperative, singular or formal) — 'write the' or 'write' + masculine singular noun or object.
additional_notes: 'escreva' is the formal or polite imperative (also used for tú in some regions) of 'escrever' (to write). 'o' is the masculine definite article 'the' or can be a direct object pronoun when attached as 'escreva-o' (write it). In the examples, 'escreva o' is followed by a masculine noun (relatório, endereço, dever de casa, nome). Use 'escreva a' for feminine nouns. To tell someone to write something directed at 'you' informally in Brazil, people often use 'escreve' (imperative familiar) or 'escreva' for formal/Polite (você).
target_language_example: Escreva o número do seu telefone aqui.
native_language_example: Write your phone number here.

meaning: 'writes with' (indicating which hand or tool someone uses to write).
additional_notes: Used with a person or subject + 'com' + instrument/part (commonly 'a mão esquerda/direita' = the left/right hand). Conjugated form of 'escrever' (ele/ela escreve). In questions or commands the verb form changes (e.g., 'Você escreve com a mão direita?').
target_language_example: Ela escreve com a mão direita.
native_language_example: She writes with her right hand.

meaning: 'write the' or 'spell the' (imperative or present) depending on context.
additional_notes: Escreve o combines the verb escrever (to write/spell) with the definite article o (the). In questions like "Como se escreve o seu sobrenome?" it means "How is your surname spelled?" In commands like "Escreve o teu nome" it means "Write your name." Verb form may change with person and register (e.g., "escreva" is the formal imperative). "Escreve o" is informal (tu) in many varieties of Portuguese.
target_language_example: Escreve o teu número de telefone aqui.
native_language_example: Write your phone number here.

meaning: to write the (masculine singular) — 'escrever' = to write; 'o' = the (masculine).
additional_notes: Used when referring to writing a specific masculine noun mentioned or understood from context (e.g., relatório, livro, roteiro, nome). In Portuguese the definite article (o) agrees in gender and number with the noun: escrever a (feminine), escrever os (plural), etc. Often the noun is present (escrever o relatório) but can be omitted if clear from context.
target_language_example: Ela vai escrever o relatório amanhã.
native_language_example: She will write the report tomorrow.

meaning: 'to write your' — a combination of the verb escrever (to write) and the possessive pronoun seu (your/his/her, context-dependent). Used when instructing or describing someone writing something that belongs to them (name, number, report, etc.).
additional_notes: The phrase is compositional: escrever + seu. 'Seu' can mean 'your' (formal or neutral in Brazilian Portuguese) or 'his/her' depending on context; clarify when needed (e.g., seu pai = your father or his father). Word order: the thing possessed usually follows the possessive (escrever seu nome). For informal contexts with a single person you know well, speakers may use 'teu' (in some regions) or add clarification (seu + name).
target_language_example: Você pode escrever seu nome aqui?
native_language_example: Can you write your name here?

meaning: 'wrote the' (past tense of 'to write' + masculine singular definite article).
additional_notes: Escreveu is the third-person singular past (pretérito perfeito) of escrever. O is the masculine singular definite article 'the'. Together they appear before masculine nouns (e.g., livro, relatório, menu, nome). Word order can change with pronouns/questions: 'Você escreveu o meu nome?' = 'Did you write my name?'. For feminine nouns use 'escreveu a'.
target_language_example: Ela escreveu o relatório ontem.
native_language_example: She wrote the report yesterday.

meaning: 'written by' (passive construction indicating the author/agent).
additional_notes: Used in passive sentences to say who wrote something. 'Escrita' is the past participle of 'escrever' (to write) and agrees in gender/number with the noun it modifies (escrita/escritas, escrito/escritos). 'Por' introduces the agent (the person who did the action).
target_language_example: A carta foi escrita por Maria.
native_language_example: The letter was written by Maria.

meaning: 'written on' or 'written in' (indicates something is written in/on a document, book, wall, etc.).
additional_notes: Used with a noun introduced by a definite article or demonstrative (e.g., 'escrito no regulamento' = written in the regulation). 'No' is the contraction of 'em + o' (in/on + the). Use 'escrito na' for feminine nouns, 'escrito nos'/'nas' for plural. Can refer to text physically on a surface or content contained in a document.
target_language_example: Está escrito no boletim que haverá mudança de horário.
native_language_example: It's written in the bulletin that there will be a schedule change.

meaning: listening to (the)...
additional_notes: Present participle of escutar (to listen) + definite article o (the). Used to describe someone actively listening to a person, speech, sound, or thing. In Portuguese word order the article follows the verb when giving a clipped phrase like this; in full sentences you'd usually see the object after the verb (e.g., escutando o discurso). Can also appear with other articles/pronouns (escutando a, escutando-os, escutando-me).
target_language_example: Eu estava escutando o rádio quando você ligou.
native_language_example: I was listening to the radio when you called.

meaning: space in / room in (something).
additional_notes: Used to ask or say whether there is physical space or room inside a vehicle, place, or group. Often appears with a noun after 'no' (contraction of 'em + o')—e.g., 'espaço no carro' = 'space in the car'. Can be used literally (physical room) or figuratively (place/acceptance in an organization or group).
target_language_example: Há espaço no banco para mais uma pessoa?
native_language_example: Is there room on the bench for one more person?

meaning: wait there / hang on (for a moment).
additional_notes: Common informal phrase used to ask someone to pause or wait where they are or to hold on briefly. Can be used literally (stay in that place) or figuratively (wait a moment while you do something). More polite alternatives: "espere um momento", "aguarde".
target_language_example: Esperar aí enquanto eu pego minha carteira.
native_language_example: Wait there while I get my wallet.

meaning: 'I/he/she/you (formal)/they expected that' followed by a feminine noun or feminine clause
additional_notes: This is the imperfect/conditional form of 'esperar' (to expect/to hope) plus the feminine singular definite article 'a' or the start of a feminine subordinate clause introduced by 'que'. Context determines whether 'a' is the article before a noun (e.g., 'esperava que a festa...' — I expected that the party...) or the pronoun/article 'a' before a feminine noun. If the speaker is first person, 'esperava que...' can mean 'I hoped/expected that...' followed by a clause with a verb (no article needed). When followed by 'a' it usually precedes a feminine noun: 'esperava que a reunião começasse mais cedo' = 'I expected that the meeting would start earlier.'
target_language_example: Esperava que a reunião começasse mais cedo.
native_language_example: I expected that the meeting would start earlier.

meaning: I expected that
additional_notes: Esperei is the past form of esperar for eu ('I'). With que, it introduces what someone expected or hoped in the past, usually followed by the imperfect subjunctive: esperei que acontecesse. In English, 'that' is often left out: 'I expected/hoped it would happen.'
target_language_example: Esperei que ele entendesse a situação.
native_language_example: I expected him to understand the situation.

meaning: 'I hope to see' (followed by a pronoun or time).
additional_notes: Commonly used with object pronouns attached to the infinitive (vê-la, vê-lo, vê-los) to mean 'to see her/him/them'. Often followed by a time expression (amanhã, logo, a próxima vez). The full correct infinitive form is 'ver' (infinitive); in writing you'll see 'espero ver' + object pronoun attached to the infinitive (espero vê-la = espero ver‑la).
target_language_example: Espero vê‑te amanhã.
native_language_example: I hope to see you tomorrow.

meaning: 'his wife is' (describing a man's wife).
additional_notes: Used to describe or identify the wife of a male person previously mentioned (dele = of him/his). 'Esposa' = wife. The phrase is followed by an adjective, nationality, occupation, or other description. In spoken Portuguese 'dele' clarifies possession and avoids ambiguity; you can also say 'a mulher dele' (his woman/wife) or use a proper name: 'a esposa do Carlos é...'.
target_language_example: A esposa dele é médica.
native_language_example: His wife is a doctor.

meaning: '(my/your/her/etc.) wife is' — a subject (esposa) + present progressive/state 'está' to say how the wife is or where she is.
additional_notes: Use 'esposa' = wife and 'está' (third-person singular of estar) to describe someone's current condition, location, or temporary state (nervous, preocupada, em casa, brava, etc.). Replace the possessive (minha, sua, a minha) as needed: 'minha esposa está...' (my wife is), 'sua esposa está...' (your wife is), 'a esposa está...' (the wife is). For asking length of pregnancy ('de quanto tempo?') the phrase asks how far along she is.
target_language_example: Minha esposa está cansada hoje.
native_language_example: My wife is tired today.

meaning: 'wife, too' or 'your wife as well' — expresses that the wife is included in whatever was just said.
additional_notes: Combine 'esposa' (wife) with 'também' (also/too). Used to ask or state that the wife shares the same characteristic or action as someone else (e.g., also Canadian, also met, also lost). Word order: subject + 'esposa também' or question form 'Sua/Tua esposa também?'. In Portuguese 'também' usually follows the noun or verb it modifies.
target_language_example: Sua esposa também fala inglês?
native_language_example: Does your wife speak English too?

meaning: to forget (something/someone) — literal failure to remember or figurative ‘forget about’/‘give up on’ an object introduced by the masculine article 'o'.
additional_notes: A transitive verb phrase: esquecer + object (here shown with the masculine definite article 'o' before a masculine noun). Use 'esquecer a' for feminine nouns. The reflexive construction 'esquecer-se de' (eu me esqueci de / eu esqueci de) is also common when followed by clauses or infinitives. Context affects meaning: can be literal (fail to recall) or idiomatic/figurative (abandon, dismiss — e.g., 'pode esquecer o empréstimo' = 'forget about the loan'). Adjust article/gender and pronouns as needed (ex.: 'esquecer o amigo', 'esquecer o passado', 'não esquecer o trabalho de casa').
target_language_example: Nosso professor nos lembrou de não esquecer o nosso trabalho de casa.
native_language_example: Our teacher reminded us not to forget our homework.

meaning: he/she/you (formal) forgot the (plural, masculine) — 'esqueceu' = forgot; 'os' = the (masculine plural).
additional_notes: This is the past (pretérito perfeito) third-person singular form of esquecer + the definite article 'os' (masculine plural). Use when referring to forgetting plural masculine nouns (e.g., óculos, brincos). Portuguese often repeats possessive (dele/dela) but it's optional: 'esqueceu os óculos' or 'esqueceu os óculos dele'. Context and capitalization (Senhor) change formality. For feminine plural nouns use 'esqueceu as'.
target_language_example: Ela esqueceu os documentos na sala.
native_language_example: She forgot the documents in the room.

meaning: I forgot to lock (something).
additional_notes: Common phrase to say you forgot to lock a door, drawer, etc. Use with the object: 'esqueci de trancar a porta' (I forgot to lock the door). Can be conjugated: 'esqueci' (I forgot), 'esqueceu' (he/she/you formal forgot), 'esquecemos' (we forgot). 'Trancar' = to lock; alternative 'trancar' vs 'fechar' (close) — locking implies securing with a key or latch.
target_language_example: Eu esqueci de trancar a porta quando saí.
native_language_example: I forgot to lock the door when I left.

meaning: I forgot my ...
additional_notes: A common way to say you left or forgot a personal item. 'Esqueci' = 'I forgot'; 'minha' = 'my' (feminine). Use 'meu' for masculine nouns (e.g., 'esqueci meu casaco'). Can be followed by any noun indicating the item. In spoken Portuguese the subject 'eu' is often omitted: 'Esqueci minha carteira.'
target_language_example: Esqueci minha chave no apartamento.
