native_language_example: I forgot my key in the apartment.

meaning: 'don't forget (about/of)'.
additional_notes: Imperative form of esquecer with the preposition 'de' (often contracted in speech as 'do' before a masculine noun). Commonly appears as 'Não esqueça de...' or 'Não se esqueça de...'. Use 'se' for reflexive polite/neutral imperative. 'Do' = de + o, so it matches the gender/definite article of the noun that follows (e.g., do vinho).
target_language_example: Não se esqueça do seu passaporte.
native_language_example: Don't forget about your passport.

target_language_multi_word_term: esqueçam de / não esqueçam de / não se esqueçam de
meaning: forget to
additional_notes: Used to tell people to remember (or not to forget) to do something. 'Esqueçam' is the plural imperative or present-subjunctive form meaning 'you (plural) forget'. Adding 'não' makes it a negative command: 'don't forget'. The reflexive particle 'se' (não se esqueçam de) is common and slightly more natural/formal but both forms are used. Followed by an infinitive verb or a noun (e.g., 'esqueçam de ligar', 'esqueçam de mim').
target_language_example: Não se esqueçam de trazer os passaportes.
native_language_example: Don't forget to bring your passports.

meaning: 'that guard' or 'that (male) goalkeeper' depending on context.
additional_notes: Esse is a demonstrative meaning 'that' (nearby or just-mentioned). Guarda can mean 'guard' (person who protects), 'goalkeeper' in sports, or 'store/keeping' in some compounds, but by itself usually refers to a guard or keeper. Together, 'esse guarda' points to a specific guard/person previously mentioned or visible: 'that guard' or 'that goalkeeper'. Use esse for masculine singular nouns. If referring to a female, use essa guarda.
target_language_example: Esse guarda não deixa ninguém entrar.
native_language_example: That guard doesn't let anyone enter.

meaning: 'that one is' or 'this one is' (pointing to something and describing its state).
additional_notes: Used to point to a specific object or item and state its condition (e.g. full, ready, good). In Brazilian Portuguese 'esse' often refers to something near the listener or just mentioned; depending on context and region, speakers may prefer 'este está' (closer to speaker) or 'aquele está' (farther away). Commonly followed by adjectives or short phrases.
target_language_example: Esse está limpo e pronto para usar.
native_language_example: That one is clean and ready to use.

meaning: these days; recently / nowadays (referring to the current period).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a recent or current period of time. Can mean 'these days' (= nowadays) or 'recently' depending on context. Often appears with a verb describing ongoing situations or feelings. Note punctuation: a comma after 'esses dias' is common but optional. Not formal slang.
target_language_example: Esses dias tenho pensado muito sobre mudar de cidade.
native_language_example: These days I've been thinking a lot about moving to another city.

meaning: 'those sons of' (usually completed by a vulgar word; commonly part of the insult 'esses filhos da puta' = 'those sons of bitches/sons of whores').
additional_notes: Incomplete phrase on its own — usually followed by a vulgar noun (often 'puta') to form an insult. Strong profanity; used to express anger or contempt about people. Avoid in polite/formal contexts. Tone and context determine intensity (can be used jokingly among close friends or aggressively in threats).
target_language_example: Esses filhos da puta estragaram tudo de novo.
native_language_example: Those sons of bitches messed everything up again.

meaning: 'this house' followed by negation — used to say something about 'this house' is not true.
additional_notes: Literal pieces: 'esta casa' = 'this house'; 'não' = 'not'. Used to negate a verb or description that follows (e.g., 'não está à venda' = 'is not for sale', 'não é minha' = 'is not mine'). Word order: subject + não + verb/adjective. Context determines the rest of the sentence.
target_language_example: Esta casa não é grande como a da praia.
native_language_example: This house is not as big as the one at the beach.

meaning: 'this photo was' (used to introduce a passive description about the photo: when, where or by whom it was taken).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a past participle (e.g., tirada) to form the passive voice: 'esta foto foi tirada...' = 'this photo was taken...'. Use to give information about time, place, or agent (por + person). Can appear in questions: 'Onde esta foto foi tirada?' = 'Where was this photo taken?'.
target_language_example: Esta foto foi tirada na festa de aniversário.
native_language_example: This photo was taken at the birthday party.

meaning: parked your/his/her (vehicle).
additional_notes: Verb phrase: 'estacionou' is the past (pretérito perfeito) of 'estacionar' (to park). 'o seu' is a possessive meaning 'your' (formal/informal depending on region), 'his', or 'her' depending on context — it agrees in gender/number with the noun it replaces (here implicitly 'carro'). Commonly used to ask or talk about where someone parked a car.
target_language_example: Ele estacionou o seu carro na rua ao lado.
native_language_example: He parked his car on the side street.

meaning: marital status (e.g., single, married, divorced, widowed).
additional_notes: Used when asking about a person's legal marital situation on forms or in conversation. Common in official contexts (forms, HR, registration). Typical answers: solteiro(a) (single), casado(a) (married), divorciado(a) (divorced), viúvo/viúva (widowed).
target_language_example: No formulário, indique o seu estado civil.
native_language_example: On the form, indicate your marital status.

meaning: been very
additional_notes: Usually appears in compound verb forms with ter + estado + an adjective or adverb, such as tenho estado muito bem ('I have been very well') or tinha estado muito feliz ('she had been very happy'). Here, estado is the past participle of estar, not the noun estado ('state').
target_language_example: Ela tem estado muito cansada ultimamente.
native_language_example: She has been very tired lately.

meaning: busy (state)
additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something being busy or unavailable. Often appears with the verb ter + estado (e.g., 'tem estado ocupado') to mean 'has been busy' or 'has been occupied' over a period of time. Can describe people (busy with work) or things (a phone line being busy).
target_language_example: Ela tem estado estado ocupado com o novo projeto.
native_language_example: She has been busy with the new project.

meaning: We're done / that's settled / no hard feelings (used to close a matter).
additional_notes: Informal Brazilian Portuguese expression. Often used to indicate a matter is finished, agreed, or forgiven — like 'we're even' or 'we're good.' Can be said after resolving a problem, settling a debt, or ending a disagreement. Tone depends on context: can be friendly ('we're good') or firm ('that's settled').
target_language_example: Ok, você pagou o que devia, então estamos conversados.
native_language_example: Okay, you paid what you owed, so we're done (we're even).

meaning: to be interested in; to fancy (someone) or to feel like doing something.
additional_notes: Commonly used in Brazil. With a person, it means to be attracted to or to like them (similar to 'to fancy' or 'to be into'). With an activity, it means to feel like doing it (e.g., 'não estou a fim' = 'I don't feel like it'). Often appears as 'estar a fim de' + verb or 'estar a fim (de alguém)'. Informal.
target_language_example: Eu estou a fim de ir ao cinema hoje. — Estou a fim de sair mais tarde?
native_language_example: I feel like going to the movies today. — Am I up for going out later?

meaning: to be about to (do something) / to be ready to happen soon
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone/something is on the verge of doing something (estar para + infinitive). It can also indicate a near-future state or that something is imminent. Common in European and Brazilian Portuguese. Tone is neutral and suitable for everyday use.
target_language_example: Estou para sair agora.
native_language_example: I'm about to leave now.

meaning: to be hanging by a thread; to be in a very fragile or near-failing situation
additional_notes: Used figuratively to describe situations, relationships, projects, health, or objects that are about to fail or collapse. Conveys high risk or imminent danger. Commonly used with the verb estar in constructions like estar por um fio, está por um fio, ficou por um fio.
target_language_example: Depois do acidente, a saúde dele está por um fio.
native_language_example: After the accident, his health is hanging by a thread.

meaning: 'was eating a' (past continuous — ongoing action in the past).
additional_notes: Combination of the imperfect/continuous past 'estava' (was) + gerund 'comendo' (eating) + indefinite article 'um' (a). Use to describe someone who was in the middle of eating something in the past. Subject can be explicit or omitted (Portuguese often drops the subject). Change 'um' to 'uma' for feminine nouns (ex.: estava comendo uma maçã).
target_language_example: Ontem à tarde eu estava comendo um sanduíche quando o telefone tocou.
native_language_example: Yesterday afternoon I was eating a sandwich when the phone rang.

meaning: was planning to do (something).
additional_notes: Past progressive construction: estava (imperfect of estar) + planejando (gerund of planejar) + fazer (infinitive). Used to describe an ongoing intention or plan in the past. Can be followed by an explicit action or left implicit when context makes the action clear.
target_language_example: Eu estava planejando fazer uma surpresa para ela.
native_language_example: I was planning to do a surprise for her.

meaning: was missing/longing for (someone or someplace).
additional_notes: Saudade is a Portuguese noun expressing longing or missing. The construction 'estar com saudades de' + [pessoa/lugar/coisa] means to feel that longing at that moment. Commonly followed by 'casa', a person's name, or a pronoun. Past tense 'estava' indicates it was felt previously.
target_language_example: Eu estava com saudades de você.
native_language_example: I was missing/longing for you.

meaning: was convinced that; firmly believed that
additional_notes: Past imperfect of estar + convencido de. Used to say someone strongly believed or was certain about something in the past. Followed by a clause introduced by que (that) or by an infinitive/nominal phrase. Tone is neutral; can express mistaken belief.
target_language_example: Eu estava convencido de que ela viria hoje.
native_language_example: I was convinced that she would come today.

meaning: was under / was beneath (something).
additional_notes: Past imperfect/preterite construction: estava (was) + debaixo (under). Used to say that something or someone was located beneath or under another object. Often followed by de/da/do + noun (debaixo da mesa, debaixo do banco). Can be used with or without an explicit subject: 'Estava debaixo da cama.' = 'It/He/She was under the bed.'
target_language_example: A chave estava debaixo do tapete.
native_language_example: The key was under the rug.

meaning: was lying (in a certain position).
additional_notes: Used with a body-position phrase after 'de' (e.g., 'de costas' = on one's back, 'de bruços' = on one's stomach). 'Estava' is the past imperfect of 'estar' (was). Commonly describes someone lying down and their orientation.
target_language_example: Eu estava deitado de costas, olhando o céu.
native_language_example: I was lying on my back, looking at the sky.

meaning: was inside; was in (somewhere).
additional_notes: Past imperfect of estar + dentro. Used to say someone or something was located inside a place or container. Can be followed by a preposition + noun (dentro do carro, dentro da casa) or stand alone when context makes the location clear (Tom estava dentro). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: O cachorro estava dentro da casa quando cheguei.
native_language_example: The dog was inside the house when I arrived.

meaning: train station.
additional_notes: Common phrase for the place where trains stop to pick up and drop off passengers. Often preceded by definite/article or a preposition (na/na/à/até). Can also be shortened to estação when context is clear, or combined with specific lines (estação central, estação de metrô for subway).
target_language_example: Vou esperar você na estação de trem às 17h.
native_language_example: I'll wait for you at the train station at 5 PM.

meaning: 'bus station' or 'bus stop' (place where buses pick up and drop off passengers).
additional_notes: Used for a location where buses stop; can mean a large bus station/terminal or a smaller bus stop depending on context. When preceded by a preposition: 'ir à estação de ônibus' (go to the bus station). 'Ônibus' uses the accent; plural is 'estações de ônibus'.
target_language_example: Vou esperar por você na estação de ônibus.
native_language_example: I'll wait for you at the bus station.

meaning: the station is / the station is located (used to say where a station is located)
additional_notes: Fica is the 3rd-person singular of 'ficar' and here means 'to be located' or 'to remain'. Common structure: [place] + fica + [location/distance]. Can be used with other places (por exemplo, 'a casa fica', 'o mercado fica'). Useful for giving or asking location. Pronunciation note: 'fica' sounds like 'FEE-kah'.
target_language_example: A estação fica perto do centro da cidade.
native_language_example: The station is located near the city center.

meaning: this guard / this keeper (masculine) — or 'this saves' when followed by an object (from the verb guardar).
additional_notes: Can be interpreted two ways depending on context and pronunciation: 1) as a noun phrase meaning 'this guard' (este = this, guarda = guard/keeper), used to point out a male guard or someone who watches/keeps something; 2) as a verb phrase if part of a larger clause (ele/ela/isso guarda = he/she/it saves/keeps) but 'este guarda' as 'this saves' is less common — more natural for the verb is 'isto guarda' or 'isso guarda' or using a pronoun subject. Gender matters: guarda (noun) can be masculine ('o guarda') or feminine in some regions. Use context to decide meaning.
target_language_example: Este guarda protege a entrada do prédio.
native_language_example: This guard protects the building entrance.

meaning: this place is not / this place no longer (depending on continuation).
additional_notes: Literal words: 'este' (this) + 'lugar' (place) + 'não' (not). Usage depends on the verb or phrase that follows. Common patterns: 'este lugar não é...' (this place is not...) and 'este lugar não é mais...' (this place is no longer...). Can express location (not in X), suitability (not for you), safety (not safe), or change over time (no longer the same). Word order is standard: subject + negation after the subject and before the verb or complement.
target_language_example: Este lugar não é seguro para crianças.
native_language_example: This place is not safe for children.

meaning: lifestyle; the way a person or group lives (habits, choices, social behavior).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone's usual way of living — including habits, spending, work–life balance, values, and daily routines. Can describe positive, neutral, or negative judgments (e.g., extravagant, healthy). Often appears with verbs like ter (to have), viver (to live), adaptar-se (to adapt), invejar (to envy).
target_language_example: Ela tem um estilo de vida mais saudável desde que começou a correr.
native_language_example: She has a healthier lifestyle since she started running.

meaning: be in
additional_notes: "estiver" is a form of estar used especially after words like quando and se for future or uncertain situations: quando estiver..., se estiver.... "na" is the contraction of em + a, so it often means "in/on/at" before a feminine noun or place name.
target_language_example: Quando eu estiver na praia, vou te mandar uma foto.
native_language_example: When I'm at the beach, I'll send you a photo.

meaning: were in the
additional_notes: "estivesse" is the imperfect subjunctive of "estar" and often appears after "se" ("if") or "como se" ("as if") to talk about hypothetical, unreal, or imagined situations. "no" is the contraction of "em + o" and usually means "in the," though English may also use "at the" or "on the" depending on context.
target_language_example: Se eu estivesse no escritório, atenderia o telefone.
native_language_example: If I were in the office, I would answer the phone.

meaning: 'I am reading a' (masculine singular object).
additional_notes: Present continuous: estou + gerund (lendo) = 'I am reading'. The indefinite article 'um' agrees in gender with a masculine noun that follows (e.g., um livro). Use 'uma' for feminine nouns (estou lendo uma revista). Often followed by the thing being read or left alone in conversation if context makes it clear.
target_language_example: Estou lendo um livro sobre história.
native_language_example: I am reading a book about history.

meaning: 'I miss (someone/something)'.
additional_notes: Used to say you miss someone or something. Literally: 'I am with saudades of' — saudades is a Portuguese noun expressing longing or missing. Commonly followed by a person (você, você, ele) or thing (a minha casa). Contractions: often spoken without 'eu' (Estou com saudades de você).
target_language_example: Estou com saudades de meus amigos do colégio.
native_language_example: I miss my school friends.

meaning: I'm not at all / I'm not (in the slightest).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize a negative state or feeling. Normally appears with adjectives or participles (e.g. 'a fim', 'arrependido', 'contente', 'satisfeito') or alone as a strong negation ('Não estou nada!'). In European Portuguese the construction 'não estou nada a + infinitive' is common for 'not at all inclined to'.
target_language_example: Não estou nada a vontade para ir à festa.
native_language_example: I'm not at all comfortable going to the party.

meaning: the road was / the road was being (past state of the road).
additional_notes: Combines estrada (road) + estava (imperfect/past of 'estar'). Used to describe the condition or situation of a road in the past. Replace 'estrada' with another noun to describe that thing's past state (e.g., 'a ponte estava', 'a rua estava'). Common constructions: 'A estrada estava + adjective/participle/prepositional phrase' (e.g., bloqueada, coberta de gelo, em construção, fechada).
target_language_example: A estrada estava perigosa por causa da neve.
native_language_example: The road was dangerous because of the snow.

meaning: ‘the road is’ — a simple subject + verb phrase used to describe the condition or status of a road.
additional_notes: Use to state or ask about the state of a road (blocked, damaged, closed, under construction, etc.). 'Estrada' = road; 'está' = third-person singular present of 'estar' (temporary states, location, ongoing actions). For permanent descriptions you might see 'é' instead of 'está'. Word order is the same as English: noun + verb.
target_language_example: A estrada está fechada por obras.
native_language_example: The road is closed for repairs.

meaning: shooting star; a meteor streaking across the sky.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a meteor that appears as a bright streak of light. Common in exclamations (e.g., to point one out). Not literal — it's not an actual star falling. Can be used in everyday speech and in expressions like 'fazer um pedido a uma estrela cadente' (make a wish on a shooting star).
target_language_example: Nós sempre pedimos um desejo quando vemos uma estrela cadente.
native_language_example: We always make a wish when we see a shooting star.

meaning: studies there
additional_notes: Used to say or ask that someone studies at a particular place mentioned or understood from context. Common in questions: 'Sua irmã estuda lá?' = 'Does your sister study there?' 'Lá' means 'there' (a place previously mentioned or visible). In Portuguese, subject pronouns and possessives vary (sua/tua) by formality/region.
target_language_example: Meu primo estuda lá desde o ano passado.
native_language_example: My cousin has been studying there since last year.

meaning: 'is watching (the)'.
additional_notes: Present continuous of assistir + definite article 'à' (a + a) used when specifying the thing being watched (e.g., a TV). Commonly used for watching TV, a movie, or a program. In Brazilian Portuguese, people often say 'está assistindo TV' (without the preposition + article) in speech; both forms are correct. Verb 'assistir' can also mean 'to attend' depending on context.
target_language_example: Ela está assistindo à novela agora.
native_language_example: She is watching the soap opera right now.

meaning: 'is running' (used for a nose: 'is running/dripping').
additional_notes: Commonly used to describe a nose producing fluid (a runny nose). Literally 'is dripping/flowing' — can be used for other things that are leaking or dripping, but in everyday speech with 'nariz' it means 'has a runny nose'. Present continuous (estar + gerund).
target_language_example: Meu nariz está escorrendo desde esta manhã.
native_language_example: My nose has been running since this morning.

meaning: 'is written in' (used to say what language something is written in).
additional_notes: Use to indicate the language of a text, label, sign, etc. 'Está' is the third-person singular of estar (temporary state), 'escrito' is the past participle of escrever (written), and 'em' means 'in'. You can change the language name after 'em' (e.g., em inglês, em alemão). For feminine/plural nouns referring to the item, the phrase can be adjusted (e.g., 'estão escritos em' for plural masculine, 'está escrita em' for feminine singular).
target_language_example: O rótulo está escrito em português.
native_language_example: The label is written in Portuguese.

meaning: 'you are wasting your' (as in 'you are wasting your time').
additional_notes: A common phrase used to tell someone they're wasting something (usually 'tempo' = time). 'Está perdendo seu...' is the impersonal/neutral form (third person singular) and often used directly to someone in polite or neutral speech (equivalent to 'you're wasting your...'). In casual speech Brazilians may say 'você está perdendo seu...' or simply 'você está perdendo tempo.' Follow with the noun (e.g., 'tempo').
target_language_example: Você está perdendo seu tempo tentando convencê-la.
native_language_example: You are wasting your time trying to convince her.

meaning: 'here/there is your' or 'how/where is your' (uses of 'estar' + possession 'sua').
additional_notes: Combines the verb estar (to be) with the possessive pronoun sua (your—formal or neutral). Used to point out possession (Aqui está a sua ... = Here is your ...) or to ask about the state/location of something/someone (Como está a sua ...? / Onde está a sua ...?). 'Sua' agrees with the noun it refers to (feminine singular). For informal speech with a male listener or to match the noun's gender, forms like 'seu' (masculine) may be used. Context determines whether it means 'here is/there is' (statement) or 'how/where is' (question using está).
target_language_example: Aqui está a sua mochila; onde está a sua casa?
native_language_example: Here is your backpack; where is your house?

meaning: 'is open to' (used to say a place is open to a group or the public).
additional_notes: Commonly used with 'o público' (the public) or other groups (e.g., 'ao público', 'ao tráfego', 'a visitantes'). 'Está' is the 3rd-person singular of 'estar' (to be) and agrees with the place: 'O museu está aberto ao público.' For feminine nouns you might see 'aberta' (e.g., 'a sala está aberta ao público').
target_language_example: O centro cultural está aberto ao público aos sábados.
native_language_example: The cultural center is open to the public on Saturdays.

meaning: okay
additional_notes: Can be used on its own to agree, accept, or say "all right/okay." It also means someone is fine or doing well. In estar bem com alguém, it can mean being on good terms or okay with someone. Because it uses estar, the form changes with the subject: estou bem, você está bem?, etc.
target_language_example: Está bem, falamos amanhã.
native_language_example: Okay, we'll talk tomorrow.

meaning: it's good
additional_notes: Common phrase used to say something is good, acceptable, or okay. Context determines nuance: can describe weather or conditions ("o clima/tempo está bom" = "the weather is good"), express agreement or approval ("está bom" = "okay/fine"), or indicate adequacy ("o que conseguirem está bom" = "what you manage is fine"). Tone and intonation can make it more polite or final (e.g., "Está bom?" = "Is that okay?").
target_language_example: Está bom, podemos começar agora.
native_language_example: That's fine, we can start now.

meaning: is good for / is fine for / works for (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is acceptable, convenient, suitable, or appropriate for a person, time, activity, or purpose. Common for arranging plans (e.g., asking if a time 'works for you') and for commenting on suitability (e.g., weather 'is good for' an activity). Can be followed by a person, time, or an infinitive clause.
target_language_example: Quarta-feira às sete está bom para mim?
native_language_example: Is Wednesday at seven OK for me?

meaning: is heartbroken / has a broken heart
additional_notes: Used with estar + 'com o coração [partido]' to describe someone who is emotionally hurt, usually from a breakup or disappointment. Often completed as 'está com o coração partido' but can appear shortened in speech/context. Use with people (ele/ela/tu/você/está).
target_language_example: Ela está com o coração partido depois do término.
native_language_example: She is heartbroken after the breakup.

meaning: is with you / is on your side / has you (possession) — depends on context.
additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone is physically with you (e.g., 'He is with you') or that someone supports you ('is on your side'). Also can mean someone has something in their possession when referring to an object (e.g., 'It is with you'). Context and intonation clarify meaning. 'Contigo' is the informal singular 'with you' (used for tu).
target_language_example: Ele está contigo agora?
native_language_example: Is he with you now?

meaning: is ten (units) off / is ten (units) — used to say something is ten (minutes, degrees) fast/slow or at ten units.
additional_notes: Commonly used with a unit after 'dez' (dez minutos, dez graus). Often describes clocks being ten minutes fast (adiantado) or slow (atrasado), or temperatures (dez graus). Context or additional words (adiantado/atrasado, abaixo/acima de zero) clarify the exact meaning.
target_language_example: O relógio está dez minutos atrasado.
native_language_example: The clock is ten minutes slow.

meaning: 'is somewhere' or 'is in some (place/state)'.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something exists in an unspecified place or in an unspecified condition. Commonly followed by lugar (place) or a prepositional phrase (em algum lugar, em algum tipo de...). Can refer to physical location or to a state/condition (e.g., 'em algum tipo de coma' = 'in some kind of coma').
target_language_example: A chave está em algum lugar na gaveta.
native_language_example: The key is somewhere in the drawer.

meaning: is in good (condition/state) — used before a noun like 'forma' (shape/health) or 'situação' (situation).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; 'boa' must agree with a following feminine noun (e.g., 'forma', 'situação'). Commonly used to say someone is in good physical shape ('está em boa forma') or in a good situation/condition. Word order: estar (está) + em + adjective (boa) + noun. Use 'bom' instead of 'boa' when the following noun is masculine (e.g., 'está em bom estado').
target_language_example: Ela está em boa forma.
native_language_example: She is in good shape.

meaning: is in (suitable/usable) condition; is able/capable
additional_notes: Used to say that a person, object or situation is in an appropriate state. Context determines whether it means physically/technically usable (e.g., 'the car is in working condition') or that a person is fit/able to do something (e.g., 'she is in a condition to work'). Often followed by 'de' + infinitive when referring to ability: 'está em condições de falar'.
target_language_example: O computador está em condições de ser usado.
native_language_example: The computer is in a condition to be used.

meaning: 'is able to' / 'is in a condition to' (can do something; often implies physical, mental, or situational capacity).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is (or is not) capable, ready, or fit to do something. Often appears in negative form (não está em condições de) to politely indicate inability, lack of fitness, or inappropriate timing. Followed by an infinitive verb.
target_language_example: Ele não está em condições de viajar hoje.
native_language_example: He is not able/fit to travel today.

meaning: is in your (or their) hands; responsibility or control lies with you/them.
additional_notes: Commonly used to say that someone's fate, decision, or responsibility depends on another person or group. 'Suas' agrees in gender/number with the thing possessed (here often feminine plural noun implied like 'mãos'). In spoken Portuguese you may also hear 'está nas suas mãos' (contraction of 'em' + 'as') — e.g. 'está nas suas mãos'. Context determines whether 'suas' means 'your' (formal/informal you) or 'their' — use surrounding context to interpret.
target_language_example: A decisão agora está em suas mãos.
native_language_example: The decision is now in your hands.

meaning: is everywhere / is all over (something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is present everywhere or widely spread. Often completed by 'a parte' (em toda a parte) or by a place/thing (em toda a mídia). Context determines whether it's literal (physically everywhere) or figurative (widely present, very common). Commonly followed by 'a parte', 'a mídia', 'a cidade', etc.
target_language_example: A alegria está em toda a cidade durante a festa.
native_language_example: Joy is everywhere in the city during the festival.

meaning: is underneath / is below (in a physical sense).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is physically under or beneath another object. Embaixo (or embaixo de) is followed by the thing it's under: 'está embaixo da cadeira' = 'is under the chair'. In spoken Portuguese you may also hear 'embaixo' without 'de' when context is clear. Not used for abstract 'below' (use 'abaixo' for some non-physical contexts).
target_language_example: O gato está embaixo do sofá.
native_language_example: The cat is underneath the sofa.

meaning: is strong / is loud / is intense (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: 'is strong'. Used to describe strength, intensity, volume, flavor, smell, weather, a person's physical strength, or that something is going well (colloquially). Context determines the nuance: e.g. 'a música está forte' = the music is loud; 'o café está forte' = the coffee is strong; 'ele está forte' = he is physically strong or recovering well. Often follows estar + adjective, so it describes a current state.
target_language_example: O café está forte hoje.
native_language_example: The coffee is strong today.

meaning: 'is/are over/way down (at a place)'; indicates someone or something is located somewhere, often emphasizing distance or position (e.g. 'over there', 'down there').
additional_notes: Common spoken expression combining the verb estar + lá (there) + a preposition (em + place or direction). Used to point out location with emphasis — can mean 'over there', 'down there', or 'back there' depending on context. After 'em' a place or direction follows (e.g. em baixo, em casa, em frente). Informal/colloquial register.
target_language_example: Ele está lá em baixo, junto ao rio.
native_language_example: He is down there, by the river.

meaning: used after a negation to emphasize that something is far from being the case (e.g., 'is not at all' / 'is nowhere near').
additional_notes: In Portuguese, 'nada' often follows a negative verb to add emphasis: 'não está nada bem' = 'is not well at all'. It's a stronger negation than just 'não está bem'. Common in everyday speech. Word order: 'não' (negation) + verb + 'nada'. Can be used with adjectives/adverbs (bem, fácil, bom, etc.).
target_language_example: Depois da doença, ele não está nada bem.
native_language_example: After the illness, he is not well at all.

meaning: literally 'is my' — part of a longer sentence (not a standalone phrase).
additional_notes: This sequence combines the verb 'está' (he/she/it/you formal is; or 'is located') with the possessive pronoun 'meu' (my). It usually appears inside a full sentence like 'Está o meu livro?' (Is my book there?) or 'Onde está o meu carro?' (Where is my car?). On its own it is incomplete and should be followed by a noun or used within a question or clause. Word order can vary: Portuguese more commonly uses 'o meu está...' (the mine is...) or 'está o meu [objeto]?' in questions with locative context.
target_language_example: Onde está o meu casaco?
native_language_example: Where is my coat?

meaning: is near / is close (feminine subject).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun to say something is physically or figuratively near in time or space. For masculine subjects use "está próximo". Can describe events (a victory, a storm) or feelings (pain) that are imminent or too close.
target_language_example: A festa está próxima — precisamos preparar tudo.
native_language_example: The party is near — we need to prepare everything.

meaning: is a bit
additional_notes: Common informal structure used with adjectives or past participles to mean 'is a bit' or 'is a little'. Often followed by an adverb like 'pouco' (a little) or directly by an adjective: e.g. 'está um pouco nervoso' = 'is a bit nervous'. Can be used for weather ('está um pouco frio') or states ('está um pouco bêbada'). Note: the verb 'estar' (está) marks temporary state. word-for-word literal translation ('is one') is not useful here.
target_language_example: Hoje está um pouco chuvoso.
native_language_example: Today it's a bit rainy.

meaning: 'are mine' or 'my ... are' (plural).
additional_notes: Combination of the verb 'estar' in the 3rd-person plural ('estão' = 'they/you all are') plus the possessive pronoun 'minhas' (feminine plural 'my'). Used when referring to plural feminine nouns that belong to the speaker (e.g., pinturas, amigas, fotos, malas). Word order in Portuguese is typically 'Aqui estão minhas pinturas' = 'Here are my paintings.' For masculine plural use 'meus' instead; for singular use 'está minha' (rare) or more commonly 'a minha' with noun: 'a minha bolsa está aqui.'
target_language_example: Onde estão minhas chaves?
native_language_example: Where are my keys?

meaning: 'where are my' (plural).
additional_notes: Used when asking the location of multiple items or people that belong to the speaker. 'Estão' is the third-person plural of 'estar' (to be) and agrees with the plural noun that follows. 'Os meus' means 'my' for masculine plural nouns; for feminine plural use 'as minhas'. Word order in questions often places the verb first: 'Onde estão os meus livros?'.
target_language_example: Onde estão os meus documentos?
native_language_example: Where are my documents?

meaning: 'they are' + soft/intensifying modifier (part of phrases like 'estão um pouco' or 'estão um tanto') — used to say 'they are a bit / somewhat'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the verb 'estão' (they are) followed by the indefinite modifier 'um' used in constructions like 'um pouco' (a little/a bit) or 'um tanto' (somewhat). Common patterns: 'estão um pouco ...' = 'they are a little ...' and 'estão um tanto ...' = 'they are somewhat ...'. Agreement depends on what 'they' refers to (plural subject). Use for describing temporary states (temperature, size, feelings, etc.).
target_language_example: As cadeiras estão um pouco desconfortáveis.
native_language_example: The chairs are a bit uncomfortable.

meaning: 'I finish' or part of the structure 'eu acabo de + [infinitive]' meaning 'I have just [done something]'.
additional_notes: Alone, 'eu acabo' can mean 'I finish' or 'I end' (often needs an object: 'eu acabo com ...' = 'I finish/end someone/something'). More commonly in spoken Portuguese is the phrase 'eu acabo de + infinitive' which means 'I have just [done something]'. Context determines whether it's ending/finishing or the 'just did' recent-past meaning.
target_language_example: Eu acabo de chegar ao escritório.
native_language_example: I have just arrived at the office.

meaning: ‘I arrived’ in a subordinate past subjunctive sense (used after expressions like 'antes que', 'até que', or in polite questions).
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular imperfect subjunctive of chegar. Commonly appears after conjunctions that require the subjunctive (antes que = before, até que = until) to talk about actions that may or may not have happened relative to another past action. Also used in polite or tentative questions/offers (Tudo bem se eu chegasse mais cedo?). In everyday speech, Brazilians often use 'chegasse' the same way native speakers use English past subjunctive/counterfactual phrasing.
target_language_example: Será que tudo bem se eu chegasse mais cedo amanhã?
native_language_example: Would it be OK if I arrived earlier tomorrow?

meaning: that I buy
additional_notes: eu compre is the first-person singular present subjunctive form of comprar (to buy). It's used after verbs or expressions that trigger the subjunctive (like querer que, esperar que, or time expressions) and in polite requests or suggestions: e.g. "Que tipo de X você quer que eu compre?" = "What kind of X do you want me to buy?" In many everyday contexts it simply means "that I buy" or functions as "I buy" when expressing desire, request, doubt, or future uncertainty. Not a standalone phrase — appears inside longer clauses.
target_language_example: Você quer que eu compre pão?
native_language_example: Do you want me to buy bread?

meaning: I know
additional_notes: Commonly appears in relative clauses introduced by ninguém/alguma pessoa/qualquer pessoa (nobody/someone/anyone) with the subjunctive verb conhecer (conheça). Literally 'that I know' or 'I know (of)'. Used to qualify people or things in relation to the speaker's knowledge or acquaintance (e.g., 'nobody I know', 'something I know'). The verb is in the subjunctive when the relative clause is non-factual or indefinite.
target_language_example: Você conhece alguém que eu conheça?
native_language_example: Do you know anyone that I know?

meaning: a conditional phrasing meaning 'if I said that...' or 'would I say that...' used to introduce a hypothetical or contrary-to-fact statement.
additional_notes: Formed with the verb 'dizer' in the imperfect subjunctive (dissesse). Commonly used in conditional or hypothetical sentences (often with 'se' or 'seria mentira se...'). It softens or questions the truth of what follows (e.g., expressing doubt, politeness, or a hypothetical). Can appear with or without the subject pronoun 'eu' (e.g., 'se eu dissesse...' or 'se dissesse...').
target_language_example: E se eu dissesse que já resolvi o problema?
native_language_example: What if I said that I already solved the problem?

meaning: 'I and my...' — used to start a phrase listing yourself plus a person you are related to (e.g. 'I and my father', 'my partner and I').
additional_notes: Common word order in Portuguese places the speaker first: 'eu e meu pai' = 'my father and I' (English normally uses 'my father and I' or 'I and my father' but 'my father and I' is more natural). The phrase is followed by a noun (pai, namorado, filho) and then the verb. Use appropriate verb agreement (plural): 'eu e meu pai somos/estamos/deixamos'. Informal register; sometimes commas appear in written examples but are not required.
target_language_example: Eu e meu irmão vamos ao mercado amanhã.
native_language_example: My brother and I are going to the market tomorrow.

meaning: I was more (used in comparisons about past age or qualities).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in phrases like 'quando eu era mais novo/velho/jovem' (when I was younger/older) or 'eu era mais [adjective/noun]' to compare past states. 'Mais' here means 'more' and often requires a following qualifier (e.g. 'novo', 'velho', 'mãe') to complete the idea. The structure uses the imperfect past 'era' to describe ongoing or habitual past situations.
target_language_example: Quando eu era mais novo, jogava futebol todos os dias.
native_language_example: When I was younger, I played soccer every day.

meaning: 'I bumped into' or 'I accidentally hit/touched (someone or something)'.
additional_notes: From the verb esbarrar (to bump into). Used for accidental physical contact (e.g., bumping into a person, object, or door). Can also be used figuratively for 'ran into' someone unexpectedly. The past simple (pretérito perfeito) here indicates a completed action. Add context (em alguém, em algo, com alguém) to specify what or whom you bumped into.
target_language_example: Eu esbarrei no meu colega no corredor ontem.
native_language_example: I bumped into my colleague in the hallway yesterday.

meaning: 'I was about (to)'.
additional_notes: Used to say you were on the point of doing something (followed by 'a' + infinitive: 'a sair', 'a ir'). Common in past contexts. Equivalent to English 'I was about to...'.
target_language_example: Eu estava prestes a sair quando ela ligou.
native_language_example: I was about to leave when she called.

meaning: I feel like / I want to (do something).
additional_notes: Use this phrase to express a desire or urge to do something. It's followed by 'de' + verb (infinitive) when specifying the action: 'estou com vontade de comer' = 'I feel like eating.' More casual than simply 'quero' (I want) and often implies a temporary feeling.
target_language_example: Eu estou com vontade de ver um filme esta noite.
native_language_example: I feel like watching a movie tonight.

meaning: that I do
additional_notes: First-person singular imperfect subjunctive of fazer ("to do" / "to make"). It often appears after que with verbs of wanting, asking, or suggesting: queria que eu fizesse = "wanted me to do". It also appears after se for hypothetical situations: se eu fizesse = "if I did" / "if I were to do".
target_language_example: Ela queria que eu fizesse o almoço.
native_language_example: She wanted me to make lunch.

meaning: 'if I were you' — used to give advice or say what you would do in someone else's situation.
additional_notes: A conditional/idiomatic expression used to introduce advice. Commonly appears in full clauses like 'Se eu fosse você, ...' (If I were you, ...). Often followed by a suggestion: 'Se eu fosse você, eu...'. Informal and formal contexts both use it; verb after is typically conditional or would + verb.
target_language_example: Se eu fosse você, eu aceitaria a oferta.
native_language_example: If I were you, I would accept the offer.

meaning: 'I refuse' (I decline to do or accept something).
additional_notes: Used to state a firm refusal or refusal to accept/do something. Often followed by 'a' + infinitive (e.g., 'a aceitar', 'a desistir', 'a sair'). More emphatic than a simple 'não' and expresses strong will or refusal.
target_language_example: Eu me recuso a mentir para você.
native_language_example: I refuse to lie to you.

meaning: 'I deserve' or 'I deserve it'.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone is worthy of or has earned something (a break, a chance, a reward). Often followed by a noun or clause (e.g. 'um descanso', 'outra chance', 'isso'). Common in everyday speech and neutral in tone.
target_language_example: Depois de todo esse trabalho, eu mereço um prêmio.
native_language_example: After all that work, I deserve a prize.

meaning: I don't understand.
additional_notes: Used to say you do not grasp or comprehend something someone said or did. Can be followed by a clause (e.g., 'o que...') or stand alone. Common in both formal and informal contexts; tone can express confusion, frustration, or lack of knowledge.
target_language_example: Eu não entendo por que você fez isso.
native_language_example: I don't understand why you did that.

meaning: I would not be
additional_notes: Conditional form of 'ser' (to be). Used to express hypothetical or conditional states about oneself (often translated as 'I wouldn't be' or 'I would not be able' when followed by 'capaz de' or similar). Common in sentences imagining a different situation or expressing inability in hypothetical contexts.
target_language_example: Eu não seria feliz sem meus amigos.
native_language_example: I wouldn't be happy without my friends.

meaning: I thought you said...
additional_notes: Use this to report a past belief about something someone else said. Often introduces a clause repeating or summarizing what you remember the other person saying. Can imply surprise, correction, or misunderstanding. Common in conversational past; the clause after 'que' can be in past or imperfect depending on context.
target_language_example: Eu pensei que você disse que viria hoje.
native_language_example: I thought you said you would come today.

meaning: 'I need to know the' (used before a clause introduced by 'que' or a question word).
additional_notes: Common phrase to express a personal need for information. Usually followed by 'que' + clause (e.g. 'o que aconteceu' = 'what happened') or other subordinating words (e.g. 'o que isto significa'). In spoken Portuguese you may also hear the shorter 'preciso saber' without the subject pronoun. Use when asking for facts or explanations.
target_language_example: Eu preciso saber o que aconteceu com o relatório.
native_language_example: I need to know what happened to the report.

meaning: 'I was almost run over' (by a vehicle).
additional_notes: Used to describe narrowly avoiding being hit by a vehicle while walking or crossing the street. Quase = almost; fui atropelado = passive past: 'was run over'. You can change the subject (e.g., 'quase fui atropelada' for a female speaker) or the vehicle ('por um carro', 'por um caminhão').
target_language_example: Ontem, ao atravessar a avenida, eu quase fui atropelado por uma moto.
native_language_example: Yesterday, while crossing the avenue, I was almost run over by a motorcycle.

meaning: 'what I want right now is' (focuses on the immediate desire)
additional_notes: Used to emphasize a current, immediate wish. Often appears in the structure 'O que eu quero agora é ...' or 'Tudo o que eu quero agora é ...' followed by a noun, noun phrase, or verb phrase. Tone is neutral and common in spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: O que eu quero agora é descansar por uma hora.
native_language_example: What I want right now is to rest for an hour.

meaning: I want to see (someone).
additional_notes: This is a colloquial contraction of "eu quero ver" plus a clitic object (la/lo/las/los) attached to the contracted verb: "vê-la" = "ver + a (her)". In full standard form you'd say "Eu quero ver (a) + object" or "Eu quero vê-la" in speech/writing. Used to express desire to see a person or people (now or again). The final pronoun changes for gender/number: vê-la (her), vê-lo (him), vê-las (them fem.), vê-los (them masc.).
target_language_example: Eu quero vê-lo amanhã no café.
native_language_example: I want to see him tomorrow at the café.

meaning: 'I am crazy' (often used as 'I'm crazy about...' someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to express strong enthusiasm, passion or love for a person or thing. When followed by 'por' + noun/pronoun (eu sou louco por ela), it means 'I'm crazy about her'. Alone it can mean 'I'm crazy' (insane) but context usually shows whether it's emotional/figurative. For feminine speaker say 'eu sou louca'.
target_language_example: Eu sou louco por música brasileira.
native_language_example: I'm crazy about Brazilian music.

meaning: 'I help you' as part of a question or offer: 'that I help you' / 'for me to help you'.
additional_notes: Common in questions or offers: Quer/Queres/Quer que eu te ajude? = Do you want me to help you? Uses the subjunctive verb form 'ajude' after 'quer que' or similar verbs expressing desire/will. 'Te' is the informal singular object (you). In more formal contexts use 'lhe' or 'você' constructions: 'quer que eu o/a ajude?' or 'quer que eu ajude você?'.
target_language_example: Você quer que eu te ajude a enviar o e-mail?
native_language_example: Do you want me to help you send the email?

meaning: 'I love you.'
additional_notes: Standard, direct way to say 'I love you' in Portuguese. 'Eu' = I, 'te' = you (object pronoun, informal singular), 'amo' = love. Used for romantic love, strong affection, or deep emotional statements. With strangers or formal situations, Portuguese speakers may use 'você' instead of 'te' ('eu amo você'), but 'eu te amo' is the most common intimate form.
target_language_example: Eu te amo mais do que tudo.
native_language_example: I love you more than anything.

meaning: 'I have the impression that' / 'I feel that' (used to express a personal sense, suspicion, or impression).
additional_notes: Common phrase to introduce what you think or suspect without being certain. Followed by 'que' + clause (eu tenho a impressão de que...). Can be used for feelings, hunches, or tentative opinions. More formal than simply 'acho' or 'sinto'.
target_language_example: Eu tenho a impressão de que vamos chegar atrasados.
native_language_example: I have the impression that we will arrive late.

meaning: I have a question.
additional_notes: Polite, common way to indicate you want to ask something. Can be used in formal or informal contexts. 'Pra' is a colloquial contraction of 'para' seen in spoken Brazilian Portuguese. You can shorten to just 'tenho uma pergunta' or simply 'uma pergunta' in some contexts. Use when raising your hand, interrupting politely, or starting to ask for information.
target_language_example: Com licença, eu tenho uma pergunta sobre a tarefa.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have a question about the assignment.

meaning: 'when I was your (age)'.
additional_notes: A common way to compare ages in Portuguese: full phrase is usually 'quando eu tinha a sua idade' (when I was your age). In examples it's shortened to 'eu tinha a sua' with 'idade' understood from context. Used to introduce something you did or experienced at the other person's current age.
target_language_example: Quando eu tinha a sua idade, eu estudava à noite.
native_language_example: When I was your age, I studied at night.

meaning: I had money / if I had money (hypothetical conditional).
additional_notes: Part of the past-subjunctive (imperfeito do subjuntivo) used in conditional sentences (often with 'se'). It expresses an unreal or hypothetical situation now or in the future (equivalent to 'if I had money' in English). The main clause typically uses a conditional: 'compraria', 'poderia', 'viajaria'.
target_language_example: Se eu tivesse dinheiro, viajaria pela Europa.
native_language_example: If I had money, I would travel around Europe.

meaning: I had a
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression, but a common fragment. "tivesse" is the imperfect subjunctive of "ter". It often appears after "se" in hypothetical sentences ("if I had ...") and after verbs or expressions that require the subjunctive ("that I had ..."). "um" is usually the masculine singular article "a/an" before a noun, but it can also mean "one".
target_language_example: Se eu tivesse um mapa, seria mais fácil.
native_language_example: If I had a map, it would be easier.

meaning: 'I saw (her/him/it) at/on/in' (used to introduce where or when you saw someone or something).
additional_notes: Eu vi na combines the subject + past tense of ver (eu vi = I saw) followed by a preposition (na = in/on/at + feminine article). Common in spoken Portuguese to start a story: 'Eu vi na semana passada' (I saw [them] last week) or 'Eu vi na TV' (I saw it on TV). The object ('her/him/it') is often omitted when obvious from context.
target_language_example: Eu vi na estação ontem à tarde.
native_language_example: I saw [them/it] at the station yesterday afternoon.

meaning: 'I go by' or 'I travel by' (used to say which mode of transport you use).
additional_notes: Used before a mode of transportation or means (ônibus, bicicleta, carro, a pé) to say how you travel. In Portuguese you often omit the article: 'vou de ônibus' = 'I go by bus'. For walking you can say 'vou a pé' instead of 'vou de a pé'. Tense and subject can change (vou, ia, fui) but the structure 'ir + de + [transport]' is common.
target_language_example: Eu vou de trem amanhã de manhã.
native_language_example: I go by train tomorrow morning.

meaning: 'that I go with' (subjunctive form used after verbs/phrases expressing desire, doubt, request, or suggestion)
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular present subjunctive of ir (vá) combined with com = 'with'. Used after verbs like querer, achar (when expressing opinion/doubt), pedir, sugerir, etc. It appears in reported requests or wishes: 'He wants that I go with him' → more natural in English: 'He wants me to go with him.' In spoken Portuguese, word order often drops the subject pronoun (eu), so you will frequently hear 'que eu vá com ele' but also 'que eu vá com o Tom' or just 'que eu vá com vocês'.
target_language_example: Ela quer que eu vá com você amanhã.
native_language_example: She wants me to go with you tomorrow.

meaning: 'I go to' (subjunctive/uncertain — used when speaking about wanting, suggesting, or possibility of going to a place).
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular of the verb 'ir' (to go) in the present subjunctive (eu vá) followed by the preposition 'para' + destination. It's used after verbs or expressions that require the subjunctive (e.g., querer que, talvez) or to express possibility/uncertainty. For simple statements of future plans or intentions, Portuguese often uses 'vou para' (eu vou para Boston = I'm going to Boston).
target_language_example: Talvez eu vá para Portugal no verão.
native_language_example: Maybe I'll go to Portugal in the summer.

meaning: the event is on (a specific day).
additional_notes: Used to say on which day a scheduled event takes place. 'Na' is the contraction of 'em' + 'a' and is used before feminine singular nouns like 'quarta' (short for 'quarta-feira'). Replace the final day word to indicate different weekdays: segunda, terça, quarta, quinta, sexta. To specify dates or times, add them after the day.
target_language_example: O evento é na quinta-feira às 19h.
native_language_example: The event is on Thursday at 7 PM.

meaning: ex-girlfriend; a woman who was someone's girlfriend in the past.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a former romantic partner (female). Commonly written with a hyphen (ex-) before the role. Neutral register; can be used in formal and informal contexts. If referring to a former boyfriend, use ex-namorado.
target_language_example: Minha ex-namorada mora em outra cidade agora.
native_language_example: My ex-girlfriend lives in another city now.

meaning: ex-boyfriend; a former romantic male partner.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a man who was previously someone's boyfriend. Commonly used in conversation and writing. Can be used with possessive: 'meu ex-namorado' (my ex-boyfriend). The hyphen is often used, but you'll also see 'ex namorado' without a hyphen.
target_language_example: O meu ex-namorado ligou ontem e pediu desculpas.
native_language_example: My ex-boyfriend called yesterday and apologized.

meaning: 'exactly the' or 'exactly' (used to emphasize precision or agreement).
additional_notes: Used to point out something precise or to emphasize that something is exactly as described. Often followed by a noun or clause (ex.: exatamente o livro; exatamente o que...). In questions, 'exatamente' can appear before the subject to ask for clarification (O que exatamente o Tom...?). Gender/number of the article may change (exatamente a, exatamente os, exatamente as).
target_language_example: Isso é exatamente o que eu precisava.
native_language_example: That's exactly what I needed.

meaning: exactly you / exactly (did) you — used to ask for precise information about someone's actions or identity
additional_notes: Used in questions to request specific details or to clarify who did something or what someone did. Often appears as part of 'O que exatamente você...?' (What exactly did you...?) or 'Quando exatamente você...?' (When exactly did you...?). 'Exatamente' emphasizes precision; 'você' is the informal/formal 'you' in Brazil (neutral).
target_language_example: O que exatamente você fez ontem à noite?
native_language_example: What exactly did you do last night?

meaning: 'no longer exists' or 'doesn't exist anymore'.
additional_notes: Used after a noun or clause to say something that used to exist or be true now does not. Often appears as 'não existe mais' or 'já não existe mais'. 'Mais' here means 'anymore'/'any longer' (not 'more').
target_language_example: A loja que vendia livros raros não existe mais.
native_language_example: The shop that sold rare books no longer exists.

meaning: 'I explained everything' (simple past / perfect: I have already explained everything).
additional_notes: Expliquei is the first-person singular preterite/pretérito perfeito of explicar (to explain). Tudo means 'everything' or 'all'. Commonly used with a recipient introduced by 'para' (e.g., para ele/para ela/para eles) or alone to say you've already explained all relevant information. Tone is neutral and appropriate in formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Expliquei tudo para o professor ontem.
native_language_example: I explained everything to the teacher yesterday.

meaning: 'expelled from' or 'kicked out of' (passive: someone was forced to leave a place or organization).
additional_notes: Used with a noun for the place or institution (escola, sala, igreja, sinagoga). 'Expulso' is the past participle of 'expulsar' and agrees in gender/number (expulso/expulsa/expulsos/expulsas). 'Da' is the contraction of 'de + a' (from the). For masculine/feminine or plural places adjust the article: 'do' (de + o), 'da' (de + a), 'dos', 'das', or sometimes without article: 'expulso de escola' (less common). Often appears with a verb like 'foi' (was) or 'será' (will be) to form passive constructions.
target_language_example: Ele foi expulso da escola.
native_language_example: He was expelled from the school.

meaning: fire extinguisher.
additional_notes: A portable device used to put out small fires. Common in buildings, vehicles and workplaces. Use definite/indefinite articles as in English (um extintor = a fire extinguisher; o extintor = the fire extinguisher).
target_language_example: Há um extintor de incêndio no corredor.
native_language_example: There is a fire extinguisher in the hallway.

meaning: Seriously? / Come on. (expresses disbelief, surprise, annoyance, or emphasis)
additional_notes: Informal spoken phrase used to react to something surprising, hard to believe, annoying, or to urge someone to be honest/stop joking. Tone depends on context and intonation: can be incredulous ("Seriously?"), impatient ("Cut it out"), or emphatic ("Be serious"). Often used alone or before a sentence.
target_language_example: Fala sério, isso custa quanto?
native_language_example: Seriously, how much does this cost?

meaning: Hey, speak up / tell me something / what's up (informal greeting or prompt to speak).
additional_notes: Informal Brazilian Portuguese. Used to prompt someone to talk, give information, or as a casual greeting equivalent to 'hey' or 'what's up'. Tone depends on context: can be an invitation to say something ('say something'), a call for a person by name ('hey, [name]'), or a casual 'hi'. Common with friends and acquaintances; avoid in formal settings.
target_language_example: Fala aí, como foi seu dia?
native_language_example: Hey, how was your day?

meaning: '(he/she/you) speaks like' or 'talks like/behaves verbally like'.
additional_notes: Literal: fala (he/she/you speak[s]) + como (like/as). Used to compare the way someone speaks to someone else (tone, words, accent, expressions). Can be used for similarities in manner of speaking. Context decides subject (fala can be imperative tú form in Brazil? Note: 'fala' is present indicative for ele/ela/você or imperative tú in informal speech depending on region).
target_language_example: Ele fala como a irmã quando conta histórias.
native_language_example: He speaks like his sister when he tells stories.

meaning: says someone 'speaks French better than' (used to compare ability).
additional_notes: This is part of the comparative construction 'fala inglês/português/francês melhor do que...' meaning 'speaks ... better than...'. The full phrase usually includes the subject and the comparison: e.g. 'Tom fala francês melhor do que Mary.' Note: In spoken Portuguese you may also hear 'fala melhor que' (omitting 'do'), which is common and acceptable in many varieties. Use 'melhor' for 'better' and 'do que' (or 'que') to introduce the thing/person being compared.
target_language_example: Ela fala francês melhor do que eu.
native_language_example: She speaks French better than I do.

meaning: 'speaks French so/that ...' used in comparisons (e.g. 'speaks French as well as...')
additional_notes: This fragment appears before a comparison introduced by 'quanto' (as ... as) or before an adverb/adjective like 'bem' (well). Common full pattern: 'fala francês tão bem quanto...' = 'speaks French as well as...'. 'Tão' amplifies degree and is usually paired with 'como' or 'quanto' for comparisons (Brazilian Portuguese often uses 'quanto').
target_language_example: Ela fala francês tão bem quanto eu.
native_language_example: She speaks French as well as I do.

meaning: speak(s) English
additional_notes: Literally 'speak English'. Used both as a statement (X speaks English) and as a question when addressing someone: 'Você fala inglês?' = 'Do you speak English?'. For polite questions, add 'Desculpe' or 'por favor' and use 'Você' or 'o senhor/a senhora'. Verb form 'fala' is informal/neutral for 'you (tu)' in some regions or 'he/she/you (você)' in standard Brazilian Portuguese.
target_language_example: Desculpe, você fala inglês?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you speak English?

meaning: spoken in
additional_notes: Used to say that a language (or something said) is used or spoken in a place. Passive construction: falado (past participle) + em (in). Common with languages and regions: 'O espanhol é falado em vinte países.' Can also appear with other subjects: 'É falado em...'
target_language_example: O português é falado em vários países da África.
native_language_example: Portuguese is spoken in several countries in Africa.

meaning: native speaker (a person who speaks a language as their first language).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who acquired a language in childhood and speaks it naturally. Commonly follows definite/indefinite articles (um/uma, o/a) and can refer to any language: 'falante nativo de inglês/francês'. Agreement: 'falante' is masculine by default; use 'falante nativo' (m) or 'falante nativa' (f) to match the person's gender. Note that in casual speech some speakers may say 'falante nativo' regardless of the person's gender, but grammatically it should agree.
target_language_example: Eu queria saber falar francês como um falante nativo.
native_language_example: I wanted to be able to speak French like a native speaker.

meaning: to speak with (someone's) mother; ask to talk to a mother.
additional_notes: Used when requesting to speak to a person's mother (formal or plural forms vary: 'do senhor' = of the gentleman, 'dos senhores' = of the gentlemen/multiple people, 'da senhora'/'das senhoras' = of the lady/ladies, 'de vocês' = of you (plural, informal)). Often used when contacting a household or calling a group and you want to talk to the mother specifically. Verb 'falar com' = 'to speak with'.
target_language_example: Posso falar com a mãe dele, por favor?
native_language_example: Can I speak with his mother, please?

meaning: 'to speak with my' (used before a feminine noun: my wife/my partner/my daughter, etc.)
additional_notes: A phrase used to request or state that someone should talk to a female person who belongs to the speaker. 'Minha' is the feminine singular possessive 'my' and must agree with the following noun (minha esposa, minha mulher, minha filha, minha parceira). For masculine nouns you would use 'falar com meu'. Common in polite requests: 'Posso falar com minha...?'
target_language_example: Posso falar com minha namorada, por favor?
native_language_example: Can I speak with my girlfriend, please?

meaning: to speak with your (someone's) — used to say you will talk to a person related to the listener (e.g., your husband, manager).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the verb falar (to speak) + com (with) + seu (your, masculine or neutral possessive). 'Seu' can refer to 'your' (formal or informal) or 'his/her' depending on context — here it means 'your' as in 'your husband/manager/partner'. Use the appropriate possessive (sua/seu) to match the gender of the person: falar com sua amiga (female), falar com seu marido (male). For formality, Portuguese often uses 'seu/sua' regardless of register; in some regions 'teu' (informal) may appear. If addressing politely, you can say 'posso falar com o seu gerente?'
target_language_example: Posso falar com seu diretor sobre isso?
native_language_example: Can I speak with your director about this?

meaning: to speak French almost (to a certain degree).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the verb 'falar' (to speak), the language 'francês' (French), and 'quase' (almost). It expresses that someone's ability in French is close to some comparison (e.g., another language, another person, or a native speaker). Often followed by a comparison phrase introduced by 'tão... quanto', 'como', or a noun phrase like 'um nativo'.
target_language_example: Ela sabe falar francês quase tão bem quanto fala inglês.
native_language_example: She can speak French almost as well as she speaks English.

meaning: 'to speak French so (well)'.
additional_notes: Used to comment on someone's ability to speak French, usually followed by an adjective like 'bem' (well) or another adverb. 'Tão' means 'so' or 'that/very' and intensifies the adjective. Common in surprised or impressed reactions (e.g., 'falar francês tão bem' = 'speak French so well'). Word order: 'falar francês tão bem' or 'tão bem falar francês' (latter less common).
target_language_example: Não sabia que você podia falar francês tão bem.
native_language_example: I didn't know you could speak French so well.

meaning: to speak badly about someone; to badmouth or criticize behind their back.
additional_notes: Used when someone talks negatively about another person (gossip, complaints, insults). Can refer to a person's character, behavior, or actions. Often used with de/da/dos (falar mal de alguém) or with alguém as object. Context determines tone: can be mild criticism or outright slander.
target_language_example: Eles costumam falar mal dos colegas durante o almoço.
native_language_example: They usually badmouth their coworkers during lunch.

meaning: to speak badly about (someone); to gossip or criticize others.
additional_notes: Used with people as the object (dos = de + os). Commonly means saying negative things or gossiping about others, often behind their backs. Frequently appears in phrases like 'falar mal dos outros' (to speak badly about others).
target_language_example: Ele tem por princípio nunca falar mal dos outros.
native_language_example: He has a principle of never speaking badly about others.

meaning: to speak seriously; to be serious (about something).
additional_notes: Used when someone wants to indicate they are not joking or want a serious conversation. Can be used intransitively (Ele fala sério.) or with que + clause (Preciso falar sério com você.). Tone depends on context—can be firm or concerned.
target_language_example: Precisamos falar sério sobre suas notas.
native_language_example: We need to talk seriously about your grades.

meaning: 'to speak a little' or 'to say a bit/more' (often used to ask someone to speak more, speak a little, or give a short amount of information).
additional_notes: Common phrase used to request someone to speak a bit (e.g., more slowly, more loudly, or to give more information). Context determines whether it means 'speak a little' (briefly) or 'speak a little more' (increase volume, speed, or add a bit more detail). Often appears with modifiers like 'mais devagar' (more slowly), 'mais alto' (louder), or 'sobre isso' (about that). Polite forms use poderia/quer/se importaria.
target_language_example: Você pode falar um pouco mais sobre seu trabalho?
native_language_example: Can you talk a little more about your work?

meaning: 'do you speak Portuguese?' (informal, singular 'you').
additional_notes: Informal question used to ask one person if they speak Portuguese. 'Falas' is the second-person singular present of 'falar' (tu). In Brazil, people usually say 'você fala português?' (using 'você') rather than 'tu falas'. You can also use the polite/formal form 'o senhor/a senhora fala português?'. Drop the question mark intonation in spoken language only if context makes it clear.
target_language_example: Desculpa, falas português?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you speak Portuguese?

meaning: talk about
additional_notes: Imperative/subjunctive plural form used to address multiple people (vocês or formal vocês/ocês depending on dialect). Commonly used to tell others not to talk about a topic: 'Não falem de...' = 'Don't talk about...'. Can be followed by noun phrases (falem de filmes, falem de outra coisa) or possessives (falem de suas vidas).
target_language_example: Por favor, não falem de política hoje.
native_language_example: Please don't talk about politics today.

meaning: said something / spoke anything
additional_notes: This phrase combines the verb 'falou' (past tense, he/she/you formal spoke/said) with 'alguma' (feminine form of 'some/any'). Alone it is incomplete and appears in questions or negative contexts, e.g. 'Ele falou alguma coisa?' (Did he say anything?) or fragmentary answers like 'Não falou alguma coisa.' Note: more common collocations are 'falou alguma coisa' or 'falou alguma coisa sobre...' — native speakers often use 'alguma coisa' (something/anything) rather than just 'alguma'.
target_language_example: Você falou alguma coisa sobre a reunião?
native_language_example: Did you say anything about the meeting?

meaning: 'family is the' — used to state that family holds a particular value or role (e.g., the base, the most important).
additional_notes: This phrase begins a sentence that assigns an important quality or role to the family. Common completions: 'base de tudo' (the foundation of everything), 'instituição básica/mais importante' (basic/most important institution). Often used in general statements about social values.
target_language_example: A família é a base de tudo na vida.
native_language_example: Family is the foundation of everything in life.

meaning: will cause (someone/something) to
additional_notes: Two main uses: 1) As part of the construction "fará com que + [clause]" meaning "will cause (that) ..." — it introduces a result/effect (e.g. "Fará com que arrume um bom emprego" = "It will cause him/her to get a good job"). 2) In questions like "O que fará com ele?/O que fará com ela?" it means "What will you/they do with him/her?" or "What will happen to him/her?" — here it means "do with" or "deal with." Context determines whether it expresses causation (cause something to happen) or an action toward a person/thing.
target_language_example: Isso fará com que ele mude de ideia.
native_language_example: That will cause him to change his mind.

meaning: will do/make the (something).
additional_notes: Combination of future tense of 'fazer' (fará = he/she/you-formal will do) + definite article 'o' before a masculine noun. Used to say someone will perform or prepare a specific task or item (e.g., fará o café = will make the coffee). Word order can change depending on the noun that follows (e.g., fará o relatório).
target_language_example: Ela fará o jantar amanhã.
native_language_example: She will make the dinner tomorrow.

meaning: 'please, take care' or 'please look after (someone/something)'.
additional_notes: A polite request combining 'por favor' (please) and the imperative 'cuide' from cuidar (to take care/look after). Often used to ask someone to look after a person, an object, or themselves. In casual speech you may hear shortened forms like 'Me faça um favor, cuide do...' or simply 'Por favor, cuide de...' Use 'cuide-se' to tell someone to take care of themselves.
target_language_example: Por favor, cuide do cachorro enquanto estou fora.
native_language_example: Please take care of the dog while I'm away.

meaning: Please tell (someone)... / Please tell someone to... (used to ask someone to pass a message).
additional_notes: A polite request formula combining 'por favor' + 'diga a' (tell to). Use 'diga a [nome]' + 'que' + clause to report information (tell someone that...). Use 'diga a [nome] para' + infinitive to ask someone to do something (tell someone to do...). If the person is plural use 'diga a eles/elas'. In spoken Portuguese you can also say 'diga para' instead of 'diga a' in many varieties.
target_language_example: Por favor, diga a Carla para me ligar amanhã.
native_language_example: Please tell Carla to call me tomorrow.

meaning: Please tell (someone) — polite request to ask another person to inform or tell someone else something.
additional_notes: This is a polite formula combining 'por favor' (please) with the imperative 'diga' (tell) and the preposition 'ao' (to the). Use 'ao' before masculine singular nouns (ao Tom, ao chefe) and 'à' before feminine singular (à cozinheira). If you name the person, you can also use 'para' + infinitive (diga ao Tom para esperar) or 'que' + clause (diga ao Tom que... ). Common in spoken and written requests.
target_language_example: Por favor, diga ao meu irmão que eu ligo mais tarde.
native_language_example: Please tell my brother that I'll call later.

meaning: 'please, write your' (polite request to write down something that belongs to the person).
additional_notes: This combines the polite marker 'por favor' (please) with the verb phrase 'escreva seu' (write your…). Use to ask someone politely to write personal information (name, address, phone number, etc.). 'Escreva' is the formal/imperative or polite imperative form of 'escrever' (to write) addressing você or o senhor/a senhora. For informal tú use 'escreve o teu' (different forms). When asking what exactly to write, add the noun: 'escreva seu nome', 'escreva seu endereço', etc.
target_language_example: Por favor, escreva seu número de telefone.
native_language_example: Please, write your phone number.

meaning: 'please, close the door.'
additional_notes: A polite request combining 'por favor' (please) and the imperative 'feche' (close) of the verb fechar. Used to ask someone to shut a door; examples add phrases like 'ao sair' (when leaving), 'atrás de você' (behind you), or 'com cuidado' (carefully). Imperative is formal/neutral (você form).
target_language_example: Por favor, feche a porta quando sair.
native_language_example: Please close the door when you leave.

meaning: please call me / please call (someone) / please get in touch with me
additional_notes: Used in two main ways: 1) asking someone to call you by a preferred name (e.g., “por favor, me chame de Jim” = please call me Jim); 2) asking someone to phone or contact you (e.g., “por favor, me chame” = please call me). Context (name vs. contact) makes the meaning clear. Polite and common; add a name after 'de' when requesting a preferred name: 'me chame de [nome]'.
target_language_example: Meu nome é Ricardo, mas por favor, me chame de Rick.
native_language_example: My name is Ricardo, but please call me Rick.

meaning: 'please, tell me' or 'please tell me...'.
additional_notes: A polite request asking someone to provide information. Often appears as 'Por favor, me diga...' or shortened to 'Por favor, diga-me...' The verb 'diga' is the imperative (formal or polite) of 'dizer' addressed to você/tu (depending on region); 'me' means 'to me'. Common in everyday and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Por favor, me diga aonde fica o banheiro.
native_language_example: Please, tell me where the bathroom is.

meaning: 'please give me' — a polite request asking someone to hand you or provide something.
additional_notes: Commonly used with 'por' as 'por favor, me dê' or simply 'me dê' in polite requests. Followed by a noun or a phrase (e.g., time, an object, advice). Use 'me dê' for informal/polite requests to someone you address as 'você' or 'tu' (conjugation may change: 'me dá' in colloquial speech).
target_language_example: Por favor, me dê cinco minutos para terminar.
native_language_example: Please give me five minutes to finish.

meaning: 'please call me' (ask someone to phone you)
additional_notes: A polite request: 'por favor' = please; 'me ligue' = call me (formal or neutral). Use when asking someone to phone you. You can change tense/person: 'me liga' (informal, Brazil), 'me ligue' (more neutral/formal). Often followed by time/place: 'mais tarde' (later), 'quando chegar' (when you arrive).
target_language_example: Por favor, me ligue quando chegar em casa.
native_language_example: Please call me when you get home.

meaning: 'please forgive me' or 'please excuse me'.
additional_notes: A polite request for forgiveness or apology. Commonly used with 'por' or 'por favor' before it (as in the examples). Can be used for minor mistakes (being late) or more serious apologies; tone and context determine formality. You can shorten to 'me perdoe' or more formally say 'perdoe-me'.
target_language_example: Por favor, me perdoe por esquecer seu aniversário.
native_language_example: Please forgive me for forgetting your birthday.

meaning: 'please, stop (doing something)'.
additional_notes: A polite request asking someone to stop an action. 'Por favor' = please; 'pare de' is the imperative of 'parar de' (to stop doing). Follow with an -ing verb (infinitive in Portuguese), e.g. 'pare de cantar' = stop singing. Can be used in urgent or firm contexts depending on tone.
target_language_example: Por favor, pare de falar no celular aqui dentro.
native_language_example: Please stop talking on your phone in here.

meaning: 'a favor to' or 'a favor for' — used when saying you're asking or doing a favor directed at someone.
