meaning: the same way; in the same manner
additional_notes: Used to compare actions, feelings, or situations. Often appears in the phrase 'da mesma forma (que...)' meaning 'in the same way (that...)' or simply 'da mesma forma' meaning 'likewise' or 'the same applies.' Can be used with verbs, feelings, or events.
target_language_example: Eu faço isso da mesma forma que você.
native_language_example: I do this the same way as you.

meaning: 'the same age as'.
additional_notes: Used to compare ages. Structure: 'ter + a mesma idade que + [person/pronoun]'. Can follow a noun or pronoun (e.g., 'ele tem a mesma idade que eu' = 'he is the same age as me'). In Portuguese, object after 'que' often uses subject pronoun ('eu') rather than object form ('mim').
target_language_example: A minha irmã tem a mesma idade que eu.
native_language_example: My sister is the same age as me.

meaning: the same idea / the same thought
additional_notes: Used to say two or more people share the same thought, plan, or opinion. 'Mesma' agrees in gender with 'idéia' (feminine). Note: modern Brazilian Portuguese typically spells 'idéia' as 'ideia' (without the accent), so you'll also encounter 'mesma ideia'. Common in sentences like 'We had the same idea' or 'She has the same idea as him.'
target_language_example: Ah, mais alguém teve a mesma idéia.
native_language_example: Ah, someone else had the same idea.

meaning: 'the same way' or 'in the same manner'
additional_notes: Used to compare how something is done, felt, or perceived. Often appears as 'da mesma maneira' (in the same way) or 'de mesma maneira' in formal contexts. Can describe actions ('did it the same way'), feelings ('felt the same way'), or viewpoints ('see things the same way').
target_language_example: Ele explicou o problema da mesma maneira para todos.
native_language_example: He explained the problem the same way to everyone.

meaning: 'same time' or 'at the same time' (simultaneously); can also mean 'meanwhile' or 'as well'.
additional_notes: Used to say that two or more actions/events occur simultaneously (equivalent to 'at the same time'). Often appears in phrases like 'ao mesmo tempo' (at the same time / meanwhile). By itself 'mesmo tempo' commonly requires a preposition (e.g., 'ao') depending on the sentence: 'ao mesmo tempo, ...'.
target_language_example: Ela estudava e, ao mesmo tempo, trabalhava em meio período.
native_language_example: She was studying and, at the same time, working part-time.

meaning: even so; nevertheless; despite that.
additional_notes: Used to contrast a previous statement and show that something remains true or will happen despite that fact. Can stand alone as a short response (e.g., "Mesmo assim!"). Common in spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: Está chovendo, mas vou sair mesmo assim.
native_language_example: It's raining, but I'll go out even so.

meaning: used to introduce a clause meaning 'even that' or 'really that'—often in questions: 'do you really think that...?'
additional_notes: Common in spoken Portuguese to add emphasis or disbelief before a subordinate clause. In the examples it appears in questions: 'Você acha/espera mesmo que o ...?' = 'Do you really think/expect that ...?' Can also appear in other structures (e.g., 'antes mesmo que o...') meaning 'even before the...'. 'O' is the masculine definite article ('the') and will change to 'a' when referring to feminine nouns.
target_language_example: Você acha mesmo que o João vai aceitar?
native_language_example: Do you really think that João will accept?

meaning: 'even if' or 'even though' (conditional concession).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical or concessive condition that does not change the main statement. Commonly followed by a verb in indicative or subjunctive depending on degree of doubt/fact. Equivalent to English 'even if' when imagining a possibility, or 'even though' when stating a contrasting fact.
target_language_example: Mesmo se chover, vamos ao parque.
native_language_example: Even if it rains, we'll go to the park.

meaning: on the same day that / the same day when
additional_notes: Used to link two events that happened on the same calendar day. Commonly appears with verbs in past or present; can be used with or without an article before a person's name (o Tom / Tom). Equivalent to English 'on the same day that...' or 'the same day when...'.
target_language_example: Cheguei ao Brasil no mesmo dia em que começou a festa.
native_language_example: I arrived in Brazil on the same day that the party started.

meaning: the same office (i.e., working in the same workplace/location)
additional_notes: Used to say that two or more people share the same office or workplace. 'Mesmo' means 'same' and agrees in gender with 'escritório' (masculine). Can refer to the same physical office, the same company/department, or the same office building depending on context. Word order: 'mesmo escritório' follows the noun ('no mesmo escritório' = 'in the same office').
target_language_example: Nós dois trabalhamos no mesmo escritório desde janeiro.
native_language_example: We both have worked in the same office since January.

meaning: the same hospital
additional_notes: Used to indicate that two or more people or events share the same hospital. 'Mesmo' means 'same' and agrees in gender/number with the noun (mesmo hospital, mesma clínica, mesmos hospitais). Commonly appears with verbs like trabalhar, trabalhar em, ou ficar (to be/stay).
target_language_example: Nós estudamos na mesma escola e agora trabalhamos no mesmo hospital.
native_language_example: We studied at the same school and now we work at the same hospital.

meaning: even if
additional_notes: Used to introduce a concession or hypothetical condition. With the subjunctive (seja, fosse, tenha) it often expresses doubt or a hypothetical situation ('even if' / 'even though'). With the indicative it can emphasize a fact ('even though'). Can begin a sentence or clause.
target_language_example: Mesmo que chova, eu irei ao parque.
native_language_example: Even if it rains, I'll go to the park.

meaning: to put in/into, to insert, to cause (followed by a masculine singular noun or the masculine singular definite article 'o'); often used in literal and idiomatic expressions (e.g., 'meter o dedo', 'meter o pé').
additional_notes: Meter is a common transitive verb meaning 'to put' or 'to place'. In colloquial Portuguese it commonly appears with articles or pronouns (meter o carro, meter a mão, meter o pé) and forms many idioms (meter-se em encrenca = get into trouble). The particle 'o' here is the masculine singular definite article and will change to 'a', 'os', 'as' or contract with clitic pronouns (ex.: 'meter-lhe', 'meter-me'). Word order and object forms follow normal Portuguese grammar. In Portugal and Brazil conjugation and usage are similar, though some idiomatic senses vary regionally.
target_language_example: Vou meter o livro na estante.
native_language_example: I will put the book on the shelf.

meaning: my God
additional_notes: An exclamation used to express surprise, shock, disbelief, frustration, annoyance, or strong emotion. Equivalent to English "oh my God" and often abbreviated as "ai, meu Deus" or just "meu Deus". Can be used formally or informally depending on tone; not a literal invocation.
target_language_example: Meu Deus, que susto você me deu!
native_language_example: Oh my God, what a scare you gave me!

meaning: my jacket / my pullover (casual outerwear).
additional_notes: Blusão refers to a casual jacket, sweater, or pullover — something warm you wear over clothes. 'Meu' is the possessive 'my'. Commonly used in everyday speech to ask if someone has seen or knows where your jacket is. Word gender: blusão is masculine (o blusão).
target_language_example: Alguém viu o meu blusão azul?
native_language_example: Has anyone seen my blue jacket?

meaning: my lap (the front part of your thighs when seated; used for holding someone/something).
additional_notes: Used when inviting someone or an animal to sit or be held on your lap. Common in affectionate contexts (parents with children, partners, pets). Can be possessive (meu/ minha) depending on speaker's gender (meu colo / meu colo is same). Often used with verbs like sentar, senta, vir, carregar. Tone is usually warm/intimate — avoid with strangers unless appropriate.
target_language_example: Vem sentar no meu colo, quero te abraçar.
native_language_example: Come sit on my lap, I want to hug you.

meu computador ainda não estava pronto

target_language_multi_word_term: meu computador ainda não estava pronto
meaning: my computer still wasn't ready / wasn't finished yet.
additional_notes: Used to report that a device (here, 'meu computador') was not yet ready/finished (for pickup, repair, setup, etc.). Common in past-tense reported speech: 'disse que...' (said that...). 'Ainda' = still/yet; 'não estava pronto' = was not ready. Useful when talking about repairs, orders, or waiting for something to be completed.
target_language_example: A loja ligou para avisar que meu computador ainda não estava pronto.
native_language_example: The store called to say that my computer still wasn't ready.

meaning: my (day) of — used to say today/tomorrow is a day for something (e.g., luck, rest).
additional_notes: Combine with a noun to say that a particular day is dedicated to or characterized by that thing: meu dia de folga (my day off), meu dia de sorte (my lucky day). Often used with hoje/amanhã or alone with a contextually understood day. Word order: meu dia de + noun. Informal/neutral, common in speech.
target_language_example: Amanhã é meu dia de descanso.
native_language_example: Tomorrow is my day of rest.

meaning: 'my movie' (literal) or idiomatically 'my way of seeing things / my story / my mental space'.
additional_notes: Usually literal when talking about actual films (e.g., 'meu filme favorito'). Idiomatically, Brazilians use 'entrar no meu filme' to mean 'get into my story / understand or accept my point of view/way of behaving' (often said negatively: someone doesn't 'fit into' or accept what I'm thinking). 'No meu filme...' means 'in my version/imagination/plan'. 'Perdi meu filme' is informal and means 'I lost my train of thought / I got confused / I freaked out.' Context determines whether it's literal or idiomatic.
target_language_example: No meu filme, isso já está resolvido.
native_language_example: In my view/plan, that's already resolved.

meaning: 'my' + 'great/large' used before a noun to mean 'my great' (important, big, close) or literally 'my large'
additional_notes: Combines the possessive meu (my) with the adjective grande (big/great). Meaning depends on context: can be literal (physically large) or figurative (important, close, intense). English equivalents: 'my great', 'my big', 'my dear' (for close friends) or 'my great/arch-' (for enemy). Word order is standard: meu grande + noun. Adjust gender/number: meu/minha; grande is invariant for gender but agrees in number (grandes). Tone can be formal or informal depending on context.
target_language_example: Além disso, é meu grande amigo.
native_language_example: Besides, he is my great/close friend.

meaning: my brother
additional_notes: Literally means your male sibling. It is a compositional phrase: meu = 'my' and irmão = 'brother'. In Brazilian Portuguese, meu irmão can also be used informally to address someone in a friendly or emphatic way, similar to 'bro' or 'man'.
target_language_example: Meu irmão mora em São Paulo.
native_language_example: My brother lives in São Paulo.

meaning: my best (used to describe the best person/thing I have or my closest/most important)
additional_notes: Used before or with a noun to mean 'my best' (e.g., best friend, best dictionary). Gender and number must agree: meu melhor (masculine singular), minha melhor (feminine singular), meus/ minhas melhores (plural). Commonly used for close relationships (meu melhor amigo) or top choices (meu melhor livro).
target_language_example: Ele é meu melhor amigo.
native_language_example: He is my best friend.

meaning: around me; in my surroundings.
additional_notes: Used to refer to things, people, or the environment surrounding the speaker. Often appears in the phrase 'ao meu redor' (= around me). It expresses physical surroundings or metaphorical/social environment (people near me, things happening around me).
target_language_example: Há muita confusão ao meu redor hoje.
native_language_example: There is a lot of confusion around me today.

meaning: 'my work as' or 'my work in' (used before a job, role, subject or type of work)
additional_notes: This phrase combines meu (my) + trabalho (work/job) + de (of/as/in). It is followed by a noun or noun phrase specifying the role, field or task: e.g. meu trabalho de professora (my work as a teacher) or meu trabalho de pesquisa (my research work). In everyday speech pode aparecer sem artigo: meu trabalho de professor or with an article: o meu trabalho de professor. Use de to link the type/area of work.
target_language_example: Meu trabalho de professora exige muito preparo.
native_language_example: My work as a teacher requires a lot of preparation.

meaning: 'my train' (referring to the train I am taking or that belongs to my travel plans).
additional_notes: A literal, common phrase used to talk about the specific train someone will catch, missed, or that is delayed. Used in everyday travel contexts; 'meu' can be contracted to 'meu' or 'o meu' (both common). Often appears with verbs like atrasar (be late), sair (leave), partir (depart), perder (miss).
target_language_example: Meu trem sai às oito; preciso ir agora.
native_language_example: My train leaves at eight; I need to go now.

meaning: my true / my real (used before a noun)
additional_notes: Combines the possessive 'meu' (my) with the adjective 'verdadeiro' (true/real). Used before nouns to indicate authenticity, genuine identity, or true feelings (e.g., 'meu verdadeiro nome' = my real name; 'meu verdadeiro amor' = my true love). Gender and number must agree with the noun (e.g., minha verdadeira, meus verdadeiros).
target_language_example: Ela finalmente encontrou o seu meu verdadeiro lugar.
native_language_example: She finally found her true place.

meaning: my bus (the bus I take or that belongs to me in context).
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to a bus that the speaker regularly uses or a specific bus they intended to catch. In Portuguese possessive 'meu' agrees in gender with the noun (ônibus is masculine). Can appear with or without the article: 'o meu ônibus' or just 'meu ônibus'.
target_language_example: Quase perdi meu ônibus hoje de manhã.
native_language_example: I almost missed my bus this morning.

meaning: 'my [something] is' — a short phrase where 'meu' (my) is followed by a form of 'estar' (to be).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's just 'meu' (my) plus the verb 'está' (he/she/it/you formal is). In Portuguese speakers often omit the noun when context makes it clear (e.g., 'o meu está com problemas' = 'my one/thing is having problems'). The omitted noun can be a device, object, or abstract thing previously mentioned. Use when the thing you refer to is understood from context.
target_language_example: O meu está sujo, preciso lavar.
native_language_example: Mine is dirty, I need to wash it.

meaning: my (past) days/years; the time period in my life (often childhood or school days).
additional_notes: Used to refer nostalgically to a past period in one's life (e.g., 'meus tempos de criança', 'meus tempos de escola'). Often followed by a specifying phrase (de criança, de escola, de juventude). Common in reminiscence; not formal or slang—neutral.
target_language_example: Meus tempos de escola foram bem divertidos.
native_language_example: My school days were really fun.

meaning: 'to mess with', 'to bother/interfere with', or 'to pick on' someone (to provoke, annoy, challenge, or cause trouble for someone).
additional_notes: Commonly used to warn someone not to provoke, bother, or interfere with a person or group. Context decides nuance: can mean physically attack, bully, challenge, or simply annoy. Often followed by a pronoun or noun (mexer com a gente / mexer com você). Informal and frequently used in spoken Brazilian Portuguese.
target_language_example: Até um idiota como você sabe que não deve mexer com a gente.
native_language_example: Even an idiot like you knows you shouldn't mess with us.

meaning: microwave (singular); a microwave oven or a microwave-frequency wave.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the microwave oven (short for forno micro-ondas) or to a microwave (electromagnetic wave). In everyday speech, people more commonly say micro-ondas (plural) for the appliance: 'o micro-ondas'. When singular 'micro-onda' appears, context determines whether it's the appliance or the wave. Pronunciation: mee-kroh-OHN-dah.
target_language_example: A comida está pronta no micro-ondas.
native_language_example: The food is ready in the microwave.

meaning: microwave (oven); microwave (appliance).
additional_notes: Refers to the kitchen appliance used to heat food quickly. Can be used with definite article or prepositions (no micro-ondas = in/into the microwave). Plural form is the same for general references (os micro-ondas) but commonly used singular when talking about one appliance (o micro-ondas).
target_language_example: Vou colocar a sopa no micro-ondas por dois minutos.
native_language_example: I'll put the soup in the microwave for two minutes.

meaning: 'a million (of)'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate the quantity 'one million' before a noun or currency (um milhão de dólares = one million dollars) or before a noun meaning people/objects (um milhão de pessoas). Informally it can be used hyperbolically (um milhão de vezes = a million times). When followed by a number or currency, include 'de' before the noun; with some proper nouns or when 'milhão' stands alone, 'de' may be omitted in speech for emphasis.
target_language_example: Eu já visitei este lugar um milhão de vezes.
native_language_example: I've visited this place a million times.

meaning: 'for me, it is' or 'to me, it is' — used to give your opinion about something
additional_notes: This is the phrase 'Para mim, está...' where 'para mim' (or shortened 'mim' in colloquial speech) means 'for me' / 'in my opinion', followed by 'está' (it is/feels). Use it to state personal judgments about how something is (good, equal, far, etc.). In informal speech speakers sometimes say 'pra mim tá...' or drop 'para' in casual contexts. The structure: Para mim, está + adjective/adverb/clause.
target_language_example: Para mim, está perfeito.
native_language_example: For me, it's perfect.

meaning: 'for me' (expressing personal opinion, perspective, or relevance).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the speaker's point of view, preference, or what applies to them. Often appears as 'para mim' (more common) or 'pra mim' in informal speech. 'Mim' follows prepositions; the comma and 'o' here reflect examples where 'mim' is followed by a comma and the masculine article 'o' begins the next phrase (the 'o' is not part of the phrase 'mim').
target_language_example: Para mim, o som da chuva é música.
native_language_example: For me, the sound of rain is music.

meaning: for me before / to me before (used to indicate something happened to or for 'me' at an earlier time).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's the object pronoun 'mim' (me) followed by 'antes' (before). Common in sentences like 'ler para mim antes de dormir' (read to me before sleeping) or 'nunca fez/mintiou em mim antes' (never did/said to me before). In careful grammar, when 'to me' is required, Portuguese often uses 'para mim' or 'a mim' (especially before verbs of giving/doing). 'Mim antes' appears when the preposition is present earlier in the clause or in colloquial speech; watch word order: 'antes de eu dormir' (before I sleep) vs. 'para mim antes' (for me before).
target_language_example: Leia uma história para mim antes de eu dormir.
native_language_example: Read a story to me before I sleep.

meaning: a sequence of pronoun + time expression used in phrases like 'para mim o tempo todo' or 'de mim o tempo todo' to mean 'to me all the time' / 'about me all the time' (indicates an action affects 'me' continuously)
additional_notes: Technically 'mim' is the unstressed object pronoun (me) and normally appears after prepositions (e.g. 'para mim', 'de mim'). It does not stand alone as 'mim o tempo' — the full idiomatic expression is typically 'para mim o tempo todo' or 'de mim o tempo todo'. Examples below show common uses. 'O tempo todo' = 'all the time' / 'constantly'. Informal register is common in speech.
target_language_example: Ela mente para mim o tempo todo.
native_language_example: She lies to me all the time.

meaning: 'my beer' — refers to a beer that belongs to or is intended for the speaker.
additional_notes: Used to indicate possession (mine). Can be literal (a bottle/can/glass of beer) or jokingly about someone's drink. In Portuguese, 'minha' is the feminine singular possessive matching 'cerveja' (a feminine noun). Common in casual, everyday speech.
target_language_example: Onde está a minha cerveja? Por favor, não a beba!
native_language_example: Where is my beer? Please don't drink it!

meaning: 'my lesson' or 'my homework/exercise' depending on context.
additional_notes: Literal composition: minha (my) + lição (lesson/task). In school contexts lição often means a lesson or school assignment/homework. Can also mean a moral lesson (something learned). Context tells whether it refers to a class lesson, a specific exercise, or a personal lesson learned.
target_language_example: Terminei minha lição antes do jantar.
native_language_example: I finished my homework before dinner.

meaning: 'my subject' (usually a school subject or topic I study)
additional_notes: Used to refer to a subject, course, or topic someone studies or teaches (e.g., matemática, história, biologia). In some contexts 'matéria' can mean 'news item' or 'material', but in school contexts it means 'class/subject'. 'Minha' marks possession ('my').
target_language_example: Essa é a minha matéria favorita.
native_language_example: This is my favorite subject.

meaning: the best/better way to do this
additional_notes: Used to talk about the most effective or improved method for doing something. Can be used with verbs or actions previously mentioned. Commonly appears in suggestions or instructions: 'O modo melhor de fazer isso é...' or 'Um modo melhor de fazer isso seria...'.
target_language_example: Um modo melhor de fazer isso é planejar antes de começar.
native_language_example: A better way to do this is to plan before starting.

meaning: tomato sauce; sauce made from tomatoes
additional_notes: Common food item used with pasta, pizzas, and as a base for many dishes. Can refer to homemade or canned sauce. In everyday speech it usually means a savory cooked tomato-based sauce (not raw tomatoes).
target_language_example: Vamos almoçar macarrão com molho de tomate.
native_language_example: Let's have pasta with tomato sauce.

meaning: a difficult time; a period of hardship or trouble.
additional_notes: Used to describe a challenging period for a person, group, or country. Common in both formal and informal contexts. Can refer to emotional, financial, political, or personal troubles. Often preceded by verbs like 'estar', 'passar por', 'atravessar', or 'ser'.
target_language_example: Ela está passando por um momento difícil agora.
native_language_example: She is going through a difficult time right now.

meaning: 'the mountain is' (used to describe the state or condition of a mountain)
additional_notes: A simple subject + verb phrase: 'montanha' = mountain, 'está' = is (temporary/state). Used to describe conditions of the mountain (e.g., covered with snow, green, visible). For permanent facts you might see 'a montanha é...' but for current states or conditions use 'a montanha está...'. Often appears with location or condition phrases: 'coberta de neve', 'coberta por neve', 'no topo'.
target_language_example: A montanha está coberta de nuvens hoje.
native_language_example: The mountain is covered in clouds today.

meaning: a pile of shit; strong vulgar insult meaning 'a mess' or calling someone/something worthless
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Can refer to a literal mess (a pile of feces) or be used figuratively to express anger about a situation ('this mess') or to insult a person ('you piece of shit'). Use with caution; not appropriate in polite contexts.
target_language_example: Vamos resolver este monte de merda agora.
native_language_example: Let's deal with this pile of shit now.

meaning: lives in that (feminine) / lives in this (depending on context) — indicates someone lives in a specific place (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Mora = 'lives' (from morar). Nessa is a contraction of 'em' + 'essa' meaning 'in that' (feminine) or sometimes 'in this' in conversational context. Use 'mora nessa' before a feminine noun like 'casa' or 'vizinhança' (e.g., 'mora nessa casa'). For masculine nouns use 'mora nesse' (em + esse).
target_language_example: Ela mora nessa casa desde 2010.
native_language_example: She has lived in that house since 2010.

meaning: 'where (do you) live' — used to ask about someone's place of residence
additional_notes: Combines the verb morar (to live) with the question word onde (where). In spoken Portuguese the subject and verb can be omitted or reordered: 'Você mora onde?' = 'Where do you live?' Colloquial variations drop pronouns or use past tense: 'Você ainda mora onde costumava (morar)?' = 'Do you still live where you used to?'
target_language_example: Você mora onde agora?
native_language_example: Where do you live now?

meaning: I lived in
additional_notes: First-person past form of 'morar' (to live). Use before a masculine singular place/article (no = em + o) — e.g. 'morei no Brasil' or 'morei no centro'. For feminine places use 'morei na' (e.g. 'morei na França'), and for plural use 'morei nos'/'morei nas'. Can also appear without the article for some country names (e.g. 'morei no Japão' is common). Often followed by a time expression: 'por três anos', 'há dez anos', etc.
target_language_example: Morei no Rio de Janeiro por dois anos.
native_language_example: I lived in Rio de Janeiro for two years.

meaning: 'to starve' (literally 'to die of hunger'); used both literally and figuratively to mean 'be very hungry' or 'refuse to endure extreme hardship'.
additional_notes: Literally means to die of hunger. Commonly used figuratively in Portuguese to say someone is very hungry (e.g., 'estou morrendo de fome') or to express refusal to accept extreme hardship ('Não vou morrer de fome' = I won't starve). Can be used emphatically or hyperbolically, as in 'prefiro morrer de fome a...' ('I'd rather starve than...'). Tone is informal to neutral depending on context.
target_language_example: Não vou morrer de fome.
native_language_example: I won't starve.

meaning: 'they died when' (introduces the time or circumstance of people's deaths)
additional_notes: A past-tense clause: morreram is the third-person plural of morrer (to die). Use morreram quando to say when multiple people died or to introduce the moment/cause of their death. The clause that follows can be a time expression, a descriptive clause, or an event (e.g., 'morreram quando o avião caiu' = 'they died when the plane crashed'). If referring to a single person, use 'morreu quando'.
target_language_example: Os soldados morreram quando o edifício desabou.
native_language_example: The soldiers died when the building collapsed.

meaning: 'died in' (used before a place or type of accident/event).
additional_notes: Combination of the verb morrer (to die) + the contraction num (em + um = in a/inside a). Commonly used to say someone died in a specific accident, in a hospital, or at an event: 'morreu num acidente' (died in an accident), 'morreu num hospital' (died in a hospital). Use num for masculine singular nouns (em + um). For feminine nouns use 'numa' (em + uma).
target_language_example: Ela morreu num acidente de carro no ano passado.
native_language_example: She died in a car accident last year.

meaning: very hungry; starving.
additional_notes: An informal idiom used to emphasize strong hunger. Literally 'dead from hunger' — common in spoken Portuguese. Use in casual contexts with friends/family. Can modify a person: Estou morto de fome (I'm starving). Not typically used in formal writing.
target_language_example: Depois do jogo, eu estava morto de fome e comi dois sanduíches.
native_language_example: After the game, I was starving and ate two sandwiches.

meaning: 'killed by a' (passive: someone or something was killed by a [male/unspecified] agent or cause).
additional_notes: Used in passive constructions: morto (dead/killed) + por (by) + um (a/an, masculine or non-gendered general agent). If the agent is feminine use 'uma' (morta por uma). Can introduce a person, animal, object or event that caused the death (e.g., 'morto por um gato', 'morto por um raio', 'morto por um tiro'). Context determines whether 'um' refers to an indefinite person ('a man/woman'), a specific masculine noun, or a non-person cause. Agreement: 'morto' agrees with a masculine subject; use 'morta' for feminine subjects.
target_language_example: Bill foi morto por um intruso.
native_language_example: Bill was killed by an intruder.

meaning: to show how to do (something); to demonstrate how to do it.
additional_notes: Used when asking or stating that someone will demonstrate the steps or process for doing something. Common with indirect object pronouns (me, lhe, nos) and infinitive phrases (mostrar como fazer isso). Can be used in questions and promises.
target_language_example: Você pode me mostrar como fazer isso?
native_language_example: Can you show me how to do this?

meaning: 'to show my' — used when indicating you will show something that belongs to you
additional_notes: Combines the verb mostrar (to show) with the possessive meu (my). Followed by a noun (meu amor, meu número, meu quarto, meu visto, meu carro). In spoken Portuguese you may hear contractions or pronoun placement with indirect objects (e.g., 'vou te mostrar' = 'I'll show you'). Adjust meu to match gender/number of the noun: minha (fem), meus/minhas (pl.).
target_language_example: Posso te mostrar meu livro amanhã?
native_language_example: Can I show you my book tomorrow?

meaning: 'show (someone) the' or 'show the' (used before a masculine noun like 'caminho').
additional_notes: Portuguese verb phrase: 'mostrar' = to show. When followed by a masculine singular noun starting with a definite article, Portuguese often contracts or places the article after the verb as in 'mostrar o caminho' = 'show the way'. In examples 'me mostrar o caminho' = 'show me the way'. Use 'mostrar a' for feminine nouns (e.g. 'mostrar a direção').
target_language_example: Você pode me mostrar o restaurante?
native_language_example: Can you show me the restaurant?

meaning: to show your (something).
additional_notes: Used to ask or say that someone should display or let someone see a personal item (car, passport, receipt, photos, etc.). 'Mostrar' = to show; 'seu' = your (masculine or neutral; can mean his/her/your depending on context). In polite requests use 'pode/por favor' (e.g., 'Pode me mostrar seu ...?'). Word order: 'mostrar' + object + 'seu' + noun (often 'mostrar seu + [noun]').
target_language_example: Você pode me mostrar seu passaporte, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you show me your passport, please?

meaning: to show (you) a (thing); 'mostrar' = to show, 'uma' = a/one (feminine).
additional_notes: Commonly used when introducing or pointing out a single item, idea, method, picture, etc. Often followed by 'coisa' (thing) or a feminine noun (e.g., forma, pintura). In spoken Portuguese the object pronoun can be te / lhe (te is informal). Word order: Vou/Posso + te/lhe + mostrar + uma + [coisa/noun].
target_language_example: Posso te mostrar uma maneira melhor de fazer isso.
native_language_example: Can I show you a better way to do this?

meaning: show him/it/you (formal) — imperative/subjunctive form of 'mostrar' + direct object pronoun 'o' (masculine singular).
additional_notes: Mostre is the formal/third-person imperative (or present subjunctive) of mostrar. The pronoun 'o' refers to a masculine singular object or a masculine person of respect (equivalent to 'him' or 'it'). Context and intonation decide if it's a command (Mostre o relatório. — Show the report.) or a polite request (Quero que mostre o caminho. — I want you to show the way.). For informal singular commands to a friend use 'mostra-o' in Portugal or 'mostra para ele/mostra isso' in Brazil; in Brazilian Portuguese clitic placement often differs (e.g., 'mostre-o' is more formal/literary).
target_language_example: Por favor, mostre o documento ao chefe.
native_language_example: Please show the document to the boss.

meaning: he/she showed his/her (something).
additional_notes: Mostrou is the past tense (pretérito perfeito) of mostrar = 'to show'. Sua is a possessive adjective meaning 'his', 'her', or 'your' (formal), and agrees in gender/number with the noun that follows. In spoken Portuguese, context tells you the possessor's gender. For neutral or ambiguous contexts English uses 'his/her' or 'their'. Commonly used to introduce the thing that was shown (e.g., coleção, tatuagem, cicatriz, agenda).
target_language_example: Ela me mostrou sua nova tatuagem.
native_language_example: She showed me her new tattoo.

meaning: doesn't change anything; it makes no difference.
additional_notes: Commonly used after a statement to say that something has no effect or consequence. Often appears as 'não muda nada' (with 'não' = 'not'). Can be used about situations, decisions, opinions, or feelings: 'Isso não muda nada.' Tone can be neutral or dismissive depending on context.
target_language_example: Mesmo se ele ligar, não muda nada.
native_language_example: Even if he calls, it doesn't change anything.

meaning: 'we moved (to)'.
additional_notes: First-person plural past tense of mudar-se (to move residence). Use 'para' to indicate destination (city, country, house). Often appears as 'nos mudamos para' or contracted 'mudamo-nos para' (less common). Can be used for moving to a place or changing houses.
target_language_example: No ano passado nos mudamos para um apartamento maior.
native_language_example: Last year we moved to a bigger apartment.

meaning: climate change (the long-term change in Earth's climate patterns)
additional_notes: Used to talk about global warming and related environmental changes. Singular in Portuguese here — often used with articles (a mudança climática) or without. Can refer to the phenomenon in general or to specific effects/policies.
target_language_example: A mudança climática exige ação de governos e pessoas.
native_language_example: Climate change requires action from governments and people.

meaning: 'to change the' (feminine plural); 'mudar' = to change, 'as' = the (fem. pl.).
additional_notes: Used before feminine plural nouns (e.g., regras, coisas). In Portuguese the article ('as') agrees with the noun; English doesn't require an article here in some contexts ('change rules' vs 'change the rules'). Word order: verb + article + noun. Can be followed by object or complement.
target_language_example: Precisamos mudar as regras deste jogo.
native_language_example: We need to change the rules of this game.

meaning: to change one's mind; to change an opinion or decision.
additional_notes: Used when someone alters a previously held opinion, decision, or plan. Common with pronouns/people (mudar de ideia, fazê‑la mudar de ideia, convencer alguém a mudar de ideia). Can be used in various tenses and with different subjects (ele pode mudar de ideia, eles ainda podem mudar de ideia). Not formed with a reflexive pronoun (use mudar de ideia, not se mudar).
target_language_example: Isso me fez mudar de ideia.
native_language_example: That made me change my mind.

meaning: moved to
additional_notes: Past tense of 'mudar-se' (to move residence). Used to say you changed where you live. Often appears with a destination (city, house, apartment) or 'cá/qui' (here). English uses 'moved to' or 'moved into' depending on context.
target_language_example: Eu me mudei para São Paulo no ano passado.
native_language_example: I moved to São Paulo last year.

meaning: 'changed my' or 'changed my (something)'.
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a noun (e.g., vida = life). Often appears in the phrase 'mudou a minha vida' meaning 'changed my life' (had a big impact). 'Minha' must agree with the noun it refers to (minha vida, meu mundo). Can be used for past actions (mudou = changed).
target_language_example: Aquela viagem mudou a minha vida.
native_language_example: That trip changed my life.

meaning: many things to (do/finish/etc.).
additional_notes: Used to say someone has many tasks, items, or matters remaining to do or deal with. Usually followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., fazer) or a clause explaining what still needs attention. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ela tem muitas coisas para organizar antes da festa.
native_language_example: She has many things to organize before the party.

meaning: many people in/at (the)...
additional_notes: Used to say that a large number of people are present somewhere. 'No' is the contraction of 'em' + 'o' (in/at the + masculine singular noun). Change 'no' to 'na', 'nos', or 'nas' depending on the gender and number of the noun that follows (e.g., muitas pessoas na festa; muitas pessoas nos shows). You can also use 'há' or 'havia' to indicate present vs. past existence: 'Há muitas pessoas no parque' (There are many people in the park); 'Havia muitas pessoas no saguão' (There were many people in the lobby).
target_language_example: Há muitas pessoas no metrô durante a manhã.
native_language_example: There are many people in the subway during the morning.

meaning: 'very well in/at' or 'doing very well in/at (something)'.
additional_notes: Used before a noun (often a place, activity, class, or test) to say someone or something performs or fits very well in that context. Portuguese structure: 'muito bem na' = 'muito bem' + feminine contraction 'na' (em + a). If the noun is masculine use 'no' (e.g. 'muito bem no jogo'). Can describe performance ('na prova', 'na escola') or how something would look/fit ('ficaria muito bem na minha cabana').
target_language_example: Ela está indo muito bem na universidade.
native_language_example: She is doing very well at university.

meaning: 'very expensive' (feminine plural).
additional_notes: Used to describe plural feminine nouns as being expensive. 'Muito' = very/very much; 'caras' is the feminine plural of 'caro' (expensive). For masculine plural nouns use 'muito caros'. Can also appear alone (e.g., 'São muito caras.') when the noun is clear from context.
target_language_example: Aquelas bolsas são muito caras.
native_language_example: Those bags are very expensive.

meaning: much from you / a lot because of you (used after verbs like 'aprender' or with emotional reactions)
additional_notes: Commonly appears after verbs to say you gain/learn/feel a lot 'from' or 'because of' someone. With verbs like aprender (to learn): 'aprendo muito com você' = 'I learn a lot from you.' With verbs of feeling (entristecer-se): 'se entristece muito com você' = 'he/she/You (formal) is very saddened by you' or 'because of you.' Word order: 'muito' (a lot) + 'com você' (with you/from you).
target_language_example: Eu aprendo muito com você todos os dias.
native_language_example: I learn a lot from you every day.

meaning: a lot of / really like (something belonging to you) or need (your)... — expresses strong liking or need for something of yours
additional_notes: Used before a noun introduced by 'sua' (your) to say you like or need that person/thing a lot. Context determines exact English phrasing: e.g. 'gosto muito da sua mãe' = 'I really like your mother'; 'preciso muito da sua ajuda' = 'I really need your help'. Contraction: 'da' = de + a (of the, from the). Formality: neutral, common in speech and writing.
target_language_example: Eu preciso muito da sua opinião sobre isso.
native_language_example: I really need your opinion about this.

meaning: ‘very happy if’ — used to express that the speaker would be very pleased if something happens.
additional_notes: This is a short phrase combining an adjective (muito feliz = very happy) with the conditional connector se (if). It's typically followed by a clause describing the condition (often with a verb like ver, encontrar, receber). Formality: neutral; common in both spoken and written Portuguese. Word order: adjective + se is natural when stating willingness or pleasure about a possible future event.
target_language_example: Ficarei muito feliz se você puder vir à reunião.
native_language_example: I'll be very happy if you can come to the meeting.

meaning: very crazy / really crazy (can mean mentally unstable or, informally, extremely bold/strange).
additional_notes: Used to describe a person or action as 'very crazy.' In neutral contexts it can mean mentally unstable; informally it often expresses amazement—either negative (reckless, stupid) or positive (wild, impressive). Tone and context determine whether it's insulting, joking, or admiring.
target_language_example: Tem que ser muito louco pra fazer isso.
native_language_example: You have to be really crazy to do that.

meaning: much younger; noticeably younger
additional_notes: Used to compare ages/appearance. Commonly appears with que (than) or without an explicit comparison when context implies it (e.g., 'parece muito mais jovem' = 'looks much younger'). 'Muito' (very/much) intensifies 'mais jovem' (younger).
target_language_example: Ela parece muito mais jovem do que diz a sua idade.
native_language_example: She looks much younger than her age says.

meaning: 'much older than' (comparative phrase; incomplete without 'que').
additional_notes: This fragment is normally part of the full comparative 'muito mais velho do que' meaning 'much older than'. On its own ('muito mais velho do') it is incomplete and will be followed by 'que' plus the clause or noun. Commonly used to compare age or relative age between people or things.
target_language_example: Ele parecia muito mais velho do que nas fotos.
native_language_example: He seemed much older than in the photos.

meaning: much less; let alone (used to emphasize that something is even less likely or appropriate).
additional_notes: Used to downplay or reject an action or possibility by saying it's even less true or acceptable than what was just mentioned. Often follows a negative statement. Can be placed after a comma (e.g., "e muito menos...") or at the start of a clause.
target_language_example: Eu não consigo resolver o problema, muito menos explicar para alguém.
native_language_example: I can't solve the problem, much less explain it to someone.

meaning: 'thank you very much' (said by a female speaker).
additional_notes: Common polite expression to thank someone. Portuguese speakers mark gender on obrigada/obrigado: 'obrigada' is used by women, 'obrigado' by men. Can be used alone or followed by a name/title (e.g., 'Muito obrigada, senhora'). For neutral/unknown speakers, choose form matching the speaker's gender identity. Tone ranges from casual to formal depending on context.
target_language_example: Muito obrigada pela ajuda!
native_language_example: Thank you very much for the help!

meaning: thank you very much
additional_notes: Polite way to say 'thank you very much.' If the speaker is male, 'obrigado' is used; females often say 'obrigada.' 'Muito' intensifies the thanks. Can be used formally or informally; repeating 'muito, muito obrigado' adds emphasis. 'Antecipadamente' in examples means 'in advance' (i.e., 'thanks in advance').
target_language_example: Muito obrigado pela ajuda!
native_language_example: Thank you very much for the help!

meaning: I'm very sorry for (what)... / very sorry about (what)...
additional_notes: Used to express sympathy or apology for something that happened or something someone said/did. Often appears in the phrase 'Sinto muito pelo que...' or 'Lamento muito pelo que...'. Followed by a clause or noun phrase describing the event or action (e.g., 'pelo que fiz', 'pelo que aconteceu'). Formal and informal contexts; tone is apologetic or consoling.
target_language_example: Sinto muito pelo que aconteceu ontem.
native_language_example: I'm very sorry for what happened yesterday.

meaning: used to do something a lot when (I/he/she) was (young/younger/child).
additional_notes: Combines 'muito' (a lot) with 'quando era' (when I/he/she was) to talk about frequent past habits or repeated actions in childhood or youth. You'll often see variations like 'muito quando era criança' or 'muito quando era mais jovem'. Use appropriate subject and tense: 'Eu' → 'Eu ... muito quando era criança.'
target_language_example: Eu brincava muito quando era criança.
native_language_example: I played a lot when I was a child.

meaning: 'nice to meet you' or 'a pleasure' (used when meeting someone or agreeing politely).
additional_notes: Common polite phrase used when being introduced or to express willingness/pleasure. In introductions it's equivalent to 'nice to meet you.' Can stand alone ('Muito prazer!') or be part of a sentence ('Com muito prazer' = 'with pleasure/I'd be glad to'). Formal and neutral — safe in most contexts.
target_language_example: Muito prazer, eu sou o João.
native_language_example: Nice to meet you, I'm João.

meaning: for a long time (since); used to talk about something that has been true for a long period
additional_notes: Often appears in phrases like 'faz muito tempo que...' or 'há muito tempo que...' to mean 'it's been a long time since...' or 'for a long time'. Can be followed by a verb or clause describing what has lasted. 'Muito tempo que' on its own is informal/truncated; learners should prefer 'faz muito tempo que' or 'há muito tempo que' in full sentences.
target_language_example: Faz muito tempo que não nos vemos.
native_language_example: It's been a long time since we last saw each other.

meaning: 'a lot to' / 'much to' (used before verbs or infinitives to say there is a large amount left to do, offer, see, etc.)
additional_notes: Commonly appears before infinitive verbs or verbal expressions (desfrutar, oferecer, ver, ensinar) to indicate there's plenty/much of something left or available. Can be used in positive and negative contexts (e.g., 'não há muito para ver' = 'there isn't much to see'). Word order: 'muito para' + infinitive or pronoun + infinitive (e.g., 'muito para lhe ensinar').
target_language_example: Ainda há muito para aprender sobre isto.
native_language_example: There is still a lot to learn about this.

meaning: 'women like' or 'women enjoy/prefer'.
additional_notes: A general statement about what women (in general) like. 'Mulheres' is the plural noun 'women'. 'Gostam' is the third-person plural of 'gostar' (to like) and requires 'de' before the thing liked. Use 'As mulheres gostam de...' to make a neutral/general observation. To talk about a specific woman, use 'A mulher gosta de...'.
target_language_example: As mulheres gostam de música ao vivo.
native_language_example: Women like live music.

meaning: 'the world in which' or 'the world that/where'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause describing the world/society/context where something happens. Followed by a verb or relative clause (e.g., 'vivemos', 'os homens vivem'). Equivalent to English 'the world in which...' or simply 'the world where...'.
target_language_example: No mundo em que vivemos, a tecnologia muda tudo rapidamente.
native_language_example: In the world in which we live, technology changes everything quickly.

meaning: the world is full (of...) — used to say there are many people/things like that or that something is common
additional_notes: Literal translation: “the world is full.” Often followed by a preposition/phrase (e.g. 'de gente', 'de oportunidades', 'de problemas') to specify what the world is full of. Used in conversational Portuguese to comment that something is common, widespread, or that there are plenty of alternatives. Tone is neutral; not idiomatic slang.
target_language_example: O mundo está cheio de gente que pensa assim.
native_language_example: The world is full of people who think that way.

meaning: the real world; real life (as opposed to an imagined, virtual, or idealized situation).
additional_notes: Used to contrast everyday reality with fantasy, theory, or online/idealized situations. Can be used literally (the physical world) or idiomatically (practical, harsh realities). Common in greetings or warnings: 'Bem-vindo ao mundo real!' = 'Welcome to the real world!'. Gender/number on greetings agrees with the person(s) addressed (bem-vindo/a(s)/os).
target_language_example: Depois da faculdade, entrei de cabeça no mundo real.
native_language_example: After college, I dove headfirst into the real world.

meaning: literally 'the world knows'; used to mean 'everyone knows' or 'it's well known'.
additional_notes: A fixed phrase formed by mundo (world) + sabe (knows). Used informally or in speech to emphasize that something is common knowledge. Often appears in expressions like 'o mundo sabe' or 'todo mundo sabe'. 'Todo mundo sabe' is more common and means 'everyone knows'.
target_language_example: Todo mundo sabe que ela é uma ótima cozinheira.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that she is a great cook.

meaning: 'the world knows that' — used to say something is widely known or obvious
additional_notes: A fixed sequence of words: mundo (the world) + sabe (knows) + que (that). Often used in spoken and written Portuguese to emphasize that a fact is common knowledge or obvious to everyone. Can appear with a subject pronoun or article before mundo (o mundo sabe que) but is frequently used without the article in casual speech. Tone can be neutral or emphatic depending on context.
target_language_example: O mundo sabe que ela é uma grande cientista.
native_language_example: The world knows that she is a great scientist.

meaning: 'worldly' or 'experienced; well-traveled' (literally 'seen world').
additional_notes: Used to describe a person who has seen a lot of life, is experienced, streetwise, or cosmopolitan. Can be positive (experienced, sophisticated) or neutral depending on context. Not a fixed idiom in all regions — more common in Brazil in expressions like 'um homem/mulher de mundo' or 'mundo visto' to praise someone's experience. Tone is not strongly informal.
target_language_example: Ela é uma pessoa mundo viu e já morou em três países.
native_language_example: She is a worldly person and has lived in three countries.

meaning: 'the world is a ...' — used to make a general statement about the world being (adjective) (e.g., dangerous, beautiful).
additional_notes: This phrase is followed by an adjective or a descriptive clause to express a speaker's general opinion about the world (e.g., "mundo é um lugar perigoso" = "the world is a dangerous place"). In Portuguese you can add articles or qualifiers (o mundo é um lugar..., o mundo pode ser um lugar...). Often appears with emotive or evaluative words (perigoso, lindo, injusto, cheio de esperança). Pronoun 'o' before 'mundo' is common: 'o mundo é um lugar...'.
target_language_example: O mundo é um lugar bonito quando as pessoas ajudam umas às outras.
native_language_example: The world is a beautiful place when people help each other.

meaning: the museum is / the museum's state (open, closed, located, etc.).
additional_notes: Combines 'museu' (museum) with the verb 'estar' to describe the museum's current condition, status, or temporary location. Used for temporary states (está aberto/fechado/aberto hoje/fechado agora) and to indicate location (está ao virar da esquina). For permanent characteristics, Portuguese uses 'ser' instead of 'estar'.
target_language_example: O museu está fechado para reformas.
native_language_example: The museum is closed for renovations.

meaning: sewing machine.
additional_notes: Refers to the mechanical or electronic device used to stitch fabric and other materials. Commonly used in household or tailoring contexts. Gender: feminine (a máquina). You can use possessives (minha máquina de costura) or describe condition (máquina de costura nova).
target_language_example: A avó dela consertou a saia com a máquina de costura.
native_language_example: Her grandmother fixed the skirt with the sewing machine.

meaning: typewriter (a mechanical or electromechanical device for typing).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a physical typewriter. Can be used in everyday contexts (losing, borrowing, owning, using). In modern contexts it may sound old-fashioned since most people use computers, but it's the standard term for the device.
target_language_example: Ela encontrou uma velha máquina de escrever no sótão.
native_language_example: She found an old typewriter in the attic.

meaning: washing machine; a machine that washes (clothes, dishes when specified).
additional_notes: Often needs a noun after it to specify what it washes: 'máquina de lavar roupa' (washing machine for clothes) or 'máquina de lavar louça' (dishwasher). In casual speech people may shorten 'máquina de lavar roupa' to just 'máquina' or 'máquina de lavar' when context is clear.
target_language_example: A minha máquina de lavar roupa quebrou ontem.
native_language_example: My washing machine broke yesterday.

meaning: time machine; a device for traveling to the past or future.
additional_notes: Used literally in sci‑fi contexts (a device that moves through time) or imaginatively (wishful talk about changing the past). 'Máquina' = machine, 'do tempo' = of time — literal, compositional translation. Can be used in questions and stories.
target_language_example: Se eu tivesse uma máquina do tempo, voltaria para corrigir meus erros.
native_language_example: If I had a time machine, I would go back to fix my mistakes.

meaning: gas mask; protective mask that filters harmful gases and particles.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a protective device worn over the face to filter toxic gases, smoke, or airborne particles. Common in contexts like military, industrial safety, civil defense, or emergency situations. Can be singular or plural (máscara de gás / máscaras de gás).
target_language_example: Os trabalhadores usam máscara de gás durante a limpeza.
native_language_example: The workers wear a gas mask during the cleanup.

meaning: 'as much as' / 'the most that' (used to indicate the greatest amount or extent possible)
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs of ability or possibility (poder, conseguir) to say 'as much as you/they can' or 'the most that can be...'. Often appears in constructions like 'o máximo que você puder' or 'o máximo que conseguirem'. It is neutral/formal and can be used in spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: Pegue o máximo que puder sem estragar nada.
native_language_example: Take as much as you can without ruining anything.

meaning: their mother (referring to a group of people)
additional_notes: Possessive phrase: mãe = mother; deles = of them/their (masculine or mixed group). Use 'deles' when the possessor group is male or mixed; for an all-female group use 'delas'. Common in everyday speech to indicate someone is the mother of the mentioned people. Word order is noun + possessive pronoun.
target_language_example: Eles mandaram flores para a mãe deles.
native_language_example: They sent flowers to their mother.

meaning: 'mother and the' (combination of 'mãe' = mother + conjunction 'e' = and + definite article 'o' = the (masculine)).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the sequence 'mãe e o' that can appear when mentioning a mother followed by a masculine noun introduced with the definite article (e.g., 'mãe e o pai' = 'mother and the father'). Word order and articles match Portuguese grammar: 'o' agrees with a masculine noun. In everyday English you'd usually say 'my mother and father' without the definite article. Watch for gender agreement ('a' for feminine, 'o' for masculine).
target_language_example: A mãe e o pai vão nos visitar amanhã.
native_language_example: The mother and the father are going to visit us tomorrow.

meaning: "(my/your/the) mother is" — the verb 'estar' used with 'mãe' to say where or how someone's mother is (location or temporary state).
additional_notes: Use 'mãe está' to describe a mother's location (e.g., 'na cozinha'), physical condition (e.g., 'muito doente'), or temporary situation (e.g., 'ocupada', 'para entrar'). Choose the possessive or subject pronoun before 'mãe' as needed: 'minha mãe está' (my mother is), 'sua mãe está' (your/his/her mother is), or just 'a mãe está' (the mother is / the mother is about to…). 'Estar' indicates temporary states or locations, not permanent characteristics.
target_language_example: Minha mãe está no trabalho agora.
native_language_example: My mother is at work right now.

meaning: my mother is sick / (the) mother is ill.
additional_notes: A simple statement saying that someone's mother is ill. Use 'minha mãe está doente' to say 'my mother is sick.' You can add time expressions: 'desde o mês passado' (since last month), 'há dois dias' (for two days). To specify location/state: 'na cama' (in bed).
target_language_example: Minha mãe está doente desde ontem e precisa descansar.
native_language_example: My mother has been sick since yesterday and needs to rest.

meaning: 'mother lives' (literally: 'mother lives/is living')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom — it's just the verb morar ('to live') used with mãe ('mother'). Use to say where someone's mother lives. Word order is subject + verb; pronouns or possessives (minha/sua) usually appear before mãe (e.g., minha mãe mora...).
target_language_example: Minha mãe mora perto da praia.
native_language_example: My mother lives near the beach.

meaning: 'mother knows' — literally 'mother knows'; often used to say that one's (or someone's) mother knows something or to stress that it's common knowledge even to one's mother.
additional_notes: Literal phrase combining mãe (mother) + sabe (knows). Used to state that a mother knows a fact or to emphasize that information is widely known (e.g., 'even my mother knows'). Can appear in questions asking whether someone's mother knows. Not idiomatic or slang.
target_language_example: Até a minha mãe sabe disso.
native_language_example: Even my mother knows that.

meaning: 'hands up' (command to raise your hands, usually by police/robbers)
additional_notes: Used as an imperative order telling people to raise their hands and stay still. Common in contexts of authority or threat (police, robberies, stop-and-search). Can be shouted alone or followed by instructions (e.g., 'e não se mexam' = 'and don't move').
target_language_example: Mãos ao alto e devagar — ninguém precisa se machucar.
native_language_example: Hands up and slowly — nobody needs to get hurt.

meaning: hands in/on (used to say someone has their hands in or on something, often pockets or a body part).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in expressions like 'mãos nos bolsos' (hands in pockets) or 'mãos nos seios' (hands on breasts). Used to describe someone's hand placement or posture. Literal and compositional. Tone is neutral but context can be informal depending on noun (e.g., 'mãos nos seios' is sexual). Verb often appears as 'ter/estar/com/colocar/enfiar as mãos nos...'.
target_language_example: Ele estava com as mãos nos bolsos enquanto esperava.
native_language_example: He had his hands in his pockets while he waited.

meaning: 'the doctor said' or 'the doctor told (someone)'.
additional_notes: A common phrase used to report what a doctor advised or stated. Followed by a direct object (who was told) + infinitive or by 'que' + clause with the reported information. Useful for talking about medical advice or diagnoses.
target_language_example: O médico disse que eu devo tomar os remédios todos os dias.
native_language_example: The doctor said that I should take the medicine every day.

meaning: literally 'doctor can' – used to talk about what a doctor is able to do or to ask if a doctor is available/able to see someone.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's simply the noun 'médico' (doctor) plus the modal verb 'pode' (can/may). Use it to state a doctor's ability or availability (e.g., scheduling an appointment, permission, or confirming capability). Pronouns and object forms change depending on the patient: consultá-la (her), consultá-lo (him), me ver (see me).
target_language_example: O médico pode vê-la na terça-feira às três.
native_language_example: The doctor can see you on Tuesday at three.

meaning: 'the slightest idea' — used to say you don't know something at all.
additional_notes: Common expression to emphasize lack of knowledge or understanding. Often appears in negative phrases: não tenho a mínima ideia (I have no idea). Can be used alone as an exclamation: Não tem a mínima ideia! Tone ranges from informal to neutral; suitable in most spoken and written contexts.
target_language_example: Eu não tenho a mínima ideia de onde deixei as chaves.
native_language_example: I have no idea where I left the keys.

meaning: classical music.
additional_notes: Refers to the Western art music tradition (e.g., Bach, Mozart, Beethoven) or more generally to orchestral/chamber/solo repertoire and formal compositions. Used like in English: gostar de música clássica = to like classical music; ouvir/escutar música clássica = to listen to classical music.
target_language_example: Eu gosto de ouvir música clássica quando estudo.
native_language_example: I like to listen to classical music when I study.

meaning: pop music (popular, mainstream music).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the popular music genre 'pop'. Can be preceded by adjectives or origin (e.g., 'música pop russa' = Russian pop). Pronunciation: música (MOO-zee-ka), pop (like English 'pop').
target_language_example: Ela adora ouvir música pop enquanto estuda.
native_language_example: She loves listening to pop music while studying.

meaning: in bed all day / in bed the whole day.
additional_notes: Used to say someone stayed in bed for the whole day. Commonly appears as 'na cama o dia todo' or 'na cama o dia inteiro'. It's neutral (not slang) and often describes resting, being sick, lazy behavior, or a day off. You can replace 'o dia' with 'o dia todo' or 'o dia inteiro' for clarity.
target_language_example: Hoje vou ficar na cama o dia todo e descansar.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to stay in bed all day and rest.

meaning: 'obviously' / 'right in (one's) face' or literally 'on the face'
additional_notes: Used both figuratively and literally. Figuratively it means something is obvious or obvious to see (e.g., "estava tão na cara" = "it was so obvious"). It can also describe something happening directly to someone's face (literal, often strong: "dar um tiro na cara" = "shoot someone in the face"). Tone ranges from neutral to strong depending on context; be careful with literal uses because they can be violent or blunt.
target_language_example: A resposta estava na cara desde o começo.
native_language_example: The answer was obvious from the start.

meaning: in the existence of; referring to whether something exists
additional_notes: Used after verbs like acreditar (to believe) or duvidar (to doubt) to talk about belief in the existence of something (e.g., bruxas = witches, fantasmas = ghosts). Commonly appears as 'acreditar na existência de ...' or 'duvidar da existência de ...'.
target_language_example: Você acredita na existência de vida em outros planetas?
native_language_example: Do you believe in the existence of life on other planets?

meaning: in front (of)
additional_notes: Used to indicate physical position in front of something or someone (e.g., 'in front of the house', 'in front of mom') or to mean 'ahead' in order/sequence (e.g., 'go ahead', 'come first'). Context determines whether it refers to spatial location or being ahead/first. Often followed by de/da/do/verb/noun (e.g., 'na frente do carro', 'na frente do computador').
target_language_example: O cachorro está na frente da casa.
native_language_example: The dog is in front of the house.

meaning: in front of; ahead of (physically or in order/position).
additional_notes: Used for physical position (standing in front of someone), for being ahead in a race or competition, or for speaking/performing before an audience. Context determines whether it means 'physically in front of', 'ahead of' (competition), or 'in front of an audience'.
target_language_example: Ela ficou nervosa em falar na frente de tanta gente.
native_language_example: She was nervous about speaking in front of so many people.

meaning: on time
additional_notes: Common phrase with several related uses depending on context: 1) 'on time' meaning punctual (e.g., chegar na hora = arrive on time); 2) 'at the time' referring to a specific moment (e.g., bem na hora = just in time); 3) used in set expressions like 'na hora de dormir' = at bedtime/when it's time to sleep. Context determines the best English equivalent.
target_language_example: Ele sempre chega na hora para as reuniões.
native_language_example: He always arrives on time for meetings.

meaning: 'for the most part' / 'mostly' (when used as 'na maior parte') ; can also appear in other uses where 'maior' means 'bigger' (e.g. 'na maior casa' = 'in the biggest house').
additional_notes: Most commonly appears as the full phrase 'na maior parte (de...)' meaning 'for the most part' or 'most of' (use with time periods, groups, situations). It is a neutral, common expression for generalizing. Separately, 'na maior' can be part of a literal phrase where 'maior' is the comparative/adjective 'bigger' (e.g. 'na maior casa' = 'in the biggest house'). Context determines which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Na maior parte do ano, chove pouco aqui.
native_language_example: For the most part of the year, it rains little here.

meaning: 'in the morning' or 'on the morning (of)'.
additional_notes: Used to specify a time during the morning. Commonly appears as 'na manhã seguinte' = 'the next morning'. 'Na' is the contraction of 'em' + 'a' (in/on + the). Can be followed by a time phrase (e.g., 'na manhã de segunda-feira' = 'on Monday morning').
target_language_example: Na manhã seguinte, fomos ao mercado.
native_language_example: The next morning, we went to the market.

meaning: 'in my opinion' or 'as I see it'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a personal view or judgment. Common in both formal and informal contexts. Can be placed at the start of a sentence (as in the examples) or elsewhere: 'Eu, na minha opinião, prefiro...' or 'Isso é, na minha opinião, errado.'
target_language_example: Na minha opinião, esse filme vale a pena.
native_language_example: In my opinion, that movie is worth watching.

meaning: in fashion; fashionable; trendy.
additional_notes: Used to say that clothing, styles, ideas or items are currently popular or fashionable. Can describe short-term trends (this season/this year) or things that became fashionable some years ago. Commonly used with estar (está/estão) or ficar (fica/ficam).
target_language_example: Aquele casaco está na moda este inverno.
native_language_example: That coat is in fashion this winter.

meaning: 'exactly' or 'right on target' (used to say something is perfectly correct or spot-on).
additional_notes: Informal, idiomatic expression. Used to praise a correct answer, a precise action, or to agree that something is exactly right. Common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese. Can be used alone as an exclamation ("Na mosca!") or in a sentence ("Ele acertou na mosca." = He hit it exactly).
target_language_example: Você descreveu a situação na mosca.
native_language_example: You described the situation exactly/right on.

meaning: on the tip of the tongue; almost remembered or ready to be said.
additional_notes: Used when a word, name, or answer is just about to be recalled or spoken but not yet said. Often describes a temporary memory lapse: you feel you know it but can't quite produce it. Common in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: O nome dela está na ponta da língua, mas não consigo me lembrar.
native_language_example: Her name is on the tip of my tongue, but I can't remember it.

meaning: a strong, vulgar emphasis roughly like 'the f***ing' or 'the damn' (used to add anger, frustration, contempt, or intensity before a noun or place).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. 'Porra' is a swear word; 'na porra' is used to intensify emotion about something and often appears with determiners/possessives (na porra da, na porra do, na porra de). Not appropriate for polite or formal contexts. Tone ranges from anger to exasperation or emphatic surprise. Use with caution.
target_language_example: Eu vou na porra da reunião e falar o que precisa ser dito.
native_language_example: I'm going to the f***ing meeting and say what needs to be said.

meaning: on the (shelf) of / on the ... shelf (used with qualifiers like 'cima' or 'baixo').
additional_notes: Used to tell someone where to place an item on a shelf. Commonly followed by a qualifier (e.g., 'cima' = top, 'baixo' = bottom) or a possessive (e.g., 'na prateleira de livros' = on the bookshelf). In the examples it's a fixed phrase meaning 'on the ... shelf' (na = in/on the + prateleira = shelf + de = of/of the).
target_language_example: Coloca a caixa na prateleira de cima.
native_language_example: Put the box on the top shelf.

meaning: 'in practice' or 'in reality' (what actually happens, as opposed to theory).
additional_notes: Used to contrast theory/expectation with real-world results or to state how things work in reality. Often appears at the start of a sentence or clause and is followed by a comma. Equivalent to 'actually' or 'in practice' in English.
target_language_example: Na prática, o plano não funcionou como esperávamos.
native_language_example: In practice, the plan didn't work as we expected.

meaning: in the capacity/role of; as (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate someone's role, position, or official capacity when performing an action or making a statement (similar to 'as' or 'in my capacity as'). Common in formal contexts, official documents, or statements. Followed by a noun: na qualidade de + [cargo/função/papel].
target_language_example: Falo na qualidade de presidente da associação.
native_language_example: I speak in my capacity as president of the association.

meaning: 'actually', 'in reality', or 'to face reality' (colloquial).
additional_notes: Common informal expression. Used two ways: as an adverb/intro (na real = honestly / actually / in fact) and in the verbal phrase 'cair na real' meaning 'to come to terms with reality' or 'to wake up/realize the truth'. Tone is conversational; avoid in formal writing.
target_language_example: Na real, eu não sabia que isso ia acontecer.
native_language_example: Honestly, I didn't know that was going to happen.

meaning: 'in reality' or 'actually' (used to contrast expectation with reality or to correct/clarify).
additional_notes: Common phrase to introduce a correction, contrast, or emphasis. Can be used like English 'actually', 'in fact', or 'in reality'. Placement is flexible: at the start of a sentence (Na realidade, ...) or inside it (..., na realidade, ...).
target_language_example: Na realidade, eu não posso ir à festa.
native_language_example: Actually, I can't go to the party.

meaning: 'in the week that' / commonly used as 'next week' when followed by 'vem' (na semana que vem).
additional_notes: Often appears as the fixed expression 'na semana que vem' meaning 'next week'. More generally 'na semana que...' introduces a time clause (the week when). In spoken Portuguese, 'na semana que vem' is the usual way to say 'next week'.
target_language_example: Na semana que vem vou começar um curso de português.
native_language_example: Next week I'll start a Portuguese course.

meaning: actually
additional_notes: Often used to correct, clarify, or contrast with what was said or assumed before. It's very common at the start of a sentence, but it can also appear before the part being corrected.
target_language_example: Na verdade, eu prefiro ficar em casa hoje.
native_language_example: Actually, I prefer to stay home today.

meaning: 'at that time' or 'back then' (referring to a specific past period).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a particular time in the past already understood from context or mentioned earlier. Can appear at the start of a sentence or after the verb. Common in storytelling or giving background information.
target_language_example: Na época, eu morava em outra cidade.
native_language_example: At that time, I lived in another city.

meaning: not related / has nothing to do with it / irrelevant
additional_notes: Used to say two things are unrelated or that someone is no longer connected to something/someone. Can be used as an interjection ("Nada a ver!") to express disagreement or that something doesn't make sense. Context determines whether it's about relevance or relationship.
target_language_example: Isso não tem nada a ver com o que eu disse.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with what I said.

meaning: has nothing to do with you / it's none of your business
additional_notes: Used to say that someone is not involved, responsible, or connected to a situation. Can be neutral (no relation) or dismissive/defensive (telling someone to mind their own business). Common variants: "isso não tem nada a ver com você" and "não tenho nada a ver com isso."
target_language_example: Isso não tem nada a ver com você, por favor não se envolva.
native_language_example: This has nothing to do with you, please don't get involved.

meaning: not bad; pretty good (mild approval).
additional_notes: Informal/colloquial phrase used to express mild praise or approval — equivalent to 'not bad' or 'pretty good' in English. Often used alone, with a name, or with 'hein?' for confirmation. Can be used positively even when describing something with minor flaws.
target_language_example: O jantar ontem não era caro e, honestamente, foi nada mau.
native_language_example: Last night's dinner wasn't expensive and, honestly, it was not bad.

meaning: as if nothing had happened; nothing had happened (subjunctive phrase)
additional_notes: This is a subjunctive clause often used after verbs or expressions that imply a hypothetical, wish, or contrasting situation (e.g., 'como se', 'agora parece', 'é como se'). It describes a situation imagined or reported in which nothing occurred. Useful in conditional or descriptive contexts: 'Ele agiu como se nada tivesse acontecido' = 'He acted as if nothing had happened.'
target_language_example: Ela entrou na sala e sorriu como se nada tivesse acontecido.
native_language_example: She entered the room and smiled as if nothing had happened.

meaning: 'to swim in this' (used before a masculine noun: 'nadar neste + noun' = 'to swim in this [river/lake/etc]').
additional_notes: A combination of the verb nadar (to swim) + the contraction neste (em + este = in/at this [masculine]). Use before masculine singular nouns (neste rio, neste lago). For feminine use 'nadar nesta'. Common in signs and warnings (É proibido/É permitido/É perigoso/É seguro nadar neste rio).
target_language_example: É perigoso nadar neste rio em julho.
native_language_example: It's dangerous to swim in this river in July.

meaning: 'her boyfriend is' (describing a characteristic or state of a woman’s boyfriend).
additional_notes: Used to state something about 'her' boyfriend (dela = of her). Commonly followed by nationality, religion, age, personality, or other descriptions. Word order: 'o namorado dela é + [adjective/noun/phrase]'. If speaker refers to a specific woman already known in context.
target_language_example: O namorado dela é muito gentil.
native_language_example: Her boyfriend is very kind.

meaning: 'in/on the back' or idiomatically 'in the back' / 'on one's back' (literal) and used in expressions like 'stab in the back' or 'carry on one's back'.
additional_notes: Can be literal (physical location: on someone's back or the backs of objects) or idiomatic. Examples: 'apunhalou a Mary nas costas' = 'stabbed Mary in the back' (betrayal), 'carregava o mundo nas costas' = 'carried the world on his back' (burden/responsibility), 'dor nas costas' = 'back pain'. Common preposition form: nas = em + as (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Ele trabalhava o dia todo e voltou com dor nas costas.
native_language_example: He worked all day and came back with back pain.

meaning: 'in the hands of' — indicates who has control, responsibility, possession, power, custody, or is causing something (literally or figuratively).
additional_notes: Used both literally (someone physically holding or possessing something) and figuratively (control, responsibility, fate, influence, or harm caused by someone). Common with verbs like estar, cair, deixar, sofrer, prefiro, and expressions invoking trust or danger (e.g., 'nas mãos de Deus' = under God's care; 'cair nas mãos de alguém' = fall into someone's hands — possibly dangerous). Tone is neutral; context determines formality and nuance.
target_language_example: A verdadeira justiça está nas mãos de Deus.
native_language_example: True justice is in the hands of God.

meaning: 'sunrise' — the moment the sun appears above the horizon or the early morning light.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the time of day when the sun rises or the visual phenomenon (colors, light). Common in expressions about early morning activities (e.g., 'ver o nascer do sol' = watch the sunrise). Can be used literally or poetically.
target_language_example: Fui à praia para ver o nascer do sol.
native_language_example: I went to the beach to see the sunrise.

meaning: 'spaceship' or 'spacecraft' (a vehicle designed for travel in outer space).
additional_notes: Used to refer to any vehicle that travels in space (manned or unmanned). Commonly interchangeable with 'foguete' when context implies a rocket, but 'nave espacial' focuses on the craft itself. Plural: 'naves espaciais'.
target_language_example: Eles lançaram a nave espacial hoje de manhã.
native_language_example: They launched the spaceship this morning.

meaning: 'necessary that' — introduces a necessity or requirement (often followed by a subjunctive verb).
additional_notes: Used to say something is required or needed. Commonly appears in impersonal constructions with 'é necessário que...' and is often followed by verbs in the subjunctive (e.g., você faça). Can be used in questions and negatives. Formal but widely used in spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: É necessário que você entregue o relatório hoje.
native_language_example: It is necessary that you submit the report today.

meaning: an informal way to refer to 'the thing/affair/issue of' or 'the ... thing' (used to point to a situation, matter, deal, or topic).
additional_notes: Very colloquial.
