meaning: 'that you (plural) are (verb) me' — the start of questions or statements describing actions others are doing to 'me'.
additional_notes: This is a fragment often used in questions introduced with 'Por que' (Why) or other clauses: e.g. 'Por que vocês estão me [verb]?' The structure: 'vocês' = you (plural), 'estão' = are (present progressive), 'me' = me (object). It signals someone asking why a group is doing something to them now. Replace the final verb to complete the sentence (agradecendo, ajudando, encarando, perguntando, perseguindo).
target_language_example: Por que vocês estão me ignorando?
native_language_example: Why are you (plural) ignoring me?

meaning: why are you (plural) so ...
additional_notes: This phrase is used to ask a group of people (vocês) why they are in a certain state or feeling. The adjective at the end changes to match gender and number (quietos = mixed/male plural, quietas = female plural). Common in spoken and written Portuguese. 'Por que' at the start means 'why'.
target_language_example: Por que vocês estão tão cansados?
native_language_example: Why are you (all) so tired?

meaning: 'that you (plural) like' or 'which you (plural) like' (referring to preferences of a group)
additional_notes: Used to refer back to something previously mentioned or to ask about the preferences of a group (vocês = you all). Common in questions introduced by 'por que' (why) or in clauses after nouns to ask which one(s) they prefer. ‘Gostam’ is third-person plural to agree with 'vocês'. Predominantly used in Brazilian Portuguese; European Portuguese may use 'vocês' less frequently or with slightly different pronoun choice.
target_language_example: Por que vocês gostam tanto disso, que vocês gostam tanto da cidade?
native_language_example: Why do you (all) like that so much, that you (all) like the city so much?

meaning: that you (plural) can / that you (plural) are able to
additional_notes: Used to express belief, encouragement, or statement about the ability of a group (informal or formal plural depending on region). 'Vocês' is the plural 'you' used in most Brazilian Portuguese; in Portugal 'vocês' is also used but sometimes replaced by 'vós' or 'vocês' with different formality. The clause often follows verbs like 'sei' (I know) or 'acho' (I think): 'Eu sei que vocês podem...' = 'I know that you (all) can...'.
target_language_example: Eu tenho certeza de que vocês podem terminar o projeto a tempo.
native_language_example: I'm sure that you (all) can finish the project on time.

meaning: 'what you (plural) want' or 'that you (plural) want' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used to ask or refer to the desires or reasons of a group (você plural = vocês). Common in questions: 'O que vocês querem?' = 'What do you want?'. In sentences starting with 'Por que vocês querem...?' it asks for the reason ('Why do you all want...'). Verb 'querem' is present tense, 3rd person plural. Formality: neutral; 'vocês' is the standard plural 'you' in Brazilian Portuguese (in European Portuguese 'vocês' is also used but may be more formal depending on region).
target_language_example: Por que vocês querem mudar de cidade?
native_language_example: Why do you (all) want to move to another city?

meaning: 'that you (plural) have' or 'that you (plural) ...' (used to report possession, feelings, states, or obligations of a group)
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction que ('that' / 'who') + vocês (you plural) + têm (third-person plural of ter = to have). Used to report what a group possesses (objects, permissions), their feelings/states (medo, certeza), or obligations (ter que = to have to). In spoken Brazilian Portuguese vocês is the common plural 'you'. Word order may change for questions (Por que vocês têm...? = Why do you have... or Why are you...).
target_language_example: Eu sei que vocês têm tempo para conversar.
native_language_example: I know that you (plural) have time to talk.

meaning: 'have to return to' (followed by a masculine singular place: o + place).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the obligation expression 'ter que' (have to) + 'voltar para' (to return to) + the masculine definite article 'o' before a masculine noun (e.g., 'o escritório', 'o trabalho', 'o jantar' used here as an event). In spoken Portuguese the 'que' often links to a previous verb (e.g., 'tenho que voltar para o...'). Replace 'o' with 'a' for feminine places (voltar para a). Use without the article for proper names or when not required.
target_language_example: Tenho que voltar para o escritório às três.
native_language_example: I have to return to the office at three.

meaning: that is the
additional_notes: A common sequence where que introduces a subordinate clause and é o literally means "is the." Used to identify or state what something/someone is. English translations often contract to "that is the" or "that it's the." Word order may vary; context determines whether que is 'that' or part of a question ("who/what do you think that is"). Not idiomatic by itself — it is a compositional chunk formed from common words.
target_language_example: Eu acho que é o fim da estrada.
native_language_example: I think that it's the end of the road.

meaning: jigsaw puzzle; any puzzle you assemble or solve.
additional_notes: Used for physical jigsaw puzzles and figuratively for puzzles/problems to solve. Literally 'break-head' but means a puzzle to piece together or a brain-teaser. Can be used with montar (assemble) or resolver (solve).
target_language_example: Ela comprou um quebra-cabeça de 500 peças.
native_language_example: She bought a 500-piece jigsaw puzzle.

meaning: to be embarrassed or proven wrong; to be disappointed; (informally) to physically hit someone's face (threat).
additional_notes: Colloquial idiom. Most commonly used to mean 'to be humiliated' or 'to be proven wrong' (e.g., 'you'll be disappointed/you'll eat your words'). In informal or violent contexts it can be a threat meaning 'to smash someone's face' (physical assault). Tone can be aggressive—use with caution; avoid in formal situations.
target_language_example: Se você acha que vai ganhar sem estudar, vai acabar por quebrar a cara.
native_language_example: If you think you'll win without studying, you'll end up being proven wrong/embarrassed.

meaning: 'who arrived' or 'who came'.
additional_notes: Used to ask or point out the person(s) who has/have arrived. Common in questions (Quem chegou?) and exclamations drawing attention (Olha/Veja quem chegou! = Look who's here!). In formal writing you might see 'quem chegou' in questions; in speech contractions like 'quem chegou?' often follow greetings or when announcing someone's arrival.
target_language_example: Olha quem chegou ao jantar!
native_language_example: Look who's arrived at the dinner!

meaning: 'I wish' / 'if only' (expresses a wish or regret)
additional_notes: Used to express a strong wish, desire, or regret about something that is unlikely or impossible. Often followed by the imperfect subjunctive (eu tivesse, tivéssemos) or 'que' + subjunctive. Tone can be wistful or hypothetical.
target_language_example: Quem dera eu pudesse viajar agora.
native_language_example: If only I could travel now.

meaning: 'who would have thought' / 'who would've guessed'.
additional_notes: Used to express surprise, irony, or unexpected outcome. Can stand alone as an exclamation (e.g., 'Mas, quem diria?') or introduce a clause ('Quem diria que...'). Tone can be amused, incredulous, or slightly sarcastic depending on context.
target_language_example: Quem diria que ela mudaria de ideia tão rápido?
native_language_example: Who would have thought she'd change her mind so quickly?

meaning: I wish (if only); expresses a wish or regret about something unlikely or impossible.
additional_notes: Used to express longing or regret for something that is unlikely or impossible. Often followed by an infinitive or a subjunctive clause (quem me dera + infinitive / que + past subjunctive). Equivalent to English 'if only' or 'I wish'. Can stand alone as an exclamation: 'Quem me dera!' = 'If only!' or 'I wish!'.
target_language_example: Quem me dera eu poder viajar agora.
native_language_example: If only I could travel now.

meaning: 'whoever' or 'whomever' (introduces an indefinite person).
additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified person(s). Often followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., diga, fale, seja) when expressing doubt, opinion, or a non-specific subject. Can be used in positive, negative, or neutral contexts: 'Quem quer que seja, entre' = 'Whoever it is, come in.'
target_language_example: Quem quer que venha, será bem-vindo.
native_language_example: Whoever comes will be welcome.

meaning: 'who knows' / 'maybe'.
additional_notes: Used both literally to ask who knows something and idiomatically as a short response meaning 'maybe' or 'it’s possible'. Often placed at the start of a sentence to suggest uncertainty (Quem sabe...) or alone as a comment (Quem sabe!). Can be followed by a question (Quem sabe?) to mean 'Who knows?'.
target_language_example: Quem sabe amanhã chova e a praia ficará vazia.
native_language_example: Who knows, maybe it will rain tomorrow and the beach will be empty.

meaning: 'If only' or 'I wish' (expressing a wish or regret that something were true).
additional_notes: Used to express a strong wish or regret about something unlikely or impossible. Often followed by a verb or a clause (explicit or implied). Tone can be wistful or resigned. Informal to neutral — common in spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: Quem te dera eu ter mais tempo para viajar.
native_language_example: If only I had more time to travel.

meaning: 'who you were (with)'.
additional_notes: This phrase appears in questions about who someone was with. In Portuguese the full expression is often 'com quem você estava' (with whom you were). Word order can change in questions: 'Com quem você estava?' = 'Who were you with?'. Informal spoken variants may drop 'você' or use 'tava' (estava → tava).
target_language_example: Com quem você estava no cinema ontem?
native_language_example: Who were you with at the cinema yesterday?

meaning: who (plural you)
additional_notes: Used to ask about the identity of people addressed to a group (plural 'you'). 'Vocês' is the plural 'you' in Brazilian Portuguese. Common constructions: 'Com quem vocês...?' (With whom are you all...?), 'Em quem vocês...?' (For whom will you all.../Who will you all vote for?). Word order can change for questions (e.g., 'Com quem vocês estão falando?' or more formally 'Com quem estão falando?').
target_language_example: Quem vocês convidaram para a festa?
native_language_example: Who did you (all) invite to the party?

meaning: 'wants/want to give to' (construction: querer + dar + preposition a, used before a person or pronoun).
additional_notes: Combination of the verb querer (to want) + dar (to give) + preposition a (to). Use when referring to giving something to a person; the object (what is given) can be stated after the person or implied from context. In speech you may also hear alternatives like 'quer dar pra ela' (colloquial) or clitic pronouns ('quer dar-lhe'), but 'quer dar a' + full pronoun is neutral and clear. Frequently appears in questions (e.g., 'O que você quer dar a ela?').
target_language_example: O que você quer dar a ela?
native_language_example: What do you want to give to her?

meaning: means
additional_notes: Two main uses: 1) as a verb phrase meaning 'to mean' or 'to signify' (e.g., 'isso quer dizer que...' = 'that means that...'); 2) as a discourse filler like 'I mean' or 'well' used to clarify, restate, or introduce a comment. Context determines if it's reporting meaning or functioning as a conversational pause. Common in spoken Portuguese.
target_language_example: Quer dizer, não podemos simplesmente ignorar o problema.
native_language_example: I mean, we can't just ignore the problem.

meaning: 'wants to write' (he/she/you want to write).
additional_notes: Literal combination of verb querer (to want) + infinitive escrever (to write). Expresses desire to do the action of writing. Subject is understood from context (quer can be eu quero, você/ele/ela quer). In questions or imperatives word order may drop the subject: "Quer escrever?" = "Do you want to write?"
target_language_example: Ele diz que quer escrever um artigo sobre música.
native_language_example: He says he wants to write an article about music.

meaning: do you really want (me) to... / you really want (me) to...
additional_notes: Used to question or express surprise at someone insisting that the speaker do something. Often followed by a verb in the subjunctive or infinitive with a personal object (e.g., 'eu fique', 'eu vá', 'eu faça...'). Tone can be incredulous, hurt, or emphatic depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Você quer mesmo que eu vá sem avisar ninguém?
native_language_example: Do you really want me to go without telling anyone?

meaning: 'wants another' or 'do you want another?'.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say someone wants an additional one of the same thing. In questions it becomes an offer: 'Quer outro?' = 'Do you want another one?'. Can be used literally (food, drink, object) or figuratively/ironically (e.g., 'Quer outro tapa na cara?' = 'Do you want another slap in the face?'). Subject may be omitted in questions (context gives person).
target_language_example: Ela quer outro pedaço de pão.
native_language_example: She wants another piece of bread.

meaning: 'whatever happens' or 'no matter what happens'.
additional_notes: Usually appears in the fixed expression 'o que quer que aconteça' (literally 'whatsoever that may happen') to express determination or acceptance regardless of the outcome. Can be used to reassure, warn, or show resolve. Commonly followed by a comma and a main clause.
target_language_example: O que quer que aconteça, eu vou te apoiar.
native_language_example: Whatever happens, I will support you.

meaning: want to know
additional_notes: Literally 'wants to know.' Depending on the subject, it can also mean 'do you want to know?' In spoken Portuguese, quer saber? can be used like 'you know what?', se quer saber means 'if you want to know / honestly', and só quer saber de... means 'only cares about...' or 'is only interested in...'
target_language_example: Ela quer saber quando o filme começa.
native_language_example: She wants to know when the movie starts.

meaning: they want you to
additional_notes: Usually followed by another verb: querem que você faça/venha/volte. In Portuguese, this pattern uses que + the subjunctive to say what someone wants another person to do. Here querem means 'they want' (though in some contexts it can also mean 'you all want').
target_language_example: Eles querem que você chegue cedo.
native_language_example: They want you to arrive early.

meaning: 'we want to book/reserve a trip'.
additional_notes: Simple present tense, first-person plural (nós/queremos). Used to express the desire to book travel (flight, tour, hotel, etc.). You can replace 'uma viagem' with a destination ('para a França') or a specific transport/accommodation ('um voo', 'um hotel'). In casual speech the subject pronoun 'nós' is often dropped: 'Queremos reservar uma viagem.'
target_language_example: Queremos reservar uma viagem para Portugal no próximo mês.
native_language_example: We want to book a trip to Portugal next month.

meaning: we want you
additional_notes: A casual order of words meaning 'we want' + direct object pronoun 'you' (informal singular). In European Portuguese the pronoun often appears after the verb (queremos-te) and is less common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese, which prefers 'queremos te' or 'queremos te ajudar'. Use when expressing that a group wants to do something involving the listener (help you, tell you something, hurt you, etc.). The pronoun 'te' is informal (tu/you singular). For formal or plural 'you' use 'queremos o(a) senhor(a)' or 'queremos vocês'.
target_language_example: Queremos te ajudar com a lição se você quiser.
native_language_example: We want to help you with the homework if you want.

meaning: to mean
additional_notes: Most often used to talk about the meaning of words, signs, sentences, or actions. The exact infinitive phrase querer dizer often appears after another verb, such as pode or vai. In many everyday contexts, a conjugated form like quer dizer means 'means' or 'does ... mean?'. Literally, it can also mean 'to want to say'.
target_language_example: É difícil saber o que "saudade" pode querer dizer.
native_language_example: It's hard to know what "saudade" can mean.

meaning: wanted to know why / wanted to find out (why).
additional_notes: Common phrase used to report that someone wanted to know the reason for something. Often completed by 'que' or 'por que' plus a clause or question word. In neutral or polite past-tense contexts (queria = conditional/polite past of querer). 'Por quê' with accent appears at the end of a sentence. Use 'queria saber por que...' for 'I/he/she wanted to know why...'.
target_language_example: Eu queria saber por que você saiu cedo ontem.
native_language_example: I wanted to know why you left early yesterday.

meaning: wanted to move (change residence).
additional_notes: Polite/neutral past or conditional form: queria is the imperfect/conditional of querer (I/he/she wanted/would like). 'se mudar' = to move (house/city). Commonly followed by destination introduced by 'para' (para Boston, para outra cidade). In Brazil you may also hear 'queria mudar-se' (less common) or 'queria se mudar daqui' (wanted to move away from here).
target_language_example: Ela dizia que queria se mudar para o litoral.
native_language_example: She said she wanted to move to the coast.

meaning: 'I wanted to sit' or polite 'I would like to sit'.
additional_notes: Combines the imperfect/conditional form of querer (queria) with the verb sentar (to sit). In everyday speech Portuguese speakers often say queria + infinitive to make a polite request (equivalent to 'I would like' or 'I'd like to sit'). Context decides past vs. polite request: 'Eu queria sentar ao lado de Tom' can mean 'I wanted to sit next to Tom' (past) or more commonly 'I'd like to sit next to Tom' when asking for a seat. You may also hear 'gostaria de sentar' as a more formal alternative.
target_language_example: Eu queria sentar ao lado dele, por favor.
native_language_example: I'd like to sit next to him, please.

meaning: 'I want mine' or 'I want my ...' (expressing desire for something that belongs to the speaker).
additional_notes: Used to state that you want something belonging to you. Often followed by a noun (quero a minha bicicleta = I want my bike) or can stand alone with context (quero a minha = I want mine). Can express emotional wants (quero a minha mãe, quero a minha liberdade). Possessive is feminine singular here (minha); change to 'meu' for masculine nouns (quero o meu).
target_language_example: Quero a minha caneta, por favor.
native_language_example: I want my pen, please.

meaning: 'I want to go home and...'; expresses a desire to go home followed by another action or purpose.
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase to say you want to go home plus do something there (rest, see family, sleep, etc.). 'Quero' can be omitted for a more colloquial 'Só quero ir para casa e...'. The clause after 'e' is whatever you want to do once home. Use appropriate conjugation and gender/number for people mentioned (meu/minha, filhos/filhas).
target_language_example: Quero ir para casa e descansar um pouco.
native_language_example: I want to go home and rest a bit.

meaning: 'I want to ask/request' or 'I want to order' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Quero = I want; pedir = to ask/request/order/apologize (pedir desculpas = to apologize). Use with direct objects or prepositions: pedir desculpa(s) (to apologize), pedir um favor (to ask a favor), pedir comida (to order food). Conjugation changes with subject (eu quero pedir, nós queremos pedir).
target_language_example: Quero pedir um favor: você pode me ajudar amanhã?
native_language_example: I want to ask a favor: can you help me tomorrow?

meaning: 'I want to have a' or 'I want to get a' (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: A common phrase used to express desire to obtain or experience something in the future. Literal words: quero (I want), ter (to have), uma (a/an, feminine). The noun after 'uma' must be feminine (e.g., palavrinha, espada, namorada). In conversational Portuguese, 'quero ter uma palavrinha com...' is a polite way to say 'I'd like to have a word with...' or 'I'd like to speak with...'.
target_language_example: Eu quero ter uma conversa com você amanhã.
native_language_example: I want to have a conversation with you tomorrow.

meaning: I want to see
additional_notes: A literal combination of quero + ver. It is used to say that you want to see something or someone; with people, it can also mean "I want to see/meet" that person.
target_language_example: Quero ver o filme hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I want to see the movie tonight.

meaning: 'a matter of life or death' — something extremely serious or urgent.
additional_notes: Used to describe situations with very high stakes or urgent consequences. Equivalent to English idiom 'a matter of life or death.' Can be used literally (health, danger) or figuratively (very important decisions).
target_language_example: Resolver esse problema agora é uma questão de vida ou morte.
native_language_example: Solving this problem now is a matter of life or death.

meaning: 'the issue is' / 'the question is' (used to introduce the main point or problem).
additional_notes: Used to introduce or emphasize the central point, problem, or topic of discussion. Often followed by a clause explaining the main concern (e.g., 'A questão é ...'). Common in both spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: A questão é como vamos resolver isso.
native_language_example: The issue is how we are going to solve this.

meaning: 'Thursday' (the day of the week).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the fourth day of the week (Thursday). In Portuguese, days of the week are feminine (a quinta-feira) and not capitalized in normal writing. Often shortened in speech to 'quinta'. Can appear with articles/time expressions (na quinta-feira, esta quinta-feira).
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar na quinta-feira à noite.
native_language_example: Let's meet on Thursday night.

meaning: If you want, I can... (offers or suggestions).
additional_notes: Polite conditional phrase used to offer help, a favor, or a suggestion. Literally 'if (you) want, I can'. Often followed by an action verb. The subject 'você/tu' is omitted — 'quiser' is the 3rd-person formal/subjunctive of 'querer' used in conditional 'se'. Suitable in both formal and informal contexts depending on tone; you can also say 'se você quiser, posso' for clarity.
target_language_example: Se quiser, posso trazer o almoço amanhã.
native_language_example: If you want, I can bring lunch tomorrow.

meaning: 'want to smoke' (used in conditional clauses: 'if you want to smoke')
additional_notes: Quiser is the future subjunctive/conditional form of querer used after 'se' to mean 'if (someone) wants'. Common in instructions or rules: 'Se quiser fumar...' = 'If you want to smoke...'. Often followed by a consequence or location (e.g., 'saia', 'vá para fora').
target_language_example: Se quiser fumar, vá para a área designada.
native_language_example: If you want to smoke, go to the designated area.

meaning: want me to
additional_notes: Used in patterns like "você quiser que eu..." = "you want me to..." It introduces what the speaker is expected or asked to do, and the following verb is normally in the subjunctive: "quiser que eu venha/faça/seja". "Quiser" is a form of "querer" often seen after words like "se" (if), "quando" (when), or "o que" (whatever).
target_language_example: Se você quiser que eu ajude, é só me chamar.
native_language_example: If you want me to help, just call me.

meaning: 'what are you' (fragment) — a nonstandard/question-fragment form that resembles the start of a question about someone's current state, action, or situation
additional_notes: This form is nonstandard. Standard Portuguese uses 'o que você está...' or simply 'o que você...' at the start of questions (e.g., 'O que você está fazendo?'). 'Quê' with an accent usually appears at the end of a sentence for emphasis before punctuation or in isolation; at the beginning use 'o que'. If you encounter 'quê você está' it may be a typo, archaic/poetic usage, or part of a larger sentence where 'quê' is emphasized. For asking 'how are you?' use 'Como você está?'. For 'what are you doing?' use 'O que você está fazendo?'.
target_language_example: Quê você está dizendo?
native_language_example: What are you saying?

meaning: 'the boy/guy who' — introduces a relative clause describing a male person.
additional_notes: Used to refer to or identify a specific young man or boy, followed by a verb or clause (the relative clause). 'Rapaz' = boy/young man; 'que' = who/that. Can be used for acquaintances, descriptions, or asking about someone. In spoken Portuguese, 'rapaz' can also mean 'guy' (informal).
target_language_example: Conheço o rapaz que mora naquela casa.
native_language_example: I know the guy who lives in that house.

meaning: 'do you really think that the...' or 'do you really believe that the...'
additional_notes: A common spoken phrase used to express surprise, doubt, or challenge about someone's belief regarding a person, thing, or situation. It is composed of 'realmente' (really), 'acha' (you think/believe — from achar), and the masculine singular article 'o' (the). Context determines what follows after 'o' (a noun or clause). In questions, subject pronoun may be omitted in Portuguese: 'Você realmente acha que o João vai ganhar?' equals 'Do you really think that João will win?'.
target_language_example: Você realmente acha que o filme vai ser bom?
native_language_example: Do you really think that the movie will be good?

meaning: did you really think that... / you really thought that...
additional_notes: Used to express surprise, disbelief, or challenge about someone's belief or assumption. Often appears at the start of a question (Você realmente achou que...?) but can also appear in statements. 'Realmente' = 'really' (intensifier). 'Achou' is past of 'achar' (to think/believe). Common in informal and neutral speech.
target_language_example: Você realmente achou que eu iria aceitar isso?
native_language_example: Did you really think I would accept that?

meaning: 'I would really like to' or 'I really wish to'.
additional_notes: Polite, slightly formal way to express a strong desire or wish about something you want or would have liked. Commonly followed by an infinitive verb (gostar de + infinitive) or a clause. Use for present wishes (Eu realmente gostaria de estudar...) or past regrets with ter + past participle (Eu realmente gostaria de ter conhecido...).
target_language_example: Eu realmente gostaria de visitar Portugal este ano.
native_language_example: I would really like to visit Portugal this year.

meaning: 'I really am' or 'I truly am' (used to emphasize the speaker's true state or identity).
additional_notes: Combines 'realmente' (really/truly) + 'sou' (I am). Used to stress that what follows (a quality, feeling, identity) is true despite appearances or doubts. Common in statements and questions. Word order can change (e.g., 'sou realmente' is less common).
target_language_example: Posso parecer confiante, mas realmente sou tímido.
native_language_example: I may seem confident, but I really am shy.

meaning: to recommend a (masculine) — used to ask someone to suggest one item/person/place.
additional_notes: Common phrase when asking for suggestions. The indefinite article 'um' agrees with masculine nouns (use 'uma' for feminine: 'recomendar uma'). You can use different verbs/forms for politeness: 'pode', 'pode me', or conditional 'poderia'. Often followed by the type of thing you want (médico, hotel, restaurante, jogo, dicionário).
target_language_example: Você pode recomendar um bom café perto daqui?
native_language_example: Can you recommend a good café near here?

meaning: to make up for lost time; to recover lost time.
additional_notes: Commonly appears as 'recuperar o tempo perdido' (make up for lost time). Used when trying to catch up after delays or lost opportunities. Can be used literally (time) or figuratively (lost opportunities, productivity). Often follows verbs like precisar/ter/temos/tenho.
target_language_example: Preciso recuperar o tempo perdido este mês.
native_language_example: I need to make up for lost time this month.

meaning: 'natural resource' — something found in nature that people can use (water, minerals, forests, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to talk about materials or elements from the environment that have economic, ecological, or social value. Plural is 'recursos naturais'. Common in discussions about environment, conservation, economy, and sustainability.
target_language_example: A água é um recurso natural essencial para a vida.
native_language_example: Water is a natural resource essential for life.

meaning: 'refused to' (they refused to ...).
additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) third-person plural of recusar + the preposition a before an infinitive verb or action. Used to say that a group declined or refused to do something. In Portuguese, reflexive form 'se recusaram a' is common (they themselves refused). English often uses 'refused to' + verb.
target_language_example: Eles se recusaram a ajudar-nos quando pedimos.
native_language_example: They refused to help us when we asked.

meaning: refused to (do something).
additional_notes: Form of the verb recusar-se (refuse) in the imperfect past tense: 'se recusava a + infinitive' = 'was refusing to' / 'refused to' (habitual or ongoing past). Commonly used when someone refuses an action or request. Pronoun 'se' is reflexive and required here. In English you can translate as 'refused to' or 'wouldn't'.
target_language_example: Ela se recusava a participar do projeto.
native_language_example: She refused to take part in the project.

meaning: refused to do (something).
additional_notes: Used to report that someone declined or refused to perform an action. Commonly appears as 'se recusou a fazer' when reflexive (he/she refused). Can be followed by an infinitive (fazer + object/clause). Polite/formal contexts may use 'recusou' without 'se' for transitive uses, but for refusing personally, use 'se recusar a + infinitive'.
target_language_example: Ele se recusou a fazer a apresentação.
native_language_example: He refused to do the presentation.

meaning: 'refused to pay'.
additional_notes: Past tense (ele/ele/ela) of 'recusar-se a pagar' — to refuse to pay. Used when someone declines to give money for a service, fee, ransom, etc. Common construction: [subject] + se recusou a pagar + [object/person].
target_language_example: Ela se recusou a pagar a conta do restaurante.
native_language_example: She refused to pay the restaurant bill.

meaning: newborn; recently born (usually a baby).
additional_notes: Used as a noun or adjective to describe a baby born very recently. Can be literal (a newborn infant) or used metaphorically in similes (e.g., 'innocent as a newborn'). Hyphenated: recém-nascido (masculine); for feminine use recém-nascida. Common in medical, news, and everyday contexts.
target_language_example: O hospital recebeu um recém-nascido prematuro.
native_language_example: The hospital received a premature newborn.

meaning: 'social network' or 'social media platform' — a website or app where people connect and share content.
additional_notes: Used to refer to any social networking site or service (Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, etc.). Can be countable (uma rede social, duas redes sociais) and is commonly used with 'conta' (account) — e.g., 'uma conta em uma rede social'.
target_language_example: Ela criou uma conta em uma nova rede social.
native_language_example: She created an account on a new social network.

meaning: 'regarding', 'concerning', or 'in relation to' (used to link a topic or subject).
additional_notes: Commonly used in formal or written Portuguese to introduce the topic that follows. Often appears in phrases like "em relação a" (in relation to / regarding). When used alone as "relação a" it usually requires a preceding preposition (e.g., "em relação a", "no que diz respeito a"). Followed by a noun or clause showing the subject being discussed.
target_language_example: Em relação a sua pergunta, temos uma resposta amanhã.
native_language_example: Regarding your question, we have an answer tomorrow.

meaning: regarding; in relation to; concerning.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic or object being referred to. Often appears as 'em relação a' or 'em relação à' (à = a + a feminine article) depending on whether a definite article follows. Common in formal and neutral contexts to link a comment to a subject (health, opinion, topic, etc.).
target_language_example: Em relação à sua pergunta, vou responder amanhã.
native_language_example: Regarding your question, I will answer tomorrow.

meaning: suddenly (someone/something) began to…
additional_notes: Used to describe a sudden change or action that started. Often followed by an infinitive verb (começar a + infinitive). Equivalent to 'suddenly' or 'all of a sudden' + 'began to...'. Common in both neutral and spoken Portuguese.
target_language_example: De repente começou a chover muito forte.
native_language_example: Suddenly it began to rain very hard.

meaning: to book/reserve a trip to (a specific country or place).
additional_notes: Common phrase used when arranging travel to a destination. The preposition 'para' = 'to'; the article 'a' agrees with feminine country names (a França, a Irlanda, a Letônia, a Sérvia, a Bielorrússia). For masculine country names you'd use 'para o' (e.g., reservar uma viagem para o Brasil). You can replace 'reservar' with 'agendar' or 'comprar' depending on context (book/schedule/buy).
target_language_example: Quero reservar uma viagem para a Espanha no próximo verão.
native_language_example: I want to book a trip to Spain next summer.

meaning: 'I solved it' or 'I solved the' (past tense of resolver + definite object pronoun/article).
additional_notes: Resolvi is the first-person singular preterite (past) of resolver (to solve, to resolve). The following 'o' can be the masculine singular direct object pronoun (meaning 'it') or the masculine definite article introducing a noun ('o problema' = 'the problem'). In speech the object pronoun may be attached after the verb (resolvi-o is more literary); in modern Brazilian Portuguese it's more common to say 'eu o resolvi' or simply 'resolvi' or 'resolvi o problema'.
target_language_example: Eu resolvi o problema ontem à noite.
native_language_example: I solved the problem last night.

meaning: 'about her' or 'regarding her'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to information, opinions, or matters concerning a female person. Commonly appears after verbs like 'saber' (to know), 'contar' (to tell), or expressions of being right/ wrong (estar certo/errado a respeito dela). 'A respeito de' + pronoun is a neutral, slightly formal way to say 'about/regarding'.
target_language_example: Tenho algumas dúvidas a respeito dela.
native_language_example: I have some questions about her.

meaning: about that; concerning that; regarding that.
additional_notes: Used after expressions to refer to a specific topic or situation already mentioned (a respeito de + isso). Common in questions and statements: 'a respeito disso' = 'about that' or 'regarding that'. Can be shortened to 'disso' in casual speech if context is clear.
target_language_example: O que podemos fazer a respeito disso?
native_language_example: What can we do about that?

meaning: to be responsible or answerable for; to vouch for someone/something.
additional_notes: Used when saying someone is accountable for an action, debt, promise, or when guaranteeing another person's behavior or obligations. Often followed by a noun (responder pelo erro) or a person (responder por alguém). Can also mean to pay for or cover something in some contexts (responder pelas despesas).
target_language_example: Eu não posso responder por ele se ele não cumprir o combinado.
native_language_example: I can't be held responsible for him if he doesn't keep the agreement.

meaning: 'answered all' (past tense — he/she/you answered all [something])
additional_notes: Combination of the verb responder in the simple past (ele/ela/voce respondeu) + the determiner todas (feminine plural) used before nouns like perguntas/questões. In Portuguese the noun (e.g., perguntas) can be omitted if clear from context. Word order often is 'respondeu todas as perguntas' but informal speech may drop the article ('respondeu todas perguntas').
target_language_example: Ela respondeu todas as perguntas da entrevista.
native_language_example: She answered all the interview questions.

meaning: 'responsibility is' or 'the responsibility is' (used to state who holds responsibility).
additional_notes: Used to assign or state responsibility for something. Often followed by a pronoun or noun indicating the responsible person(s): 'deles' (theirs), 'minha' (mine), 'nossa' (ours). Can appear in full sentences like 'A responsabilidade é minha' (I am responsible). In the example with 'ter responsabilidade é ser idiota', the structure generalizes to 'to have responsibility is to be ...' — here it's a more general statement about what responsibility means or implies.
target_language_example: A responsabilidade é sua neste projeto.
native_language_example: The responsibility is yours on this project.

meaning: an answer to this (one) / the answer to this
additional_notes: Used to refer to 'an answer' or 'the answer' for a specific question or issue that is close in context (esta = this). Word order: 'resposta a esta pergunta' = 'answer to this question'. In spoken Portuguese you may also hear 'resposta a essa' (that/near you) or 'resposta a esta' without repeating 'pergunta' when context is clear.
target_language_example: Ainda não encontrei resposta a esta pergunta.
native_language_example: I still haven't found an answer to this question.

meaning: 'answer' or 'response to (something)'.
additional_notes: Used when saying that something is an answer or response directed at a specific thing (followed by a noun or phrase). 'À' is the contraction of the preposition 'a' + the feminine definite article 'a' (a + a = à) and agrees with feminine nouns like 'pergunta', 'mensagem', 'carta'. For masculine nouns you'd see 'resposta ao' (a + o = ao).
target_language_example: Enviei um e-mail e recebi uma resposta à minha dúvida.
native_language_example: I sent an email and received a response to my question.

meaning: 'the restaurant is' — a subject (o restaurante) + the verb 'estar' used to describe location or temporary states.
additional_notes: Use 'o restaurante está' to say where the restaurant is (location) or how it is right now (open/closed, busy, clean, etc.). 'Estar' indicates temporary conditions or current status. For location you can add prepositions (em, na, ao lado de). For descriptions of state use adjectives (cheio, aberto, fechado).
target_language_example: O restaurante está fechado hoje à noite.
native_language_example: The restaurant is closed tonight.

meaning: 'the result of' or 'as a result of'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate cause or origin: 'o resultado do X' = the result of X. Often followed by a noun or noun phrase introduced by 'do' (contraction of de + o). Can also appear in phrases like 'como resultado do' = 'as a result of'.
target_language_example: A mudança aconteceu como resultado do aumento de preços.
native_language_example: The change happened as a result of the price increase.

meaning: 'the meeting was' (past tense statement about a meeting).
additional_notes: Combines reunião (meeting) + foi (past of ser/ir, here 'was'). Used to say when or how a meeting occurred or to give an evaluation (e.g., 'was a waste of time'). Commonly followed by a time expression (esta tarde, no mês passado) or a description/opinion.
target_language_example: A reunião foi muito produtiva ontem.
native_language_example: The meeting was very productive yesterday.

meaning: 'rich in resources' — having abundant natural or material resources.
additional_notes: Used to describe countries, regions, or places that have plenty of natural (e.g., minerals, forests, water) or material resources. Often followed by a specific type: rico em recursos naturais (natural resources) or rico em recursos minerais (mineral resources). Can be used in neutral, formal, or informal contexts.
target_language_example: O país é rico em recursos naturais, especialmente florestas e água.
native_language_example: The country is rich in natural resources, especially forests and water.

meaning: laughing at (someone or something).
additional_notes: Formed from the verb rir (to laugh) in the gerund rindo + preposition 'de' (often contracted with pronouns: rindo dele/dela/deles). Used to say someone is laughing at or making fun of someone/something. Typical structure: 'estar rindo do ...' or simply 'rindo do ...' in context. Can be followed by a noun, pronoun, or clause (e.g. 'rindo do erro', 'rindo dele', 'rindo do que aconteceu').
target_language_example: Ele está rindo do meu erro.
native_language_example: He is laughing at my mistake.

meaning: rock and roll (music genre); used to refer to rock music in general.
additional_notes: This is an English loan phrase commonly used in Portuguese exactly as in English. It refers to the musical style (often classic rock). Use with gostar (gosta/gostam) to ask if someone likes this genre. Pronunciation follows Portuguese phonetics but the words remain English.
target_language_example: Você gosta de rock and roll clássico?
native_language_example: Do you like classic rock?

meaning: Ferris wheel (large amusement-park wheel with passenger cars).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the big observation/entertainment wheel at fairs, parks or beaches. Often preceded by verbs like andar de/ir na/subir na (to ride/go on). Can be used literally (riding the wheel) and in contexts implying seeing a view from above.
target_language_example: Vamos andar de roda-gigante amanhã à noite.
native_language_example: Let's ride the Ferris wheel tomorrow night.

meaning: 'stolen' (masculine, past participle used after a masculine noun with the definite article placed before the noun, e.g., 'o [objeto] roubado')
additional_notes: 'Roubado' is the past participle of 'roubar' (to steal). The ordering 'roubado o' is not the neutral noun phrase order in Portuguese (which is 'o [objeto] roubado'), but you may encounter 'roubado o' in contexts that split the phrase (for emphasis, in poetry, or in reported speech) or when the participle and article are separated by other elements. More commonly, the definite article 'o' precedes the noun it modifies: 'o carro roubado' = 'the stolen car.'
target_language_example: Disseram que havia roubado o relógio, mas o dono negou que o relógio tivesse sido roubado o.
native_language_example: They said he had stolen the watch, but the owner denied that the watch had been the stolen one.

meaning: swimsuit; swimwear (clothing you wear for swimming or at the beach/pool).
additional_notes: Used for any swim garment (bathing suit, bikini, trunks). Can be singular or plural depending on context. Common in Portugal and Brazil. To ask 'Do you have a swimsuit?' use 'Você tem uma roupa de banho?'
target_language_example: Ela comprou uma nova roupa de banho para as férias.
native_language_example: She bought a new swimsuit for the vacation.

meaning: the street is / the road is (describing the state or condition of a street)
additional_notes: Combines 'rua' (street) + the verb 'estar' (to be) to describe temporary conditions of a street: how it looks, whether it's full/empty, wet, closed, etc. Use for current or temporary states (not permanent qualities). In conversation you can swap 'rua' for other places (a praça está, o caminho está).
target_language_example: A rua está bloqueada por causa do acidente.
native_language_example: The street is blocked because of the accident.

meaning: the streets were (past description of street conditions)
additional_notes: A simple past descriptive phrase using ruas (streets) + estavam (imperfect past of estar). Use to describe how streets looked or what they contained (e.g., covered, crowded, empty). Commonly followed by adjectives (vazias, lotadas) or prepositional phrases (cobertas de neve). Use estavam for ongoing/picture-like past actions or states.
target_language_example: As ruas estavam cobertas de folhas no outono.
native_language_example: The streets were covered with leaves in autumn.

meaning: 'the streets are' (a subject + present continuous/state of being)
additional_notes: Combines plural noun 'ruas' (streets) with the verb 'estar' in the third person plural present (estão). Use to describe the current state or condition of streets (full, empty, clean, covered, etc.). In Portuguese, 'estar' indicates temporary states or locations. Swap 'ruas' for another plural noun to describe other things (e.g., 'as lojas estão...').
target_language_example: As ruas estão molhadas depois da chuva.
native_language_example: The streets are wet after the rain.

meaning: 'as bad as' (used to compare how bad something is relative to something else)
additional_notes: Often appears in comparisons with 'tão' or 'não' (e.g., 'não é tão ruim quanto...') to say something is not as bad as another thing or to ask if it's as bad as it seems. Common structure: 'tão ruim quanto' = 'as bad as'; 'não é tão ruim quanto...' = 'it's not as bad as...'.
target_language_example: O concerto não foi tão ruim quanto eu esperava.
native_language_example: The concert wasn't as bad as I expected.

meaning: 'rumors of/about' — used to introduce unconfirmed reports or gossip about something or someone.
additional_notes: Followed by a clause or noun phrase describing the subject of the rumor (often introduced with que + clause). Common in news and everyday speech to report unverified information; implies uncertainty. Neutral register — can be used formally or informally depending on context.
target_language_example: Há rumores de que eles vão se mudar para outra cidade.
native_language_example: There are rumors that they're going to move to another city.

meaning: the radio is (followed by a state or condition).
additional_notes: A simple subject + verb phrase using the noun 'rádio' and the verb 'estar' to describe the radio's current condition (off, on, loud, broken, without signal, etc.). Use 'o rádio está...' for a specific radio. Common adjectives or past participles follow: 'desligado' (off), 'ligado' (on), 'muito alto' (very loud), 'quebrado' (broken), 'sem sinal' (no signal).
target_language_example: O rádio está sem bateria agora.
native_language_example: The radio is out of battery right now.

meaning: 'faster than' (used to compare speed or rate)
additional_notes: This phrase is part of comparative constructions with 'mais' + adjective + 'do que' (mais rápido do que = faster than). Use with subjects and verbs: 'X corre mais rápido do que Y' = X runs faster than Y. Can also compare non-physical speed (e.g., 'fala mais rápido do que eu' = speaks faster than I do). In casual speech you may also hear 'que' instead of 'do que' in some regions, but 'do que' is standard.
target_language_example: Ela escreve mais rápido do que eu.
native_language_example: She writes faster than I do.

meaning: faster than (the)… — used to compare speed or rate to something/someone.
additional_notes: This is a comparative structure: 'mais rápido do que o...' (more fast than the...). You will often see 'mais rápido do que' followed by a noun, pronoun, or phrase (e.g., 'o som', 'o normal', 'o resto de nós'). In spoken/written Portuguese the article ('o', 'a', etc.) agrees with the noun referenced. You can replace 'rápido' with other adjectives (mais lento, mais alto) to make other comparisons.
target_language_example: Ela corre mais rápido do que o irmão.
native_language_example: She runs faster than (her) brother.

meaning: as fast as possible; as quickly as possible
additional_notes: Commonly used after expressions like "o mais" to form "o mais rápido possível" (the fastest/as soon as possible). Alone, "rápido possível" is incomplete in Portuguese; native speakers usually say "o mais rápido possível" or "o mais rápido que puder". Use to ask someone to do something with urgency.
target_language_example: Preciso que você responda o e‑mail o mais rápido possível.
native_language_example: I need you to reply to the email as quickly as possible.

meaning: as fast as (used to compare speed)
additional_notes: Used in comparisons to say that one person/thing is as fast as another. Often appears in structures like 'tão rápido quanto' (as/so fast as) or simply 'rápido quanto' after an adjective or adverb. Can compare people, animals, vehicles, processes, etc. Word order: subject + (é/foi/está) + tão/mais/menos + rápido quanto + object. If comparing verbs, use 'tão rapidamente quanto' or 'tão rápido quanto' colloquially.
target_language_example: Ele corre tão rápido quanto o irmão.
native_language_example: He runs as fast as his brother.

meaning: as fast as (she/he) could; as quickly as possible (emphasizes ability/effort in the past).
additional_notes: Often appears as part of the phrase 'o mais rápido que podia' (or 'o mais rápido que pôde'). Use 'rápida' for feminine subjects. 'Podia' (imperfect) highlights ongoing ability or repeated/continuous effort; 'pôde' (preterite) indicates a single completed ability in the past. Common in spoken and written Portuguese to describe trying to move or act at maximum speed.
target_language_example: Ela correu o mais rápido que podia.
native_language_example: She ran as fast as she could.

meaning: 'know anything' or 'know something' (used to ask if someone has information about a person or topic).
additional_notes: Common question form using the verb saber (to know). Often appears as 'Você sabe algo...' or simply 'Sabe algo...?' in informal contexts. Use to ask whether someone has any information or news about a person, situation, or topic. Can be followed by 'de', 'sobre' or a direct object (e.g., 'sabe algo de Maria?', 'sabe algo sobre isso?').
target_language_example: Você sabe algo sobre o evento de sábado?
native_language_example: Do you know anything about Saturday's event?

meaning: to find out / to know immediately; to have inside information or to be told something straightaway (colloquial).
additional_notes: Informal Brazilian Portuguese expression. Often used in conversational shortcuts like 'ele sabe de uma' (he knows right away/has inside info) or 'vou saber de uma' (I'll find out immediately). Not typically used in formal writing. Can appear with or without an explicit object.
target_language_example: Se tiver novidades, me avisa — eu quero saber de uma.
native_language_example: If there are any updates, tell me — I want to know right away.

meaning: 'knows nothing' or 'doesn't know anything'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone has no knowledge about a topic. In standard Portuguese, negative sentences more commonly place 'não' before the verb: 'não sabe nada' or 'não sabe de nada'. However 'sabe nada' can appear in spoken language or following contexts where 'não' is omitted for emphasis or in elliptical sentences. Use with subjects (ele/ela/você) as in examples.
target_language_example: Ele sabe nada sobre programação.
native_language_example: He knows nothing about programming.

meaning: 'does (someone) know his/her/your (something)'.
additional_notes: Literal components: sabe = (he/she/you formal) knows; o seu = his/your/their (depending on context) + noun that follows. In the examples, 'sabe o seu' is followed by a noun (número, endereço, nome, segredo) and asks or states whether someone knows that specific piece of information. Subject and possessive agree by context: the subject (ela, ninguém, todo o mundo, Tom) determines the verb conjugation and 'seu' refers to the possessor (his/her/your/their) understood from context. In spoken Portuguese, 'seu' can be ambiguous — use 'dela', 'dele', 'dele/a' for clarity if needed (e.g., 'o número dela' = her number).
target_language_example: Você sabe o seu e-mail?
native_language_example: Do you know your e‑mail?

meaning: 'do you/they/he/she know what this/that means' (phrase used to ask or state that someone knows the meaning or significance of something).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in questions or exclamations. In Portuguese word order can vary: 'Você sabe o que isso significa?' = 'Do you know what this means?'. Can also be used in statements: 'Ele sabe o que isso significa.' Note pronoun (você, ele, todo mundo) determines subject. 'Isso' usually refers to something just mentioned or visible.
target_language_example: Você sabe o que isso significa para a nossa família?
native_language_example: Do you know what this means for our family?

meaning: 'do you/does [someone] know where she is' (part of questions about someone's location or place related to 'she')
additional_notes: This fragment appears in questions asking whether someone knows the location, residence, or birthplace of a female person (ela = she). In Portuguese questions, the subject or auxiliary can be omitted or reordered (e.g., 'Você sabe onde ela mora?' or 'Sabe onde ela está?'). Depending on context, it can be formal or informal. To make it a complete question in English, add the subject ('you', 'he', etc.) or invert: 'Do you know where she...?'
target_language_example: Você sabe onde ela trabalha?
native_language_example: Do you know where she works?

meaning: 'do you know why' (informal question asking for the reason).
additional_notes: A common spoken way to ask if someone knows the reason for something. In European Portuguese you may also hear 'sabes por que' or 'sabe por que é que' (or in Brazil 'sabe por que' / 'você sabe por que'). Word order and pronoun (sabe/sabes/você sabe) change with formality and number. 'Porque' here introduces a question meaning 'why' — note written Portuguese sometimes splits into 'por que' in questions, but 'porque' as one word is frequently used in speech.
target_language_example: Você sabe porque o cinema fechou tão cedo?
native_language_example: Do you know why the cinema closed so early?

meaning: 'do you know which' or 'do you know what (which)'.
additional_notes: Common informal spoken phrase combining the verb saber (to know) with qual (which/what). Often used to ask someone if they know a specific thing or choice (e.g., 'Sabe qual é?' = 'Do you know which one it is?'). In full sentences you will usually see a verb or clause after qual (qual é, qual foi, qual é o nome). Can be followed by a noun or by 'é' + clause.
target_language_example: Sabe qual é o endereço?
native_language_example: Do you know what the address is?

meaning: 'do you know how much' or 'you know how much' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Common phrase built from the verb saber (to know) + quanto (how much/how many). Used in questions (Sabe quanto custa? — Do you know how much it costs?) or as a conversational opener/remark (Sabe quanto eu paguei? — You know how much I paid?). The subject can be omitted; verb form (sabe) is informal/neutral second person (you) or third person (he/she/it) in formal speech depending on tone and context. To make a clear question, intonation or a question mark is used.
target_language_example: Sabe quanto custa este ingresso?
native_language_example: Do you know how much this ticket costs?

meaning: literally 'knows who I (am)'; used as part of a question or statement about whether someone knows the speaker's identity
additional_notes: This is not a complete sentence by itself in Portuguese; it's typically followed by a verb or used in questions like 'Você sabe quem eu sou?' ('Do you know who I am?') or in reported speech 'Ele sabe quem eu sou.' It can also appear in fragments for emphasis or informal speech. Pronoun 'eu' = 'I', and the verb 'saber' means 'to know.'
target_language_example: Você sabe quem eu sou?
native_language_example: Do you know who I am?

meaning: 'knows who you (are)'.
additional_notes: This is part of the clause 'sabe quem você é' = 'knows who you are'. 'Sabe' is the third-person singular (or formal second-person singular) of 'saber' (to know). Useful in sentences stating or asking whether someone knows another person's identity. In questions word order can be 'Sabe quem você é?' or 'Você sabe quem eu/ele/ela é?'.
target_language_example: Ninguém sabe quem você é aqui.
native_language_example: Nobody knows who you are here.

meaning: 'they/you (plural) know it' or 'they/you know (something)'.
additional_notes: Sabem is the third-person plural (eles/elas) or formal/plural usted form (vocês/Os senhores) of saber (to know). The short phrase 'sabem o' often appears before a clause or object: 'sabem o que…' (know what…) or 'sabem o suficiente' (know enough). In English you may translate depending on context as 'they know', 'you (plural) know', or 'do you (plural) know...?' Verb agrees with the subject (eles/elas/vocês/Os senhores).
target_language_example: Eles sabem o que fazer amanhã.
native_language_example: They know what to do tomorrow.

meaning: 'they know what they are...' (start of a clause meaning 'they know what they are doing/saying/losing/etc.')
additional_notes: This is a common Portuguese pattern: verb (sabem = they know) + 'o que' + estar (estão) + present participle or gerund (e.g., fazendo, dizendo, perdendo). It introduces what the subjects know (or don't know). In negative sentences use 'não sabem o que estão...' For questions, intonation or a question mark is added. The pronoun implied is 'eles/elas' (they).
target_language_example: Eles sabem o que estão fazendo no projeto.
native_language_example: They know what they are doing on the project.

meaning: 'we know nothing' (we don't know anything)
additional_notes: A negative frase built with saber (to know). In standard Portuguese, the preferred form is 'não sabemos nada' (with não before the verb). In spoken or reduced contexts you may hear 'sabemos nada' or 'a gente sabe nada', but always means lack of information. Use when saying you have no information about a person, event, or fact. If you want to make a question: 'Sabemos de algo?' or 'Sabemos alguma coisa?'.
target_language_example: Não sabemos nada sobre o que aconteceu naquela noite.
native_language_example: We know nothing about what happened that night.

meaning: 'who knows' / 'I don't know; it's anyone's guess' (colloquial hesitation)
additional_notes: Used informally to express uncertainty, doubt, or lack of knowledge about something. Often appears in speech as part of a phrase like "saber lá o que..." (who knows what...) or alone as a brief comment. Tone can be dismissive or resigned depending on context.
target_language_example: Saber lá o que vai acontecer amanhã.
native_language_example: Who knows what will happen tomorrow.

meaning: 'to know why' or 'to find out why'.
additional_notes: Used to ask or state a desire to learn the reason for something. In European Portuguese you'll often see 'porquê', 'porque', or 'por que' variations depending on grammar: here 'porque' functions as 'why' in informal speech. When forming direct questions, native speakers may add 'é que' (e.g., 'sabes por que é que...?').
target_language_example: Eu queria saber porque ele não veio à festa.
native_language_example: I wanted to know why he didn't come to the party.

meaning: 'didn't know anything about' (past tense).
additional_notes: Used to say you (or someone) had no knowledge of something in the past. Commonly appears with a subject and an object introduced by sobre (sobre aquilo/isso/ela). In spoken Portuguese the subject or pronoun may be omitted (e.g., “Não sabia nada sobre isso”).
target_language_example: Eu não sabia nada sobre o plano.
native_language_example: I didn't know anything about the plan.

meaning: we knew that
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect form of saber (nós sabíamos) + que to introduce a clause about something known in the past. It often gives background information or shared knowledge: 'sabíamos que...' = 'we knew that...'. In Portuguese, the subject pronoun nós is often omitted.
target_language_example: Sabíamos que ele voltaria cedo.
native_language_example: We knew that he would come back early.

meaning: 'Are you kidding me?' / 'You must be joking with me.' (expresses disbelief or annoyance)
additional_notes: Informal expression used when someone is surprised, annoyed or finds something hard to believe. Common in Brazil. Often appears as 'Tá de sacanagem comigo?' or 'Você tá de sacanagem comigo?'. Can be directed at a person or situation. Stronger than a polite 'are you kidding?' — can sound confrontational depending on tone.
target_language_example: Sério? Tá de sacanagem comigo?
native_language_example: Seriously? Are you kidding me?

meaning: 'sleeping bag' (a padded bag for sleeping outdoors or while camping).
additional_notes: Used for camping, traveling, or when someone needs a portable bed covering. Can be singular or plural (saco(s) de dormir). Commonly used when asking to borrow, buy, or describe sleeping arrangements.
target_language_example: Você pode me emprestar seu saco de dormir?
native_language_example: Can you lend me your sleeping bag?

meaning: 'go away' / 'get out' (informal, often forceful)
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to leave or to express strong rejection. Common in Brazil; tone can be angry, dismissive, or playful depending on context. Often used alone as an exclamation. Can be directed at a person or at an idea/comment (like 'yeah, right' or 'no way' in some contexts).
target_language_example: Sai fora, não quero mais conversar com você.
native_language_example: Go away, I don't want to talk to you anymore.

meaning: 'go away' / 'leave' (informal), or 'get out' (leave a place or conversation).
additional_notes: Common colloquial Brazilian Portuguese expression. Often used like 'sair' but with extra emphasis; can mean physically leaving a place, stepping out for a moment, or telling someone to go away. Tone ranges from neutral to brusque depending on context. Not typically used in very formal speech.
target_language_example: Ele pediu para eu sair fora porque precisava descansar.
native_language_example: He asked me to go away because he needed to rest.

meaning: classroom; the room where classes are held.
additional_notes: Common, neutral term for a room used for teaching in schools, colleges, or other educational settings. Used with articles and possessives (a sala de aula, minha sala de aula, sua sala de aula). Can appear with prepositions: dentro da sala de aula (inside the classroom), sair da sala de aula (leave the classroom).
target_language_example: Os alunos deixaram a sala de aula depois da aula.
native_language_example: The students left the classroom after class.

meaning: waiting room; a room where people wait (e.g., at a clinic, office, station).
additional_notes: Commonly used for places where people wait for appointments, meetings, transport, or services. Can be literal (a physical room) or used figuratively in contexts like staging areas. Plural: salas de espera. Often preceded by definite/indefinite articles (a/na/na sala de espera).
target_language_example: Há uma sala de espera fora do consultório.
native_language_example: There is a waiting room outside the office.

meaning: living room; lounge (the main sitting room in a house).
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to the main room for relaxing, entertaining guests, watching TV, etc. 'Sala' means room; 'de estar' literally 'of being' — together 'room for being' = living room. Can be used in formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Vamos assistir ao filme na sala de estar.
native_language_example: Let's watch the movie in the living room.

meaning: dining room (the room in a house where meals are eaten).
additional_notes: Common household term. Used to refer to the room where people eat meals or where a dining table is placed. Can be used in instructions (e.g., 'take it to the dining room') or to ask about furniture placement. 'Sala' = room, 'jantar' = dinner; literal composition matches the English phrase.
target_language_example: Por favor, leve isso para a sala de jantar.
native_language_example: Please take that to the dining room.

meaning: the room was / the living room was (past description).
additional_notes: Used to describe the state or condition of a room (sala) in the past. 'Sala' can mean living room, classroom, or any room depending on context. 'Estava' is the past imperfect of 'estar' (to be) and indicates a temporary state or ongoing past condition. Commonly followed by adjectives or phrases (e.g., 'abarrotada' = packed, 'cheia de crianças' = full of children).
target_language_example: A sala estava silenciosa depois da aula.
native_language_example: The room was quiet after class.

meaning: the room is (followed by a description or condition).
additional_notes: Combines sala (room) + está (third-person singular of estar). Use to describe the current state or condition of a room (e.g., empty, hot, clean). Estar is used for temporary states or locations. Insert an adjective or phrase after 'está' (e.g., 'vazia', 'muito quente').
target_language_example: A sala está limpa e organizada.
native_language_example: The room is clean and tidy.

meaning: lifeboat(s) or life-saving boat(s); also 'lifesaver' as a person when used as 'salva-vidas' (lifeguard) in some contexts.
additional_notes: Usually plural; literally 'save-lives'. Commonly refers to lifeboats or inflatable rescue boats at beaches and ships. In some contexts, salva-vidas can refer to a lifeguard (person) but more typical word for lifeguard is salva-vidas (singular) or 'guarda-vidas' depending on region. Used when pointing out emergency rescue boats or equipment.
target_language_example: Há botes salva-vidas disponíveis na praia em frente ao quiosque.
native_language_example: There are lifeboats available on the beach in front of the kiosk.

meaning: 'to save you' or 'to rescue you'.
additional_notes: Literal phrase: salvar = to save/rescue; você = you (formal/informal in Brazil often used generally). Used when talking about rescuing someone from danger, helping them avoid harm, or figuratively saving someone (e.g., from trouble, embarrassment, or financial loss). In spoken Brazilian Portuguese, 'te salvar' is more common in informal contexts (using the clitic 'te' instead of 'você').
target_language_example: Eu vou fazer tudo para salvar você.
native_language_example: I'll do everything to save you.

meaning: 'saved my' (as part of 'saved my life' or 'saved my ___').
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of salvar + possessive minha (feminine). Commonly appears in the phrase salvou a minha vida = 'saved my life'. Use minha when the possessed noun is feminine (vida). For masculine nouns use meu (e.g., salvou o meu carro). Context usually indicates what was saved; the full phrase often includes the noun (vida, carreira, pele, etc.).
target_language_example: Ela salvou a minha vida naquela viagem.
native_language_example: She saved my life on that trip.

meaning: 'saved the' (past tense of 'salvar' + masculine singular definite article 'o')
additional_notes: Salvou is the third-person singular past (pretérito perfeito) of salvar = to save, to rescue, to save (a file). The following 'o' is the masculine singular direct object article ('the') and agrees with a masculine noun (mundo, arquivo, dia). Use salvou a for feminine nouns. Can mean rescuing someone/thing, saving the day, or saving a file on a computer depending on context.
target_language_example: Ele salvou o documento no computador.
native_language_example: He saved the document on the computer.

meaning: beauty salon; hair and beauty salon.
additional_notes: Common place for haircuts, styling, manicure/pedicure and other beauty services. 'Salão' means 'salon' or 'large room' and 'beleza' means 'beauty' — literal translation matches the English phrase. Use with verbs like ir ao (go to) or estar (to be).
target_language_example: Vou ao salão de beleza na sexta-feira para cortar o cabelo.
native_language_example: I'm going to the beauty salon on Friday to get a haircut.

meaning: (ask someone to) remove their shoes before entering (the house/room).
additional_notes: Used in requests or instructions telling people to take off their shoes before entering a home or specific room. Often appears with verbs like tirar, retirar or expressions like 'faça o favor de'. The phrase is not a fixed idiom by itself — it combines 'sapatos' (shoes) with the instruction 'antes de entrar na(o)' (before entering the...). Complete the phrase with the place: casa, sala, cozinha, etc.
target_language_example: Por favor, tire os sapatos antes de entrar na casa.
native_language_example: Please take off your shoes before entering the house.

meaning: mental health
additional_notes: Refers to a person's psychological and emotional well-being. Used in the same contexts as English 'mental health' (concern, treatment, professionals, importance). Can be used formally or informally depending on context.
target_language_example: A saúde mental dela melhorou depois da terapia.
native_language_example: Her mental health improved after therapy.

meaning: a shortened expression emphasizing that health is more important (Health is more important).
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself; likely part of a larger sentence such as 'a saúde é mais importante' or a slogan 'saúde é mais' implying 'health matters more' or 'health comes first.' Used to stress priority of health over other things (money, work, etc.). Commonly appears in informal speech or written slogans. If you want to say 'health is more important,' use 'a saúde é mais importante' or 'a saúde vem em primeiro lugar.'
target_language_example: A saúde é mais — não vale a pena arriscar por dinheiro.
native_language_example: Health is more important — it's not worth risking for money.

meaning: health is more important (than ...).
additional_notes: A comparative phrase used to say health matters more than something else (wealth, money, etc.). Commonly completed with 'do que' or 'que' + the thing you're comparing. Use 'A saúde' (the health) — Portuguese often uses the definite article with body/abstract nouns.
target_language_example: A saúde é mais importante do que o dinheiro.
native_language_example: Health is more important than money.

meaning: 'sit next to me' / 'sit at my (side)'.
additional_notes: This appears as part of the phrase sentar-se ao meu lado or sente-se ao meu lado. Sentar-se = 'to sit down' (reflexive); ao meu lado = 'at my side' / 'next to me'. Use sente-se (imperative/formal polite) or senta-te (informal in Portugal) / senta (Brazil) for commands. Common in contexts inviting someone to sit beside you.
target_language_example: Sente-se ao meu lado e fique à vontade.
native_language_example: Sit next to me and make yourself comfortable.

meaning: to be late for (something).
additional_notes: Reflexive construction: 'se atrasar' = 'to be late'. Followed by 'para' + noun or event (e.g., 'para a escola', 'para a cerimônia'). Commonly used with a person as subject (ele/ela/você/tu). You can drop 'a' when the following noun doesn't require the article (e.g., 'se atrasar para escola' is informal but standard is 'para a escola').
target_language_example: Se você não sair agora, vai se atrasar para a reunião.
native_language_example: If you don't leave now, you'll be late for the meeting.

meaning: 'to get married in' (followed by a month, year, or time expression).
additional_notes: Used to indicate when someone will marry. 'Se casar' is a reflexive construction commonly used in Portuguese to mean 'to get married.' 'Em' is followed by a month, year, or time expression (em junho, em outubro, em 2025). Can be conjugated for different subjects (ele/ela vai se casar em..., nós vamos nos casar em... — note placement of reflexive pronoun can vary by regional usage).
target_language_example: A minha filha vai se casar em junho.
native_language_example: My daughter is going to get married in June.

meaning: 'take care of yourself' / 'take care'
additional_notes: A reflexive informal goodbye or caring instruction used to tell someone to look after their health/safety. Common in Brazil. Can be said alone as a farewell (like 'take care') or as a comment about someone (e.g., 'He takes care of himself'). Tone depends on context: friendly, concerned, or casual. Use with a name (Se cuida, Maria) when saying goodbye.
target_language_example: Tchau, se cuida.
native_language_example: Bye, take care.

meaning: 'how do you say this' (literally: 'is said this'); used to ask how to say or name something in another language or to ask what something is called.
additional_notes: Common in questions like "Como se diz isso em [língua]?" to request a translation or the word for an object/idea. The structure uses impersonal/reflective voice (se diz = 'one says' / 'is said'). You can replace "isso" with "isto", "aquilo" or a specific word/phrase. To address a person more directly, use alternatives like "Como você diz isso?" or "Como se fala isso?". Capitalization of language names (russo/francês) is typically lowercase in Portuguese.
target_language_example: Como se diz isso em russo?
native_language_example: How do you say this in Russian?

meaning: to forget
additional_notes: Reflexive verb meaning 'to forget' (often used with 'de' + object: 'se esquecer de algo' = 'to forget something'). Can also mean 'to try to forget' when used with context like 'querer se esquecer disso' (to want to forget that). Common constructions: 'não se esquecer' = 'don't forget'. Pronoun 'se' agrees with subject and is required in Portuguese.
target_language_example: Vou repetir para você não se esquecer disso.
native_language_example: I'll repeat it so you don't forget this.

meaning: 'you're screwed' / 'you're fucked' (vulgar) — used to say someone is in big trouble or will suffer the consequences.
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Literal components: 'se' (reflexive) + 'foder' (to fuck). Commonly used in spoken Portuguese (Brazil) to express that someone is doomed, has bad luck, or will be punished. Can be directed at someone (tu/ele se fode) or used impersonally (vai se foder — go screw yourself). Avoid in polite contexts; use milder alternatives like 'você está ferrado' or 'você está em apuros'.
target_language_example: Se continuar mentindo, você se fode quando descobrirem.
native_language_example: If you keep lying, you're screwed when they find out.

meaning: 'forming' / 'being formed' or 'graduating' (depending on context)
additional_notes: This is the gerund form of 'formar' used with the reflexive 'se'. It can describe something in the process of forming (e.g., a storm is forming) or the process of graduating from a course (Tom is graduating). Context tells you which meaning applies. Commonly appears with 'estar' (está se formando / está formando).
target_language_example: A nuvem está se formando no horizonte.
native_language_example: The cloud is forming on the horizon.

meaning: do you mind that / would you mind if (used to ask permission or check if something bothers someone)
additional_notes: Polite phrase used to ask if an action would bother someone or to request permission. Commonly appears as 'Você se importa que...' or 'Você se importa de... + infinitive'. When followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., 'abra', 'saibam'), it asks about a hypothetical or future action. Can be used formally or casually depending on tone.
target_language_example: Você se importa que eu feche a janela?
native_language_example: Do you mind if I close the window?

meaning: to mind; to be bothered (by something).
additional_notes: Used to ask politely whether an action would bother or inconvenience someone. Often appears in negative questions with não (e.g., 'Você não se incomoda...?') or as a polite request 'Você se incomoda de...?' followed by an infinitive. Commonly translated as 'Do you mind...?' or 'Would you mind...?'
target_language_example: Você se incomoda de fechar a porta?
native_language_example: Do you mind closing the door?

meaning: to join the forces (e.g., military or special forces).
additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about joining armed groups or military units; 'forças' often implies 'forças armadas' or 'forças especiais' (special forces). 'Se juntar a' is a pronominal verb meaning 'to join' or 'to become part of.' The contraction 'às' = 'a + as' (to the, feminine plural).
target_language_example: Ele decidiu se juntar às forças especiais no próximo ano.
native_language_example: He decided to join the special forces next year.

meaning: on the sofa / in the sofa (used with reflexive verbs like sentar-se, deitar-se).
additional_notes: This phrase combines a reflexive pronoun (se) with a location (no sofá). In sentences it appears after verbs like sentar-se (to sit down) or deitar-se (to lie down). In natural Portuguese the reflexive pronoun attaches to the infinitive (sentar-se) or follows/attaches to a conjugated verb (sente-se, sentou-se). English equivalents: sit on the sofa, lie on the sofa. 'No' = em + o (in/on the).
target_language_example: Por favor, sente-se no sofá e descanse.
native_language_example: Please sit on the sofa and rest.

meaning: to look like
additional_notes: Used reflexively (se) with a person as the subject to say someone looks like or resembles another person. Common structures: 'parecer-se com [alguém]' or in spoken Brazilian Portuguese 'se parecer com [alguém]'. Can be followed by a noun or a pronoun (com o pai, comigo, com você).
target_language_example: Ela começa a se parecer com a avó.
native_language_example: She is starting to look like her grandmother.

meaning: 'wondering' (thinking to oneself or asking oneself).
additional_notes: Reflexive gerund form of perguntar (to ask). Used when someone is asking themselves or wondering about something. Common in continuous tenses: estar + se perguntando = to be wondering. Often followed by a clause introduced by 'por que', 'qual', 'de onde', etc.
target_language_example: Ela está se perguntando se tomou a decisão certa.
native_language_example: She is wondering whether she made the right decision.

meaning: 'wondered why' or 'asked himself/herself why'.
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive verb (se perguntou) to express that someone wondered/questioned to themselves. Common construction: [subject] + se perguntou por que + [clause]. 'Por que' here means 'why'. Often appears in past tenses (se perguntou, já se perguntou).
target_language_example: Ela se perguntou por que ele não atendeu o telefone.
native_language_example: She wondered why he didn't answer the phone.

meaning: worry
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the negative imperative phrase 'não se preocupe' meaning 'don't worry' or 'don't be worried'.
