Usually appears as tomar a liberdade de + infinitive (or in past tense: tomei a liberdade de ...). Common in formal or polite contexts to soften an action that might require permission.
target_language_example: Ele decidiu tomar a liberdade de corrigir o texto sem consultar a autora.
native_language_example: He decided to take the liberty of correcting the text without consulting the author.

meaning: to take care of; to look after; to manage (responsibility for someone or something).
additional_notes: Used with de/da/dos to indicate what or whom is being cared for (tomar conta de mim, tomar conta das crianças). Can mean self-care or managing one's life/time (tomar conta da minha vida). Context determines whether it's temporary babysitting/looking after or a more general responsibility. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Posso tomar conta das plantas enquanto você estiver fora.
native_language_example: I can take care of the plants while you're away.

meaning: 'to take care of' or 'to look after' (someone or oneself).
additional_notes: Used when talking about caring for a person (or oneself), supervising, or being responsible for someone's needs. Commonly reflexive with 'de mim/si mesmo/nós/eles' to say 'take care of oneself/ourselves/them.'
target_language_example: Ela precisa aprender a tomar conta de si mesma.
native_language_example: She needs to learn to take care of herself.

meaning: 'to be careful' / 'to take care' (to act with caution).
additional_notes: Common impersonal or personal phrase used to advise caution. Often appears with modal verbs (dever, precisar, ter que, poder) or impersonal 'deve-se'. Can be followed by 'com' + noun (tomar cuidado com a rua) or used alone (tomar cuidado!).
target_language_example: Você deve tomar cuidado ao usar ferramentas elétricas.
native_language_example: You should be careful when using power tools.

meaning: to have a cup (of something), usually to drink tea or coffee.
additional_notes: Commonly used when inviting someone or saying you'll drink a beverage: e.g. 'tomar uma xícara de café' or 'tomar uma xícara de chá'. Can be shortened to 'tomar uma' in casual speech if context is clear. Not idiomatic — literal meaning.
target_language_example: Vamos tomar uma xícara de chá depois do trabalho?
native_language_example: Shall we have a cup of tea after work?

meaning: have a drink
additional_notes: Informal Brazilian Portuguese phrase meaning to drink (usually alcoholic) — often implies going for a casual drink with someone. Can be used as an invitation: "Tomar uma?" = "Want to have a drink?" Context may change exact translation (e.g., "tomar uma por minha conta" = "she'll buy one for me/on my tab"). Literally "tomar" = "to take" and "uma" = "one (feminine)" referring to a drink.
target_language_example: Vamos tomar uma depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: Let's grab a drink after work.

meaning: 'I hope' / 'let's hope' (expresses a wish or hope)
additional_notes: Used to express a wish or hope about something. Often followed by the subjunctive verb form (e.g., 'tomara que chova', 'tomara que eu tenha'). Can be used alone (Tomara!) or with 'que' + clause. Tone can range from casual to neutral; common in spoken Portuguese.
target_language_example: Tomara que tudo dê certo amanhã.
native_language_example: I hope everything goes well tomorrow.

meaning: 'I took' or 'I drank' (past tense of 'tomar') followed by a feminine noun or set phrase (e.g. 'tomei a liberdade').
additional_notes: Tomar is a versatile verb: it can mean 'to take' (an action, opportunity, injection), 'to drink' (a beverage), or be part of set phrases like 'tomar a liberdade' (to take the liberty). When followed by a feminine noun, use 'tomei a' (masculine nouns use 'tomei o'). Context tells the meaning: 'tomei a injeção' = I took/received the injection; 'tomei a minha primeira cerveja' = I drank my first beer; 'tomei a liberdade' = I took the liberty (did something without asking).
target_language_example: Tomei a decisão de aceitar o trabalho.
native_language_example: I made/took the decision to accept the job.

meaning: 'I took the...' or 'I drank the...' (first-person past of 'tomar' + definite article)
additional_notes: Tomei is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) first-person singular of tomar. It can mean 'took' (e.g., took transportation, took care, took/used something) or 'drank' (e.g., took medicine, finished a drink) depending on context. The following article o (the) makes the phrase specific: 'the medicine', 'the subway', 'the care', 'the rest'. Verb meaning changes with objects; choose translation according to the noun that follows or the situation.
target_language_example: Tomei o ônibus das sete para ir ao trabalho.
native_language_example: I took the 7:00 bus to go to work.

meaning: I take a shower / I take a bath (depending on context).
additional_notes: Common present-tense phrase meaning 'I take a shower' or 'I take a bath'. In Brazilian Portuguese, tomar um banho usually implies taking a shower. Used for habitual actions (often with sempre, normalmente, geralmente). Conjugate verb (tomar) for other subjects: 'tomas um banho', 'toma um banho', 'tomamos um banho', etc.
target_language_example: Hoje eu sempre tomo um banho pela manhã.
native_language_example: Today I always take a shower in the morning.

meaning: 'took the' or 'did you take the' (past tense of 'tomar' + definite article 'o')
additional_notes: Tomou is the third-person singular past (pretérito perfeito) of tomar (to take) and can also be used as a polite/formal second-person past in some regions. With 'o' it means 'the' (masculine). Depending on context, it can mean physically took something (took the newspaper), took control (took the remote/control), or took medication (took your medicine). Word order can change (Você tomou o seu remédio?).
target_language_example: Ela tomou o guarda-chuva sem avisar.
native_language_example: She took the umbrella without saying anything.

meaning: 'touch the' (imperative/command with feminine noun) or general imperative 'touch [something]'.
additional_notes: From the verb tocar (to touch) + preposition na (a + a). Used in commands: 'Não toque na ...' = 'Don't touch the ...'. With masculine nouns it becomes 'toque no'. 'Toque na' can also appear as a neutral instruction 'Touch the...' (polite/neutral imperative). Context shows both prohibition and permission. The verb form 'toque' is the formal/informal imperative (você) or present-subjunctive used for polite commands.
target_language_example: Toque na janela para ver se está fechada.
native_language_example: Touch the window to see if it's closed.

meaning: 'touch' + object warning: used to tell someone not to touch something (do not touch the ...).
additional_notes: Imperative structure: often appears after a negative imperative like "Não toque no...". "Toque" is the imperative (from tocar) or present subjunctive form; "no" = contraction of "em + o" (on/the) used before masculine singular nouns. For feminine nouns use "na" (não toque na...). Use to forbid touching people or objects; polite alternatives include "Por favor, não toque..."
target_language_example: Por favor, não toque no meu telefone.
native_language_example: Please do not touch my phone.

meaning: imperative 'ring the' or 'touch the' (command) — tú/you (formal/informal) + direct article 'o' before a masculine noun (e.g., 'sino' = bell).
additional_notes: A command form using the verb tocar (to touch/play/ring). 'Toque' is the formal (você) or third-person singular imperative/subjunctive form; in spoken Brazilian Portuguese it's often used to address someone politely: 'Toque o sino' = 'Ring the bell' or 'Touch the bell'. The 'o' is the masculine definite article and must match a masculine noun that follows (sino, telefone, botão). For informal tu in some regions you'd say 'toca o'.
target_language_example: Por favor, toque o botão para chamar o elevador.
native_language_example: Please press (touch) the button to call the elevator.

meaning: curfew (a rule requiring people to be home by a specific time).
additional_notes: Used for government or household rules that restrict people — often youth — from being outside after a set hour. Can refer to official emergency curfews or simple parental/home curfews. Commonly used with verbs like 'haver' (is there), 'perder' (to miss/violate), 'violar' (to break).
target_language_example: Os vizinhos reclamaram porque os adolescentes violaram o toque de recolher.
native_language_example: The neighbors complained because the teenagers broke the curfew.

meaning: 'around' or 'around the' (indicating movement or position surrounding something).
additional_notes: Used to say 'around' or 'around the' + feminine singular noun (da = de + a). Can indicate movement (running around the house) or position (sitting around the table) and also used for abstract ideas (around the idea of). For masculine nouns use 'em torno do' (de + o).
target_language_example: As crianças brincavam em torno da árvore.
native_language_example: The children were playing around the tree.

meaning: around; about; in the vicinity of; used with motion or location (literally 'around the').
additional_notes: Usually appears in the prepositional phrase 'em torno de' (or 'em torno do/da' when combined with definite article) meaning 'around' or 'about' — used for physical motion around something (planets around the sun) or figurative sense (tension around an issue). When used as 'girar em torno do/da', it means 'to revolve around' or 'to focus on' someone/something. Note the form changes with the article: 'em torno do' (masculine), 'em torno da' (feminine).
target_language_example: Os alunos discutiram em torno do projeto durante horas.
native_language_example: The students discussed around/about the project for hours.

meaning: no longer works here / doesn't work here anymore.
additional_notes: Used to say someone stopped working at a place. Often appears with a subject and a negative particle (não) before the verb: 'não trabalha mais aqui' = 'doesn't work here anymore.' In Portuguese word order the verb (trabalha) follows the subject in neutral sentences, but in short statements the subject can be omitted: 'Não trabalha mais aqui.' Use 'mais' to mean 'anymore/no longer.'
target_language_example: Ela não trabalha mais aqui desde o mês passado.
native_language_example: She doesn't work here anymore since last month.

meaning: 'I work for' / 'to work for (someone or an organization)'
additional_notes: Used to indicate employment or working on behalf of a person, group or organization. With subject implied or explicit: Eu trabalho para... / (Eu) trabalho para.... Can be followed by a proper name, company, agency, pronoun (você), or noun phrase. Close equivalent in English is 'work for'.
target_language_example: Eu trabalho para uma escola particular.
native_language_example: I work for a private school.

meaning: homework (school assignments to do at home).
additional_notes: Used to refer to schoolwork assigned to be completed outside class. Can be used with possessives (meu trabalho de casa, o trabalho de casa dela) or plural sense (muito trabalho de casa). Common in everyday speech and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Eu preciso terminar o meu trabalho de casa de matemática.
native_language_example: I need to finish my math homework.

meaning: 'their job is' / 'what they do is'.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone else's regular task or role. 'Trabalho' = job/work, 'deles' = theirs, and 'é' = is. Commonly followed by an infinitive verb (comprar, cortar, cozinhar) or a noun phrase describing the task.
target_language_example: O trabalho deles é cuidar das plantas do prédio.
native_language_example: Their job is to take care of the building's plants.

meaning: the job/work is (followed by a state or condition).
additional_notes: Common construction: 'trabalho está' + adjective, past participle, or phrase to describe the state of a task (e.g., feito, terminado, por um fio, quase feito). Used to say whether work is done, nearly done, in danger, etc. 'Trabalho' can be replaced by 'o trabalho' or 'meu trabalho'.
target_language_example: O trabalho está quase pronto.
native_language_example: The work is almost ready.

meaning: locked (someone) in / locked (oneself) in (a room or space).
additional_notes: From the verb trancar (to lock). 'Trancou no' is often used with a person as subject: either someone locked someone else in (A trancou B no quarto) or a reflexive form is used (se trancou no quarto) meaning they locked themselves in. Common with rooms, bathrooms, or other enclosed spaces. Use past forms (trancou = he/she/you formal locked).
target_language_example: Ele se trancou no quarto depois da briga.
native_language_example: He locked himself in the room after the fight.

meaning: 'becomes' or 'turns into' (indicates something changes into something else).
additional_notes: Used with reflexive verb form (transformar-se) or as third-person present (ele/ela se transforma em). Followed by the new state or thing introduced by 'em' + noun. Common for physical, emotional, or abstract changes. Can be used in many tenses: transforma em (present), transformou em (past), vai se transformar em (future).
target_language_example: A chuva se transforma em neve nas montanhas.
native_language_example: The rain turns into snow in the mountains.

meaning: public transportation; transport services available to the general public (buses, trains, trams, metro, etc.).
additional_notes: Common phrase for the systems people use to travel in a city or region. Can refer to a single mode (o transporte público — the public transport system) or multiple 'meios de transporte público' (means/modes of public transport). Used in everyday conversation and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Vou ao trabalho de transporte público todos os dias.
native_language_example: I go to work by public transportation every day.

meaning: bring me a
additional_notes: Common phrase used when asking someone to bring something (or someone) to you or to a place. In Portuguese word order can vary: 'trazer um copo de água' = 'bring a glass of water'. Change the article/gender/quantity as needed (um/uma/algum/alguns). When addressing someone formally or politely, add 'por favor' or use conditional 'poderia me trazer...'.
target_language_example: Você pode trazer um garfo, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you bring a fork, please?

meaning: the train was ... (past/state description)
additional_notes: A simple past/state construction: trem (train) + estava (imperfect of 'estar') describes the train's condition or situation in the past (e.g., delayed, ready). Use to report ongoing or background states in the past. To say 'the train is...' in present, use 'o trem está'.
target_language_example: O trem estava cheio ontem de manhã.
native_language_example: The train was crowded yesterday morning.

meaning: by train or by (…); used to offer/ask transport options (e.g. by train or by plane).
additional_notes: This phrase appears when listing transport methods with the preposition 'de' (meaning 'by' for means of transport). In Portuguese you repeat 'de' before each noun in a list (optional in casual speech), e.g. 'de trem ou de avião' = 'by train or by plane'. Use it to ask or give alternatives for how someone will travel.
target_language_example: Vamos para a cidade de trem ou de ônibus?
native_language_example: Are we going to the city by train or by bus?

meaning: 'thirty-six' (the number 36).
additional_notes: Used for counting, ages, measurements, math, prices, etc. In Portuguese numbers are written as words with 'e' (and) between tens and units. Pronunciation: /ˈtɾi.n.tɐ i ˈsejʃ/.
target_language_example: Tenho trinta e seis livros na estante.
native_language_example: I have thirty-six books on the shelf.

meaning: the number thirty-one (31).
additional_notes: Used to state the cardinal number 31 in dates, ages, counts, etc. Portuguese numbers are composed with 'e' (and) between tens and units. Pronunciation: 'TREE-n-tah ee OOM' (approx.).
target_language_example: Ela tem trinta e um anos.
native_language_example: She is thirty-one years old.

meaning: to change or replace the (masculine) [something].
additional_notes: Trocar means 'to change', 'to exchange', or 'to swap'. When followed by the definite article 'o' it signals a specific masculine noun will follow (e.g., trocar o nome, trocar o canal, trocar o dinheiro). Use trocar por to indicate what something is being exchanged for (trocar A por B). Can mean changing settings (trocar de canal), replacing objects (trocar o motor), or exchanging money (trocar dinheiro).
target_language_example: Posso trocar o canal?
native_language_example: Can I change the channel?

meaning: three years older (than someone).
additional_notes: Used to compare ages: (subject) é três anos mais velho (do) que (object). For feminine subject use 'mais velha'. Both 'do que' and 'que' are commonly used after 'mais velho'. The number 'três' can be replaced with any number.
target_language_example: Meu pai é três anos mais velho que minha mãe.
native_language_example: My father is three years older than my mother.

meaning: three balls (literal count) — here used to say someone can juggle three balls.
additional_notes: Literal phrase: três = three, bolas = balls. Commonly used to state quantity or describe juggling (fazer malabarismos/com/— to juggle with). Can appear in sentences with verbs like conseguir, poder, or ver to talk about ability or observation: "Consigo fazer malabarismos com três bolas."
target_language_example: Ela aprendeu a fazer malabarismos com três bolas.
native_language_example: She learned to juggle with three balls.

meaning: three glasses/cups (of something).
additional_notes: Used to count containers of liquid (glasses, cups). Followed by 'de' + beverage: e.g. 'três copos de água' = three glasses of water. Can refer to glasses or cups depending on context; use with verbs like beber/tomar. Number and noun agree: 'três copos'.
target_language_example: Ela pediu três copos de água, por favor.
native_language_example: She asked for three glasses of water, please.

meaning: 'three stitches' (in medical context) or 'three points' (score); literal: three dots/points.
additional_notes: Literal phrase meaning "three points/dots." Common uses: (1) medical: levar/trazer três pontos = to receive three stitches (sutures) after a cut; (2) sports/games: winning/losing by three points (Tom venceu por três pontos = Tom won by three points); (3) can also refer to three dots or items counted as points in songs/chanting. Context determines the meaning.
target_language_example: Ela levou três pontos no braço depois do acidente.
native_language_example: She got three stitches in her arm after the accident.

meaning: because of you; on your account.
additional_notes: Used to blame someone for something negative (often angrily). 'Tua' is the informal singular 'your' (tu). In more formal or plural contexts Brazilians often use 'sua causa' (but 'sua' can be ambiguous) or 'por sua causa'. Word order can also be 'por tua causa' (common) or just 'tua causa' after a verb/exclamation as in the examples.
target_language_example: Chegámos atrasados por tua causa.
native_language_example: We arrived late because of you.

meaning: 'waiting for you' (informal singular 'you')
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is waiting for a specific person (informal singular tu). Common in Portugal; in Brazil 'à sua espera' (formal) or 'te esperando' are more typical. Structure: à + pronoun + espera = 'in (the) your wait' → 'waiting for you.'
target_language_example: Eles estão à tua espera na estação.
native_language_example: They are waiting for you at the station.

meaning: your party (informal, singular 'you').
additional_notes: Tua is the possessive for 'your' when speaking informally to one person (tu). Use 'sua festa' in more formal or when using 'você'. 'Festa' means party, celebration. In Brazil, 'tu' is less common in some regions; match possessive to the pronoun you use.
target_language_example: Posso levar um amigo à tua festa?
native_language_example: Can I bring a friend to your party?

meaning: 'your mother' (informal/neutral, singular, familiar 'tua').
additional_notes: Tua is the familiar singular 'your' (used with friends, family, or people you address informally). In some regions of Brazil, 'tua' is less common than 'sua' for polite/formal speech. Use 'sua mãe' to be more neutral or formal. Context examples show both statements and questions about someone's mother.
target_language_example: Onde está a tua mãe?
native_language_example: Where is your mother?

meaning: okay
additional_notes: A very common expression meaning that something is okay, fine, or acceptable. It can be used to agree, reassure someone, or move a conversation along. As a question, especially just "Tudo bem?", it can also mean "How are you?" or "Are you okay?".
target_language_example: Se você quiser sair mais cedo, tudo bem.
native_language_example: If you want to leave earlier, that's okay.

meaning: all I can / everything I can (do)
additional_notes: Used to express doing the maximum possible effort or everything one is able to do. Often appears in contexts like 'faço tudo o que posso' (I do everything I can) or 'fiz tudo o que pude' (I did all I could). Tone is neutral and common in spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: Eu faço tudo o que posso para ajudar.
native_language_example: I do everything I can to help.

meaning: 'everything will (be) ...' — start of a reassuring sentence meaning things will turn out a certain way (usually 'better' or 'okay').
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a future-tense reassurance: 'tudo vai ficar bem' (everything will be fine), 'tudo vai ficar resolvido' (everything will be resolved), etc. Alone it is incomplete and normally followed by an adjective or past participle. Used to comfort someone or predict an outcome.
target_language_example: Não se preocupe — tudo vai ficar bem.
native_language_example: Don't worry — everything will be fine.

meaning: 'the ... shift' (used to specify a work shift at a particular time, e.g. 'turno da noite' = the night shift).
additional_notes: Used with a time or period (noite, manhã, tarde, madrugada, meia-noite) to indicate which work shift or duty period. 'Turno' = shift; 'da' is the contraction of 'de + a' ('of the'). Common in workplace contexts and asking/talking about schedules.
target_language_example: Ela prefere trabalhar no turno da manhã.
native_language_example: She prefers to work the morning shift.

meaning: 'okay' / 'is okay' (short for 'está bem')
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction of 'está bem'. Used to say something is okay/fine, to ask if someone is okay, or to acknowledge/agreed (like 'alright' or 'okay, fine'). Common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese. Context determines tone: question (Are you okay?), statement (it's okay), or agreement (Okay, bye).
target_language_example: Tá bem, vou ligar mais tarde.
native_language_example: Okay, I'll call later.

meaning: 'okay' or 'all right' (agreement, acceptance, or to end a conversation).
additional_notes: Informal contraction of 'está bom'. Used to agree, accept something, confirm understanding, or to close a topic. Tone and context decide nuance: friendly acceptance ('okay, thanks'), mild resignation ('fine'), or to signal the end of discussion. Common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese.
target_language_example: Tá bom, obrigada.
native_language_example: Okay, thank you.

meaning: 'you know' / 'you see' (colloquial filler to check agreement or attention); also 'it's on' or 'it's connected' in literal sense
additional_notes: Informal, contraction of 'está ligado'. Common in Brazilian Portuguese as a conversational tag meaning 'you know'/'you get it' or to ask 'are you paying attention?' e.g. 'Tá ligado?' = 'You know? / Right?'. Can also be literal about something being switched on or connected (e.g. a aparelho tá ligado = the device is on). Use in informal speech and with friends.
target_language_example: Ele explicou tudo, tá ligado?
native_language_example: He explained everything, you know?

meaning: 'as soon as' or 'as soon as possible' (indicating immediate action or time right after something happens).
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen immediately after another event (as soon as) or, in fixed phrase 'tão logo quanto possível', to mean 'as soon as possible.' Often followed by a clause introduced by que or by a verb. Can appear alone in short responses (e.g., 'Tão logo assim?') to express surprise about how soon something happened.
target_language_example: Tão logo termine o trabalho, me avise.
native_language_example: As soon as you finish the work, tell me.

meaning: 'are afraid of' or 'fear (something)'.
additional_notes: Plural form of 'ter medo de' (to be afraid of). 'Têm' is the third-person plural of 'ter'. 'da' is the contraction of 'de + a' (of the/from the) and agrees when the noun is feminine singular; use 'do' (de + o) for masculine nouns, or 'de' alone before pronouns or indefinite nouns. Common structure: [subject] + têm medo de/da + [noun/verb-infinitive].
target_language_example: Eles têm medo da tempestade.
native_language_example: They are afraid of the storm.

meaning: they are nosy / eavesdrop / can overhear things (literally: 'they have long ears')
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression used to say someone listens in, overhears conversations, or is likely to find out information—often implying gossip or that others may be listening. Context matters: can be playful or a warning to speak carefully. Plural form here (têm) = 'they have'.
target_language_example: Não fale sobre surpresas aqui — eles têm orelhas compridas.
native_language_example: Don't talk about the surprise here — they have long ears (i.e. they're likely to overhear).

meaning: table tennis (ping-pong).
additional_notes: Refers to the sport played on a table with paddles and a lightweight ball. Common synonyms in English: table tennis or ping-pong. Used in Portuguese exactly like the English name split into words (tênis = tennis, de = of, mesa = table).
target_language_example: Eles começaram a jogar tênis de mesa no clube todas as sextas.
native_language_example: They started playing table tennis at the club every Friday.

meaning: lit. 'sneakers by/through' — not a fixed phrase; likely part of a larger sentence (e.g. 'tênis pela manhã' or 'tênis pela loja') and needs more context.
additional_notes: This sequence is not a standalone idiom in Portuguese. 'tênis' means 'sneakers' or the sport 'tennis' (context decides). 'pela' is the contraction of 'por' + 'a' meaning 'by/through/for the'. Together they typically appear as part of a longer phrase (for example 'tênis pela manhã' wouldn't be natural — more natural would be 'corrida pela manhã' or 'uso de tênis pela cidade'; or 'comprei tênis pela internet' — 'I bought sneakers online'). Watch for meaning based on context: 'tênis' (shoe) vs 'tênis' (sport).
target_language_example: Comprei tênis pela internet.
native_language_example: I bought sneakers online.

meaning: shy and (followed by another adjective/personality trait)
additional_notes: Combines the adjective tímido (shy) with the conjunction e (and) to link another description. Used before another adjective to describe a person or animal (e.g., tímido e solitário). Word order in Portuguese is typically adjective + e + adjective when describing traits.
target_language_example: Tom é um garoto tímido e solitário.
native_language_example: Tom is a shy and lonely boy.

meaning: I'm (at) / I'm on — informal contraction of 'estou no' used to say you're at a place, on the phone, or doing something.
additional_notes: Tô is an informal spoken contraction of estou (I am). 'No' is the contraction of 'em' + 'o' (in/at the) or part of fixed expressions like 'no telefone' (on the phone). Used in casual conversation to say where you are or what you're doing (e.g., at work, on the phone, on the ground). For feminine nouns you'd hear 'tô na'.
target_language_example: Tô no café esperando você.
native_language_example: I'm at the café waiting for you.

meaning: 'a Gray Falcon' (a proper name or code name for a person, vehicle, or unit)
additional_notes: Used as a name or code — probably a proper noun (e.g., a callsign, code name, or nickname). The capitalized words and repeated sentences suggest it's being called/invoked ("I'll call a Gray Falcon Ten"). In Portuguese the article 'um' + capitalized name feels like introducing or summoning that entity. If you hear this in conversation, treat it like naming someone/something rather than describing a random gray falcon bird.
target_language_example: Vou chamar um Falcão Cinzento para nos ajudar.
native_language_example: I'll call a Gray Falcon to help us.

meaning: 'a hug' or 'an embrace'.
additional_notes: Used both literally (to hug someone) and figuratively (to ask for comfort). Common in greetings/closings in messages (e.g., 'Um abraço' = 'Best regards' or 'Hugs'). Can be used with verbs like dar (dar um abraço), receber, precisar de. Tone can be affectionate or friendly depending on context.
target_language_example: Depois do jogo, ela me deu um abraço apertado.
native_language_example: After the game, she gave me a tight hug.

meaning: 'a friend whose father is...'.
additional_notes: Use to describe possession or relationship: 'cujo' = 'whose' (agrees in gender/number with the possessed noun). Here 'um amigo' (masculine singular) so 'cujo' is used. Followed by the possessed noun ('pai') and a verb or complement. Common in formal and neutral registers.
target_language_example: Tenho um amigo cujo pai é médico.
native_language_example: I have a friend whose father is a doctor.

meaning: 'a kiss' (used as a short goodbye or request).
additional_notes: Literally means 'a kiss'. Commonly used as a casual farewell (like 'kisses' or 'love' at the end of a message), as a question/request for a kiss, or to say someone owes you a kiss. Tone depends on context and familiarity — can be affectionate, playful, or flirty.
target_language_example: Ele terminou a ligação com um beijo.
native_language_example: He ended the call with a kiss.

meaning: one fine day; a nice/beautiful day (literal) or 'one day' (in the future, often unexpectedly).
additional_notes: Can be used literally to describe good weather (a beautiful day). Also used idiomatically to mean 'one day' or 'someday' — often introducing an event that will happen unexpectedly or in the future (e.g., "Um belo dia, ele foi embora" = "One day, he just left"). Tone is neutral; context tells whether it's literal weather or a narrative time phrase.
target_language_example: Um belo dia, ela decidiu viajar pelo mundo.
native_language_example: One fine day, she decided to travel the world.

meaning: a little / a bit / somewhat (can indicate small amount, degree, or a short time)
additional_notes: Common informal expression. Depending on context, it can mean 'a little' (quantity), 'a bit' or 'somewhat' (degree), or 'for a short while' (time). Often used with verbs and adjectives: 'um bocado bêbado' = somewhat drunk; 'um bocado de coisas' = a few things; 'voltei por um bocado' = I returned for a bit. Tone is conversational.
target_language_example: Fico um bocado cansado depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: I get a bit tired after work.

meaning: one day
additional_notes: Literally means "one day." It often introduces an unspecified day in a story ("one day...") and can also mean "someday" when talking about the future. The exact meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Um dia, quero aprender a surfar.
native_language_example: One day, I want to learn to surf.

meaning: a (male) student of/from; used to say someone (male) is a student in a particular school, grade, program, or country.
additional_notes: Literal components: um (a/an), estudante (student), do (contraction of de + o = of the / from the). 'Do' is used before masculine singular nouns (e.g., ensino médio, terceiro ano, Canadá). For a female student use 'uma estudante da' (de + a = da). Context determines whether 'do' conveys membership ('student of a program') or origin ('student from a country').
target_language_example: Eu era um estudante do ensino médio naquela época.
native_language_example: I was a high school student at that time.

meaning: 'a large number' or 'many'.
additional_notes: Formal/neutral expression used before countable nouns to mean 'a large number of' or 'many'. Common in writing and speech; often followed by de + noun (um grande número de pessoas). Equivalent to 'muitas' but slightly more formal/quantitative.
target_language_example: Um grande número de estudantes compareceu à palestra.
native_language_example: A large number of students attended the lecture.

meaning: 'a man in/on' or 'a man at' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Literal sequence: um (a/an), homem (man), na (contraction of em + a = in/at/on the). Used before a feminine noun: 'na casa' = 'in the house'. Meaning depends on the following noun and context — e.g. 'um homem na casa' = 'a man in the house', 'um homem na porta' = 'a man at/in the door/doorway', and in idiomatic or emotional contexts ('um homem na cadeia' = 'a man in jail').
target_language_example: Há um homem na cozinha.
native_language_example: There is a man in the kitchen.

meaning: 'a player of' or 'a ... player' (used to say someone plays a sport, game or is a fan of something).
additional_notes: Followed by a sport, game, or activity: e.g. 'um jogador de futebol' = a soccer player. Can also describe someone who plays an instrument or is a fan when context allows (less common). Use 'uma jogadora de' for a female player. If referring to a team member, you might also see 'jogador do' or 'da' (contracting 'de' + 'o/a') when specifying 'of the' (e.g. 'jogador do Flamengo').
target_language_example: Ele é um jogador de vôlei da escola.
native_language_example: He is a school volleyball player.

meaning: 'a long way to go' or 'a long road ahead'.
additional_notes: Used to say there is still a lot to do or a long process ahead. Often appears as 'um longo caminho pela frente' (literally: 'a long road in front of us'). Can refer to tasks, progress, personal development, or literal distance. Common in both singular and plural subjects.
target_language_example: Ainda temos um longo caminho pela frente.
native_language_example: We still have a long way to go.

meaning: a lot
additional_notes: Informal, used to indicate a large quantity or many of something. Commonly followed by 'de' + noun (um monte de coisas = a lot of things) but can stand alone as an exclamation meaning 'a lot!' or 'loads!'.
target_language_example: Tenho um monte de trabalho hoje.
native_language_example: I have a lot of work today.

meaning: a lot of things to (do) / many things to (do).
additional_notes: Informal expression used to say you have many tasks or things to do. Often followed by a verb or left implicit (e.g., 'para fazer' = 'to do'). 'Um monte de' is a common colloquial quantifier meaning 'a lot of' or 'lots of.'
target_language_example: Tenho um monte de coisas para resolver hoje.
native_language_example: I have a lot of things to take care of today.

meaning: a very beautiful country
additional_notes: Used to describe a country as attractive or scenic. Common in spoken and written Portuguese. Word-by-word: um (a/an), país (country), muito (very), bonito (beautiful). Replace país with a city's or region's name as needed (e.g., 'um lugar muito bonito'). Can be used with adjectives or extra info: 'um país muito bonito e interessante'.
target_language_example: O Brasil é um país muito bonito para visitar.
native_language_example: Brazil is a very beautiful country to visit.

meaning: a little
additional_notes: Used for a small amount or degree. It can describe how much of something there is or how much someone does something. Before a noun, it often appears as um pouco de: um pouco de água, um pouco de francês. It can also be used on its own to mean some/a little.
target_language_example: Preciso descansar um pouco.
native_language_example: I need to rest a little.

meaning: 'Nice to meet you' (literal: 'a pleasure to meet').
additional_notes: Common polite phrase used when meeting someone for the first time. In Portuguese the full forms are "É um prazer conhecê-lo" (to a man), "É um prazer conhecê-la" (to a woman), or the neutral "É um prazer conhecê-lo/conhecê-la" depending on formality and gender. Plural: "É um prazer conhecê-los" (masculine/mixed) or "É um prazer conhecê-las" (feminine). Often shortened in speech to "Prazer" or "Muito prazer."
target_language_example: É um prazer conhecê-la, Maria.
native_language_example: It's a pleasure to meet you, Maria.

meaning: 'a feeling' or 'a hunch'—an intuitive sense that something will or has happened.
additional_notes: Used to describe an instinctive or premonitory feeling about a future event or situation. Can be neutral, positive, or negative (good/bad hunch). Common in everyday speech: É só um pressentimento = It's just a hunch/feeling.
target_language_example: Tenho um pressentimento de que tudo vai correr bem.
native_language_example: I have a hunch that everything will go well.

meaning: a (baseball) bat; can also mean 'a stick' or 'club' used to hit or attack.
additional_notes: Most often appears as 'um taco de beisebol' (a baseball bat). Context determines meaning: literal sports equipment (I bought a bat) or a weapon used to hit/attack. Masculine noun: 'o taco'. Can be used without 'de beisebol' when context is clear.
target_language_example: Ele pegou um taco do carro e quebrou a janela.
native_language_example: He grabbed a bat from the car and broke the window.

meaning: a transplant (a medical organ or tissue transplant).
additional_notes: Used to talk about receiving an organ or tissue from a donor (e.g., kidney, heart). Often followed by the organ: 'um transplante de rim', 'um transplante de coração'. Common in medical contexts; can be used alone to mean 'an organ transplant' when context is clear.
target_language_example: Ela recebeu um transplante de fígado no ano passado.
native_language_example: She received a liver transplant last year.

meaning: 'one to ten' — used to indicate a range or scale from 1 through 10.
additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about counting (contar de um a dez) or to give/ask ratings on a 1–10 scale (em uma escala de um a dez). Can appear with verbs like contar (to count) or achar/avaliar (to rate).
target_language_example: Avalie o serviço de um a dez.
native_language_example: Rate the service from one to ten.

meaning: 'one by one' or 'one at a time'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate items or people acted on individually in sequence. Can describe people entering, objects being brought, or events happening one after another. Common and neutral; context may be literal or figurative (e.g., defeated one by one).
target_language_example: Entraram um por um pela porta.
native_language_example: They entered one by one through the door.

meaning: 'each other' or 'one another' (reciprocal action).
additional_notes: Used to indicate reciprocal actions between two or more people. Can also appear as 'uns aos outros' in plural contexts or 'um ao outro' when referring to two people; Portuguese often uses reflexive constructions (nos ajudamos) together with 'um ao outro' for clarity or emphasis.
target_language_example: Eles se respeitam e ajudam um ao outro.
native_language_example: They respect each other and help one another.

meaning: a combination meaning 'one with the' or 'a [thing] with the [thing]' used when linking a singular noun (um/uma) with 'com o' before a masculine singular noun.
additional_notes: This is not an idiom — it's simply the sequence of the indefinite article 'um' (one/a) + the preposition 'com' (with) + the definite article 'o' (the). You will see it in phrases like 'um com o fato' (one with the suit) or 'um com o outro' (one with the other). Agreement matters: use 'uma com a' for feminine nouns, 'um com a' / 'uma com o' are incorrect. Often contracted in speech when followed by a pronoun or in informal contexts, but standard written form keeps the three words separate.
target_language_example: Ele trouxe um com o casaco que lhe dei.
native_language_example: He brought one with the coat I gave him.

meaning: 'one for the' or 'one per the' — used before a masculine singular noun or phrase
additional_notes: Literal sequence: um (one) + para (for/to) + o (the, masculine). Often appears in contexts like giving one item to someone or indicating one of something per unit (e.g., "um para o João" = one for João; "um para o dia" = one per day). Word order and contraction may vary in speech (e.g., 'um pro' where para + o = pro). Make sure the following noun is masculine singular.
target_language_example: Vou deixar um para o Pedro.
native_language_example: I'll leave one for Pedro.

meaning: a (female) friend who lives (in/of).
additional_notes: Used to introduce or describe a female friend and where she lives. 'Uma amiga' = 'a (female) friend'. 'Que' = 'who/that'. 'Mora' = third-person singular of 'morar' (to live). To mention location, follow with preposition + place: 'mora em Londres', 'mora na Alemanha' (feminine country uses 'na' = 'em + a'). You can drop 'uma' in some contexts: 'Tenho amiga que mora...' is less common; more natural: 'Tenho uma amiga...'.
target_language_example: Eu tenho uma amiga que mora em Lisboa.
native_language_example: I have a friend who lives in Lisbon.

meaning: a letter from a (male) / a letter from one
additional_notes: Common phrase meaning 'a letter from someone.' 'Um' can mean 'a' (indefinite article) or 'one.' Context determines if it refers to a specific person ('a letter from a friend') or simply 'one of' a group ('a letter from one of my friends'). Gender: 'um' is masculine — used with masculine nouns like 'amigo'. For female senders use 'uma carta de uma (amiga)'.
target_language_example: Recebi uma carta de um amigo ontem.
native_language_example: I received a letter from a friend yesterday.

meaning: a crown (a circular decorative headpiece).
additional_notes: Used to refer to any crown or ring-shaped head ornament (royal crown, flower crown, wreath). 'Uma' is the indefinite article 'a/an'. Context tells whether it's a royal crown (rei) or a decorative crown (de flores). Pronounced [ˈuma koˈɾoɐ].
target_language_example: Ela colocou uma coroa de flores na cabeça.
native_language_example: She put a flower crown on her head.

meaning: a delivery (or item) for; meant for someone or something
additional_notes: Commonly used to say you have a delivery/package addressed to someone, or an order/task to deliver. Can refer to a physical package, a delivery job, or that something is intended for a person. Depending on context, 'entrega' can also mean 'delivery' as a task (e.g., I have a delivery to make = 'uma entrega para fazer').
target_language_example: Eu tenho uma entrega para o João.
native_language_example: I have a delivery for João.

meaning: a native (female) speaker
additional_notes: Used to refer to a woman who speaks a language as her mother tongue. 'Falante' = speaker; 'nativa' agrees in gender with the person described. For a male speaker say 'um falante nativo' or more commonly 'um falante nativo' / 'um falante nativo' (less common) — many speakers instead use 'nativo'/'nativa' with 'falante' omitted: 'uma nativa' is informal. Often used in contexts like language learning, translation, or linguistics.
target_language_example: Ela é uma falante nativa de português do Brasil.
native_language_example: She is a native speaker of Brazilian Portuguese.

meaning: a ribbon, tape, or cassette (depending on context).
additional_notes: Uma fita is a general word for a long, thin strip: can mean a decorative ribbon (for hair or clothing), adhesive tape, or an audio/video cassette/tape (fita cassete, fita VHS). Context (words like 'cassete', 'em branco', or mention of hair/clothing) tells which meaning applies. Feminine noun; indefinite article 'uma' = 'a'.
target_language_example: Ela colocou uma fita vermelha no cabelo.
native_language_example: She put a red ribbon in her hair.

meaning: one hour
additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration of 60 minutes. Can appear with quantifiers (uma hora, menos de uma hora, mais de uma hora, por uma hora) and with verbs of time (ter, esperar, tentar, nadar). Neutral register and very common. Use "one hour" or "an hour" in English depending on context ("one hour" for emphasis/precision, "an hour" for general duration).
target_language_example: Eu preciso de uma hora para terminar isso.
native_language_example: I need an hour to finish this.

meaning: a better way to do (something).
additional_notes: Used to offer or suggest an improved method for doing something. Often followed by 'isso' (that) or a verb/phrase describing the action. Polite phrases in the examples use different pronouns/forms (te, lhe, senhora, senhoras).
target_language_example: Posso mostrar uma maneira melhor de fazer esse bolo.
native_language_example: I can show a better way to make this cake.

meaning: a coin to make a (telephone) call / a coin to use in a payphone.
additional_notes: Used when searching for a coin needed to operate a payphone or another coin-operated device. The phrase is typically completed with the object (e.g., 'uma ligação' — a call). In Brazil, payphones (orelhões) and coin-operated machines are less common today, but the expression still clearly communicates needing small change. Word order can vary (e.g., 'procurei no meu bolso uma moeda para fazer uma ligação').
target_language_example: Procurei no bolso uma moeda para fazer uma ligação.
native_language_example: I looked in my pocket for a coin to make a call.

meaning: in one hand ... and in the other (hand) ... — used to describe holding two different things.
additional_notes: This phrase appears as part of a larger structure: 'em uma mão e (em) outra' or 'uma mão e um/uma ... na outra'. It describes that a person is holding one object in one hand and another object in the other hand. You will usually see the full pattern: 'segurava/em uma mão X e (em) outra Y' or 'tinha/em uma mão X e na outra Y'.
target_language_example: Ela entrava com uma bolsa em uma mão e um casaco na outra.
native_language_example: She came in with a bag in one hand and a coat in the other.

meaning: a loss of; a waste of (time/resources) depending on context.
additional_notes: Used before a noun to indicate loss, depletion, or waste. Common contexts: 'uma perda de tempo' (a waste of time), 'uma perda de sangue' (a loss of blood), 'uma perda de dinheiro' (a financial loss). Followed by a noun or noun phrase. Tone is neutral.
target_language_example: Foi uma perda de tempo tentar consertar aquilo.
native_language_example: It was a waste of time trying to fix that.

meaning: a bridge here; (there) used to be a bridge here.
additional_notes: Literal phrase combining 'uma ponte' (a bridge) + 'aqui' (here). Commonly used in past-tense sentences to say that a bridge existed at this location in the past: 'Havia uma ponte aqui' or 'Havia um tempo em que havia uma ponte aqui' (There used to be a bridge here / There was once a bridge here). Use 'há muito tempo' or 'um tempo' to emphasize that it was long ago.
target_language_example: Havia uma ponte aqui, mas foi levada pela enchente.
native_language_example: There used to be a bridge here, but it was carried away by the flood.

meaning: a portion; a serving; also informally 'a lot' or 'a bunch' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Primary meaning: a portion or serving of food (e.g., uma porção de batatas). Informal/colloquial usage: can mean 'a lot' or 'many' when referring to quantity or intensity (e.g., uma porção de atividades = lots of activities). Use context to determine whether it's literal (food) or figurative (many).
target_language_example: Pedi uma porção de batatas para compartilhar.
native_language_example: I ordered a portion of fries to share.

meaning: a shovel; a spade (a single shovel).
additional_notes: Used to refer to one shovel as a tool for digging, scooping sand/dirt, or moving materials. Common in everyday contexts (gardening, construction). Can be used in questions to ask if someone has a shovel (Você tem uma pá?). Gender: pá is feminine, so use 'uma'. Pronunciation tip: 'pá' sounds like 'pah'.
target_language_example: Você tem uma pá para cavar o buraco?
native_language_example: Do you have a shovel to dig the hole?

meaning: once
additional_notes: Used to talk about a single occurrence, either in the past or as frequency: uma vez ao mês = once a month, vi uma vez = I saw it once. In some expressions like uma vez na vida, it emphasizes that something happens very rarely.
target_language_example: Eu estive em Lisboa uma vez.
native_language_example: I was in Lisbon once.

meaning: 'since' or 'because' (gives a reason); can also mean 'once' in the sense of 'after' or 'as soon as' depending on context.
additional_notes: Common conjunction used to introduce a reason or cause (similar to 'since'/'because'). In some contexts it can mean 'once' ('after' or 'once something happens'), but for beginners the causal use ('because/since') is most frequent. Formal-register neutral.
target_language_example: Uma vez que você chegou cedo, podemos começar.
native_language_example: Since you arrived early, we can start.

meaning: to take a (short) walk/ride/turn in something (e.g., around a place or in a vehicle).
additional_notes: Common, everyday expression used for going for a short walk, stroll, drive, or lap. The preposition and article after 'volta' change with the noun: 'dar uma volta no parque' (no = em + o), 'dar uma volta na cidade' (na = em + a), or 'dar uma volta por aí' (around/around town). Can imply a leisurely, casual outing rather than a long trip.
target_language_example: Vamos dar uma volta no bairro antes do jantar.
native_language_example: Let's take a walk/drive around the neighborhood before dinner.

meaning: a short walk/ride/quick stroll (a little trip)
additional_notes: Informal, diminutive of 'volta' (turn/round/trip). Used to suggest or describe going out briefly — walking, driving, or just stepping outside. Often used in questions or casual plans: 'Quer dar uma voltinha?' = 'Want to go for a quick walk/ride?'. Context determines whether it's walking or driving.
target_language_example: Quer dar uma voltinha no parque?
native_language_example: Do you want to go for a quick walk in the park?

meaning: 'no way' / 'not a chance' (informal, dismissive refusal)
additional_notes: Colloquial and emphatic. Used to reject or deny something strongly—similar to 'no way', 'not on your life', or 'as if' in English. Often follows or replaces a statement to show disbelief or refusal. Can be rude depending on tone and context; avoid in formal situations.
target_language_example: Você acha que eu vou emprestar meu carro? Uma ova!
native_language_example: You think I'll lend you my car? No way!

meaning: each other / one another (used in plural contexts)
additional_notes: Used as part of the reciprocal expression 'uns aos outros' or 'uns aos outros/as' meaning 'each other' or 'one another'. Often appears with plural subjects and verbs (e.g., 'lambem uns aos outros'). Can be shortened in speech to 'uns aos'. Place it before or after other pronouns as in examples. Used for reciprocal actions or relationships among members of a group.
target_language_example: Eles escrevem mensagens uns aos outros todos os dias.
native_language_example: They write messages to each other every day.

meaning: to use my (something).
additional_notes: Combines the verb usar (to use) with the possessive meu (my). It's not a fixed phrase — it precedes a noun: usar meu carro, usar meu telefone. Word order: verb + possessive + noun. Possessive must agree in gender/number with the noun (meu/minha/meus/minhas).
target_language_example: Posso usar meu telefone por um minuto?
native_language_example: Can I use my phone for a minute?

meaning: 'cows are' (present tense statement about cows)
additional_notes: A simple subject + verb phrase: vacas (cows) + são (they are / are). Used to make general statements about cows. 'São' is the 3rd-person plural present of 'ser' (to be). Replace 'vacas' with another noun to form similar sentences (e.g., 'os cães são', 'as árvores são').
target_language_example: As vacas são importantes na agricultura.
native_language_example: Cows are important in agriculture.

meaning: 'will understand' (future tense of 'entender').
additional_notes: Used to say someone will understand something in the future. Can be a simple statement (He will understand), a question (Will you understand?), or a prediction/assurance (You will understand when...). Common in spoken Portuguese; 'vai' is the present indicative of 'ir' used as a future auxiliary. Formal written Portuguese may use the simple future 'entenderá' but 'vai entender' is more frequent in conversation.
target_language_example: Você vai entender quando vir aqui.
native_language_example: You will understand when you come here.

meaning: 'is going to do the' or 'will do the' (future, masculine singular object).
additional_notes: Combination of the verb 'ir' in the present (vai = he/she/you formal is going) + infinitive 'fazer' (to do/make) + definite masculine singular article 'o'. Used to indicate a future action directed at a specific masculine noun implied or stated after 'o' (e.g., 'vai fazer o trabalho' = 'is going to do the work'). In spoken Portuguese parts after 'o' may be omitted if context makes the object clear. For feminine objects use 'vai fazer a'.
target_language_example: Ele vai fazer o jantar hoje à noite.
native_language_example: He is going to make the dinner tonight.

meaning: 'will know' (literally) / used idiomatically as 'who knows' or 'nobody will know' depending on context.
additional_notes: Literally the future of 'saber' (to know): 'vai saber' = 'will know'. In conversation it appears both in literal statements (Someone will know / You will know) and as an idiomatic skeptical phrase equivalent to English 'who knows' or 'go figure' (often used alone at the start of a sentence). Tone and context determine whether it's literal or idiomatic.
target_language_example: Vai saber se ele vem amanhã.
native_language_example: Who knows if he'll come tomorrow.

meaning: an aggressive insult: 'fuck off' / 'go fuck yourself'.
additional_notes: Very vulgar and offensive. Used to tell someone to go away or to express strong anger. Literally 'go fuck yourself' (vai = go, se foder = fuck yourself). Do not use in polite contexts; can provoke confrontation.
target_language_example: Vai se foder, eu não quero mais conversar com você.
native_language_example: Fuck off, I don't want to talk to you anymore.

meaning: will see
additional_notes: Literal meaning is 'will see' (from ir + ver). Used both as a literal future tense ('you/he/it will see') and idiomatically as a warning, threat, or promise ('you'll see' — implying consequences or that something will become clear). Context determines subject: with subject pronoun it can be 'you will see' (você vai ver) or 'he/she/it will see' (ele/ela vai ver). Informal speech often drops the subject pronoun: 'Vai ver!' = 'You'll see!'
target_language_example: Vai ver que tudo vai dar certo.
native_language_example: You'll see that everything will work out.

meaning: goes/going anywhere (often in negative constructions meaning 'goes nowhere' or 'won't go anywhere').
additional_notes: Used most often in negative sentences with words like 'não' and 'nenhum/nenhum(a)/algum' to mean 'not going anywhere' or 'won't go anywhere'. Common fixed expressions: 'não vai a lugar algum/nenhum' = 'doesn't go anywhere' or 'won't go anywhere'. Can be used literally (physically going) or figuratively (making no progress).
target_language_example: Ela não vai a lugar algum sem o mapa.
native_language_example: She doesn't go anywhere without the map.

meaning: goes/walks (somewhere) on foot; 'vai a pé para a' = 'he/she goes on foot to the (feminine place)'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone walks to a destination. 'Vai' is the 3rd-person singular of 'ir' (to go); replace with other forms for different subjects (vou, vamos, vão, etc.). 'A' before the place is the feminine definite/article 'to the' (e.g., 'a escola' = to the school). For masculine places use 'ao' (e.g., 'vai a pé ao trabalho'). Can be turned into a question by intonation or adding question marks.
target_language_example: Ela vai a pé para a biblioteca todos os dias.
native_language_example: She walks to the library every day.

meaning: what if
additional_notes: Informal spoken Brazilian Portuguese. Used before a clause to suggest a possibility, often when explaining a precaution or plan: 'what if...', 'maybe...', sometimes 'just in case'. It is not a literal use of vai ('goes').
target_language_example: Vou sair mais cedo, vai que tem trânsito.
native_language_example: I'll leave earlier, in case there's traffic.

meaning: 'is worth nothing' / 'is worthless' (can also mean 'is no good' or 'is useless').
additional_notes: Used to say that a person, thing, idea or power has no value or is useless. Common in negative sentences: 'não vale nada' = 'is worth nothing'. When said about a person (e.g., 'ele não vale nada') it's insulting — equivalent to 'he's good for nothing.' Tone can be strong; avoid in polite contexts.
target_language_example: Esse contrato não vale nada para mim.
native_language_example: That contract is worth nothing to me.

meaning: 'applies to' or 'is valid for' (someone or something); can also mean 'is worth' in contexts about value or price.
additional_notes: Most commonly used to say that a statement, rule or situation also concerns someone/something (e.g., "Isso vale para todos" = "This applies to everyone"). In other contexts, especially when followed by a question about quantity or price, vale can mean 'is worth' (e.g., "Quanto isso vale para você?" = "How much is that worth to you?"). The construction is composed of the verb valer (to be worth/to apply) + preposition para (to/for).
target_language_example: Essa regra vale para visitantes também.
native_language_example: That rule applies to visitors too.

meaning: 'to be worth it' / 'to be worthwhile'.
additional_notes: Used to say that an action, effort or situation justifies the cost, trouble or risk. Common in phrases like "pode valer a pena" (it may be worth it) and imperative encouragements like "faz valer a pena" (make it worthwhile). Often followed by an infinitive or clause describing what's at stake.
target_language_example: Pode valer a pena tentar uma vez.
native_language_example: It might be worth trying once.

meaning: 'let's put' (first-person plural imperative + verb stem with clitic attached)
additional_notes: This is the informal contracted form of vamos colocar + object clitic (me, o, a, os, as). In full: vamos colocar + pronoun (e.g., vamos colocá-lo = let's put him/it; vamos colocá-la = let's put her/it). The pronoun attaches to the infinitive with an accent added to keep the stress (colocar → colocá‑). Used to give a suggestion or command for a group including the speaker. English translations depend on the object: him, her, it, them, you (formal), etc.
target_language_example: Vamos colocá-lo na mesa.
native_language_example: Let's put him/it on the table.

meaning: let's catch/get (him/her/them/it)
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction of 'vamos pegar' with the object pronoun attached (e.g. pegá-lo, pegá-la, pegá-los). Used to mean 'let's catch', 'let's get', or 'let's grab' someone or something. Tone can be playful, urgent, or physical depending on context (e.g. catching a person, grabbing an object, or grabbing someone's attention). The final vowel is often dropped in casual speech or writing: 'pegá' = 'pegar'. Choose the correct pronoun form when completing the phrase (pegá-lo, pegá-la, pegá-los, etc.).
target_language_example: Calma, vamos pegá-lo antes que ele corra.
native_language_example: Calm down, let's catch him before he runs.

meaning: let's go
additional_notes: Common informal phrase used to encourage action, to get people moving, or to urge someone to try/continue. Can be used literally (to start moving) or figuratively (to motivate, express impatience, or prompt someone). Tone depends on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Vamos lá, você consegue terminar isso hoje?
native_language_example: Come on, you can finish this today?

meaning: 'vassoura' = broom; here used in the instruction '(take) a broom and ...' (imperative construction).
additional_notes: This appears as the phrase 'pegar uma vassoura e ...' or 'pegue uma vassoura e ...' meaning 'take/get a broom and (do something)'. It's an imperative instruction telling someone to grab a broom and then sweep. The 'e' (and) connects to the following verb: e varra = and sweep (or start sweeping). Common in commands: 'Pegue uma vassoura e varra aqui.'
target_language_example: Maria, pegue uma vassoura e varra a cozinha.
native_language_example: Maria, get a broom and sweep the kitchen.

meaning: 'see you tomorrow' (informal way to say you'll meet or see someone the next day).
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase used when arranging to meet or saying goodbye. Often appears as 'Te vejo amanhã' or 'Eu te vejo amanhã' (with or without the subject). Can be used as a statement or a question to confirm plans. Polite/formal alternative: 'Nos vemos amanhã.'
target_language_example: Te vejo amanhã no parque às 10h.
native_language_example: See you tomorrow at the park at 10am.

meaning: I/you/he/she/... haven't seen (someone) for (a period).
additional_notes: Used with a negative verb form (não vejo/Não te vejo) plus há + time expression to say how long it has been since you last saw someone. Há here means 'ago' or 'for' when indicating elapsed time. Subjects and object pronouns change (não o vejo, não a vejo, não te vejo).
target_language_example: Não o vejo há três meses.
native_language_example: I haven't seen him for three months.

meaning: 'see you later' (I'll see you later / see you soon).
additional_notes: Casual farewell used to say you'll see the person later the same day or soon. Commonly appears as 'Te vejo mais tarde' (informal 'I/I'll see you later'). Can be used with friends, family or colleagues in informal contexts. If addressing formally, use 'Vejo você mais tarde.' Tone depends on context and rising intonation can make it a question ('See you later?').
target_language_example: Te vejo mais tarde no trabalho.
native_language_example: See you later at work.

meaning: 'I don't see anything' (colloquial/contracted Portuguese for 'não vejo nada').
additional_notes: This phrase is used to say you cannot see anything. Standard Portuguese places 'não' before the verb (não vejo nada). In spoken or colloquial contexts, speakers sometimes omit the initial 'não' in casual phrases like 'vejo nada' for emphasis or regional speech, but grammatically the negative particle is needed: 'Eu não vejo nada.' It can also be used figuratively to mean 'I don't notice/understand anything.'
target_language_example: Eu não vejo nada no escuro sem a lanterna.
native_language_example: I can't see anything in the dark without the flashlight.

meaning: 'older than' (feminine form) — used to compare ages or to say someone/something is older than someone/something else.
additional_notes: velha is the feminine form of 'old' (velho/velha). In comparisons use 'mais velha do que' or simply 'mais velha que' (both are common). When comparing a female to someone else, use velha; for males use 'velho' (e.g., mais velho do que). Informal contexts often drop 'do' and use 'que' instead. Word order: subject + é/é + mais velha do que + comparison.
target_language_example: Ela é mais velha do que eu.
native_language_example: She is older than me.

meaning: older than you
additional_notes: Used in comparisons with 'mais' (mais velho do que você = older than you). Can refer to people, animals or things (e.g., 'esse uísque é mais velho do que você' = the whiskey is older than you). Often shortened in speech to 'mais velho que você' (dropping 'do'). When comparing age with names: 'X é mais velho do que você' or with verbs: 'mais velho do que você pensa' (older than you think).
target_language_example: Meu cachorro é mais velho do que você imagina.
native_language_example: My dog is older than you imagine.

meaning: 'as old as' (used to compare ages).
additional_notes: Combines velho (old) with quanto (as...as) to form a comparison, normally used with the particle tão or another degree word: 'tão velho quanto' = 'as old as'. It can compare people or things and often appears with pronouns, names or nouns (e.g., 'sou tão velho quanto ele', 'é tão velho quanto meu pai'). Use 'tão' before the adjective to mark equality; without 'tão' the phrase is ungrammatical in most contexts.
target_language_example: Eu sou tão velho quanto ele.
native_language_example: I am as old as him.

meaning: 'older than' (used in comparisons to state that someone/something is older than another).
additional_notes: Commonly appears with 'mais' as 'mais velho que o...' to form comparative ('more old than'). The definite article (o/a) may be included or omitted depending on grammar and emphasis: 'mais velho que o João' vs 'mais velho que João'. Use 'mais novo' or 'mais jovem' for 'younger than'.
target_language_example: Ele é muito mais velho que o Ken.
native_language_example: He is much older than Ken.

meaning: 'older than you' (part of the comparative construction 'mais velho que você').
additional_notes: This phrase appears in the comparative structure 'mais velho que você' meaning someone is older than you. In Portuguese you can replace 'velho' with 'novo' or 'novo/novo(a)' for 'younger' ('mais novo que você' / 'mais jovem que você'). For questions, word order and intonation indicate it's a question (e.g., 'Você é mais velho que eu?' is also common—note: grammatically 'do que eu' or 'que eu' is preferred in formal written Portuguese).
target_language_example: Ele é mais velho que você.
native_language_example: He is older than you.

meaning: 'come here' (used to call someone nearer; can be direct or attention-getting).
additional_notes: Common informal phrase to call someone to come closer or to get their attention. Used with a name or alone (e.g., "Vem cá!"). Tone can be friendly, urgent, or commanding depending on intonation and context. Not rude in itself but can sound abrupt if used with strangers or in formal situations.
target_language_example: Vem cá, preciso falar com você um segundo.
native_language_example: Come here, I need to talk to you for a second.

meaning: 'to beat/defeat the' or 'to win the' (followed by a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Vencer is a regular verb meaning to defeat or to win. When followed by the masculine definite article 'o' it introduces a specific masculine noun (vencer o inimigo, vencer o campeonato). Use 'vencer a' for feminine nouns. Can be used for people, teams, competitions, or abstract opponents.
target_language_example: Nós precisamos vencer o time visitante amanhã.
native_language_example: We need to beat the visiting team tomorrow.

meaning: 'to sell the' (masculine singular object).
additional_notes: This is the verb vender (to sell) followed by the masculine singular definite article o. It appears before a masculine noun: e.g., vender o carro (to sell the car). Word order can change in questions or with pronouns: 'venderam o livro?' (Did they sell the book?). When using a direct object pronoun, the article is replaced: 'venderam-no' or in modern spoken Brazilian Portuguese 'venderam para ele' depending on meaning.
target_language_example: Quero vender o carro no próximo mês.
native_language_example: I want to sell the car next month.

meaning: to sell yours / to sell your (thing).
additional_notes: A phrase combining the verb vender (to sell) with the possessive 'o seu' (your / yours). Used when talking about selling something that belongs to the listener or a third person (depending on context and gender/number agreement). In Portuguese the possessive must agree in gender/number with the noun (e.g., vender o seu carro, vender a sua casa, vender os seus livros). The subject (who sells) can be explicit or implied: 'vender o seu' often appears in questions or statements about selling the listener's possession.
target_language_example: Você vai vender o seu apartamento?
native_language_example: Are you going to sell your apartment?

meaning: to have to do with that; to be related to that.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is connected or relevant to a particular thing/situation. Often appears in sentences like 'Não tem ver com isso' (It has nothing to do with that) or 'Tem a ver com isso' (It has to do with that). Verb 'ver' here is idiomatic and doesn't mean 'see'.
target_language_example: Isso não tem ver com isso; foi só um mal-entendido.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with that; it was just a misunderstanding.

meaning: to have to do with; to be related to (something/someone).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is connected or related to another thing. Often appears as part of the expression 'ter/ver a ver com' (e.g. 'isso tem a ver com...' = 'that has to do with...'). 'Ver com o' by itself is typically followed by a noun or pronoun (o/ a/ os/ as) and indicates relationship or relevance.
target_language_example: Isso não tem ver com o problema que discutimos.
native_language_example: That doesn't have anything to do with the problem we discussed.

meaning: to see (someone/something) from time to time; occasionally
additional_notes: Used to say you meet or see someone occasionally, not regularly. Can refer to people, things, or events. Commonly used in conversational Portuguese. Structure: ver (to see) + de vez em quando (occasionally).
target_language_example: Eu gosto de ver de vez em quando os meus amigos da universidade.
native_language_example: I like to see my university friends from time to time.

meaning: 'to see stars' — to feel dizzy or briefly lose consciousness (often after a blow to the head); can also be literal (to see stars in the sky).
additional_notes: Common idiom used when someone is dazed after a hit, fall, or sudden pain: 'Ele levou um soco e começou a ver estrelas.' For beginners, note there are both figurative (dazed) and literal (stargazing) uses; context determines meaning. Often used in the past: ver estrelas/começar a ver estrelas/ficar a ver estrelas.
target_language_example: Ele bateu a cabeça e começou a ver estrelas.
native_language_example: He hit his head and began to see stars.

meaning: to check/see whether you (you) ...; 'to see if you...'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce checking whether someone is in a certain state, knows something, or can do something. Common in casual and neutral contexts. Often follows verbs like 'queria' (I wanted) or 'vamos' (let's) and is followed by a clause: ver se você + verb (verb conjugated for 'você').
target_language_example: Só quero ver se você pode me ajudar.
native_language_example: I just want to see if you can help me.

meaning: to see only; to look and nothing else / to be left to see only (depends on context).
additional_notes: Literal composition: ver = to see, só = only / alone. Alone, 'ver só' is uncommon as a fixed phrase; it can mean 'to see only' (e.g., ver só uma coisa = to see only one thing) or 'to be left to see alone' in colloquial uses (context needed). More natural alternatives: 'apenas ver' or 'ver apenas' for 'only see', and 'ver sozinho' for 'see alone' (i.e., by oneself).
target_language_example: Eu vou ver só a parte final do filme.
native_language_example: I'll only watch the final part of the movie.

meaning: 'actually / to tell the truth' + 'I don't' (used to correct or contradict something about oneself)
additional_notes: This phrase combines ways to introduce honesty or correction (e.g., 'Na verdade' or 'Para dizer a verdade') with a negation about the speaker ('eu não' = 'I don't' / 'I am not'). Commonly used to disagree, correct a mistaken assumption, or admit something you did not do. In English you might say 'actually, I don't' or 'to tell the truth, I don't/I'm not.' Word order in Portuguese can vary: 'Na verdade, eu não...' or 'Para dizer a verdade, eu não...'.
target_language_example: Para dizer a verdade, eu não conheço essa pessoa.
native_language_example: To tell the truth, I don't know that person.

meaning: 'is it true that...' (used to ask if a statement is true)
additional_notes: Commonly used at the start of yes/no questions to ask whether some information is true. Structure: 'É verdade que + [clause]?' Often followed by the definite article 'o/a' when the clause begins with a masculine/feminine noun (É verdade que o Tom...? É verdade que a Maria...?). Can be slightly formal; in casual speech you might also hear 'é verdade?' or 'é mesmo?'
target_language_example: É verdade que o voo foi cancelado?
native_language_example: Is it true that the flight was canceled?

meaning: 'is it true that you (plural)?' — used to ask if something about 'you' (plural) is true.
additional_notes: Common in questions introduced by 'É verdade que...' to confirm or ask about a reported fact involving 'vocês' (you plural). Formality: neutral; 'vocês' is the plural 'you' used in Brazil (in Portugal, 'vocês' exists but 'vós' is rare). Structure: É verdade que + statement. Can be used with different tenses and verbs.
target_language_example: É verdade que vocês viajaram para o Brasil no ano passado?
native_language_example: Is it true that you (all) traveled to Brazil last year?

meaning: 'the truth about' or 'truth regarding'.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the true facts or reality concerning a person, event, topic, etc. Commonly appears with a topic or clause after 'sobre' (e.g., 'a verdade sobre a Palestina' = the truth about Palestine). Can be used in statements, questions, and reported speech.
target_language_example: Ele quer saber a verdade sobre o que aconteceu.
native_language_example: He wants to know the truth about what happened.

meaning: 'you (do something) next time' or phrases using 'vez' with 'você' to refer to someone's turn or a future occasion (e.g., 'da próxima vez, você...'; 'quando for sua vez, você...').
additional_notes: This pattern combines vez (time/occasion/turn) with você (you). Common expressions: 'da próxima vez, você...' (next time you...), 'na próxima vez' (same meaning), 'pela última vez' (for the last time), and 'quando for sua vez' (when it's your turn). Use to give instructions, make requests, warn, or point out someone's turn. Word order can vary: 'da próxima vez, você...' or 'você, da próxima vez,...'.
target_language_example: Da próxima vez, você me avisa antes de trazer visitas.
native_language_example: Next time, you let me know before bringing visitors.

meaning: 'once a year' or 'one time per year'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate an action or event that happens (or is done) one time each year. Often appears after quantities like 'uma vez ao ano' or 'uma vez por ano' (both mean the same). Can be placed after the verb or at the end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Eu visito meus pais uma vez ao ano.
native_language_example: I visit my parents once a year.

meaning: 'instead' or 'in its place' (used after 'em' as 'em vez disso').
additional_notes: Usually appears as the phrase 'em vez disso' meaning 'instead' or 'rather than that'. It contrasts one action/choice with an alternative. Can follow a clause (Em vez disso, ...), or appear after a verb to ask for an alternative (O que você quer em vez disso?). Not to be confused with 'vez' alone (time/turn).
target_language_example: Em vez disso, vamos ficar em casa e assistir a um filme.
native_language_example: Instead, let's stay home and watch a movie.

meaning: once a month; one time per month.
additional_notes: Used to indicate frequency — how often something happens. Commonly placed after the verb or at the end of the sentence: e.g. "Eu vou ao cinema vez por mês" (less natural) or more commonly with numeral: "uma vez por mês". Native speakers often say "uma vez por mês" or simply "por mês" with context. Can be combined with numbers: "duas vezes por mês" (twice a month).
target_language_example: Vou ao dentista vez por mês.
native_language_example: I go to the dentist once a month.

meaning: once a week; per week.
additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens. Replace 'vez' with a number to change frequency (e.g., 'duas vezes por semana' = twice a week). Can appear after the verb or at sentence end: 'Eu vou ao ginásio uma vez por semana.'
target_language_example: Eu estudo português uma vez por semana.
native_language_example: I study Portuguese once a week.

meaning: 'the (last) time I saw (someone)'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific occasion when the speaker saw someone. Often appears as 'a última vez que vi' = 'the last time I saw (X)'. Can be used with other time expressions (na última vez que vi, da última vez que vi). Verb 'vi' is the first‑person past of 'ver' (to see).
target_language_example: A última vez que vi Maria foi no Natal.
native_language_example: The last time I saw Maria was at Christmas.

meaning: because you / since you (used to give a reason directed at 'you')
additional_notes: A causal phrase used to introduce a reason or explanation related to the person 'você'. Equivalent to 'porque você' or 'já que você' but slightly more formal/neutral. Common in written and spoken Portuguese: 'Vez que' can also appear without 'você' (e.g., 'vez que estava atrasado...').
target_language_example: Vez que você está ocupado, eu posso cuidar disso hoje.
native_language_example: Since you are busy, I can take care of this today.

meaning: '... times before' — indicates how many times something happened previously.
additional_notes: Used after a number or adverb (duas vezes, muitas vezes, três vezes) to say that an action occurred that many times prior to some reference point. Common in past contexts. Word order: [number/adverb] + vezes + antes. Can be translated as '... times before' or simply 'before' depending on context (e.g., 'many times before').
target_language_example: Eu já falei com ela duas vezes antes.
native_language_example: I have already spoken to her two times before.

meaning: ‘times more’ — used to compare quantities (e.g., three times more = 3× as many).
additional_notes: Placed after a number to form multiplicative comparisons: 'três vezes mais' = three times more/as many. Often appears in structures like 'Eu tenho três vezes mais X que Y' (I have three times more X than Y). Can be used with large numbers ('dez vezes mais'). In Portuguese, word order may vary: 'Tem três vezes mais livros que eu' = 'He/She has three times more books than I do.'
target_language_example: Ela tem cinco vezes mais experiência do que eu.
native_language_example: She has five times more experience than I do.

meaning: 'how many times you' (used to ask how often someone has done something)
additional_notes: Commonly appears in questions with 'Quantas vezes você...' to ask about frequency or number of occurrences. 'Vezes' means 'times' (occurrences); 'você' is the pronoun 'you'.
